LONDON, May 4 (4) - George VI was “crowned” today with neither pomp nor ceremony. In fact, he was “crowned” four times. The king paid an unheralded visit to Westminster Abbey to rehearse for his coronation May 12 and practiced the ritual with the archbishop of Canterbury for two hours. He wore a coronation robe over his civilian suit. Queen Elizabeth accompanied him and rehearsed part of the processional. She looked on, however, while the archbishop and the king practiced the rite which will enthrone the new monarch. Her own crowning was not rehearsed.

1937-02-19.text: — LONDON, Feb. 19—Great Britain’s munitions and war equipment factories were thrown into high gear today for production of shells, guns and aircraft in the nation’s undisguised fear of “the next war.” Spurred by favorable parliamentary vote on the resolution authorizing a two billion dollar government “war loan in peace,” the country forged ahead on a seven billion five hundred million dollar rearmament program. Observers of a bitter two-day debate in the House of Commons over the unprecedented peace time preparations for conflict were impressed by the bald way in which government leaders, especially in the conservative ranks, spoke of “the next war,” rather than “the possibility of war.”

NEW YORK, Feb. 19--(UP)— Frances Clyne, New York society modiste, returned on the S. S. Bremen today with word that the Duke of Windsor and Mrs. Wallis Simpson will be married May 12 in the English chapel in Vienna. She said the date was “stated definitely” at a cocktail party in London attended by Lord Brownlow, close friend of the former king.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 18 WP President Roosevelt, acting shortly after announcement of England’s proposed $7,500,000,000 defense program, called in naval heads today to discuss means of speeding American naval construction. Mr. Roosevelt met with assistant secretary of navy, Charles Edison, to consider the effects of Britain's newly announced naval program and operations of the Walsh-Healey act, which concurrently is delaying the naval construction program. Edison said Mr. Roosevelt asked him to study the effect of Britain’s announcement on the American fleet program and investigate the Walsh-Healey act situation thoroughly. As a result of the stringent provisions of the Walsh-Healey act, government navy yards have found no bidders to supply their steel requirements. Edison said he had informed the President that navy yards, according to present indications, will not be forced to close down un

LONDON, Feb. 18.—One of the worst fires in London in many years destroyed two factories today, causing damage estimated by fire inspectors at $500,000. More than 250 firemen and 50 pieces of equipment were summoned to fight the blaze, whose cause was not determined. The flames spread to tenements adjoining the factories while the intense heat cracked thousands of panes of glass in nearby buildings. Several persons suffered minor injuries from falling beams and masonry.

BAGHDAD, Iraq, Feb. 16.—Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh flew from Rutbah Wells, Iraq, to Basrah, Iraq, at the upper end of the Persian Gulf today and took off half an hour later for Bahrein, a British island in the gulf on the way to India. After a night at Rutbah Wells, where they took refuge from a dangerous sand storm, the Lindberghs flew the 490 miles to Basrah, across the desert and down the Euphrates. During his half hour stay at Basrah, Lindbergh said that he and his wife were enjoying their vacation flight. Lindbergh before he left England obtained permission to land either at Bushire or Jask, Iran (Persia), way stations on the eastern air route. Bahrein is well past Bushire and it was expected they would continue on to Jask. The American flyers made a forced landing at Rutbah Wells in the desert yesterday when they encountered a sand storm that reduced visibility to 100 yards

Paris, Feb. 19.—(?)—Dr. Hjalmar Schacht, Nazi minister of economics, was reported in government circles today to be ready to undertake preliminary negotiations for a new western European peace pact to break the diplomatic deadlock between France, Germany and Britain. As the first step toward the new security alignment—believed to have been brought nearer by France's “tougher” attitude toward Germany—the Nazi minister was expected to come to Paris within the week to sign a new Franco-German trade treaty. His government, official circles indicated, named him special ambassador to secure suggestions for a wide political settlement in Europe. France and Great Britain have agreed, foreign office sources said, Germany now must take the first step toward establishing diplomatic peace. The two powers have agreed, it was said, to try to force Chancellor Adolf Hitler to a clear, specific statement

LONDON, Feb. 18—(4)—Britain’s giant rearmament program passed its first legislative hurdle tonight after Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin told the House of Commons the plan was designed “to put ourselves in a position to deter aggression.” The House passed by a vote of 329 to 145 a resolution authorizing the government to borrow up to $2,000,000,000 in the next five years for the defense scheme which calls for expenditures of $7,500,000,000. The vote ended a two-day debate in which the opposition sharply criticized the plan and the statements by government leaders in its defense. Laborite Sir Stafford Cripps earlier, censuring the plan, charged ‘we're witnessing the most magnificent subscription to a world suicide pact yet made public in any country in the world.’

LONDON, Feb. 18.— Operation of a “Committee of Industrial Intelligence”— to aid Britain's rearmament program by reporting on stocks of raw materials in foreign countries—was announced today by Sir Thomas Inskip, minister of defense coordination in the House of Commons. Informed sources declared the committee would furnish information to be used in the purchase of armament materials. Thomas did not give a detailed summary of the committee's duties to the parliamentary chamber, however. The defense minister also disclosed formation of another group --the Joint Intelligence Committee—to coordinate defense plans of the British army, navy and air force. He made his statement in reply to opposition charges there is no director or coordination in the government’s $7,500,000,000 armament program, now before the Commons for debate. Laborite A. V. Alexander had charged the arms proposal a “prof-

1937-03-02.text: (By The Associated Press) London, March 1—The Duke of Windsor has set May 2 as the day for his wedding to Wallis Simpson, it was reported here today. The report aroused fear that the royal romance would overshadow the coronation of his brother-successor, just 10 days later. After Divorce Former King Edward VIII generally was believed to have made it clear in week-end inferences that he intended to marry the woman for whom he abdicated the throne as soon as her divorce from Ernest Simpson becomes absolute, April 27. It has been becoming daily more apparent the people of England will not have forgotten their self-exiled ruler by May 12, when his brother, George VI, is to be crowned.

LONDON, March 2, (P).—The British Broadcasting Company, convinced there has been too much crooning, took steps today to limit the number of throaty singers on English airways. While declining to define the difference between crooners and straight singing, the company, effective next Monday, limited dance bands to one croon for every three numbers.

LONDON, March 1 (*)—Floating mines crippled another foreign ship off Spain today while official British pronouncements hinted at certain renewal of attempts to bring Spanish peace. The stricken ship—third to be menaced by mines in the ship-lanes off Spain's east coast within five days—was the French freighter Marie. She made port at Palamos, Spain, but shipping circles showed alarm. The place where she hit the mine was near the spot where the British merchantman Llandov-ery Castle was damaged similarly last week. Moreover, the French transport Sebaa reported she narrowly had avoided a mine off Barcelona. Hope for new international efforts to find a peaceful solution of the Spanish war, now 73 months old, was buoyed by Foreign Minister Anthony Eden's declaration to Commons that the government had proposals for halting the war 'constantly in mind'. Authoritative sources said they believed

By The Associated Press Italy answered the challenge of the world armament race today with an order for virtual lifetime military readiness of all her men and strengthening of her war preparations. Answering Great Britain’s recently announced defense program the Fascist grand council decreed ‘the “integral militarization of all active forces between the ages of 18 and 55, with periodical recall of the mobilizable classes.” Official British sources would not comment on Premier Benito Mussolini’s move. On the other side of the globe the Japanese naval minister openly professed to see a “menace to Japan in any enlargement of the United States air fleet in the Pacific.” In Spain the government rounded up many spies who had gotten important posts within its own military ranks. Desultory fighting dragged on in the seventh month of civil war.

Paris — “® — Howard Hughes, American transcontinental speed pilot, and Jean Batten, New Zealand woman flyer, were recognized today as the outstanding aviators of 1936. Miss Batten was awarded the Harmon international trophy for 1936 for a record-breaking solo hop from England to New Zealand, and Hughes for the transcontinental non-stop flights. Hughes, flying from Los Angeles to Newark in seven hours, 28 minutes and 25 seconds, set a new non-stop record last Jan. 19.

PARIS, March 2—(AP)—Wallis Warfield Simpson has ordered five new creations from the establishment of British Captain Edward Molyneux, Parisian dressmaker, it was disclosed today. Her order, placed through the Cannes branch of the Molyneux salon, includes an evening fur coat, an evening ensemble, a wool coat for afternoon wear, an afternoon dress, and a sports outfit. Ten silver fox skins will be used for the coat, primarily an evening model of fingertip length with long sleeves. Cut on straight lines, the coat may also be worn for formal afternoon functions by the future wife of the former British King. EVENING ENSEMBLE IN BLUE PASTEL Her next choice was an evening ensemble of lustrous pastel blue satin, cut straight with a floor length skirt and a square neck. A matching jacket is designed in cutaway, tailored style with plain sleeves and revers. Blue mirror glass is used for buttons an

London, March 1.—(/?)—British tradesmen—among them many of the throne’s most loyal subjects—threatened tonight to engage in open controversy with the office of works over distribution of 85,000 tickets for the coronation parade of King George and Queen Elizabeth. The newest murmur of dissent mounted into an angry clamor for tickets on two sides, with co-operative work societies pitted against federated trade organizations. The possibility the duke of Windsor may marry Mrs. Wallis Simpson before the coronation date of May 12 was even momentarily pushed into the background, despite reports the wedding has already been set for May 2. Support Their Demands. First hints of the dispute over parade seats arose with published reports the co-operatives would get the best places for the color procession. Fishmongers, diamond dealers, poultry, game and rabbit workers in the trade organizations aros

ROME, March 2 ()—The fascist Brand council, today met Great Britain’s rearmament threat with a five-point program to increase Italy’s armaments and war forces. The governing body of fascism, meeting at the call of Premier Mussolini, decreed: the “integral militarization of all active forces between the ages of 18 and 55 with periodical recalls of the mobilizable classes.” Duce, who recently boasted Italy could put 8,000,000 armed men into battle, personally put through the far-reaching program, to answer the British announcement that $7,500,000,000 would be spent on war defense in the next five years. The other four points announced by the official communique, after a session lasting until near dawn, reached through every phase of Italian life: 1. An “adequate increase” in the armed forces. 2. Extension for five years of the general commission for war supplies. 3. “Total sacrifice” if ne

1937-06-04.text: CHATEAU DE CANDE, MONTS, France, June 3. (AP) — The radiant Duke of Windsor took Wallis Warfield as his bride and duchess today in two serene and dignified marriage ceremonies. Just 25 weeks ago today he gave up his crown of England and empire because she could not be his queen. “I will,” the duke supremely happy, answered in a firm loud voice to the Anglican poor man’s parson who gave him the unsanctioned blessing of the Church of England. As far as I could see neither the duke nor anyone else kissed the bride. The duke raised his voice so high in his eagerness to take the “woman I love” as his wife that he startled the 34 guests in the flower-banked music room of this old chateau. After him, his blue-eyed lady answered “I will.” Her voice was just as firm as Edward's, but more hushed. The religious service ended at 12:14 p.m. (5:14 a.m., central standard time) after the wedding.

CHATEAU DE CANDE, Monts, France. (By TransAtlantic Telephone to New York) — The Duke of Windsor, sovereign of the British empire for 326 unhappy days as Edward VIII, married today Mrs. Wallis Warfield, the American-born woman for whom he gave up his throne, defied his church and went into exile. The civil and religious ceremonies that brought this romance of a century to its triumphant culmination were solemnized by a French village mayor-physician and a provincial clergyman from the British Midlands here in the Chateau De Cande before some 50 persons. The religious ceremony was held in open defiance of the leaders of the Church of England, as the Duke had defied the British government to make the twice divorced Mrs. Warfield his wife. There was a wedding breakfast after the ceremonies, and late today the Duke and Her Grace the Duchess were to leave on their honeymoon, to Wasserleonburg

MONTS, France. UM. Edward of England and blue-eyed American-born Wallis Warfield were married in the ancient and turreted Chateau de Cande in this pastoral village of sunny France, and with a wistful plea for privacy to work out their own happiness departed for honeymoon in Austria. Two simple services united the couple, whose romance roused Britain's empire to grave debate over the rights of constitutional monarchs and led Edward to quit the throne of his father because he could not have the radiant Wallis as his queen. The rotund country doctor and mayor of Monts, Charles Mercier, read the civil service prescribed by French law before required witnesses in the chateau salon. The wilful “poor man’s parson,” who ignored the Church of England's opposition to remarriage of Mrs. Warfield, read the religious service. He was the Rev. R. Anderson Jardine, vicar of St. Paul's church, Darlington

London — (4) — British sources considered it likely Friday their abdicated monarch, Edward of Windsor, might drop the title of “Royal Highness” which his brother-successor, King George VI, denied his American-born bride of Thursday. They pointed to three significant omissions of the coveted “Royal Highness” in connection with the wedding yesterday—a style which the Duke unavailing sought to have conferred on Wallis Warfield as Duchess of Windsor. Initials Dropped. These things, they speculated, might mean Windsor would give up the royal designation which the British government did not think it fitting his twice-divorced wife should bear: 1. Departing from custom he did “not use the royal initials “H. R. H.” when he signed the French marriage.

LONDON, June 3 (UP).—The Church of England, outwitted by an obscure country clergyman and confronted by an angry public controversy over its refusal to sanction the marriage of the Duke of Windsor, still does not recognize his wedding as blessed by the church, the bishop of Fulham made it plain today. Apparently because of the public temper and resentment against the church, Rev. Robert Anderson Jardine, who performed the ceremony, has been victorious with his defiance. The bishop of Fulham, who has jurisdiction over Anglican Church affairs in France, admitted he would not be disciplined. No Action Planned The bishop, who sent Rev. Mr. Jardine a telegram of strong protest and rebuke, told the United Press:— "No further action will be taken by me. My telegram to Mr. Jardine only protested against his officiating at an Anglican service in a jurisdiction where he had no license or permissio

LONDON, June 3 ()—Great Britain today laid a three-point program before France, Italy and Germany to restore the broken naval ring around Spain. She suggested: 1. That safety zones for neutral ships be established in Spanish waters. 2. That the Spanish government and the insurgent administration be asked to guarantee protection of warships of the patrolling powers, 3. That Britain, France, Italy and Germany consult immediately if a warship of any of them is attacked. Germany gave no advance warning to the other powers when her ships shelled the Spanish government port of Almeria Monday in retaliation for an attack on the German pocket battleship Deutsch- SEE NO. 38, PAGE &

| SMECON —— Lhe wedding day | of Wallis Warfield and the Duke of Windsor was just another day at the office for Ernest Aldrich Simpson, the new duchess’ second husband. While his former wife and his former king were being married at Monts, France, Simpson sat lunching at one of London’s famous chop houses with an old friend, who was a close friend of the duke and the new duchess. He lunched as thousands of other London business men lunch — off cold roast beef and salad. At some tables nearby, people were reading the latest editions of afternoon newspapers with large pictures of the former king and his American-born bride. But nobody, apparently, noticed Simpson. Nobody disturbed his noonday meal.

London, June 3.—The wedding of its former king and the American woman who could not become its queen today stirred the British public to a new pitch of excitement over the abdication-coronation drama. The government maintained official silence. The royal family remained in seclusion. Bishops of the Church of England protested the Rev. R. Anderson Jardine’s action in performing the religious ceremony for the former King Edward VIII and Mrs. Wallis Warfield, his twice-divorced bride, at Monts, France. But the London press blazoned news of the marriage along with full-length portraits of the Duke and his new Duchess in their wedding attire, and the British public read avidly. Recognition Demanded: Outspoken Laborite J. McGovern demanded in the House of Commons: “Has the government already decided to send or are they sending a message of congratulations to Windsor on his wedding?” Prime Mini

1937-04-11.text: Worcester, Eng.—{INS}—Announcing his intention to retire, probably immediately after the coronation, Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin warned his constituents Saturday against permitting Fascism or Communism to gain a foothold in Britain. “You cannot graft them to our system any more than you could graft a Siberian crab to an oak,” he said. Baldwin, who will be 70 in August, said he felt his vitality “to a certain extent canned.”

LONDON, April 10.—(AP)—Sudden departure of the mighty battle cruiser Hood from Gibraltar tonight led to reports Britain was reinforcing her naval strength on the Basque coast as a result of Spanish insurgent threats to interfere with foreign shipping. The Hood, world's largest warship, sailed west from Gibraltar after officers and sailors were rounded up hurriedly from cafes and Gibraltar's streets. The admiralty did not disclose her destination. Four British vessels loaded with food consigned to Bilbao, besieged Basque port held by Spanish government forces, meanwhile were being held up at St. Jean de Luz, France, after reported threats by Spanish insurgents they would seek to prevent all food ships entering the port--even at the risk of an incident with the British navy. The captain of one of the waiting merchantmen, it was reported from the French port, asserted he had been informed o

WORCESTER, England, April 10 (AP)—Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin, the sturdy conservative of British conservatism, warned his people earnestly away from either communism or fascism today in a homely speech that sounded like a swan song. He announced his imminent retirement, but set no date for it. He has been prime minister three times. Addressing his constituents, he warned Britain against “mass consciousness” and “the virus of either communism or fascism.” And then the 69-year-old government leader declared of himself: “It is far better to go when the people may still think of you as perhaps not incompetent than to stay until perhaps they know before you do that you are becoming incompetent.” Political observers generally agreed Neville Chamberlain, who is a year and a half younger than Baldwin, would be his successor.

GIBRALTAR, April 10 — (UP—Rebel airplanes were reported here today to have bombarded and damaged a British destroyer off Malaga port in southern Spain. The report of the British destroyer bombing followed two aerial attempts to bomb the destroyer Gallant by rebel planes earlier in the week, for which the insurgent authorities on the island of Mallorca formally apologized. The Gallant was not hit. Four rebel planes were understood here to have participated in the bombing of the British warship off Malaga while it was proceeding to Gibraltar, bringing refugees from Valencia, wartime capital of Spain.

London—(4)—George Arliss observed his 69th birthday Saturday with an eye to the future. "The man who made Disraeli famous," insofar as most moviegoers are concerned, deeply resents the idea he is giving up anything about the theater. He is emphatic that he has not forsaken the legitimate stage and is eager to lay the ghost of rumors that he has deserted or retired from Hollywood.

| NEW DELHI, India, Sunday, April 11. (U.P)—Twenty-five members of a military convoy, including six British officers, were killed when renegades of the Fakir of Ipi ambushed the contingent in the mountains of Waziristan, it was revealed today. | Two British bombing squadrons have been sent across the mountains to wipe out the followers of the Fakir, who is known as the “firebrand of the northwest frontier.” The 25 soldiers and officers were killed and 40 others, including five officers, were wounded when the tribesmen attacked the convoy along the Manzaih-Wana road on Friday morning, it was reported here. The convoy consisted of 45 lorries protected by two armored cars. The lorries carried British infantry while native soldiers tramped along the road, keeping a sharp lookout for snipers in the mountain crags. The convoy was a punitive expedition sent into the desolate Waziri country foll

NEW DELHI, India. — Six British officers were officially reported killed and five wounded Saturday in a skirmish with tribesmen on the northwest frontier. Unconfirmed reports placed the casualties at 25 killed, 40 wounded in the remote territory where spasmodic guerilla warfare recently has cropped out again.

Hoylake, Cheshire, Eng., April 10 (UP)—Mrs. J. Spy announced tonight that she would ask King George VI “as a special coronation favor” to repeal a 200-year-old law under which every person by the name “Spy” may be shot on sight. There are about 200 Spys in Great Britain, she said, and all are descendants of the Scottish clan MacDonald, the members of which were outlawed. The law never was repealed and, technically, still permits shooting on sight anyone by the name of Spy.

1937-02-14.text: LONDON, Feb. 13.—(P)—A source close to the royal family said tonight Edward, duke of Windsor, will not return to England for at least three years. The princess royal, countess of Harewood, who wept on parting with her brother at Vienna today, will bring to Queen Mother Mary and the brothers of the former king full details of his plans.

LONDON, Wednesday March 10. —UP—Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin will resign the last week of May and will be succeeded by Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, political circles reported today. Several other members of the Baldwin cabinet also are expected to retire, including Ramsay MacDonald, lord president of the council; Viscount Halifax, lord privy seal; and Viscount Hailsham, lord high chancellor. According to the London Daily Herald the new cabinet will mark a transition period in which the conservative party will gradually disappear and finally emerge as the “National” party.

Tokyo, Feb. 14.—The newspaper Asahi reported today more than 300 women and children died in a moving picture theater fire in Antung, Manchoukuo. Japanese troops were called out, the paper said, and distinguished themselves by saving many lives. (Antung is on the Yalu river, about seven miles above its mouth in the Bay of Korea.)

By RICHARD G. MASSOCK By The Associated Press. WITH FASCIST FORCES SOUTHEAST OF MADRID, Feb. 13. —Generalissimo Francisco Franco's Fascist insurgents today ripped another spoke from the wheel of vital highways about Madrid. They tightened the ring of steel which they have been drawing closer and closer around the city in more than three months of fighting. The objective is complete strangulation of arteries through which Madrid draws her supplies for life and defense. But one segment of the circle apparently remains open for communications between Madrid and the eastern Mediterranean seaboard. This provides only for a circuitous detour from the Madrid-Valencia highway through Alcala De Henares 20 miles east of the city on a northeastern route to Guadalajara. The maneuver, carried out by air attack and a push by land under heavy fire of Socialist government artillery, sheared a nine-mile

MADRID, Feb. 13. (UP) The Inés of rebels threw themselves against Madrid's defenses tonight in what appeared to be the start of a supreme effort to seize the city. They were thrown back across a battlefield littered with dead. General Francisco Franco, the rebel dictator, drove the main force of his attack against the Jarama River sector near Arganda Bridge, about 12 miles southeast of the capital, key to the Valencia Highway upon which Madrid is dependent for food and supplies. Loyalists met the charge with hand grenades. ITALIAN PILOT IS BURNED IN WRECK One of the enemy ships crashed in flames and its pilot burned to death in the wreckage. Loyalists identified him as an Italian from papers found on the body. At 10:30 p.m. the defense Junta announced that the rebels had been repulsed at Arganda Bridge. Loyalist military leaders tonight asked their government to order immediate conscript

BERLIN, Feb. 13.--(4)--Three Germans met death at dawn today in macabre formalities of the Nazi chopping block. Three times the top-hatted headsman swung his gleaming axe to execute one man for high treason and two others for “non-political” murders. At least six more remain in Reich jail cells waiting a similar fate. Kurl Stangl, of Dresden, was beheaded for high treason, while Bruno Busse and Georg Grammens were beheaded for ‘non-political’ killings. Four others met a like death during the past week.

| Madrid, Feb. 13.—(4?)—Decision to create a single unified command of all government forces in Spain—now poorly coordinated and in some cases virtually independent—appeared imminent tonight. | A committee from the defense junta, in command of the forces holding Madrid, was en route to Valencia to request establishment of obligatory military service for all able-bodied males between the ages of 20 and 45. | Insurgent planes bombed the main ward of a hospital in Arganda, 15 miles southeast of the capital, killing three persons.
PARIS, France. (UP) — The cabinet in a meeting Saturday decided to invite the American Legion to attend the 1937 exposition in France.

1937-05-18.text: > May 18./)—Britain’s newly-crowned monarchs King George VI and Queen Elizabeth, revived an old royal custom today by accepting an invitation to a ball at the home of one of their subjects. The king and queen planned to be among the 40 royal guests of the Duke and Duchess of Sutherland at historic Hampden House tonight. Two kings and three queens will be present; Britain's rulers, Queen Mother Mary, King Farouk of Egypt and Queen Mother Nazli of Egypt.

LONDON, May 18.—(UP)—J. P. Morgan, his health improved, expects to leave for the United States in about 10 days, a spokesman at his office said today. Morgan's associates expressed astonishment at a rumor which originated in New York last night that he was dead.

MONTS, France, May 17, UP — The Duke of Windsor tonight sent his equerry to London with a bulky bundle of "important papers" believed to be invitations to the royal family to attend his marriage to Mrs. Wallis Warfield. The papers which Dudley Forwood, who is Edward's "Man Friday," carried across the English Channel were known to be in connection with the wedding which will be held soon, probably the first week in June. Forwood will return to the Chateau de Cande Thursday, stopping off at Le Havre where he will greet Mrs. Warfield’s "Aunt Bessie," Mrs. Buchanan Merryman of Washington, D. C., upon her arrival from the United States. He will escort her to Monts, Mrs. Merryman, who was with Mrs. Warfield in London during the days of Edward's abdication crisis, (Continued on Page 2, Col. 8)

MADRID, May 18,--()—American volunteer battalions, used continually as government shock troops in the Spanish civil war, were estimated today to have lost almost a third of their number in death. Reliable sources placed the number of United States citizens killed while fighting on the government side at more than 500, or 30 per cent of the 1,700 reported to have enlisted since the conflict started just ten months ago. A few of the volunteers were professional air pilots and technicians, and a few were soldiers of fortune, but the overwhelming majority lacked previous military experience. The largest contingent of Americans in the service of the Republic has been the 16th infantry, or Abraham Lincoln battalion, which members of the unit said was recruited in the United States. This battalion originally was composed of 487 men who entered Spain last December and January and went into the t

Valencia, Spain, May 17 (P). Dr. Juan Negrin formed a new “Win the War” Spanish government tonight. Negrin, 48-year-old physician and a Socialist, heads Spain's sixth wartime government as Premier. Negrin also will serve as minister of finance. The number of seats in the new cabinet were reduced from nineteen to nine. All ministers represent the Popular Front political Parties. The CNT Trades Union which had four posts in the old cabinet was left out after refusal to participate. The new cabinet set-up: Foreign Affairs, Joe Giral, Left Republican. National Defense, Indalecio Prieto, Socialist. Justice, Manuel Iribe, Basque Nationalist. Interior, Julian Zugazagoitia, Socialist. Instruction and Wealth, Jesus Hernandez, Communist. Agriculture, Vincent Uribe, Communist. Public Works and Communications, Bernardo Giner de Los Rios, Union Republican. Labor and Social Assistance, Jaime Ayguade,

Hendaye, Franco-Spanish Frontier. — General Franco's insurgent command announced today its armies had “completely dominated” the important Basque defense of Amorebieta and that columns were pushing on toward Bilbao, nine miles to the northwest. The insurgents reported Amorebieta was in flames and apparently empty of defenders, and that they had advanced to a point 1,300 feet from it. They took the nearby villages of Echano, Epalza, Anacha, Avinda, Dudagoitia and the monastery of San Miguel. The insurgents, it was announced, were hastening the destruction of Amorebieta. They captured considerable quantities of war materials which they said the Basques, with heavy casualties, had left on the field.

Madrid, May 18.—Anarcho-Syndicalists refused today to co-operate with the new cabinet of Dr. Juan Negrin. Their stand overshadowed the relief of many Madrilenos that the governmental crisis, caused by the resignation of Premier Francisco Largo Caballero and his failure to bring extreme left elements into a new ministry, was solved by Negrin’s “win the War cabinet.” Concern mounted for the government’s defenses against the insurgent revolt. “The Negrin cabinet was formed without our participation and we will not collaborate with it,” the national committee of Anarcho-Syndicalist national confederation of labor (CNT) declared. “At the moment we only advise the ‘CNT membership that now more than ever it must hold itself loyal to responsible (CNT) committees. Let nobody act on his own account! “Only through unity of action shall we frustrate the counter-revolution and avoid an ‘embrace of ve

CASTEL GANDOLFO, May 18 — Pope Pius today ordered loud speakers placed in the public audience chamber of his villa to magnify his failing voice. Due to a heart condition, prelates said, the pontiff’s voice has been failing after a few minutes and only pilgrims close by could hear him. He received Cardinal Chelli and several other prelates today.

1937-11-16.text: London, Nov. 16 (UP)—Twelve persons were reported killed today when an airliner bound to London from Brussels crashed in flames near Ostend, Belgium. An Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Ostend said the plane was bound to London from Frankfurt, via Brussels. The dispatch said the plane, belonging to the Belgian S. B. E. N. A. line, was lost in a thick fog which made it difficult for the pilot to locate the airport for a forced landing. The landing lights were switched on and flares were lighted, but near the airdrome the plane hit a chimney and crashed. The victims were burned to death.

LONDON, Nov. 16—(AP)— Britain today dispatched Viscount Halifax on a “feeler” visit to Germany and welcomed youthful Leopold, king of the Belgians, to her shores for diplomatic talks of possibly far-reaching effect. A flotilla of British destroyers, escorted by nine Royal Air Force planes, steamed out to meet the visiting king in mid-channel—the first of the fanfare for Leopold’s formal state visit to seal the friendship of his tiny kingdom and the British Empire. Halifax, Lord President of the Council, en route to Germany by train and channel boat, will arrive at Berlin tomorrow morning and, among other things, probably will discuss Germany’s colonial aspirations with Hitler at Bavarian Berchtesgaden on Thursday. Halifax’s conversations with Hitler and other German leaders were expected to enable the Briton to report to Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain as to whether there were any rea

LONDON, Nov. 16, ()—Leopold, king of the Belgians, arrived at flag-draped Victoria station today on a state visit to England. King George, resplendent in the crimson tunic of a field marshal, snapped to a salute and shook hands with Leopold as the young visiting monarch stepped from his train to a platform carpeted with scarlet plush. Prime Minister Neville Chamber-

London, Nov. 16.—Halifax, one of Britain’s most expert political negotiators, left for Berlin today to talk European peace with Fuehrer Adolf Hitler, Col.-Gen Hermann Goering, and other Nazi leaders. It was believed here that the talks, officially termed private as they are, might prove one of the most important developments in recent European diplomatic activities. Apparently in an effort to cut short rumors that the visit might be postponed, the government advanced Lord Halifax’s departure by one day.

London, Nov. 16 (UP)—Highly reliable diplomatic quarters reported today that Japan recently gave France a virtual ultimatum to cease allowing men and munitions to enter China through French Indo-China. Failing such action, these sources said, Japan is reported to have threatened immediate seizure of the big Chinese island of Hainan off the coast of Kwantung province, strategically dominating the whole of northern Indo-China.

BARCELONA, Nov. 16.—(UP)—It was reported today that the S. S. Cardium, believed to be a British ship, sent out an SOS for assistance from the international patrol today when "attacked by pirates" between Ibiza and Alicante.

LONDON, Nov. 16 (U.A)--The German embassy said today that those killed in the crash of a Belgian airliner at Ostend included Prince George, grand duke of Hessen; his wife and two children, Ludwig and Aldenbach, and his mother, the dowager grand duchess.

LONDON, Nov, 15 (#)--A three-point preparedness program to safeguard the British empire against airplane attacks was outlined by Sir Samuel Hoare, home secretary, in the House of Commons today. Sir Samuel, moving second reading of the government's air raids precautions bill, told the house that “we have got to make the airplane as little dangerous to the British empire as we have made the submarine.” His plan envisaged: 1. An airforce strong enough not only to defend the empire, but strong enough to maintain the offense. 2. Antiaircraft guns, searchlights, and other weapons of ground protection, far more numerous and accurate than in the World War; 3. A system of air raid precautions to “ensure the country against panic and ensure that services without such a civilized community cannot exist will be maintained.” The home secretary said Britain's supply of gas masks for civilians was bett

1937-11-09.text: JERUSALEM, Nov. 9 ()—Five young Jews were shot to death today in a new outbreak of Arab-Jewish violence. They were attacked by the Holy Land's hill terrorists near a quarry where four of the group worked. The fifth was their armed guard. Low skimming British military planes and steel-helmeted police with dogs immediately spread a tight net in the Judean hills for the suspected Arab killers.

PARIS, Nov. 9 (U.P)—The Duke and Duchess of Windsor plan to visit the United States immediately after Christmas, English friends of the couple said today. They will go to Honolulu, it was said, after a tour of several weeks in the United States, during which they will make no attempt to study housing or industrial conditions.

London, Nov. 8—Growing fear was aroused in many parts of the world tonight that the Italy-German-Japanese pact against international communism was designed chiefly for territorial expansion. Skepticism was voiced in several countries at the signatories’ assurances the agreement signed at Rome Saturday was directed exclusively against bolshevism and constituted a safeguard against war. Recent Italian support of German colonial demands heightened suspicion of Italy's purpose in adhering to the pact at a time when the Japanese army is occupying large sections of China. Out in Cold Some British quarters expected Japan to grant Italy and Germany special economic advantages in occupied portions of China, excluding the United States and Great Britain. A source close to the German chancellery disclosed Germany would attempt to end the Chinese-Japanese war by bringing China into the anti-communis

LONDON, Nov. 9—Führer Adolf Hitler, following up his diplomatic victory in persuading Italy to join the German-Japanese anti-Comintern alliance, may soon ask Great Britain to discuss his demand for colonies in Africa, it was reported today. There seemed indications that Britain might consent to a discussion provided that any colonial concessions would bring guarantees calculated to contribute to European peace.

London, Nov. 8.—-()—-Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden told the house of commons today that Spanish insurgent General Francisco Franco has sent a note expressing regret for the sinking of the British merchantman Jean Weems, October 31. He said the insurgents offered to submit the question of liability and compensation to arbitration. The foreign secretary turned aside questions as to the identity of the pilot of the attacking plane, who some have hinted might have been Bruno Mussolini, son of the Italian premier.

New York, Nov. 9.—(4—Interest in the markets for basic commodities, where prices have declined precipitously during the last few weeks, shifted today to the buying side, and quotations turned moderately upward for a wide range of staples. A sharp rise in the London metal market had an almost immediate repercussion here. Copper for export gained more than half a cent a pound, and scrap copper was advanced by the same margin. In the futures markets, other nonferrous metals turned higher, and wheat, cotton, coffee, rubber, hides, and sugar futures joined the upturn. The coming session of Congress, at which specific measures designed to benefit agricultural prices will be considered, was likewise regarded as “bullish.” The stock market rallied from yesterday's low levels, with utility and copper shares in the van, and many stocks profiting to the tune of a few cents to $1 or more. Bonds also

PARIS, Nov. 8 -- A source close to the Duke and Duchess of Windsor said today the couple had decided tentatively on February as a possible new date for their postponed trip to the United States. The Duke and Duchess believe that by that time "the criticism will have subsided," making the tour possible, one of their associates said. Postponement of the tour, which was to have brought the Windsors to America Nov. 1, was announced Friday night. At that time the Duke said there had been "grave misconceptions" over his motives. To Stay in Paris The Windsors expected to remain Continued on ‘Second Page

Shanghai, Nov. 8 (4) - Chinese declared tonight they had launched a counter-offensive to isolate a Japanese force south of Shanghai, estimated at 25,000 men, from its landing base on the seacoast. Severe fighting broke out both south and west of Shanghai. In Chekiang province, to the south, Chinese declared they had repulsed a surprise Japanese thrust toward Shanghai from the Hangchow bay area. Japanese reported advances south of Soochow creek, on the western edge of Shanghai's International Settlement. Chinese reinforcements rushed to Sunkiang, a vital point in the Chinese defenses against which one of three Japanese columns was striking from the south. Another Japanese column, Chinese army communiques reported, was held on the far side of the Whangpoo river from Shanghai when Chinese defenders forced its vanguard back across the stream at Minhang, 15 miles south of Shanghai.

1937-11-03.text: New York, Nov. 3 (UP)—A tentative and partial itinerary for the Duke and Duchess of Windsor’s American tour was announced today by the spokesman for the former King of Great Britain who said the party would visit industrial plants in Mohawk Valley and inspect textile plants in the south. The spokesman was unable to list definite cities in which the duke and duchess would stop but said that the rough plans for the first three weeks of the tour would be as follows: Arrive Nov. 11. The duke and duchess will arrive in New York on the Bremen Nov. 11 and probably will go to Washington by train that evening. The next day they will be dinner guests at the British embassy and during the afternoon of Nov. 12 will inspect the greenbelt resettlement project outside Washington. That evening the duke will speak from the capital. He and the duchess plan to return to New York on Nov. 13, spending two or

BRUSSELS, Nov. 3,—(P)—The United States, Great Britain and France took the lead today in an international effort to end the Chinese-Japanese war. Norman H. Davis, official delegate of the United States opened a conference of 19 nations convened here to promote a speedy armistice in the far eastern hostilities with an offer of full co-operation. Great Britain and France, through their delegates announced their support. Davis appealed to the international representatives for "equitable adjustment" of the Chinese-Japanese war and warned that its end was essential to the peace of the world. China will continue to fight until Japan halts her aggression, Dr. Wellington Koo, declared. The Chinese delegates said Japan's actions might lead to a world war.

LONDON, Nov. 2.—(P)—A guarded Soviet concession on belligerent rights today led to an eleventh hour agreement by the nine-power non-intervention sub-committee on procedure for getting foreign armies out of Spain. At the same time the sub-committee, including British, Russian and Italian representatives, sideslipped the still unsettled Soviet-Fascist dispute over when belligerent rights actually should be granted the warring Spaniards. Thus the future was left open to possible deadlocks while Britain was understood to be preparing regularization at least of her trade relations with insurgent Spain by a commercial agreement. Informed sources were "optimistic" about the sub-committee’s progress but admitted that the date had not been set either for the beginning of foreign troop withdrawals or for the departure of commissions to Spain to determine how many volunteers are fighting there. The

LONDON —(U.P.)— An international non-intervention subcommittee has decided to ask both factions in Spain if they are ready to withdraw their foreign "volunteers," a step which diplomatic sources agreed today was the most important the committee has taken in a year’s discussions. While Soviet Russia abstained from voting on one of the chief points — the granting of belligerent rights — the nine-power subcommittee decided to follow the French and British lead and summon the main committee to decide the question.

PARIS, Nov 3 (AP)—Sources close to French diplomats reported today there was a growing belief among them that Britain was seeking to have Francisco Franco, the Spanish insurgent chieftain, break away from Italy and Germany. Quai d’Orsay sources declared diplomats saw such a move in the background of Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden's speech before the British Commons on Monday. Pointing to Eden’s statement that foreign assistance was likely to cost Franco heavily, these quarters declared “without a single doubt these words ring like an exhortation to Franco: ‘Get rid of your allies and we will let you establish a blockade of republican Spain.’” Informed observers asserted the British attitude was “plainly” hinting in favor of Franco since recent insurgent victories. In some circles there were hints that Britain was applying pressure to eliminate Italy and Germany in order to gain commercia

BERLIN — (U.P.) — Joachim Von Ribbentrop, German ambassador to London, will go to Rome for the purpose of signing an agreement by which Italy will be included in the German-Japanese anti-Communist pact, a reliable source said today. The agreement, which includes no military clauses, is expected to be signed Friday or Saturday.

Washington, Nov. 2 (AP) — The United States government prepared today to welcome England's abdicated King and his American wife as it would any exceptionally distinguished foreign visitors. George T. Summerlin, chief of protocol for the State Department, received personal orders from President Roosevelt to assist in coordinating any appointments the Duke and Duchess of Windsor may desire with other government departments. Summerlin himself will go to New York to meet the Windsors and accompany them to Washington. That is customary only upon the arrival of heads of foreign states, prime ministers, ministers of foreign affairs, or persons of similar importance. Arrangements for the couple's reception at the White House were being held in abeyance until the return of President Roosevelt from Hyde Park. But the British Ambassador, Sir Ronald Lindsay, and Lady Lindsay, announced they would en

SHANGHAI, Nov. 3.—(#)—Negotiations were under way today to move Shanghai warfare away from fringes of the French concession, where many Americans make their homes. A Japanese spokesman told of the conversations to neutralize the Nantai area just south of the concession. He declared that representatives of neutral powers had approached Japanese with a plan designed to avoid further endangering of foreign and Chinese non-combatants. Coincidentally, foreign military observers reported that Chinese lines extending west from the International Settlement were thinning, and added that they would not be surprised if Chinese withdrew from the area immediately around Shanghai within the next few days. While neutrality conversations were in progress, Japanese resumed their drive southward from spearhead bases on the south bank of Soochow Creek. There were indications that Chinese troops were fallin

1937-10-01.text: LONDON, ENG, OCT. 1. (AP).-Britain and France today phrased the final draft of their implied demand on Italy for a showdown on intervention in Spain's civil war despite a reported attempt by Premier Mussolini to prevent such an invitation from ever reaching Rome. The momentous overture will not be forwarded until the French cabinet, probably tomorrow, gives final approval. The British cabinet already has approved the draft of the invitation. France and Britain were determined to block any move by Mussolini to sidestep the proposed tri-power conference aimed at forcing prompt withdrawals of the thousands of Italian soldiers fighting for insurgent Spain. Count Dino Grandi, Mussolini's envoy to London, was believed to have attempted to forestall actual presentation of the invitation at Rome. His call Wednesday on Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden was interpreted generally as Il Duce's first at

Jerusalem —()—Britain struck with an iron fist Friday to crush a new wave of terrorism in the Holy Land. In a sweeping offensive mandate, authorities outlawed the Arab higher committee and started rounding up its influential members. With telephone communication from the city suspended and roads Mufti Is Ousted The Grand Mufti of Jerusalem, head of the higher committee, was deprived of his office and rumor was he had been arrested. (There was a report in Cairo, Egypt, that the Mufti had been arrested.) The mandate

GOSPORT, England, Oct. 1, (A. P.) The racing yacht Endeavour I, proud and defiant, reached the slip of her berth today, bringing back from the Atlantic one of the most thrilling sagas of the sea this historic English port town ever has known. Standing on deck as the America's cup challenger slipped through the calm waters of the Solent was Ned Heard, Endeavour's bronzed, 50-year-old skipper, who, 20 days ago, was swept overboard in an Atlantic hurricane, caught a loose wire and pulled himself back aboard to make an epic 2700-mile voyage under sail. For the last 20 miles of the voyage, up through the Needles and down the Solent, Captain Heard had nothing to do. The yacht Viva Ti, from which he cut loose off Nantucket September 13, had picked him up again and towed him home. Two hours before he arrived Gosport was exulting. The wayside was strung with stars and stripes and union jacks. All

GOSPORT, England (AP)—The legendary cup yacht Endeavour I, 'back from the grave,' arrived home in triumph Friday. Nineteen days ago she left Newport, R. I., in tow of the motor yacht Viva II. Next day she broke her steel tow line in a storm that roused immediate fear for her. Vain search was made for her for days. It was feared that she had foundered. One false report was received that she was safe, and when it proved untrue she was all but given up. Sighted On Monday the British tanker Cheyenne sighted her 260 miles off the southwest tip of Ireland, and flashed the news that she was safe. Under her own sail, Endeavour I kept on. She was sighted yesterday at Lizard Point, at the southwest tip of England. She kept on up the channel. Her tow, Viva II, long home, went out to meet her and this morning, in the haze off the south coast of England, eager to get home, Endeavour consented again t

Victoria, B. C., Sept. 30, (4).— The spirit of peace and good will brought President Roosevelt to Canada today, Emphasizing United States’ friendliness toward Canada, the Chief Executive came—by paradox, on a warship—to the picturesque capital of British Columbia, Shore batteries boomed a salute of 21 guns as the U.S.S. Destroyer Phelps, bearing the President, Mrs. Roosevelt and their party, nosed into the Ogden Point dock after a three hour journey from Seattle. Despite the weather, Victoria police estimated at close to 40,000 the crowd lining the route of the presidential procession. It was the first visit of any President of the United States to Victoria, but Mr. Roosevelt's second to Canada in little more than a year.

ATHENS, Greece, Oct. 1—(7— The British Imperial Airways flying boat courier, sister ship of the Atlantic-flying Caledonia and Cambria, sank today when it sat down on Phaleron Bay. Two passengers were missing and seven were reported to have been dragged alive from the water. Of the seven, five were said to have been injured. The five-man crew also escaped. Bad visibility was blamed.

TOKYO, Oct. 1—(7)—The Japanese foreign office made it clear today Japan would not stand for third party mediation of its conflict with China. This reiteration of policy came simultaneously with sharp newspaper criticism of Great Britain, and apparently aimed directly at that power, A foreign office spokesman hinted strongly Japan regards British influence at Geneva as responsible for the League of Nations condemning Japanese bombardment of cities in China. “We desire to make clear that we do not think mediation is called for at the present stage of affairs,” the spokesman asserted. “If any power wants to mediate, let her first acquire a full appreciation of our aims and aspirations.” From the naval ministry came the admission Japanese warships were (Continued on Page 6. Col. 6)

London, Sept. 30.—(/P)—British liberals and laborites promoted an anti-Japanese boycott throughout the empire tonight. Public gatherings denounced the Japanese invasion of China. An informed source disclosed the British colonial authorities at Hongkong had opened an official inquiry into the reported sinking of Chinese fishing junks and loss of 300 lives under attack by a Japanese submarine. Although sponsors of the boycott admitted privately there was little hope of obtaining the government's open endorsement, they expressed confidence the movement would spread to other countries. The National Council of Labor, which declared a boycott, said a wide response had been given its proposal to hold demonstrations throughout Britain over the weekend. The British Red Cross sent medical supplies to China and announced an appeal for funds to aid the Chinese would be launched. The British Labor pa

1937-04-02.text: LONDON, April 2 (4)—A crowded rush-hour commuting train plowed into the rear of another on a 60-foot high viaduct between Battersea Park and Victoria station today, killing eight persons, injuring 40 and sending dazed survivors teetering like tight-rope walkers along the narrow trackway. Even a worse tragedy was averted by the presence of mind of one passenger, who struggled from the wreckage and ran, swaying, along the tracks to flag down a third train speeding from Victoria station, Airbrakes screaming, it pulled to a stop a few yards from the wreck. The last carriage of the first train, which had stopped on the tracks, was a shambles. Its wooden body was ripped off completely. Four men were killed in one compartment, three women in another. Rescue crews, reaching the viaduct with long ladders, worked in a soaking rain to pull the dead and injured from the wreckage. It took three hours

London, April 1.—Great Britain and France embarked on a joint armament race today to back up the allied might of the British fleet and the French army with at least 3,000 additional fighting planes in the next twelve months. France announced she will build 1,500 planes during 1937 to reinforce the 3,000 to 4,000 first line fighting craft she already possesses. How many planes Great Britain will build was a closely held secret of the air ministry but it is estimated that 1,750 were delivered in the last fiscal year—just the start of the drive to have 2,600 first line planes in the air by the spring of 1939. April 1 is a significant date in the air history of the two democracies whose world war alliance has been strengthened by the fact they are the only two nations in western Europe who have steered a middle course between Communism and Fascism. To Britain, today is memorable

(By The Associated Press) LONDON, Apr. 2—Eight persons were killed today and more than 40 injured when two suburban trains, crowded with city-bound workers during London's morning rush hour, crashed on a 60-foot high viaduct. One coach was badly telescoped across a live rail and burst into flames. The blaze was quickly extinguished. Scores of passengers narrowly escaped death in the smash which was one of the worst train accidents in the London area in recent years.

LONDON, April 2.—(U.P)—Seven persons, including one woman, were killed today in a collision of electric passenger trains near Victoria station in central London, an official railway announcement said. Earlier estimates reported 12 killed and 30 injured. One train was on a viaduct near Poupart’s Junction outside the station, awaiting a signal to go ahead. The second train, speeding in from Coulsdon, south of London, crashed into it. Because the crash occurred on a viaduct, rescue work was impeded. Police had difficulty in restraining crowds and making way for stretcher bearers, surgeons and nurses.

LONDON. (AP). Norman H. Davis, America's ambassador at large, said he will discuss world economic and peace co-operation with British statesmen, but that the time is not yet ripe for an international disarmament conference. Tension created by the Spanish civil war and widespread suspicion in the European mind made disarmament impracticable now, he asserted. His disavowal of any U.S. intention to propose an amendment conference now coincided with that of Secretary of State Hull in Washington. And it came, too, after general reaction in European capitals against such a conference at this time, a stepping up of Franco-British aerial armaments, and new efforts by those two nations to settle the question of foreign volunteers in Spain. An apparent softening of the Italo-German attitude inspired France and Britain to urge again that non-Spanish fighters be withdrawn from the Spanish civil war.

LONDON, (AP).—Delegates from 22 countries assembled today to seek an international five year plan to stabilize the world’s $1,300,000,000 sugar industry and put it on a paying basis for producers. The sessions, looking to coordination of both production and sale in exporting and producing countries, will open Monday with a formal session at the British foreign office. Former Premier Ramsay MacDonald will preside. The initiative for the conference came from MacDonald as president of the world monetary and economic conference of 1933 and Dr. Yendrvk Kolijn, prime minister of The Netherlands, who served as chairman of the economic committee of the conference. Over the weekend, representatives are expected from the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, Union of South Africa, India, France, Germany, Italy, Russia, Portugal, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Cuba, Peru, Brazi

LONDON, April 2 (UP)—Belief is growing in London that the Spanish nationalists face ultimate defeat after a further prolonged struggle unless they obtain fresh supplies of manpower and war material from Italy and Germany. The belief is based not on momentary developments but a long view of the resources of the combatants. The loyalists shifted the scene of heaviest fighting today to the Basque country in the north. The rebel siege at Madrid was lessened temporarily, if not lifted. The insurgents apparently withdrew forces long concentrated there to meet government troops on offensives the loyalists are pressing on other fronts in the provinces, thus dividing the rebel armies in a series of scattered attacks north and south. 75,000 Loyalists Battle In the north, a fleet of loyalist warplanes cooperated with a Basque (loyalist) land force of 75,000 men on a drive along a 100-mile front to

CALCUTTA, India. April 1 @ British India assumed autonomy government today with a general strike and widespread demonstrations. There was no violence, but millions observed the day in mourning and protest against the new constitution which granted the provinces self-government. There were arrests in the centers, as followers of the congress party, which bitterly opposed the constitution, demonstrated in the streets. The congress party members looked to their former leader, Mahatma K. Gandhi, who has indicated he has a new plan in mind regarding independence grants for India.

1937-04-06.text: (By THE ASSOCIATED PRESS) Great Britain and France were reported ready today to try to line up the Balkans against Italy if Premier Mussolini moves to quit the international "hands off Spain" agreement. That plan was recounted by an informed Paris source as the Spanish insurgents, friendly to Italy, claimed new important successes on the northern front. Their commanders asserted 2000 government soldiers had been killed in recent fighting for Durango and Bilbao. Italy Accuses France The possibility Italy might quit the 27-nation non-intervention accord was raised by an Italian spokesman as the outgrowth of authoritative Italian charges that France had "flagrantly violated" it, allowing aid to be sent to the Madrid-Valencia government. Britain and France would act to isolate the Balkans from Italy only as a "last resort", the Paris source said, as they are not anxious to attempt a major po

BY The Associated Press. LONDON, April 6.—France and Great Britain were reported today ready to bring “last resort” pressure against Premier Mussolini to halt any possibility of Italian withdrawal from the agreement to isolate the Spanish civil war. The two governments, informed sources in Paris declared, would attempt to hold Italy in line with the 27-nation nonintervention agreement by a threat to steer the Balkan states away from that friendship with Italy which Il Duce is so eager to obtain. Such a move, in answer to statements by an Italian spokesman that his country might withdraw from the efforts to keep the Spanish war from spreading, the Paris source said, would be taken only as a “last resort.” French Aid Charged “The Italian threat of withdrawal and reassumption of “full liberty of action’ in Spain was based on authoritative charges in Rome that France had given aid to the Mad

LONDON, April 5 (47)—A concerted world effort to combat barriers to trade was hinted tonight as the International Sugar Conference began its deliberations to deal with one troubled industry. Belgium, at the instigation of France and Britain, began a survey of economic conditions in Europe with a view to “exploring how it may prove possible to reduce international trade barriers.” Brussels reports indicated a visit next week by Dr. Hjalmar Schacht, German Reichsbank president, would mark the beginning of economic conversations. Whether these conversations would result in eventual convocation of an international economic conference remained to be seen, but reliable observers emphasized that such a parley was not in immediate prospect and that no bilateral agreements were envisaged as part of the tri-party survey. The United States chief of the sugar delegation, Norman H. Davis, expressed h
Zagreb, Yugoslavia, Apr. 5. (P) — Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh tonight postponed until Tuesday their takeoff on a return flight to England. They came here yesterday from Athens.

PARIS, Apr. 6 (4)—France and Great Britain, in fear that war may come to Europe again, have become more insistent in wooing the support of the United States for such an eventuality today, 20 years after America entered the World War. So fixed has the idea become that the United States would once again come to the aid of her former allies that no speech on international politics by French and British statesmen is complete without some reference to “the ties that bind us to our brothers in the great democracy over the water.” Both Great Britain and France have based their efforts to insure an alliance with Washington through appeals to a common democratic form of government. The French, in particular, have emphasized that the United States can ill afford to have her “two outposts of democracy”—France and Britain—beaten by an array of fascist powers which would then be free to turn their at

LONDON, (U.P) — Londoners thought they knew today what the American strip-tease was, and were all the more convinced that the American boiling-point in amusement is very low. Miss Diane Raye, after some weeks of censor trouble, appeared last night at the Victoria Palace vaudeville theatre. From behind a slightly transparent curtain, with the dimmest of blue lights playing on the ink-dark stage, Miss Raye appeared to the audience. She smilingly threw a voluminous chiffon cape back from her shoulders and then, making rapidly for the wings, took off a split skirt and showed her thigh at the moment of exit. This was the signal for the audience to applaud Miss Raye back for additional stripping but the audience did not know it and there was a somewhat embarrassing silent pause. Miss Raye, gesturing her despair, went back on the stage. The dim blue lights went dimmer and she dropped the front

Santander, Spain, Apr. 6—The mineral boat Andra of Panama, said to be under charter to a British shipping firm, was reported today to have been sunk by the insurgent cruiser Almirante Cervera off Castro Urdiales, 12 miles east of Bilbao on the Bay of Biscay. Reports of the Basque government, allied with the Madrid-Valencia government, asserted insurgent warships had launched a heavy bombardment of the Basque coast as a part of their drive against Bilbao. Radio messages, said to have been picked up from insurgent sources, indicated a concentration of virtually an entire fleet in the Bay of Biscay. The cruisers España Canarias and Almirante Cervera were said to be the nucleus of the concentration.

By Associated Press LONDON, April 6.—Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh charted a course for London today from Zagreb, Yugoslavia, skirting the Alpine barrier on the last leg of what was believed to have been a survey for a new commercial skyway route from England to India. His flight indicated that he believes the only possible course for an airliner is to go around the Alps and his courses were laid around both sides of the formidable range.

1937-10-25.text: LONDON, OCT. 25, (AP). -- British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden sought a compromise formula meant to save European non-intervention in Spain from collapse, but the outlook was gloomy. Amid efforts to bring the bickering powers into harmony, two mysterious incidents in the Mediterranean created what some quarters regarded as the gravest situation since the Nyon accord established the anti-piracy patrol. The 2,413-ton French freighter Oued Mellag was bombed by an unidentified plane off Barcelona, Spain, yesterday, and abandoned at sea by her crew. The master of the British liner Kaiser-1-Hing reported by radio from off the North African coast that a seaplane was seen “dropping two heavy bombs from which columns of water shot up at a great height” at a submarine which “apparently submerged.” The British admiralty, after saying for several hours that it was without information, first announ

SHANGHAI, Oct. 25.—(U.P)—British defense lines on the west fringe of the international area were provided with anti-aircraft machine guns today. Their crews were ordered to fire on any airplane that approached dangerously close, it was said on reliable authority. This grave move was the direct sequel to a Japanese airplane attack on a British army outpost yesterday in which a rifleman of the Royal Ulster Rifles was killed. Foreign naval and military authorities, increasingly anxious over the mounting fury of the Japanese attack, considered means of safeguarding the international settlement and French concession. Not only had Japanese airplanes killed the Ulster rifleman, on sentry duty in the British defense lines, but planes apparently of the same squadron had machine-gunned two parties of excursioning foreign civilian men and women, including eight Americans. So gravely did British and

LONDON (U.P) — Jean Batten, 27-year-old New Zealand girl who gave up a musical career to become a flier, rested Monday after an adventurous flight from Australia to England that established a new solo record. She made the flight from Port Darwin, Australia, to Croydon airdrome in five days, eight hours and 32 minutes. The previous record was six days, eight hours and 25 minutes which Harry F. Broadbent, the Australian distance flier, established May 3.

SHANGHAI. (CP). A British soldier was killed and five Americans and about a score of other foreigners were endangered gravely Sunday when a Japanese warplane, with machine guns blazing, swooped five times over grounds near the western edge of Shanghai’s international settlement. U.S. Consul General Clarence E. Gauss protested to the Japanese consulate general. A British sentry at the scene said British soldiers returned the Japanese airman’s fire with automatic rifles. British army authorities officially branded the affair a “deliberate attack.” Japanese naval and civilian officers quickly expressed regret to the British. British army officers disclosed three British outposts in the Keswick road area were sprayed by the Japanese airman’s bullets, and that a second British soldier escaped serious injury when a cigarette case stopped a bullet which pierced his uniform. A Japanese spokesman

HONGKONG, Oct. 25, (4).—The steamer Nanning radioed today she was proceeding to Hongkong with 29 survivors of the gasoline laden British freighter Kaitangata which burst into flame. The survivors included all five Europeans aboard the Kaitangata, the Nanning reported, but 19 Chinese were missing. The Kaitangata, chartered to the Standard Oil Company, was entering the Hainan Straits in the South China Sea bound from Hongkong to Haiphong, China, when the fire broke out last night.

LYMPNE, England (*) — Jean Batten, New Zealand woman flier, landed here Sunday, setting a new record for a solo flight from Australia to England. She clipped 14 hours and 10 minutes from the record set by Jim Broadbent last May. Her time from Darwin, Australia, was five days, 18 hours and 15 minutes. While Miss Batten was flying the last leg of her journey from Naples, where she rested Saturday night, Broadbent was flying toward Australia in an attempt to beat her record in the opposite direction. He was meeting bad weather, however, and was forced to Bagdad, Iraq, after a hop off for Basra.

London, Oct. 25 (UP) — Great Britain and the United States intend to work together at the far eastern conference at Brussels toward international action to end the Japanese-Chinese war by mediation and will resist any excited demands for penal action against Japan. Strong intimations that both countries oppose any action that would antagonize Japan, and thus tend to stiffen her determination to fight in China to a finish, were supplemented here by their policy. The American delegation headed by Norman W. Davis is due at Brussels Wednesday and the British delegation, with Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden in command, is due Friday. It was expected that Davis and Eden would confer at once on the program for the conference, due to open Saturday.

LONDON, Oct. 25.--The diplomatic reporter of the Evening Standard reported today that the Soviet government has instructed Ambassador Ivan Maiski to inform the Spanish non-intervention committee that Russia is withdrawing. "Russia takes the stand, the Evening Standard claimed, that the whole machinery has broken down at the present and is camouflaging an entirely different situation." Both the Soviet embassy and the foreign office professed to have no knowledge of the report, the foreign office saying that Maiski has no appointment to see Eden. Maiski denied that there were any new developments since he presented, more than a fortnight ago, the Soviet’s observations on the Vanduilm-Hemming report regarding control, when it was intimated: that if the control was not completely effective the Soviets might not desire to continue financial support of the control scheme. 1937-10-12.text: BANGOR, Me., Oct. 12. (?)—G-men wiped out the notorious Indiana gunman-gangster, Al Brady, and one of his mobsmen today in a sensational five-minute gunfight on Bangor’s busiest downtown street. A third gangster, superficially wounded, threw down his gun and surrendered. James Walsh, federal agent, was wounded in the thigh. The Dead Al Brady, 35, wanted for three slayings and several robberies; Clarence Shaffer Jr., a Brady mobsman; James Dalhover, Brady mobsman; head grazed by bullet. The gangsters, who long have terrorized the Mid-West with their forays upon banks and their armed bravado against officers of the law, had been traced to Bangor by the Department of Justice agents, working with Indiana State Police. Brady and his two companions went early today to a sporting goods store to buy ammunition. A squad of G-men stationed themselves in a vacant building across the street, with ma

Bangor, Me., Oct. 12, — Two Indiana gangsters were slain and a G-man wounded today in a spectacular gun battle witnessed by hundreds of motorists and pedestrians on the main street of Bangor. Slain were gang-leader A. Brady, 31, and his lieutenant, Clarence Lee Shaffer Jr., 22, who had been hunted by federal agents as the outstanding members of a mid-west desperado mob charged with three murders and robberies with loot totaling more than $85,000. At Eastern Maine General Hospital, the wounded federal agent was identified as Walter Walsh, 28, of Washington, D.C., he was shot in the right chest. An early report that the slain gangsters had been henchmen of the notorious Alvin Karpis, one-time midwestern public enemy No. 1, was denied by Indiana State Patrolman Meredith K. Steward. Though the 10 G-men, Indiana and Maine state police who participated in the battle withheld details, it was un

SHANGHAI, Oct. 12 — (UR) — Three motor cars carrying attaches of the British embassy and a Soviet consulate car were attacked and machine-gunned by airplanes today on the Nanking-Shanghai road. The Soviet consulate said one of the attacked cars flew the stars and stripes. Less than six weeks ago, the British ambassador was shot and gravely wounded on the same road. The Soviet consulate announced that a Japanese plane turned a machine gun on a consulate car which went out to pick up Leonid Shahov, secretary to the military attache, who had been with the British party. Shahov’s car broke down and the British picked him up. A spokesman for the consulate said one of the cars attacked was owned by the Bills Motors Co. and flew the American flag.

LONDON, OCT. 12, (AP). — Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain and Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden, in joint command of British foreign policy, drafted insistent but moderate action today to change Premier Mussolini's mind regarding foreign volunteers in Spain. Diplomatic sources indicated this course, supported by France, would not increase the danger of a general war but was expected to bring the Italian Premier into line on non-intervention. The change of course was plotted in the face of a gathering insurgent offensive in the Spanish civil war. Meanwhile, at Paris, sources close to the foreign office said a French proposal that Italy be given “a last chance” to agree to withdraw troops from Spain or face “action” has been drafted for submission to the British foreign office. The “suggestions” were drafted by the French government following Italy's refusal to join with France and Great Br

By United Press PARIS, Oct. 12. — Responsible quarters said today that the British government was exerting extreme pressure on France to open the Spanish frontier at once to permit a full flow of men and munitions to the Loyalists. This assertion caused astonishment here, but it seemed to be a fact and to represent a definite new turn in the general European situation. France and Britain seem agreed that Italy must be forced completely to evacuate the Balearic Islands at once and that Mussolini must be stopped from sending substantial reinforcements to Spain proper now or later. France, according to the informants, was determined to weigh all consequences first. It was represented that the French government wanted something more than the "moral" support Britain had offered, in event that the frontier was opened and France found herself in a dangerous position. It was emphasized here that

Bangor, Oct. 12.—(/?)—Federal sleuths, operating with characteristic precision and self-effacement, today erased with a hail of machine-gun fire the notorious Al Brady gang of Indiana outlaws. Swept to swift death as the federals struck with the suddenness of summer lightning were Brady, leader of the gang, and Clarence Shaffer, Jr., one of his henchmen. A third member of the gang, James Dalhover, threw down his pistol and surrendered after a machine-gun bullet flecked his nose. He was quickly lodged in a jail cell. Only one G-man suffered injury and he, Walter Walsh, was shot in the shoulder. At the Eastern Maine General Hospital, surgeons said they did not believe his wound serious. The show-down between the government men and the gangsters came as the latter left a sporting goods store they had visited to purchase pistol cartridges.
