The flying colonel and his flying wife paused in Rome today, assured by Il Duce himself they will have privacy—before resuming the birthday air tour that may take them to Cairo. The American flier called on undersecretary for air Giuseppe Valle and visited the United States embassy.

Rome, Feb. 3 (#)—Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh spent most of this afternoon seeing Rome from a limousine followed by a police escort to insure the privacy the famous flying couple desires. The Lindberghs interrupted an air tour of which the destination was believed to be Cairo, to devote two or three days to sightseeing here.

1937-09-04.text: SHANGHAI, SEPT. 4. (AP).- American, British and French consuls-general demanded today that Chinese land forces and Japanese warships withdraw from the vicinity of the international settlement and the French concession, havens for thousands of foreigners in this international city and splattered by artillery shelling in the bitter warfare between Chinese and Japanese. The consular officials addressed a joint communication to Mayor C. K. Yul, protesting further endangering the international settlement where about 100 civilians were killed yesterday. The mayor sped the message to the Nanking central government. The consular chiefs asked that Chinese troops be withdrawn to the east of Pootung road. They requested the Japanese national commander to remove Japanese gunboats to a point beyond the seventh section of the Whangpoo river, to get them out of immediate range of the international area

LONDON, SEPT. 4 (AP) - The British Admiralty today drew up secret plans for presentation at a Mediterranean conference to drive "mystery" submarines from a sea that is Britain's lifeline of empire. "Important proposals" will be made, the British government announced, when the Mediterranean powers gather next week in Geneva to discuss the grave under-sea threats to European peace, precipitated by submarine attacks on international shipping. As Europe's chancellors pored over plans for the hurriedly-summoned meeting, these developments added new elements to the situation: 1. Official Russian newspapers accused Italy of "piracy" in the Mediterranean and said the Soviets would make "fascist bandits pay dearly" for the sinking of a Russian vessel off Algiers Monday. 2. Diplomats reported the Spanish government, as well as Insurgent Generalissimo Francisco Franco, would be excluded from the co

SHANGHAI, Sept. 5. (U.P)— Alarmed at an immediate menace to the lives of more than 2,000 Americans in the International Settlement and the French Concession of this city, the United States tonight joined with Great Britain and France in demanding that Japan remove her warships from Shanghai. The intervention followed a rain of explosives on the foreign areas. SHANGHAI, Sept. 5. (WP) Chinese news dispatches reported today that the second division of the Japanese-controlled Manchukuoan army had revolted, proclaiming allegiance to the Chinese government at Nanking. The agency also reported rebellion of other Manchukuoan units who were alleged to have joined Chinese troops.

By The Associated Press. London, Sept. 3.—Great Britain led the way tonight in Europe’s effort through naval might and diplomacy to end mysterious submarine attacks on Mediterranean shipping and their threat to the continent's peace, The British government announced that it would “submit important proposals” at a conference of Mediterranean powers next week at Geneva. The statement, abandoning the British precedent of silence before such a meeting, was made while four additional destroyers sped into the Western Mediterranean with orders to capture or sink the submarine “pirates” molesting British ships of war and peace. Both steps were interpreted in well-informed quarters as evidence that the British Foreign Office intends to force a showdown. The British are aroused by the sinking of the British tanker, Woodford, and an effort to torpedo the destroyer, Havock, both by unidentified subm

Nanking, Sept. 4.—(CP)—The first lady of China today predicted the Japanese empire might some day wage bitter offensive warfare against the United States or Great Britain. That grim possibility was foreseen by Mme. Chiang Kai-shek, wife of the Chinese premier-generalissimo, who in her own right is the chieftain of China’s air forces and the Far East's most powerful feminine figure. “As Japan has torn up all treaties and violated international laws, it is possible the same devastating undeclared war which hitherto has cost China and foreign countries great losses in Manchuria and which now is being waged against the important seaports of China may be started against the United States, England or any other country having interests in China,” she said. “In China we are obliged to suffer more because we have been weakened through a delay in organizing after the revolution, but we are determi

Washington, Sept. 3. Secretary Hull restating his policy of international cooperation, said today that America and Great Britain have been working in close consultation in meeting the problems of the strife in China. With this he coupled an announcement that the department had issued the strongest possible warnings to Americans to evacuate the danger zone immediately. Naval vessels, he said, are ready to take them out of the area. At the same time, commerce department figures showed that China purchased more American aircraft in the first six months of 1937 than did any other nation. Its total was $2,415,922. Japan, which has its own plane making facilities, bought $382,883 in the same period. Another development was an announcement by the Red Cross today authorizing its 3,700 chapters to accept contributions for relief work in China. The Red Cross does not, however, contemplate a nation

JERUSALEM, Sept. 4.—(P)—A bomb was hurled into a crowded Arab bus center today, killing one woman in a new outbreak of the Arab-Jew terrorism that has claimed seven lives in recent days. The assailant, described as a Jew, managed to escape although he was fired on by a British constable who was wounded slightly by the bomb.

(Copyright, 1937) LONDON, Sept. 4.--Angered by Japan's failure to make a prompt apology for the wounding of British Ambassador Sir Hughe Knatchbull-Hugessen in China, or to reply immediately to London’s note of protest, the British government today instructed its new ambassador to Japan not to present his credentials at once. The new British envoy to Japan, Robert Leslie Craigie, has just arrived at Tokio. He was instructed not to present his credentials until Japan’s formal reply to Britain’s protest has been received in London, International News Service learned. Sir Hughe, the British envoy to China, was wounded by machine gun fire from a Japanese plane while he was motoring from Nanking to Shanghai. Britain is extremely reluctant to sever all diplomatic relations with the Land of the Rising Sun. The decision to withhold Craigie's credentials was reached at a recent meeting of British

1937-12-08.text: Winter spread itself along the Atlantic seaboard from Maine to Florida today, bringing snow and icy temperatures to parts of New England and the Middle Atlantic states, and the threat of a fresh cold wave for the South. Northern and central sections of the country, east of the Rockies, also suffered from cold. Ten deaths were attributed to the weather. Five in the South were reported from exposure. Two children died in western Pennsylvania in coasting accidents, and a Pittsburgh man collapsed and died from the cold. A Buffalo man also died from the cold; icy roads sent a physician skidding to death in the Barge Canal near Fulton, N. Y. Eleven inches of snow lay in Buffalo. Snow fell in western Massachusetts and upper New York State, and snow flurries were predicted for New York City.

| London, Dec. 8. — The fall of Nanking will mark the real beginning of Japan's difficulties in China unless the regime of Generalissimo Chiang Kai-Shek crumples and immediately seeks peace, reliable British observers predicted today. Experts on far eastern affairs believed that the Japanese high command would halt their offensive after the occupation of Nanking.

London, Dec. 8 (AP)—The 1937 edition of Jane's famous "All the World’s Aircraft," out today, ranked the United States’ airforce as one of the largest and "possibly the most efficiently equipped in the world." The authoritative survey of the international aerial rearmament race, however, credited Germany’s fighting planes with being the equal of both the United States and Great Britain in power and performance, but not in numbers. Jane’s editor, C. G. Grey, said France had fallen sadly behind in the performance of its airplanes while increasing the size of its aerial fleet. In reference to the successful performances attributed to "Russian airplanes in support of the red (Madrid) government in Spain," Grey said flatly: "Those airplanes definitely have been of American design and most likely of American construction." The volume said little was known of Russia's airforce although it was co

London, Dec. 8. (AP)--Japan apologized today to Great Britain for the aerial bombing of the British steamers Tuckwo and Tatung at Wuhu, December 5. It was learned that the question of indemnity was being considered. The apology was made by the chief of staff of the Japanese command at Shanghai who went aboard the British patrol sloop Falmouth, of the Asiatic fleet.

LONDON (UP) — Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden told a questioner in the House of Commons today that the British government not only has informed the Spanish insurgents that Britain will not admit their right to blockade the Spanish coast but also warned them against any interference with British shipping. "It has been made clear that such shipping will continue to be protected," Eden added.

SHANGHAI, Dec. 8.—()—Japanese ministry authorities tonight warned all foreigners and Chinese non-combatants to evacuate beleaguered Nanking as quickly as possible. “Hostilities may engulf the city any moment,” they said. Through Suemasa Okamoto, Japanese consul general at Shanghai, the authorities requested representatives of foreign powers, including the United States, to inform their respective nationals of the impending struggle in the evacuated Chinese capital. There were 17 Americans in Nanking. The Japanese said they considered the former capital “one large fortification” and therefore could not give the Chinese non-combatants and foreigners the assurance of safety in the so-called refugee zone. Thousands of Chinese, who took active part in the defense of the city, were huddled in the refugee district. A safety zone, established by Americans and other foreigners, flew American flag

SHANGHAI, Dec. 5 (UP).— The Japanese armies took recourse to long range bombardment today in their siege of Nanking, pounding the walls of the capital from the air, land and water when infantry assaults failed to dislodge the Chinese defenders. Land and river batteries shelled the capital and airplanes made bombing raids throughout the day, the Domei news agency reported. It said the Japanese had met stiff resistance and the final assault on the walls was uncertain. The Japanese forces charged on Nanking from three sides but found a stubborn wall of Chinese resistance. There was furious fighting a few miles outside the city, directly in line with the east gate, but the Chinese were withdrawing inside the east gate and the Japanese vanguard had not caught up with them. Foreign military experts here believed the Japanese were preparing for a final push toward the east wall, following the C

Shanghai.- (/P) ~ (Thursday)- The possibility that China might form a new government without Premier-Generalissimo Chiang Kai-Shek and make peace with Japan, was advanced by authoritative quarters here today. The generalissimo's departure from Nanking in the face of the advancing Japanese army, these authorities reasoned, likely would cause subordinates to undertake whatever settlement was obtainable. (Chiang and Madame Chiang were reported to have left Nanking by air on Tuesday.)

1937-10-18.text: LONDON, Oct. 18 (#)—Italy and Germany today held an ace which informed sources said may enable them to gain another diplomatic victory in the Spanish civil war non-intervention crisis. Observers said Premier Benito Mussolini of Italy and Chancellor Adolf Hitler of Germany can agree to the Anglo-French plan for withdrawal of foreign volunteers from Spanish armies and then let Insurgent Generalissimo Francisco Franco scrap the plan by refusing to call off his foreign fighters. Thus, they said, Germany and Italy were in a position which might permit them to prolong discussion over the problem and evade blame in the event that non-intervention machinery collapses. The non-intervention sub-committee is to meet Tuesday in London. It was pointed out that although Franco orally has agreed to a withdrawal of foreign soldiers, he has done so with a reservation. He has stipulated "equal withdrawal"

JERUSALEM, Oct. 18 (WP) — Violence increased throughout Palestine today while neutral observers voiced the opinion that peace between Jews and Arabs under present conditions was impossible. General A. P. Wavell, commander of the 10,000 British troops in Palestine, ordered the homes of Arab terrorists burned, following the destruction of Kalandia airport, near Lydda, with an estimated loss of $50,000. Sixty persons were arrested for breaking the 24-hour curfew which amounts to virtual martial law. The newest violence was the bombing of the Jewish orthodox quarters of Jerusalem. Two bombs were thrown, both of them striking a building. The damage was slight. The Jews seized a Bedouin whom they accused of the bombing, and turned him over to the police. Two Italian-speaking officers who deserted from the French foreign legion in Syria were arrested near Acre, and charged with responsibility f

KDON, (AP)——Definite abatement of the Spanish crisis was predicted last night in informed quarters as a result of diplomatic developments over the weekend. Confidence was expressed that the meeting of the non-intervention subcommittee set for Tuesday in London would yield real progress toward a settlement. The effort to recall foreign volunteers from Spain was expressed by a high Italian official in Rome. In London and Paris informed persons said Britain and France were equally ready to grant belligerent rights to both factions in the Spanish conflict. The Observer, one of London’s most influential Sunday newspapers, argued at length that Britain and the other great powers should give equal diplomatic and belligerent rights to both sides in Spain as the only obvious solution. This, it was pointed out, is what Italy and Germany have been waiting for all along. The problem before the non-i

ROME, Oct. 18. (UP)—Premier Benito Mussolini’s newspaper, Popolo D’Italia of Milan, leading a bitter campaign of criticism against Great Britain’s Palestine policy, asserted today that “news from Palestine can not but arouse a sense of horror throughout the civilized world.” Coincidently, dispatches from Addis Ababa reported that Moslem leaders of Ethiopia had telegraphed the League of Nations and the British Government expressing disapproval of British policy and an- (Continued on page 2)

LONDON—UP—The Duke of Windsor was reported by the Daily Mirror today to have made a secret airplane flight to England on Oct. 7 for a visit with his mother, Dowager Queen Mary. It was stated that the Duke flew from Paris to the airdrome at Yapton near Bognor, Sussex, and Queen Mary was driven to the airdrome in a closed car from the Bolembre estate of the Earl and Countess of Athlone with whom she was staying on Oct. 7. The report gained support by the fact that no mention was made of the Duchess of Windsor's movements on Oct. 6 and 7, two days immediately following a visit to the Paris exposition. The newspaper added that no confirmation of the report could be found but that no official denial had been issued from Buckingham Palace.

Jerusalem —{t}— British authorities, although hopeful of restoring quiet shortly to strife-torn Palestine, maintained close watch today and continued the curfew here and at Lydda. Sporadic attacks on Jews and Britons marked the weekend but stern British measures prevented any recurrence of widespread violence. A new solution to the conflict between the Holy Land's Arabs and Jews was suggested in a plan to convert Palestine, now ruled by Great Britain under a League of Nations mandate, into a British crown colony. An organization called the “Palestine Crown Colony Association,” which had been officially discouraged, applied to the Palestine attorney general's office for registration.

Bristol, Eng., Oct. 14.—(P)— Roger Babson, American economist, told the Congregational Union assembly today “if Britain needed any help to defend civilization America would always send men, money and goods.” Speaking as moderator general of the council of Congregational Churches of America, he said all American Congregationalists are 100 per cent behind President Roosevelt's Chicago address on peace.

SOUTH PARIS, Me., Oct. 18—(P)—Eighteen-year-old Paul Dwyer today faced police charges that he murdered an elderly South Paris physician and his wife and drove an automobile through New England, New York and New Jersey with their bodies in the car. In nearby Norway municipal court Dwyer was scheduled to be arraigned for slaying Dr. James G. Littlefield, 67, last Wednesday during the doctor’s visit to his home. Regardless of the outcome, police said, the slim, sallow-faced youth would be called to answer a second murder charge tomorrow in Portland in the death of the doctor’s 65-year-old wife, Lydia. Police said Dwyer strangled Mrs. Littlefield when she “became suspicious” after he had driven her around since Wednesday night ostensibly seeking her husband. 1937-07-06.text: LONDON, July 6 (AP)—Lloyds’ reported today two British warships steamed to the assistance of the British steamer Gordonia today after she was stopped near Santander, Spain, by an Insurgent Spanish warship. The ship wirelessed she was stopped about 5 miles northeast of Cape Mayo, in the general area where blockading Insurgent naval forces earlier in the week seized a French freighter under charter to a Spanish leftist aid group. Later, however, the Gordonia reported: “Have two H. M. ships alongside now and awaiting instructions from United Kingdom.” Admiralty and foreign office officials went into hasty conference. It was assumed here the British men of war were holding the Insurgent warship alongside for the time being. MINDON, July 5—(4)—Britain’s cabinet met for an hour tonight to hear Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden's detailed report on the European non-intervention-in-Spain deadlock. It was believed the imperial defense committee met earlier in secret session devoted extensively to the Mediterranean—Britain’s vital communications link with her empire—which has been increasingly threatened by political events of the past few years. Eden told Commons today that all German warships, withdrawn from the European non-intervention patrol, had left the Mediterranean. His report to the cabinet was believed to have included a scheme for compromise by which Germany and Italy will return to the non-intervention committee. British hopes of an early compromise to restore All-European cooperation to isolate the Spanish war rose as reports from other capitals indicated greater readiness to make concessions. The pres

NEW YORK —(U.P)— Two huge flying boats — one British, the other American—landed on opposite sides of the North Atlantic today, completing “without incident” two survey flights preliminary to the proposed establishment of regular trans-Atlantic flying service. First to land, at Foynes, Ireland, was the Pan American Clipper III which reached its west-east destination 12 hours and 31 minutes after leaving Botwood, Newfoundland on the 1,994-mile flight. Less than an hour later, Imperial Airways’ four-engined flying boat, the Caledonia, landed at Botwood. It made the east-west crossing from Foynes in 15 hours and 10 minutes. Pan American Airways reported that the flights, which were over the often stormy Great Circle Route, were made “without incident.” The Clipper averaged approximately 155 miles an hour. The Caledonia flew at about 135 miles an hour. Both ships carried a full complement of

FOYNES, Ireland, July 8.—(AP)—The Imperial Airways flying boat, Caledonia, was poised at the mouth of the River Shannon today for a pioneering 1,800-mile commercial survey flight across the Atlantic. Given favorable weather, the ship was scheduled to leave Western Ireland at 7 p.m. (1 p.m. EST) and head out over the Atlantic toward Botwood, Newfoundland, on the proposed transatlantic commercial air route. Almost simultaneously the Pan-American Clipper III was to shoot down the runways at Botwood airport and point her nose eastward across the ocean. It was possible the two huge flying boats, cooperating in the commercial survey, might sight one another passing somewhere in mid-ocean. West-to-east headwinds were to be against the Caledonia, and it was estimated the flight to Newfoundland would require about 16 hours. ———«- Concluded On Page 2)
LYMPNE AIRDROME Eng () Col Charles A Lindbergh landed here Tuesday afternoon from France after four days of conferences on St Gildas island with the scientist Dr Alexis Car.

CARNOUSTIE, Scotland, July 6—(AP)—Carving out his second straight 69, Horton Smith of Chicago today took the lead in the 36-hole qualifying test for the British open golf championship with a total score of 138, four strokes under par. After setting a course record by clipping two strokes off Carnoustie's par yesterday, Smith carved as many off standard figures for the adjoining Burnside course in his second round. His qualifying score was three strokes better than that of Gene Sarazen, veteran internationalist who tacked a par 71 for Carnoustie to his initial 70. Americans also held down the next two places, Byron Nelson and Sam Snead, both making their bows in this competition, being bracketed at 142. Another shot back, at 143, came Alastair McLeod, tall Scottish amateur, with rounds of 73-70. Three Americans were grouped at 144, trick shot artist Joe Kirkwood, with 77-67; Ed Dudley of

London,-(A’)- Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden indicated to the House of Commons today a possible compromise in Europe's Spanish neutrality deadlock, saying the British will consider “any other proposals which are just and fair.” The deadlock finds Britain and France on one side and Germany and Italy on the other, unable to agree on methods for continuing future attempts to isolate Spain's year-old civil war. The newest international repercussion of that conflict today found British warships standing alongside a British freighter, near ‘Santander, Spain, to protect her from capture by a Spanish insurgent blockade ship. Eden, speaking to the House, said a full session of the 27-member nonintervention committee was to be held Friday and that this should allow “a little time for reflection on the serious issues involved.” This was taken to mean that Germany and Italy might “reflect” with a vi

Dublin, Irish Free State, (4)— County Limerick sprang a last-minute election surprise early today and pushed President Eamon de Valera’s slim government majority in the Dail to four. The government, with eight seats still to be tabulated, holds 67, the Cosgrove opposition, 44, Labor, 11, and Independents 8. The latest count on the proposed new constitution, which would sever the free state's last links with the British crown, was 514,080 for and 404,661 against.

1937-07-10.text: Quebec, July 10, 10, hep gas Delano Roosevelt, Jr. and his bride, the former Ethel du Pont, embarked on the Liner Empress of Britain this afternoon for a honeymoon in Europe, They arrived here last night from Campobello Island, N. B.

London, July 9 (#) France, weary of prolonged bickering over Europe's efforts to isolate the Spanish War, today intimated to other powers that unless they can agree on some formula "beginning next week" she may throw open her Spanish border to passage of arms and men. The French stand, presented by ambassador Charles Corbin in two meetings of the full 27-nations non-intervention committee, confronted that group with a new problem but apparently did little to break its deadlock. France favors the Spanish government and her threatened action would aid its cause. The negotiators turned to Britain, in her familiar role of conciliator, to urge that she put forward a solution of their dilemma. Thereon rested continued hopes that the opposed Anglo-French and Italo-German stands could be reconciled. Corbin was understood to have warned that France will end the system of international frontier su

LONDON, July 10, ().—William Frank James of Fulham, South London, used to have a wife and a racing greyhound. Today he has a racing greyhound. Mrs. James told a magistrate her husband gambled and spent considerable time at dog tracks. "If he gave up his dog it might keep him away from racing," she sobbed. The magistrate gave James a fortnight to weigh his choice between his wife and the dog. Yesterday he announced he would stick to the dog. A separation order was granted and James was told to pay his wife six dollars a week.

Jerusalem, July 9.—(AP)—Both Jews and Arabs, although disagreeing among themselves, plunged tonight into the work of organizing opposition to Great Britain's plan to partition Palestine. The Jewish labor party met to try to form a united front against the report of the British royal commission proposing division of the Holy Land into a Jewish state, an Arab state, and a British mandated territory.

London, July 9.——-Great Britain was intrusted with finding a quick solution of the present deadlock over the Spanish non-intervention scheme tonight after France had threatened to suspend frontier patrols Monday along the Pyrenees. France threatened thus to open the Spanish border to arms traffic on Monday unless the non-intervention equilibrium was restored. An afternoon session of the non-intervention committee ended with the participating nations still deadlocked and without any useful suggestion for compromise being advanced. Britain, whose proposal that she and France take over the entire international naval patrol around Spain was turned down by Germany and Italy, had looked to those nations for new proposals on how a non-intervention program could be carried out effectively. Opening of the French frontier along the Pyrenees would clear the way for the Spanish government to obtain

JERUSALEM, July 9 —(U.P)-- The Arab high committee tonight appealed to kings, princes and emirs of the Moslem world to save Palestine from the ‘“iniquities’’ of the British plan to divide the Holy Land into sovereign Jewish and Arab states. The plea was broadcast on the Moslem Sabbath as steel-helmeted and heavily armed police patrolled the ancient streets of Jerusalem, Jaffa and Haifa to prevent further disorders between Jews and Arabs. At scattered posts more than 8,000 British troops were in readiness for trouble.

By JOSEPH W. GRIGG, JK. (United Press Staff Correspondent) LONDON—The dim hope for continuance of the policy of non-intervention in the Spanish civil war rested today in Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden and Lord Plymouth, the Non-Intervention Committee's chairman. A meeting of the committee yesterday—two sessions—served only to show how widely divergent were the views of Germany and Italy on one hand and Britain and France on the other. Plymouth, as chairman of the committee, and Eden, as his superior, were delegated to find a compromise solution. France threatened plainly that unless the solution was found quickly and proved satisfactory to her she would reopen her Spanish frontier, this permitting an unlimited flow of smuggled munitions and men to the loyalists. 1937-08-14.text: London, Aug. 14 —(P)—‘Bulldog Drummond’ is dead. Lieutenant Colonel Cyril McNeile, creator of the well-known detective character, died today at his home in Pulborough, Sussex. He was 49 years old.

Newcastle, England, Aug. 12 (Fy. Lord Runciman, 80, father of the president of the British Board of Trade, died here today. For years Lord Runciman had been a foremost figure in British shipping and owner of a fleet of liners.

Edmonton, Alta., Aug. 14 (UP)— Province police here said today a plane carrying three persons was missing in northern British Columbia near Dawson. The plane left here Friday for Dawson, stopped at Pouce Coupe, then started for Fort Nelson in the extreme northeast corner of British Columbia.

BOSTON, Aug. 13 (PI)--A coalition of mythical foreign powers, taking advantage Friday night of the American navy in Pacific waters, menaced New England's vast industrial centers and heavily populated area. To meet the pending invasion, the entire American First Army was ordered into action from Maine to Virginia. That, briefly, was the outline made public by army headquarters of a command post exercise designed to determine the effectiveness of the nation’s defense measures. The First Army comprises 176,180 troops, regulars and national guardsmen, in the 12 eastern states. Major General Fox Conner, commanding general of the First Army, ordered 147 officers of various ranks to report immediately to Fort Devens, where, in 1917 and 1918, two full war divisions were trained. These officers will act as umpires in the vast war game that will have ramifications in all sections of the northern A

(1. N.S. Staff Correspondent) Shanghai, Aug. 14— Flaming death from storm-wracked skies snuffed out the lives of four Americans, and hundreds of other civilians today, as Japanese and Chinese aerial, naval and land forces turned the teeming water-front metropolis into a bloody battlefield. Huge incendiary bombs dropped from Chinese airplanes and carried far out of range by winds of a typhoon that roared in from the China Sea wrought death and destruction. So grave had the situation become by evening that all guests were evacuated from the Palace and the Cathay Hotel in the International Settlement. In the indescribable horror and confusion, an adequate check of the foreign casualties was impossible. But it appeared definitely that Dr. Frank Rawlinson, one of the leading American missionaries in Shanghai, and his daughter, were among those killed.

SHANGHAI (AP). At least three prominent American residents of Shanghai were killed and two other Americans wounded in Chinese-Japanese aerial warfare that hurled death into crowded parts of the international settlement. Dr. Frank J. Rawlinson, one of the outstanding missionaries in China, and H. S. Honisberg, wealthy motorcar dealer, met death as Chinese bombing planes, supposedly aiming at Chinese concentrations, dumped their missiles into crowded downtown areas killing hundreds.

SHANGHAI, Aug. 14—(Saturday)—()—Three Chinese warplanes bombed the Japanese cruiser Izumo today at the northern end of Shanghai's famous bund but apparently missed their mark by the narrowest margin. The attackers, appearing over the cruiser with lightning suddenness, dived and loosed one bomb each, the explosions reverberating through the city and engulfing the vessel, flagship of the Japanese fleet here, in a wall of smoke. As the smoke lifted, the Izumo appeared to be undamaged but the docks nearby were splintered.

HENDAYE, France, Aug. 14.— Government troops thrust forward a mile in a surprise attack on the Brunette front outside of Madrid, as insurgents hammered out against the long Teruel Spearhead. One hundred miles east of Madrid opponents concentrated battle efforts on separate Central Spanish fronts. Each charged up victories in the shell-torn zone. Government sources declared their troops had forced their way into entrenchments near Brunette.

1937-06-14.text: DARLINGTON, Eng., (AP).—The Rev. R. Anderson Jardine, who stirred up a Church of England storm when he married the Duke and Duchess of Windsor, gave up his post today as Vicar of St. Paul's church. In announcing his resignation last night, the “poor man’s parson” asserted recent events—presumably the wedding in which he said he had been “just a simple channel for God’s will”—had nothing to do with his decision. (At Noetsch, Austria, associates of the duke and duchess said they were surprised to hear of the resignation). Although an official of the parish recalled that the vicar indicated at the last annual parochial meeting he might resign, the announcement came as a surprise to his congregation and even to his wife.

Waupaca, Wis., June 14—(®)—The blood heirs and the adopted heirs of the late William Hatton, millionaire New London lumberman, reached an agreement today settling the dispute over administration of the estate. Hatton died intestate. Under terms of the settlement approved by Judge A. M. Scheller in Waupaca county court, the blood heirs of Hatton are to receive one-third of the estimated one and one-half million dollar estate, and the adopted heirs to divide the remaining two-thirds.

Madrid, June 14,—(?)-—Government commanders sent troops and aircraft into action on long-quiet fronts today to relieve insurgent pressure on besieged Bilbao. While Generalissimo Francisco Franco maintained his chief drive against the Basque capital, the Madrid-Valencia forces rushed into action above Cordoba, in southern Spain, and along the Aragon front to the northeast. Government commanders plainly hoped these thrusts at the backdoors of insurgent territory would force withdrawal of some of the attacking power from the Bilbao front. In addition to Bilbao, two other of Spain's chief cities were under siege. At Madrid and Oviedo, besieging forces were actually within the outer limits of the cities at strategic points.

Bilbao, Spain, June 13.—Basque leaders admitted tonight the first line of the "iron ring" defending Bilbao had been broken by the insurgent drive, the most vicious offensive loosed by either side in the civil war. They declared the situation of the capital was dangerous, but not desperate. Several British and French destroyers were reported lying in Bilbao’s port near the mouth of the Nervion river, ready to evacuate President Jose Antonio Aguirre and other members of the government if necessary. Planes Active From 50 to 80 insurgent airplanes, without opposition in the air, were constantly flying over the Basque positions, machine gunning and bombing trenches and troop concentrations. General Gamir Uribarri, commander-in-chief of the defense, said the worst insurgent attacks against Madrid were tame compared to the pounding Bilbao has received. Rome, June 14.—Condition of Pope Pius has taken a turn for the worse, it was learned today. His physician, Dr. Milani, now spends every night at Castel Gandolfo ready to administer restoratives if necessary.

The Basque Loyalist defense seemed shattered and the Nationalists advanced all along the line east of the city. Their superiority in men, organization and spirit apparently was overwhelming and the final attack seemed delayed only because of Gen. Fidel Davila’s insistence that all of the dominant hills outside the city be occupied and consolidated first. MOSCOW, June 14—(4)—James H. R. Cromwell, free after his arrest for taking pictures of proscribed areas of the grim Kremlin walls, planned to leave today with his wife, the former Doris Duke, for Leningrad. Cromwell was detained in the National Hotel for an hour and a half yesterday for attempting to take pictures in front of the hotel which adjoins the American embassy. The Kremlin walls form the background for both buildings. He said he was photographing the hotel when a uniformed officer placed him under arrest. He was taken into the hotel where he was held until he made clear he had no illegal purpose in making the pictures. Cromwell was allowed to leave the hotel after his films were confiscated. The co-author of “In Defense of Capitalism” was told that all pictures not proscribed would be returned. Cromwell and his wife, who had a cold since their arrival here Thursday, will go dir

OTTAWA, Ont. (UP) — Canadian authorities are mobilizing forces for a drive against the saw fly, scourge of Canadian spruce forests. The saw fly causes millions of dollars damage in Eastern Canadian forests every year.

1937-01-19.text: London, Jan. 18.— (#) — The prospect that Europe yet would succeed in conquering the Spanish civil war's threat to general European peace appeared slightly improved tonight, neutral observers declared. In London, where a subcommittee of the international neutrality group met in an effort to include a ban on foreign volunteers in the general nonintervention agreement, informed sources expressed belief Portugal would consent to a separate accord to block enlistment of foreigners. Germany and Italy already had said they favored elimination of all non-Spaniards from participation in the civil struggle. Portuguese, German and Italian soldiers have been fighting with the Spanish fascists and soldiers from Russia, France and other countries have joined the Spanish socialists.

London, Jan. 19—Spanish Socialists and the insurgent governments rejected today the non-intervention committee’s proposal to control munition shipments to both sides in the Spanish civil war. The action by the Burgos and Valencia governments met a gloomy response in British circles where it was stated “everything is now up to Italy and Germany depending on whether they will shut off the flow of volunteers.” Fascist General Franco’s rejection was flat and accompanied by complaint that “thousands of volunteers” were crossing the French frontier to fight for the Socialist government. The Valencia reply, imposing numerous conditions to the suggested plan, also complained of enlistments of foreigners in the insurgent legion. Gen. Franco not only refused to accept these specific suggestions, but also sidestepped the question of whether he would accept the principle of international control to

LONDON, Jan. 19 ()—Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden told the House of Commons tonight the danger of a continental war growing out of the Spanish conflict had been definitely diminished. He warned, however, that the risk was not entirely removed. The Foreign Secretary spoke on the opening day of the new session of Parliament. A short time before his speech, he told an inquiring member that Britain intends to ban her foreign volunteers from Spain "by enforcing the existing law of the land." Of foreign powers mixing in Spain, Eden added: "Intervention in Spain is not only bad for humanity; it is bad politics." He sounded the most optimistic note of any responsible British spokesman since the Spanish war became the greatest menace to Europe's peace.

LONDON, Jan. 19 (-.- Laborites in the House of Commons, criticizing as “Episcopal spleen” the Archbishop of Canterbury’s recent radio attack on former King Edward's friends, threw the chamber into an uproar today. The heated debate was started by Ernest Thurtle, Shoreditch laborite, who asked Major G. C. Tyson, postmaster general, if the Archbishop's speech was submitted to British Broadcasting Corporation officials for approval before delivery. “No, sir,” answered Major Tryon emphatically. Speaker Fitzroy interrupted Thurtle's statement about the Archbishop's “Episcopal spleen” by declaring the member was expressing his own opinions. “May I ask if the postmaster general (spokesman for the BBC in Commons) doesn’t think the Archbishop's criticism might have been expressed while the late king was on the throne?

NANKING, China, Jan. 19 — (Tuesday) — (AP) — The United States embassy today was advised 75 foreigners had arrived in Tungkwan, Shensi province, from Siafu, where their safety had been thought endangered. Three British subjects and five Russians were the only foreigners remaining in Siafu, capital of Shensi province, according to the advices the embassy received from Loyang. Americans were not specifically mentioned, but it was assumed here that the entire group, understood to total 21, was among those arriving in Tungkwan.

PARIS, Jan. 18.—(U.9)—Failure of the British plan to stem the flow of foreign volunteers to Spain appeared imminent tonight when France refused to consider Italo-German reservations affecting "indirect intervention" in the civil war. French officials learned that the German and Italian replies to the British plan, which probably will be sent to London this week, would be identical in demanding that the proposal be extended to include, not only the problem of recruits, but indirect financial and moral aid to either Spanish faction. Demands Unacceptable, Such demands could not be accepted, it was pointed out, because of the difficulty in applying them under a democratic form of government. As a result, officials said, the entire scheme faced abandonment. LONDON, Jan. 19.—(UP)—The House of Commons, convening after the Christmas recess, was thrown into an uproar today when the speaker intervened to protect the Archbishop of Canterbury from the criticisms of Ernest Thurtle and James Maxton, laborites. The two members attacked the archbishop for his radio broadcast after the abdication of King Edward VIII, in which he denounced the social group which Edward had around him.

INNSBRUCK, Austria, Jan. 19. — A motorcycle policeman’s quick action was credited with saving Queen Wilhelmina of the Netherlands today from a plunge down a 650-foot Alpine precipice. The heavy automobile in which the queen was riding with a lady of her court skidded on the old Roman road at Matrie, south of Innsbruck. One wheel of the machine slid off the driveway at a point where there was almost sheer drop of 650 feet to the frozen river below. The automobile was traveling as slowly as possible because of the ice-covered road and Policeman Heinrich Neuberger, who had been following closely on his motorcycle, threw his weight against the slipping car until help arrived. The queen, after expressing her gratitude, returned to Innsbruck by a safer route.

1937-02-22.text: Reports of government successes came from Valencia and Madrid today as Europe's nations laid final plans for placing an embargo on the war-torn peninsula at midnight tonight. Portugal, not entirely favorable to the blockade plans, was expected to fall in line over the weekend, allowing British inspectors to see that she does not send armaments to her neighbors. The nations took official individual steps to punish volunteers for the war as hundreds of last minute battle-minded men rushed toward the Franco-Spanish border—trying to beat the midnight deadline. The final rush through Perpignan, France, was expected to total 500—some 11,000 foreign volunteers were authoritatively estimated to have passed through the city since the war started. Government troops changing their tactics reported gains northwest of Madrid. Insurgents, Madrid said, were chased from coveted Aravaca heights, bringing

LONDON, Feb. 22. 1a" - Prices leaped spectacularly on the London metal exchange today as the nations of Europe began to scramble in a big way for metals used in the manufacture of war materials. Germany was prominent among the buyers. The price of tin rose $30 a ton to approximately $1,245 a ton, the highest since 1928 and a rise of about $107 a ton since Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, announced plans for the loan to finance Britain's huge armament program just eight business days ago. Feverish buying by both speculative interest and industries, helped by a brisk demand from the United States, where markets were closed, caused copper to jump as much as $30 a ton during the day to $349 a ton. Traders and brokers, shouting and perspiring in their efforts to execute the seemingly unending stream of orders, envisaged the return of inflated world war prices when copper touc

| VIENNA, (AP). —Sir Walter Monckton, attorney general for the Duchy of Cornwall, left Vienna today in the Duke of Windsor’s airplane, presumably for London. He carried a briefcase in which, it was reported, were documents relating to royal financial provisions for the former King of England,

LONDON, Feb. 22—(AP)—Ellen Wilkinson, fiery little laborite, created a brief scene in the House of Commons today by demanding: “Can we have some guarantee that we shall not be insulted by the presence of General Goering as Germany's representative at the coronation?”

ADDIS ABABA, Feb. 22 (4—-All Ethiopians connected with the attempted assassination of Viceroy Rodolfo Graziani will be shot by an Italian firing squad on direct orders from Premier Mussolini, colonial officers announced today. A second series of instructions from Il Duce decreed death for all native chieftains continuing opposition to the Italian government, they declared. Reprisals for the wounding of Viceroy Graziani and several oth-

The Spanish war raged today from Oviedo, near the Bay of Biscay, where the government launched an offensive, to Aragon, where the insurgents started driving a wedge to the Mediterranean between Valencia and Barcelona. The insurgents, ramming fiercely up the Jarama River Valley in the heaviest fighting in recent months, reported seizure of four miles of Madrid's vital Valencia Highway. They are endeavoring to close the only remaining trunk of the highway exit.

Tokyo, Feb. 22. 22—UP—The Japanese government, reported ready to mend its strained relations with China, turned its attention to Russian armament in Siberia today and frankly told parliament that was the reason it demanded the empire’s army be Shortly after an official government spokesman had indicated a distinct modification of policy toward China, General Gen Sugiyama, minister of war, told the House of Representatives a tremendous increase in the Soviet army in Asia necessitated the Japanese army’s replenishment program. The Japanese forces, the war minister declared, were decidedly inferior to the Soviet’s far eastern army, which he said now totalled 15 divisions. He outlined the defense expansion program under four headings. 1. Replenishment of the air force and air defense equipment and personnel. 2. Strengthening of the Japanese army units in the protectorate state of Manchoukuo

MADRID (UP) Loyalist troops loosed a general offensive Monday on the front south of Madrid and official dispatches reported them advancing all along the line. It was asserted that loyalist storm troops captured La Maranosa, 15 miles south of the capital, at 11 a.m., and that troops were advancing all along a battle line that ran southeastward from the capital to the Arganda sector, 16 miles southeast of Madrid, along the vitally important Valencia road. The loyalist attack was started at dawn, upon personal orders of Gen. Jose Miaja, commander in chief. The loyalist battle line extended altogether over a twisted 37½ mile front. Heavy machine gun fire from new weapons taken into the rebel trenches for a decisive battle raked the loyalist shock troops, but despite the fire, dispatches from the front said, loyalists broke through at several points and either captured machine gun nests or fo

1937-02-16.text: London, — (P) — The international "hands off Spain committee," with only Portugal dissenting, approved a plan today to dam the flow of foreign volunteers and munitions into Spain by Saturday midnight. As 26 members of the neutrality group agreed to the control plan. A rush of military recruits over the Spanish border was apparently originating in France and Italy, to meet the deadline. An estimated 1,000 Frenchmen were said to have gone to the Spanish civil war since the first of the month with sympathizers of the Valencia government still pouring across the frontier. Rome Sends Aid Informed sources in Rome intimated there would be no let up in the aid to General Francisco Franco's insurgents until the ban becomes effective. The neutrality proposals were: 1. Each nation to ban voluntary aid to either Spanish faction by February 20. 2. The committee, also by February 20, to complete a pla

The international "hands off Spain" committee was called into session today to confirm three recommendations to insulate the rest of Europe from the Spanish civil war. Approached by a sub-committee, with only Portugal dissenting and Germany and Italy in agreement with France, Great Britain and Russia, the proposals were: 1. Each nation to ban voluntary aid to either Spanish faction by February 20. 2. The committee, also by February 20, to complete a plan to stop shipment of men and guns to Spain. 3. An agreement to put the supervisory plan into operation by March 6. Portugal Is Ignored Portugal’s opposition to establishment of an international patrol on her frontiers was ignored by the other powers, which, while hopeful of ultimate Portuguese cooperation, determined to police Portuguese entrances to Spain by a naval blockade. In effect, the plan embodies two main points: 1. Establishment

LONDON, (UP).—The main international intervention committee today provisionally decided that the ban against "volunteers" going to Spain's civil war should be made effective at midnight Saturday. The delegates agreed also that the committee’s scheme for supervising non-interference on land and sea should be operative from March 6. The non-intervention committee decided to communicate their action and these two dates to the 18 governments not represented on its subcommittee for final approval. The nine governments of the delegates on the sub-committee endorsed Monday these proposals to "put teeth" in the long delayed effectiveness of non-intervention in Spain. LONDON, (UP).—Delegates of 2 European powers began today a final effort to effect neutrality in the Spanish civil war and leave the nationalist and loyalist combatants to fight it out alone. They assembled at the foreign office for

By the Associated Press LONDON — Representatives of Europe's major powers last night set two deadlines in their drives to isolate the Spanish civil war in Spain. Sitting as a sub-committee of the international "hands-off-Spain" committee, they decided: 1. The ban on the flow of foreign volunteers to Spain must be made effective at midnight Saturday, Feb. 20; 2. Plans for complete isolation of the war, including the stationing of neutral observers and a naval blockade, must be perfected by the same time and must be brought into operation by midnight, March 6. The full non-intervention committee was called to meet at 2:30 p.m. today to ratify the decisions. The sub-committee, composed of representatives of Great Britain, France, Italy, Germany, Russia and Portugal, acted in face of Portugal’s continued refusal to cooperate in the complete control plan. Portugal's delegate said he awaited a
ALFRETON, Nottinghamshire, Eng., Feb. 16—Seven miners were killed and four injured, it was learned today, in an explosion last night at the Waterloo seam of the South Normanton Colliery.

London, Feb. 16—(4)—One hundred and fifty servants, not to mention a host of court officials, secretaries and ladies and gentlemen-in-waiting, bustled about Buckingham Palace today to make King George VI, Queen Elizabeth and their two daughters feel at home. The family moved into the vast palace yesterday from their comparatively modest quarters at 145 Piccadilly. Only a handful of spectators witnessed the change.

London, Feb. 15. — (®) — Europe’s major powers lined up tonight in an agreement to try to keep foreign volunteers from entering strife-torn Spain after March 6. They acted in the face of Portugal’s continued refusal to cooperate. Informed persons said if Portugal maintained that stand, it was likely she would be subjected to a naval blockade to prevent foreigners entering Spain through her territory. Agreed Representatives of Great Britain, France, Italy, Germany and Russia—which with Portugal form a sub-committee of international “hands-off-Spain” group—agreed at a meeting that all the 27 countries on the committee must complete plans for controlling the influx of foreign fighters by midnight Saturday, Feb. 20. The complete control program to isolate the civil war, they agreed, must become effective by March 6.
