London—(U.P.)—Great Britain has exacted from Spanish nationalist authorities an apology for an airplane attack on a British destroyer and a promise to examine marks of all craft along the Spanish east coast before attacking in the future, it was announced today. The apology and the promise were made under the guns of the cruiser Shropshire and the destroyer Garland, dispatched at full speed to Majorca island in the Balearics yesterday. From the military governor of the island, the chief nationalist authority in the Balearics, the Shropshire's captain obtained the apology. From the part admiral and commander of the island air force, the captain exacted a pledge that nationalist airplanes would be instructed in future to exercise the greatest care in examining identity marks of all craft in waters between Valencia and Alicante, on the east coast, before taking hostile action against them.

London, April 8—(UP)—Renewed reports of difficulties confronting the Spanish Nationalists spread through Europe today as Fascist Italy again refused to withdraw its own volunteers in the civil war. A dispatch to the Daily Herald (pro-Loyalist organ of the labor party) from Madrid quoted reports that Gen. Francisco Franco had given up hope of capturing Madrid and intended to withdraw his “battered” forces from south of Madrid, including the vicinity of the Madrid-Valencia highway. The dispatch said that the reports of impending Nationalist withdrawal were based on something more definite than optimistic rumors. Information received from behind the Nationalist lines regarding movements of reinforcements and a gradual slowing up of munition supplies to the front were bases for the reports, it was asserted. A Briton arriving at Gibraltar from Seville alleged that he saw 256 Italian soldiers

London, April 7—a—The British destroyer Garland sped to the Spanish insurgent island of Mallorca tonight to present an imperial demand for explanation of aerial attacks against the destroyer Gallant. There were indications that the government later would make strong representations to Gen. Francisco Franco at his Salamanca headquarters, for the Gallant incident added to numerous other incidents with insurgents at sea and to British fears that other European nations may yet be dragged into the Spanish civil war. Insurgent warplanes which, apparently came from Mallorca dropped 5 bombs alongside the Garland yesterday in two attacks off the eastern coast of Spain. They were timely driven away by anti-aircraft fire. The Spanish Valencia regime added to tension here with a new charge that German warships were (Continued on Page 16—Col. 6)

(Copyright, 1987, by United Press) LONDON, April 7. (UP)— International tension growing out of Spain’s civil war appeared dangerously near the breaking point tonight as reports of neutrality violations poured in from the capitals of Europe. Great Britain, angered by two bombing attacks on one of her destroyers in the Mediterranean by British rebel planes, heard bitter charges and counter-charges of open intervention in the war. The newest developments imperiling the peace of Europe were: 1——Dispatch of the British destroyer Garland to the rebel-held Balearic islands to protest direct to insurgent authorities against the attacks on H.M.S. Gallant. 2——Strong but cautious British suspicions that the planes which dropped 18 bombs near the Gallant may have been Italian aircraft from the rebel air base at Majorca, 3——Charges by the Spanish loyalist government at Valencia that the German warshi

Munich -- (P) — Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh, temporarily dropping their self-imposed seclusion, took a short sight-seeing trip thru Munich Thursday with an American friend. Except for the brief tour, the Lindberghs stayed in their hotel room. Special guards were posted outside to assure the fliers' privacy. The Lindberghs landed at Munich Tuesday from Zagreb, Yugoslavia. Their arrival was kept secret until late Wednesday, when a chance remark by an airport attendant disclosed their presence.

1937-12-29.text: TOKYO, 17i—Foreign Minister Koki Hirota delivered to British Ambassador Sir Robert Leslie Craigie Japan's reply to a protest against the Japanese attack on the British gunboat Ladybird. The text of the note was not made public, but the military section of imperial headquarters issued a statement saying the attack was a “mistake” and expressing regrets. One sailor was killed in the attack.

TOKYO, Dec. 29. —(#)— The British embassy today informed the Japanese foreign office that it could not accept the Japanese military version of attacks on the British gunboats Ladybird and Bee. The military section of Imperial headquarters yesterday issued a statement explaining that the attacks were a “mistake” and expressing regrets. One British sailor was killed in the incident, which occurred on the Yangtze River on the same day the United States gunboat Panay was bombed.

SHANGHAI -— (UR) — Chinese troops have recaptured 16 counties in Shansi Province as the result of removal of Japanese troops for a drive on Tsingtao, Chinese sources said today. British missionaries at Taian, in Shantung Province, where the Japanese are driving for Tsingtao, reported in telegrams to their headquarters here that the Japanese in a Christmas Day airplane raid on the city damaged the British and German missions and caused scores of casualties. An additional 26 Americans were expected to leave Tsingtao today in commercial ships, leaving 159 Americans there and 13 in the country near there. Consular authorities understood that there were 11 Americans in the Tsinan area. Nothing was known of their fate.

DUBLIN, Dec. 29.—(7)—The 15-year-old Irish Free State passed officially into history today and its 26 counties of old Ireland became “Éire.” A new constitution took effect, giving the former free state a new government and a new name—Éire in Gaelic and Ireland in English. Eamon de Valera, its sponsor, has declared the new document marks an important milestone in Dublin’s political march away from London. Religious and military ceremonies throughout the country commemorated the first “Constitution Day.” De Valera was to broadcast to America tonight. Republicans planned to hold protest meetings in the center of Dublin, but no special precautions, apparently, had been taken to prevent possible disorders. Both official London and official (Concluded on Page 3)

Dublin, Dec. 28. (AP)—A new era in Irish history will be ushered in tomorrow when a new constitution becomes effective. The old name of the Irish Free State vanishes in favor of “Éire,” or Ireland, and Eamon de Valera takes his first state ride as “Taoiseach,” or prime minister. The presidency relinquished by de Valera will be filled June 29, 1938, the government's nominee probably being Vice-President Sean O'Kelly. Meanwhile, a three-man commission will administer the president’s duties.

JERUSALEM, Dec. 29—(7) Prospects of a radio propaganda war between the Italians and the British delighted Arabs today, leading them to believe they would receive thousands of free radio sets from London and Rome. The Italian government already has distributed free medium-wave sets among Arabs so that they might pick up regular government broadcasts of news and propaganda to Palestine and the Near East from a station at Bari in Southern Italy. British authorities were understood to be ready to flood the Holy Land with short-wave sets, which would not be able to get Bari, but could be turned in on a British station at Daventry, England.

DUBLIN.--(UP)--A black flag flew over the headquarters of Sinn Fein today as the new Irish Free State constitution came into effect—a constitution which, though it is called only 'near republican', severs most of the remaining ties with Great Britain and brings the country close to the status of an independent republic. Neither left wing elements, as represented by Sinn Fein, nor conservatives, seemed to think much of the constitution, but officially it was a day of rejoicing. There were special church services and there were ceremonies at garrison centers. It was called 'Constitution Day'.

DUBLIN, Dec. 28 (VP)—A new government and a new name will go into effect Wednesday for the Irish Free State. Under the new constitution to take force then, the country will be known as Éire (pronounced airy) in Gaelic and Ireland in English. There will be a two-chambered legislature, a prime minister and a president. Becomes Minister With the inauguration of the new instrument, Eamon de Valera, New York-born government leader, will cease to be president and will become taoiseach, or prime minister. A 21-gun salute will herald the beginning of operation of the constitution. De Valera and other officials will attend a votive mass at the cathedral and parades and religious services will be held throughout the land. Bonfires Wednesday there will be bonfires and a speech by De Valera at 7:45 p.m. (2:45 p.m. E.S.T.) will be broadcast. It will be relayed to the United States. On the eve of the

1937-06-15.text: LONDON, June 14.—()—Sir James Barrie, famous playwright and teller of Scottish stories, was gravely ill today in a nursing home. The 77-year-old creator of Peter Pan was disclosed to have been in ill health for some time, and last Friday was ordered taken to the nursing home. Among the plays which made Sir James famous are The Little Minister, The Admirable Crichton, Peter Pan, What Every Woman Knows, and Dear Brutus.

Darlington, England (7#)—The Rev. R. Anderson Jardine who performed the Duke of Windsor’s religious wedding ceremony in spite of the opposition of his bishops announced today, following his resignation, he hoped to lecture for two months in the United States, TO TELL WHY He described his intended trip as a combined holiday and lecture tour presumably he will talk about why he performed the ceremony at Monts. He hopes to leave for America shortly. Mr. Jardine continued to insist his resignation as Vicar of St. Paul's at Darlington had nothing to do with his performing of the wedding ceremony. NO COMMENT The bishop of Durham today announced without comment that he had received the resignation which the “poor man’s parson” announced to his congregation last night.

SAINT-JEAN-DE-LUZ, France, June 15 (CP) -- A landing party of British sailors rescued the British consul, R. C. Stevenson from Bilbao under a hail of insurgent fire today. The sailors, with bullets whistling all about them, landed from a warship outside the besieged Basque capital, escorted the consul aboard and brought him to this French port.

PARIS, June 14 (#)—Paul Bastid, French minister of commerce, warned Great Britain and the United States today that France might be forced to abandon the tri-partite monetary agreement unless they meet France in lowering tariff barriers. His speech was made at the opening session of the International Exchange Congress and followed the raising of the Bank of France's discount rate to 6 per cent. At the same time, Premier Leon Blum called a special session of his cabinet to find a way out of the financial tangle. Pleading for “simultaneous collective efforts” to revive world exchanges, Bastid said France had the “impression” her action in lowering tariffs and easing the import quota system last fall had been strictly unilateral. “The result has been a campaign in France for the return to protection and abandonment of liberal measures,” Bastid said. The Bank of France raised the discount rat

London, June 13.—(#)—The United States’ World War allies today prepared once more to give “regretful notice” they will default the installments due June 15 on the obligations they incurred in wartime two decades ago. The British government was expected to make the same negative reply it has made each six months since three years ago to Washington's reminder that another semi-annual installment is due on the $4,277,000,000 Britain borrowed, which, with accrued interest, has grown to $5,198,000,000. Only from Finland, a creation of the World War, could the United States expect payment. Twelve other war debtors already are in default to a grand total of $1,314,821,109, and $205,338,754 due Tuesday will swell that to $1,520,159,863. (Finland notified the State Department May 29 its debt installment of $163,143 would be paid on schedule.)

London, June 15—(UP)— Sir James M. Barrie, distinguished author and playwright, who is ill of bronchial pneumonia, “had a fair night and his progress was maintained,” a bulletin by his doctors said today. Lord Horder, physician in ordinary to the king, and Dr. Mackay Huey visited Barrie at 8 a.m. for 45 minutes.

Valera, president of the executive council, The lower chamber, or Dail, of the Parliament, approved the Constitution last night by a vote of 62 to 48 with Labor party men and followers of W. T. Cosgrave, De Valera's predecessor in office, opposing. Coincidently the Dail was dissolved. A new one will be elected July 1 coincident with the constitutional plebiscite, and the new one will meet July 21. Law on Dec. 29 If the Constitution is approved it will become law after 181 days from the date of the plebiscite, on Dec. 29. Opposing the Constitution bill, Cosgrave asserted that it was forced through by a party vote and that it would restrict freedom of the press. De Valera denied Continued on Page 1

HENDAYE, French - Spanish Nationalists authorities at Irun, near the front, asserted Tuesday that Nationalist troops had begun to move in on Bilbao proper. They moved in slowly, systematically occupying house by house, it was said. French and British consulate officials left Bilbao in destroyers. Liasques insisted that their defense position still was good, that they held important posts in the hills outside the city. Francisco Franco, insurgent generalissimo, was reported preparing to proclaim a constituted Nationalist government for all Spain as soon as his victory was consolidated. It was indicated that Franco might give himself a position roughly comparable to that of Adolf Hitler of Germany, with a similar order. Bilbao was cut off from the outside. All British ships had left.

1937-07-23.text: London, July 23.—(#)—A 25-year fight to liberalize Britain's divorce laws ended today with parliamentary enactment of a law whereby cruelty, desertion for three years and insanity for five years become grounds for divorce. Adultery hitherto was the only cause for divorce in Britain.

NEW YORK, July 22.—(AP)— A second radio message which appeared to confirm a report of a mystery airplane droning over the Atlantic towards Europe was received here today by Radiomarine Corporation. The American freighter Scanmail, which replayed the first message last night, reported the British steamship Coryton, bound from Pensacola, Fla., to Glasgow, Scotland, had sighted the plane’s lights. The Scanmail reported last night that a ship, which it supposed was the British freighter Ranee, had seen and heard the plane 500 miles east of Cape Race, Newfoundland. The Ranee, it was learned later, is in the West Indies. The Radiomarine station at Chatham, Mass., which intercepted the first message, relayed to New York today a second report from the Scanmail that the Coryton had sighted the lights of a plane bound east parallel with the ship at 7:04 p.m. (C.S.T.), the same hour at which the fi

| LONDON, July 22-(AP)--Opponents of the proposed partition of Palestine today drew encouragement from parliament’s decision that Britain must tread slowly. Enemies of the British royal commission’s plan for a “surgical operation” to remove the empire’s major difficulties in the Holy Land said parliament's vote early today to defer Britain’s definite commitment to the scheme increased hopes of revising or blocking it. The partition plan, embodied in a government white paper, proposing that Palestine be divided into a Jewish state, an Arab state and a British mandate, will go now to the League of Nations. This will give opportunity for further investigation and study of the scheme in London. The vote to defer action came after a heated debate in which Laborites attacked the partition. William G. A. Ormsby Gore, colonial secretary, called for outright approval of the royal commission’s rep

Baltimore, July 23..-(AP) - The Rev. R. Anderson Jardine, the “poor man’s parson,” who wed the Duke and Duchess of Windsor, believes Edward is the man to “steer the nations toward the star of peace.” With this glowing tribute to the former King of England, the Rev. Mr. Jardine ended a lecture in which he had promised to “rip the lid off” the abdication of Edward for the love of Mrs. Wallis Warfield. He said what really forced Edward to abdicate was an alliance between the archbishop of Canterbury, whom he called an “ecclesiastical cad,” and Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin, whom he described as “grandmotherly.”

London, - (4) ~ Another British flying boat will test north Atlantic commercial air lanes next week, Imperial Airways announced today that the Cambria, sister ship of the Caledonia which made the first survey flight, will take off from Foynes, Irish Free State, next Thursday, July 29, commanded by Capt. G. J. Powell.

BLAIR OVER GORE Bed sie ‘Bath, England, July 23.--(?%)—The ousted Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia was 46 Friday and observed the second of his birthdays in exile at this English resort with a quiet family party.

London, July 22.—(AP)—Five persons were killed tonight when a Royal Air Force bombing plane crashed in flames on a peak in Derbyshire after dropping flares as a distress signal. All the occupants were burned before a rescue party could clamber up the mountainside.

News dispatch: London, July 19—The United States was charged today by an official of the Church of England with “debasing England’s social standards.” The Very Rev. W. E. R. Morrow, provost of Chelmsford Cathedral, in a sermon, blamed American influence for the hotly contested bill to relax British divorce laws. “In every contact with the United States,” said the provost, “there has been a lowering of moral standards and a flippancy in which the noblest ideals of domestic life have been derided.” At first thought, this writer, once an Englishman, felt inclined to say, “Stuff and nonsense,” and pass on to other subjects. On second thought, however, the provost raises an interesting point which deserves some honest airing. It is unqualifiedly the most arrant nonsense to say that Britain’s moral standards are imperiled by the United States for the most basic reason of all—there are more wom

1937-06-08.text: LONDON, June 8.—(P—Fears that blond “Didi” Battye may have been abducted were raised today after her fiancé disclosed he had received a note threatening to “remove” the missing society beauty. High officials of Scotland Yard took personal charge of the far-flung search and issued instructions to watch every port and airfield in the country. The fiancé, Michael Asquith, son of the Hon. Herbert and Lady Cynthia Asquith, was expected to interrupt his final examination for an Oxford degree to come to London and confer with Yard officials. Threats Numerous The message was received by young Asquith, whose father is heir presumptive to the Earl of Oxford and Asquith, before the disappearance of the former photographers’ model June 1 from the London home of her childhood friend, Viscountess Long. The letter mysteriously warned Asquith: “Unless you take better care of Miss Battye she will be remo

LONDON, June 8 — (UP) — Great Britain, France, Germany and Italy have reached agreement in principle on British proposals to revise the non-intervention plan in the Spanish civil war, it was said authoritatively today. The plan as agreed on in principle, it was said, is: 1. Extension of “safety zones” in which warships of the four powers on neutrality patrol in waters outside Spain might seek shelter for refueling and supplying, 2. Seeking of guarantees from the Spanish belligerents against molestation of patrol vessels. 3. Immediate consultation among the four powers regarding action to be taken if a patrol ship is attacked. It was understood that under the plan, warships would have the right to defend themselves in a legitimate manner against attack but there would be no right to take reprisals such as the German bombardment of Almeria without previous consultation. The plan is being d

Birmingham, England ()—A rift in the Church of England was seen today in the demand by the outspoken bishop of Birmingham for a reform of the divorce laws which caused the church’s opposition to the marriage of Edward of Windsor and twice divorced Wallis Warfield. Dr. Ernest William Barnes, bishop of the industrial diocese since 1924, coupled his support of reform in the nation’s divorce laws with a suggestion that communion be given by the church to divorced persons. The bishop’s address to the diocesan conference, of which he is president, brought into the open again the issue which led the Anglican church to refuse to bless the marriage, June 3, of abdicated Edward VIII and the woman for whom he gave up his throne.

LONDON, June 7—(P)—Britain hiked the price of gold 9.8 cents today to $34.72 an ounce to discourage shipment abroad, and the government assured investors that the monetary stabilization agreement with the United States and France would be continued. These two steps clarified the financial situation to such a degree that the ‘gold scare’ of the past two weeks appeared tonight to have disappeared. The new gold price had a two-fold purpose: 1. It narrowed the margin between the London and New York price of $35 an ounce, making shipment abroad less profitable. At today’s price, for the pound sterling, shippers stood to profit about five cents an ounce, compared with 14 cents on Saturday. There had been fear continued export of bullion would upset the British-United States stabilization set-up about $84,000,000 in gold was sold on the London market the past two weeks. 3. The higher London pri

DUBLIN, June 8. (P)—News Reels of the Duke of Windsor’s wedding, which will not be shown in England, will be exhibited in the Irish Free State, it was made known today. News reels of George VI's coronation, on the other hand, were virtually banned here.

Omaha, Neb., June 8.—(U.P.)—Efforts of a 21-year-old Cedar Rapids, Ia., girl to assume the blame for causing two traffic deaths here failed today when County Attorney James T. English ordered charges filed against the girl's sister, Mrs. R. E. Harrington, formerly of Cedar Rapids. Mrs. Harrington is charged with manslaughter and with causing death while operating a motor vehicle under the influence of intoxicating liquor. Conviction on either might mean a prison term. “We have five witnesses who will swear that Mrs. Harrington was the driver of the car,” said English upon being informed that Miss Lowe was taking the blame. Mrs. Harrington, English said, also admitted that she was at the wheel (Continued on Page Fourteen.)

London, June 5.--(LP)—A settlement has been agreed upon in the slander suit which Ernest A. Simpson, divorced husband of the Duchess of Windsor, brought to protect himself from gossip, it was understood today: Simpson's suit against Mrs. Joan Sutherland, a society woman, is No. 23 in the high court list of special jury cases to be heard this session. Until today it was expected that the suit would not be reached for weeks. Now information is that it will be up this week—probably Thursday—and that there would be but a brief hearing, ending in the issuance of an agreed statement. It was taken for granted that this statement would constitute a complete vindication for Simpson against the charge which he complained that Mrs. Sutherland made at a luncheon here—that he was “well paid” for permitting the duchess to divorce him.
London, June 8. (UP)—The Spanish Press Agency reported from Bilbao today that enemy aircraft had bombed the city heavily, killing and wounding many civilians.

1937-03-18.text: Dead—Reliably estimated at or more each as seen. Injured—Estimated at 179. Missing and believed dead—Estimated at near 100. Scene—High school building, London, Texas, Consolidated district. Geography—Located between London, a very old town, and New London, Rusk county, in the midst of the gigantic east Texas oil field. Estimated population of two communities 2000, Enrollment from 30-mile area, approximately 1200. Time—3:20 p. m. Thursday, Cause—W. C. Shaw, superintendent, said blast undoubtedly due to an accumulation of natural gas. Austin—Governor James V. Allred acted quickly and ordered martial law and sent troops into stricken communities. Washington—Headquarters of Red Cross ordered relief workers to the scene. Warm Springs—President Roosevelt, appalled, instructed government agencies to render all necessary aid, ten minutes before dismissal time.

London—(U.P)—The king’s proctor, in what was interpreted by legal authorities as a step to remove the last legal barrier to Mrs. Wallis Simpson’s final divorce decree, applied today for instructions on procedure to the president of the divorce court, Sir Boyd Merriman. Tomorrow’s official court cause list contained the following entry: “Undefended divorce case: “Simpson, W., vs. Simpson, E. A., (application by the king’s proctor for directions). “The hearing is fixed for 10:30 a.m.” (4:30 a.m. Central Standard time). The step was considered unusual, because the routine method of handling undefended cases, such as that of the Simpsons, is automatic announcement of a final decree six months after the intermediary decree is handed down. In Mrs. Simpson’s case, this would be April 27. She received her decree nisi from Earnest Aldrich Simpson at Ipswich on Oct. 27, 1936.

London, March 18 (UP)—An undisclosed person is intervening in the divorce of Mrs. Wallis Simpson, tomorrow’s cause list of the law courts disclosed today. The cause list announced that the king’s proctor will appear at 10:30 a.m. tomorrow in chambers before the president of the divorce courts, Sir Boyd Merriman, in connection with the intervention. Mrs. Simpson’s divorce from Ernest Simpson is not due to become final before April 27. Under the law, any interested person can intervene to show cause why the divorce should not be made final. The king’s proctor will ask Sir Boyd for directions on how to proceed in the intervention. The intervener’s name was not published but it was understood to be a private person.

By The Associated Press. Insurgent artillery pounded at Madrid today, scoring direct hits in the center of the capital, while the Spanish government protested in London against what was termed a threatened violation of the European neutrality agreement. The Spanish ambassador told Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden that two German ships, the August Cords and Consul Cords, loaded with war materials, were en route to an insurgent port—in violation of the neutrality pact. Eden agreed to bring the matter before the non-intervention control board, whose land and sea patrol to halt flow of arms and volunteers to Spain is expected to be fully underway by next Tuesday. Reports that a Dutch coaling ship, the Jonge Johanna, had been seized by an insurgent warship near Ceuta, Morocco, prompted the Dutch government to order four submarines prepared for active service. The insurgent bombardment of Madrid

London, March 18.—The divorce case of Mrs. Wallis Warfield Simpson against Ernest Aldrich Simpson will be reopened in the London divorce court Friday, it was learned today. An application by the king’s proctor “for direction” in the case will be heard by the president of the divorce court, Sir Boyd Merriman. The king’s proctor has the power to intervene in a divorce case between the time an interlocutory degree is granted and the divorce made final. Mrs. Simpson was granted an interlocutory decree at Ipswich assizes last fall, accusing her husband, a former officer in the Coldstream Guards of infidelity.

LONDON (W.P) — Impending legal action to annul the divorce of Mrs. Wallis Simpson and prevent her marriage to the Duke of Windsor, who abdicated as King Edward VIII for love of her, was indicated Thursday by a brief item in tomorrow's cause list of the law courts. The item did not name the intervener, who was understood to be a private person. The announcement merely said that the king’s proctor, who has the power to step in and show cause why a decree nisi should be set aside, will appear at 10:30 a.m. tomorrow in chambers before the president of the divorce courts, Sir Boyd Merriam, to ask for ‘direction.’ It is understood that the intervention is of the “common informer” type of action in which any member of the public may appear to give information. A reliable source said the intervener is not an individual of prominence and is not directly involved in the case. Mrs. Simpson's divorc

Dublin, March 17.—(CAP)— There was a near-famine of shamrocks for Dublin’s celebration of St. Patrick’s Day today. Hundreds of acres of the little green plants were buried under a heavy blizzard. The shortage, however, failed to dampen holiday spirits. A military parade, sports, dancing, singing and festive dinners were on the programme.

HENDERSON, Tex., March 18—W. C. Shaw — superintendent of the New London school eight miles Northwest of here, telephoned here this afternoon that he believed between 300 and 400 school children died in an explosion at the school. The information was given to J. W. Harris of the Rusk County News. Harris spread an alarm and fire fighting equipment, nurses and physicians from towns in this area were rushed to New London. Further details were unavailable.

1937-03-17.text: LONDON, March 16.— (7) — The British government will not pay a pension to the Duke of Windsor, presentation of King George VI's civil list message disclosed today. Instead the royal family, from its own pockets, will make an allowance to former King Edward. There was no mention of the Duke of Windsor in the message, presented in the House of Commons. It turned over to Commons the hereditary revenues from the Duchy of Cornwall, formerly held by Edward. It asked in return that Commons make provisions for certain members of the royal family. Those for whom provisions were requested were the queen, the children of the royal couple and the Duke of Gloucester.

London, March 17.—(AP)—British statesmen joined in eulogy of Sir Austen Chamberlain, “father” of the Locarno treaty, today in recounting his 45 years of public service which ended last night in death. The 73-year-old dean of conservative elder statesmen in the House of Commons succumbed to a heart attack in his West End home. He had been Chancellor of the Exchequer twice, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, Secretary of State for India, and a member of the wartime cabinet of David Lloyd George. He was the elder son of the distinguished statesman, Joseph Chamberlain, and a half-brother of Neville Chamberlain, present Chancellor of the Exchequer. There was a flood of press tributes.

London, March 16 (UP)—Merle Oberon, movie star, suffered cuts about the head and face and slight concussion today in an automobile collision. Badly shaken she was taken to a hospital. A hospital official said that Miss Oberon was cut above the eyebrow and that there was a second cut toward the back of the head. Both cuts were superficial, he said, adding: “There is little fear that they will leave any trace.”

London, March 16.—(UP)—Sir Austen Chamberlain, one of England's greatest imperialists who twice failed to attain the goal of his political life—the premiership when it was almost within his grasp, died tonight in his London home. Death, which came at 6 P. M. (1 P. M. EST), was due to a heart attack. The tall, sharp-faced statesman, who had been confined to his Egerton Terrace residence for several days, arose from his bed and started to descend the stairs to his library when he collapsed. He died a few minutes later without regaining consciousness. Sir Austen, a half-brother of Chancellor of the Exchequer Neville Chamberlain, had been ill only a few days. He was 73 years old. His death drew the mantle on a career in which he frequently was the talk of the moment but never the man of the hour. His was a life of climax and anti-climax, the tragedy of a man whose personal power in Parliamen

HENDAYE, Franco-Spanish Frontier—(U.P)—Gen. Francisco Franco's Italian troops on Madrid's northeastern front fled in panic before repeated attacks on an SS-ship Loyalist air fleet which dropped more than eight tons of explosives on them, Madrid dispatches reported today. Many French, English and American fliers were reported to have participated in the Loyalist aerial counter-attack.

LONDON, March 17—AP—Great Britain and France have received, and have decided to reject, an offer by the Spanish Loyalist government to grant them special rights in Spanish Morocco in return for aid to the Loyalists, it was understood today. Experts of the British and French foreign offices were ordered to draft identical notes for dispatch soon to Foreign Minister Julio Alvarez Del Vayo of the Loyalist government, it was said, announcing that the proposal could not be entertained. The Spanish offer was not one of territorial concessions but of special facilities, presumably mainly of military, naval and aerial nature, on condition that Britain and France help the Loyalist government, for instance by frustrating continued Italian and German intervention in behalf of the Loyalists. Experts on foreign affairs called it the biggest diplomatic blunder of the civil war. In some way, it reached

| Muskogee, Okla, March 17—(AP)—County Attorney Camp Bonds said today a calm 16-year-old high school girl, held in jail here, told him she tried to “figure some way around” firing shots at her English teacher who gave her low marks—“but couldn't.” Slender Ramona Porter, who appeared younger than 16, was in the city-federal jail after wild shots were fired at Miss Charlotte Kennedy, the English teacher, in the corridor of the high school late yesterday. “She apparently has no regret over her actions and seems rather defiant,” Bonds said. Miss Kennedy did not plan to press charges against the girl from whom she fled down the corridor. Ricocheting shots struck a leg of James Litten, janitor, and grazed the arm of Betty Janes Peckenpaugh, 17, a student. Bonds said the pistol was found at the home of the girl, daughter of an unemployed carpenter.

London, March 16.—— (4) —-Edward of England, a $2,000,000-a-year man in 1936, is off the payroll and will get no pension from the British government. Instead, the abdicated monarch must depend upon the royal family for any probable allowance from home, it became apparent tonight with submission of the civil list message to parliament. The message from his brother-successor, King George VI, made no mention of Edward, Duke of Windsor, but it did return to commons the hereditary revenues from the Duchy of Cornwall. These formerly went to Edward, now living in Austria. For Royal Family In return, commons was asked to make provisions for certain members of the royal family.

1937-08-10.text: LONDON, Aug. 9 (P)—Germany protested formally to Great Britain today against the expulsion of three Nazi newspapermen. The three, Werner von Crome, of the Berlin Lokal-Anzeiger, and the younger writers Franz Otto Wrede and Wold Dietrich Langen, working for a news agency which reports news and opinions of Germans abroad, were ordered to leave England by the home office last weekend. There was no explanation of the order. Dr. E. Woermann, charge d’affaires of the German embassy, made the protest today at the foreign office. It was described by the British as couched in “restrained terms.” The protest followed conferences of German diplomats at Renfrew, Scotland, where German Ambassador Joachim von Ribbentrop is on holiday.

BERLIN, Aug. 10 (*)—Nazi expulsion of a London Times correspondent was declared today to be “only the beginning” of sweeping action to be taken against foreign newspapermen for allegedly “meddling in the internal affairs of Germany.” An official inspired editorial in the Boersen Zeitung made this statement. A number of such correspondents, says the newspaper, are in “real press chiefs of anti-government cliques and actively cooperate with these cliques and groups.” “A comprehensive investigation of this matter is nearly concluded,” the paper declared, emphasizing that it can be regarded as certain that expulsion proceedings will be taken against other correspondents as well. The Times of London announced there “could be no question” of accepting the “dictation” of the Nazi government by replacing its Berlin correspondent with one amenable. LONDON, Aug. 10 (UP), — Great Britain presented Spanish Nationalist authorities today with a formal, peremptory demand that they release at once three British merchantmen—Malton, Candleston Castle and Mirupano—which they hold. The ships were seized by Nationalist warships blockading the Loyalist coasts of Spain. Sir Henry Chilton, British ambassador to Spain who remains on the French side of the frontier, presented the Nationalist governing Junta with the demand. Britain's demand contained no ultimatum as it set no time limit, but it was plain immediate action was sought.

Paterson, N. J., Aug. 9—(AP)—A CIO strike call to 60,000 silk workers in New Jersey, Pennsylvania, New England and New York caused thousands of men and women to leave their looms today in an announced effort to secure union contracts to improve labor conditions and stabilize the industry. The only disorder reported along the wide front was at Hazleton, Pa., where a picket at the large Duplan Silk Corporation mill was stabbed in the arm. His alleged assailant was arrested after being almost mobbed by the crowd which gathered. Earlier four sheriff's deputies were sent from Wilkes-Barre to aid nine city policemen on duty. The Duplan management said pickets, some of whom were recruited from the ranks of anthracite mine workers, jammed so tightly about the gates that some of the 1,100 workers who pushed through the lines emerged with torn clothing. Representatives of the union and employers d

London, Aug. 9.—(AP)—Great Britain protested directly to Insurgent General Franco today against the bombing last Friday of the British tanker British Corporal, off Algeria. Italian and French ships were bombed in the same place and the captain of the Italian ship was killed. Today’s protest, lodged through British Ambassador Sir Henry Chilton at Hendaye, France, was based on the presumption that insurgent planes carried out the attack, although British officials said they were “not sure.” (The insurgents have denied they were responsible.) An earlier protest was lodged with insurgent authorities at Palma, Mallorca, by British naval officials.

LONDON. Aug. 10 (#)--Despite the death of two airmen, officials announced today that London had successfully demonstrated her power to resist a mass air raid. The two men were killed when their plane crashed near the city during last night's maneuvers. Officials said 80 per cent of the raids were spotted before completion and the bombers were “attacked” by fighting planes before they reached their targets. COLD SNAP COMING! London, Aug. 10.—(AP)—The Times of London announced today there "could be no question" of accepting the "dictation" of the Nazi government by replacing its expelled Berlin correspondent with one "more amenable." The German government yesterday ordered Norman Ebbutt, widely-quoted Berlin correspondent of the Times for about 15 years, to leave Germany within two weeks in retaliation for the expulsion of three German correspondents from Great Britain. The Times was informed by the British foreign office that the German government wanted its correspondent in Berlin to be a man "who will pay less attention to work considered here as trivial- (Continued on Page Three)

LONDON, Aug. 9.—(#)—Britain tested London’s vulnerability to attack from the skies tonight with the greatest air defense maneuvers in her history. To the inexperienced eye, the mock warfare was just a realistic pageant, a play battle of flares, flashbulbs, cameras and Fourth of July toys. But to Londoners who experienced the harrowing night air raids of German Gothas and zeppelins during the World War, the thunder of 400 war planes dramatized the recent grim warning to parliament that their city “is the choiciest target in the world.” Nineteen squadrons of tiny fighting craft, 222 planes like flying torpedoes, roared across the night skies to drive off 172 bombers that flew in from the west in fighting formation. Although London—with its vast docks, oil depots, and the Enfield Munitions Works—is the nerve-center of England’s defenses, most of the targets tonight were in outlying district

1937-02-28.text: London, Feb. 27.—()—International diplomats called for two key men tonight to direct a cordon of foreign warships and military observers around warring Spain. Their jobs would be to hold the civil war inside the country and keep both men and munitions from crossing the frontiers from the outside. One would supervise the sea patrol, the other the land guards along the French and Portuguese boundaries. The danger of the conflict spreading into other parts of Europe was dissipated, it was believed, by a 27-power agreement in the international non-intervention committee to ban foreign volunteers in Spain -- effective a week from Saturday midnight. Actually, so many details of the plan remained to be completed that it appeared most unlikely the machinery for barricading Spain's borders and seaports would start operating as scheduled. Diplomats felt it was unimportant at the moment, however, s

LONDON, Eng. (UP)—Gossipers with usually good sources of information said Saturday that a good part of the difficulty over the financial affairs of the Duke of Windsor concerns the magnificent emeralds which his grandmother, Queen Alexandra, gave him. It has been generally understood that the Duke gave these jewels to Mrs. Wallis Simpson before his abdication, and that she later gave the jewels to the government. The duke is said to have been exceedingly angry, alleging that the government brought pressure on Mrs. Simpson, and to have replaced the jewels. There is no authentic estimate of the value of the jewels. The lowest ever made by gossips was $50,000. But estimates of the total indebtedness of the duke, also by gossips, range as high as $1,500,000. The story has been that Mrs. Simpson's lawyer went to Canada and got the Alexandra emeralds from her. Now it is said that she gave them

LONDON, Feb. 27—(UP)—The sensational Sunday Referee said to-night that a group of "famous Mayfair hostes and hostesses" are facing government treason charges because of a whispering campaign against King George VI. (The United Press London bureau was unable to obtain any confirmation of the Referee’s report regarding the consideration of treason charges.) The newspaper said the cabinet has discussed the advisability of action against the scandal-spreaders but that Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin is anxious to avoid any direct action. The whispering campaign was described as taking the course of exaggerated rumors about the king's health and his inability to cope with the arduous duties of his position. MADRID, Feb. 27 (AP)--The whine and crash of insurgent shells broke a five weeks’ respite for central Madrid today. The shelling was slow, the insurgents apparently correcting their first shots for precision. Street cars continued to run, the passengers' startled faces peering from the windows, excited refugees clustered in basements, asking about their friends. The shelling, in mid-afternoon, came after a quiet morning during which the only shots heard were occasional bursts from West Park and University City, western and northwestern Madrid battlegrounds through most of the siege that has lasted since November. General Jose Miaja, newly named to supreme command of all the central Spanish government troops, agreed with Valencia and Barcelona leaders that decisive united action was needed to combat the insurgent armies, especially with the imminence of a Europe-wide plan to block off Spa

Polson, Mont. (INS)—Seven men were killed and three others injured today when a rock slide, 100 feet in width, tore down the steep side of a canyon near here. The dead, bodies of whom were still buried under thousands of tons of rock that swept down the wall, were all Indian workmen. The slide occurred on the Flathead hydroelectrical project being constructed by a Butte firm. Recent mild weather caused a thaw that loosened the rock.

A PLATA, ARGENTINA, Feb. 27 (#) — Baby Eugenio Peyrera Ira- ola, Argentina's “Lindbergh Baby” was found today, the life choked out of his little body, five years almost to the day after Charles A. Lindbergh, Jr., was kidnapped from Jersey's sourland hills. Like baby Lindbergh, 2-year-old Eugenio, the seventh child of baronial cattle wealth, was killed by his kidnapper. He was stripped of his little suit, choked and wounded, and left, his arms crossed on his chest, in the slime of a pigpen at the edges of beautiful ‘La Sorpresa,” his parents’ estate. Five years ago next Monday, the Lindbergh baby was kidnapped from his famous parents’ Hopewell, N. J. estate, precipitating perhaps the most intense manhunt in American annals. It led to the finding of the child's broken body two months later. Richard Hauptmann paid for the crime in Jersey's electric chair. Argentina’s greatest murder hunt wa

A woman and two men were injured. Gov. Frank Murphy offered the service of State Labor Commissioner G. A. Krogstad in adjusting a score of labor disputes in progress here. A strike of 100 workers forced 1000 into idleness at the Michigan Malleable Iron Co. Approximately 160 salesgirls at the F. W. Woolworth five and ten cent store and 15 drivers and salesmen at the Canada Dry Ginger Ale Co. started “sitdown” strikes. Six hundred went out at Thompson Products, Inc. In its annual burlesque of national affairs—attended by the president—the White House correspondents association nominated these: J. Edgar Hoover, chief of the federal bureau of investigation. Curley of Massachusetts. Dr. Stanley “all-time” high, of the good neighbor league, which represented for the president last. At the newsmen’s dinner with the president were three of his sons, John, Franklin and James, the latter recently named a White House aide. 1937-06-28.text: London, June 28—(P)—British statesmen tonight looked to a gathering tomorrow of spokesmen for Europe’s great powers to disclose whether cooperation for keeping the Spanish war from spreading can be maintained. Official spokesmen said Britain’s future foreign policy may hinge on its decisions. The directing subcommittee of the 27-nation committee for isolating the Spanish conflict will convene at 11 a.m. The immediate question is whether Italy and Germany will return to the naval patrol around Spain they left last week, It was admitted the outlook was clouded by the declaration of Reichsfuehrer Adolf Hitler at Wurzburg that Germany renounced further efforts at international cooperation in the patrol. In Rome Virginio Gayda, often spokesman for the fascist regime, declared Italy and Germany would not accept a "complete" patrol of Spanish coasts by Britain and France. That, he said, would f

LONDON, June 27.—(AP)—British and French diplomats tonight faced with undisguised anxiety the task of restoring the international patrol of Spanish waters and preventing the manifold frictions involved from exploding in Europe's face. They agreed that how far this can be accomplished — depends entirely on the replies of Berlin and Rome to the Anglo-French proposal that Britain and France use their own naval vessels to close the gap in the patrol left by the withdrawals of Italy and Germany. This reply is expected Tuesday at a meeting of the subcommittee of the 27-nation "hands off Spain" committee. Tuesday's decision can either "split the nations wide apart again" or create more friendly relations, said a French official spokesman in Paris. Oakland, Calif.-(P)-R. T. (Dick) Merrill and Jack Lambie said today they would attempt another trans-Atlantic flight.—this time New York to Rome. The aviators, who recently flew round trip to England, expected to take off in about three weeks.

NEW YORK, June 27 (P)—Another thrilling rescue at sea was written into maritime records Sunday as the steamship President Pierce resumed its course for New York after saving the 40 crew members of the fire-swept British freighter Sandgate Castle. Forced from their ship approximately 650 miles southeast of New York, the British sailors tossed about in lifeboats for more than eight hours until the President Pierce reached them near midnight. Their ship, which sailed June 25 from New York with a general cargo for Capetown, Africa, was a fire-blackened derelict when the President Pierce arrived in response to a radioed appeal for aid. The President Pierce reported as it picked up the ship's boats that the Sandgate Castle had burned itself out and was floating low in the Atlantic swells, a menace to navigation.

Wimbledon, Eng. June 28 ()—Den Budge, America’s red-headed Davis Cup ace, eliminated Vivian McGrath of Australia, 6-3, 6-1, 6-4, in the quarter-finals of the All-England tennis championships today but his tiny compatriot, Bryan M. "Bitsy" Grant of Atlanta fell before the sound strokes of Henry Wilfred "Bunny" Austin of England, 6-1, 7-5, 6-4. Budge’s triumph came after Helen Jacobs of Berkeley, Calif., the defending titleholder, and Alice Marble, United States champion from San Francisco, had gained the quarter-finals of the women's division. Frankie Parker, a youngster from Milwaukee, gave the United States two semi-finalists in men's singles when he defeated the third seeded Heinrich Henkel of Germany in a stunning surprise 6-3, 7-5, 4-6, 4-6, 6-2. Haron Gottfried von Cramm, seeded second to Budge, outlasted veteran Jack Crawford of Australia in the remaining quarter-final, 6-3, 8-6, 3

NEW YORK (#) — Globe wireless reported Saturday night that the crew of 40 men off the flaming British freighter Sandgate Castle had been rescued far out in the Atlantic Ocean by the S. S. President Pierce, which was proceeding to New York. The Sandgate Castle, swept by fire, was abandoned and reported to the coast guard as dangerous to navigation, the radioed reports from the S. S. President Pierce said.

BERLIN, June 28, (U.P)—Nazi Germany opened a world congress of business men today with assertions that it will take direct action in any future Spanish war crisis, that it wants a Nationalist victory in Spain, and that it will continue searching for colonial territories until it gets them. The occasion was the ninth congress of the International Chamber of Commerce, said to be the greatest gathering of world business leaders ever assembled—1,600 delegates from 40 nations in addition to hundreds of specially invited guests. Col.-Gen. Hermann Goering, air minister, economic dictator and right-hand man of Fuehrer Adolf Hitler, in his speech of welcome at the opening of the congress, said bluntly: “You may be sure Germany will continue to bring up the colonial problem until its urgent and legitimate desires as regards colonies are fulfilled.” He made a bid, too, for a system of trade treatie
SOVIET NORTH POLE CAMP (By Radio to Moscow June 22).—The temperature today was just at the freezing point, 32 degrees above zero Fahrenheit. A mist hung low and visibility was only 50 to 200 yards.

1937-11-29.text: (By Associated Press). LONDON, Nov. 29—Great Britain and France began today their most determined effort since Adolf Hitler became ruler of Germany in 1933 to make a compact with him insuring the peace of western Europe. Premiers and foreign ministers of the two countries meeting in a two day conference turned first to Hitler’s increasingly strident demands for return of Germany’s former colonies. The meeting also had in view a formidable range of major world sore spots including the Chinese-Japanese situation which was regarded here as becoming more critical every day.

Cairo, Egypt, Nov. 29.—(4?)—British-directed police clamped down today on the Green Shirts party, organization of extreme nationalists hostile to Britain, following an attempt on the life of Premier Mustapha Nahas Pasha. The president of the group, Ahmed Hussein, and all of its 300 members were arrested.

London, Nov. 29—Great Britain and France, engaged in diplomatic conversations of great importance, renewed concerted efforts today to bring Germany and Italy into a new European peace settlement. At the same time, their leaders—Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain and Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden of Britain and Premier Camille Chautemps and Foreign Minister Yvon Delbos of France—were believed to be re-establishing a strong Anglo-French front in the face of the growing menace of Germany and Italy and to provide means of protecting their vast interests in the Far East. The conversations among the leaders which began today will consume nearly 27 hours. Taking place at 10 Downing Street, the foreign office, they will be continued even at luncheon and at a dinner tonight where Eden will be the host. So as not to waste time, his guests will not dress formally. The discussions probably will be

LONDON, Nov. 29--The British government instructed the commander-in-chief in the Mediterranean today to make representations to Spanish insurgent naval authorities at Palma, Majorca, against a reported threat to abolish neutral shipping zones as part of the blockade of Loyalist Spain. The neutral zones were established by the powers in connection with the Mediterranean patrol plan. Britain will point out that she cannot admit the right of blockade, since no belligerent rights have been granted, nor can she admit the right of attack in territorial waters, which would not be tolerated even if belligerent rights were accorded.

| LONDON, Nov. 28.— (AP) — With British and French statesmen scheduled to begin talks on major policy tomorrow, authoritative sources said tonight Britain and France had worked out detailed military plans to defend their Mediterranean lifelines against the ultimate victor in the Spanish civil war. Recent developments were considered to have lessened the possibility of a new Spanish regime entirely hostile to Britain and France. Among these were London's agreement for exchange of commercial agents with the Insurgent regime. Also, it was felt the airing of the German colonial problem should ease Mediterranean tension. Seek to Balk Duce, Hitler Nevertheless, the French and British naval and army staffs were said to have drafted plans to balk Italo-German control of the western and southeastern portions of the sea Premier Benito Mussolini calls “Mare Nostrum”—our sea. Even as they talk of the warring nations of the world, keen developments add to the seriousness of the crisis. London — Britain seeks a stern Anglo-French front on the Far East, with constant communication with the United States. Both countries hope to bring Germany into a new European peace structure, but France resolutely objected to the “free hand” which Hitler seeks in central Europe. The scope of the conference, inspired by Lord Halifax’s recent explorations of German territorial and political claims, suddenly had been widened to include the Japanese threat to Anglo-French interests in the Far East. 1937-03-06.text: PLYMOUTH, Eng., March 6 (4)— Frank Vosper, 37, one of England's “brilliant young men” of the theater, walked out of a British beauty queen's champagne party aboard the French liner Paris today and vanished. Passengers who attended the gay affair in the cabin of Muriel Oxford, “Miss Great Britain” of 1936, were reported summoned for an investigation by officers of the liner. Another inquiry was likely when the ship reached Le Havre, France. Vosper disappeared two hours out of Plymouth. The comely Miss Oxford, who had been appearing in a New York revue, was deeply distressed. She said Vosper, an actor-playwright, stepped out of her cabin onto a deck and “did not come back.” Friends said she and Vosper became acquainted on the voyage from New York. LONDON, Eng. (UP) — Frank Vosper, 37, British actor and author, disappeared from the liner Paris a few hours before it arrived at Plymouth Saturday from New York. Muriel Oxford, 22, chosen “Miss Great Britain” in a beauty contest last year, told Plymouth police that he had attended a party in her stateroom just before he disappeared and that they had talked together “quite normally.” She denied that Vosper had threatened to “jump overboard” if she did not promise to marry him, as another passenger, unnamed, was quoted as saying. Miss Oxford said that her stateroom had a small veranda from which a window opened directly above the sea. She said she and Vosper had stood talking on this veranda for a short time. She left Vosper there and rejoined the party, she said. Soon afterward members of the party notified the ship's commander that Vosper had disappeared. The ship turned immediately and

(—Britain’s 97,500,000,000 rearmament program promised today not only to cut into taxable incomes an extra 12 per cent but threatened to hamper normal industrial production for three years. ‘The five-year program of perfecting war defenses, with its prospective inroads into supplies of steel and other materials, would take precedence over regular peace time industry, Sir Thomas Inskip, defense co-ordination minister, suggested. “It would be no bad thing,” he declared in a speech last night, “if some orders were postponed two or three years while contractors are busy on the government program.” The airplane industry, for example, is so busy with government orders that even now it is not attempting to meet private orders. LONDON, March 6 (4i)—Britain’s War-machine budget topped the billion-dollar mark for 193 today with the air ministry proposing to gauge in the capital from air raids and asking £32,550,000 ($412,500,000) for air defense alone. Viscount Swinton, secretary of state for air, said large fleets of balloons would be sent into the air at the first alarm of a hostile raid. These balloons would drop a network of steel cables caging in the city and blocking any enemy planes from breaking through. He added the Royal Air Force would be increased to 70,000 officers and men with a first line strength of 1,760 aircraft formed in 12 squadrons. The air estimates pushed the 1937 cost of Great Britain's national defense to £207,580,000 ($1,548,099,200). The Navy has asked for £42,233,000, and the Army £10,870,000. The Canadian prime minister was an overnight guest at the White House following an hour's conference with Secretary of State Cordell Hull late Friday. IRTHLINGBOROUGH, Eng. March 6—(UP)—Ernest Greasley, a “double” for Clark Gable, would rather be a hero to the 300 girls who work under him in a local laundry than accept a motion picture contract. That he had declined three such offers — one reputedly from an American company—became known yesterday when the 300 girls went on strike because someone mentioned that Greasley might be transferred to another branch of the laundry in a different town. “I prefer to stay in Irthlingborough,” he said. “When you have 300 girls working under you it’s something to be proud of. They stood loyally by me and I don't want to let them down by leaving the country. “There was a time when I thought I would like a film career, but that's all changed now. The laundry girls want me here—and here I stay.”

London, March 5. (UP) - Edward, Duke of Windsor, and Mrs. Wallis Warfield Simpson will be married immediately after her divorce decree becomes final, April 27, a close friend of the former British monarch revealed tonight. The friend received a letter from Edward saying that his honeymoon would be spent near Arondstetten, Austria. Edward visited there recently. Mrs. Simpson plans to have her effects transferred late this month from Cannes to Emzesfeld, Edward's temporary home. Legal experts said today that although the decree nisi period expires on April 27, the final divorce might be granted a few days either before or after that date.

1937-10-17.text: London, Oct. 16.—(A?)—Count Dino Grandi, Italy’s delegate, told the non-intervention subcommittee today that Italy “accepts the proposal for partial withdrawal of a certain number of volunteers” from the Spanish civil war. The nine-power sub-committee adjourned until early next week after hearing statements by the British, French, Italian and German members. The nine diplomats, meeting in a tense atmosphere created by British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden’s demand for prompt action, heard the Italian delegate promise his country’s “loyal and firm desire to cooperate.” The main question before the meeting was that of withdrawing foreign volunteers—especially Italian—from the Spanish war to remove the principal source of danger that a general European conflict would emanate from Spain. J., Oct. 16.—The bodies of an elderly physician and his wife, beaten to death with a hammer in Maine days ago and then driven leisurely through the New England states to New Jersey by a young school boy, Prosecutor John J. Breslin said, were found today in a parked automobile. The high school boy, Paul Dwyer, 18, of South Paris, Me., who had stopped the machine with its gruesome cargo to get some sleep, confessed the double slaying, Bergen County Prosecutor John J.
