MARSEILLES, Aug. 23—(/)—The British steamer Noemijulia wirelessed today that she was being bombed by two airplanes off Ajaccio, the capital of Corsica, in the western Mediterranean. The ship, listed as being 2,499 tons, is owned by the Noemijulia Steamship Company of London. It was sailing near the waters of civil war-torn Spain where several bombings and torpedoings of commercial vessels have occurred lately. The Noemijulia’s message, picked up by a Marseilles radio station, read: “We are being bombarded. Position 42 degrees seven minutes north, five degrees 32 minutes east. Signs two planes numbers 528 and 529 black circle with white cross two black bars.” No further message was received immediately, leaving in doubt the fate of the vessel. In view of recent raids, French and British governments have ordered their warships and planes to aid merchantmen attacked on the high seas and cou

Marseilles. Aug. 23—The Jetee radio station picked up distress signals from the British freighter Noemijulia that “we are being bombarded by two planes marked with white crosses in the middle of black circles.” The freighter’s position was off the Catalan coast of Spain. The Noemijulia did not indicate the nationality of the planes but the position of the ship indicated they apparently came from Majorca. They bore the numbers 528 and 529. Lloyd’s register of shipping lists the Noemijulia as of 2,499 tons and London as her home port. It is owned by the Noemijulia Steamship Co.

Shanghai. (4?) - An American eyewitness stated tonight he had seen one Japanese destroyer badly damaged and a Japanese gunboat sunk by Chinese air bombers as the warships were covering the landing of Japanese army units near Woosung. Michael Hermann of Chicago, an oil chemist, said he viewed the battle from the deck of a Texas Co. tanker. The Japanese destroyer, he said, was hurried from the scene in tow of a sister destroyer. ‘The gunboat keeled over at an angle of 45 degrees and went down. This fight apparently was one of many that raged along the banks of the Yangtze river as a new Japanese army sought a foothold on Chinese soil.

Copyright 1937 by United Press SHANGHAI, Aug. 23—(UP)—A huge aerial bomb crashed into upper Nanking road, between the Chinese-owned Wing-on and Sincere department stores at 1:10 p. m. today, and killed from 300 to 700 persons. More than 1,000 were wounded including Anthony Billingham, a correspondent of the New York Times, and Miss Blanche Tenney, an American, born in Shanghai. Several Europeans also were hurt. Japanese said the bomb came from a Chinese plane which had been flying high over the city. A second aerial bomb, 18 inches in diameter, crashed through the roof of the U. S. navy warehouse, adjacent to the U. S. and British consulates general, but did not explode.

Genoa, Italy (#7)—Ten Italian sailors and a trainman were killed and forty sailors were injured today in a head-on collision of their excursion train and a freight train on Vigo Morasso curve. The ten sailors and the freight train engineer died on their way to a hospital or at the hospital.

YB, Franco's Spanish Frontier, Aug. 23. — Insurgent legions stormed through Santander’s “iron ring” today. They reached the besieged and hungry city’s outlying fortifications, pounded them with artillery and occupied several important towns in the strategic Villacarriedo sector. A communique from the Valencia National Defense Ministry, acknowledging the insurgent advance, said the enemy had suffered severe losses before taking the towns. It quoted an Italian sergeant who was taken prisoner as asserting four divisions of regular Italian troops were operating on this front. A surprise insurgent assault, said a Salamanca communique, opened the way through strategic Villacarriedo and other important positions over hill towns, including Alceda and Ontaneda. Franco's men claimed in taking Selaya, just south of Villacarriedo, that an entire garrison of prisoners and three tanks were captured in

1937-02-08.text: LONDON, Feb. 8 (#)—Torrential rains deluged both France and England today and spread menacing floods over large areas. The threat centered in southern England where more rain fell in the past seven days than normally during the whole month of February. Coming on the heels of earlier gales and blizzards, the downpour sent rivers on a new rampage. In Dorset, on the English channel, hundreds of persons fled to higher ground when floods isolated many villages and inundated farmlands. Besides Dorset, the hardest hit counties were Kent and Essex, neighboring London. The Thames river, overflowing for the second time within 10 days, flooded the famed playing fields of Eton and the private grounds of Windsor Castle.

LONDON, Eng. (UP) — The Daily Mirror, in a copyrighted article, today reported that Princess Royal Mary went to see her brother, the Duke of Windsor, in a final effort to prevent him from marrying Mrs. Wallis Simpson. “She has gone as an ambassadress for her brothers,” said the Daily Mirror. “During her stay with the Duke of Windsor she will plead with him in their behalf and in the behalf of Queen Mary not to marry Mrs. Simpson. “There is no doubt the Duke of Windsor still is determined as ever to marry Mrs. Simpson. He talks of their wedding openly to friends.” This report came after a surge of gossip regarding the possibility he might not be headed to matrimony — assuming in the event that Mrs. Simpson's final decree of divorce from Ernest Simpson is not granted. In so far as the duke is determined to marry is concerned the gossip agrees with the Daily Mirror article but added that it

LONDON, Feb. 8 —(AP)—The Duke of Kent today registered the birth of his second child, disclosing her name will be Alexandra Helen Elizabeth Olga Christabel. The infant, born Christmas day, will be christened tomorrow. The little princess ranks sixth in the line of succession to the throne.

VIENNA, Feb. 6.—(INS)—As the time for the Duke of Windsor to marry Mrs. Wallis Simpson draws near, certain high British personalities have launched a campaign to prevent the marriage, it was learned today. Several of the most important figures in British public and social life have written to the former ruler seeking to dissuade him from marrying the American born divorcee for whom he forsook his throne. Because of this campaign, the duke has become somewhat concerned. Declaring he would “not wait longer than necessary,” he has told friends he would marry Mrs. Simpson the day after her divorce becomes final. The final decree probably will be handed down April 27. In an effort to silence critics, the duke is striving to have two of his brothers, the dukes of Gloucester and Kent, attend his wedding. The duke also has asked his third brother and successor as king, George VI, to consent to a

PALERMO, Sicily, Feb. 8.—(AP)—Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh landed at Palermo at 3:19 p. m. today (8:10 a. m., C. S. T.) after fighting a 65-mile-an-hour gale in their flight from Rome. Their flight from the capital took slightly less than five hours, with an average speed of only 60 miles an hour because of the heavy wind blowing near the island of Ustica. Shortly before their orange and black monoplane was sighted over Bocca Di Falco airport, officials ordered emergency landing fields to be on the alert for the American fliers, whose ultimate destination was believed to be Cairo, Egypt. Regional air squadrons had been ordered to be ready to give assistance to the Lindberghs if they were forced down. United States Vice Consul W. E. Scotten and a group of Italian air officials breathed deep sighs of relief when the plane finally

Malaga, Spain (By Courier to Gibraltar), Feb. 8 (#).—Victorious Fascist legions of General Francisco Franco swept into terror-stricken Malaga today and occupied completely the last important seaport held by the Socialist government on the southern coast. The surrender was unconditional. The defense simply melted away. No government authorities remained to proclaim submission to the insurgent war machine as it moved with precision into the city.

| VIENNA, Feb. 8 (4)—Carefree, affectionate, the Duke of Windsor took his sister Mary to browse among the Hapsburg art collections in Schoenbrunn Palace today—seemingly not so anxious as before to make haste in wedding Wallis Simpson. It was reported authoritatively the duke, after several intimate fireside chats with the Princess Royal, now was inclined to more deliberation in making the wedding arrangements. All authoritative quarters said they were “completely in the dark” as to rumors circulated in London that the Princess Royal was trying to persuade Edward not to marry the woman for whom he abdicated the mightiest throne in the world.

- WITH FASCISTS OUTSIDE MALAGA, Feb. 8.—()—A double threat of death struck terror in a city. A Uy Enc, Sey Dagiaeto Ok up by a Fascist army hammering at the gates. Insurgents observed on the hilltops overlooking the Mediterranean port described the situation in the provincial capital as “complete chaos.” The population, with all land and sea exits blocked so escape appeared impossible, was panic stricken. Bands of anarchists in the city, left virtually unprotected by the sudden crumbling of its defenses, and the blazing fire from Fascist guns, the observers declared, formed an equal menace to civilian inhabitants. The strategic shipping center’s defense collapsed yesterday before a sweeping drive of the insurgent Southern Army.

1937-12-23.text: SHANGHAI, Dec. 22 (U.P)—Col. Shingoro Hashimoto commanding Japanese troops along the upper Yangtse, has been removed from his post as the result of troops' attack on United States and British warships, Americans arriving here asserted today. It was asserted that Hashimoto, politically powerful firebrand of the extremist element in the Japanese army, was relieved of his command last Saturday and replaced by a fellow colonel who “showed a much more cooperative spirit.” The Americans, who arrived here from Wuhu, did not know whether Hashimoto had been recalled or transferred to another command. Foreign military experts suggested that he probably was given another command. His mere removal, they said, would be sufficient indication of the concern of the Japanese army at attacks on United States and British ships. Man Responsible Hashimoto was regarded by forces here as the man really respons

London—7)—Great Britain took steps today to insure quick movement of part of her Mediterranean fleet to the Orient in any emergency. A decision was understood to have been reached, however, against immediate naval reinforcements in the Far East. Authoritative sources said the cabinet, at yesterday's and night sessions, considered the admiralty’s technical plan for naval reinforcements but left further decision to Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain and Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden over the Christmas holidays. The cabinet was understood to have decided large fleet movements now might be considered by the Japanese as unduly provocative. It was believed it decided on a restrained policy at least until Japan replies to protests against attacks on British shipping on the Yangtze river. The reply is expected soon.

LONDON, Dec. 23.—(U.P)—Great Britain intends to give China a full measure of moral support, but cannot prohibit the export of arms to Japan, Viscount Cranborne, foreign undersecretary, told a questioner in the House of Commons today. However, Lord Cranborne iterated the declaration of Oliver Stanley, president of the Board of Trade, to Commons on Tuesday that only one license for arms export to Japan had been issued in the last three months.

SHANGHAI, Dec. 23.—(#)—Japanese authorities warned foreigners tonight to evacuate Hangchow, Chekiang province capital and seaport, to escape the danger of rapidly approaching Japanese siege. The United States and Great Britain, both of which have nationals in the area south of Shanghai, were among powers whose consuls received the warning from Japanese consular officers. The notification also included Shaoshing, near the Gulf of Hangchow, about 35 miles southeast of the provincial capital. Japanese declared the defenders of Hangchow would be trapped or compelled to withdraw by forces steadily completing encirclement of the seaport from three sides. American and other foreign residents were endangered by the Japanese thrust against Hangchow, capital of Chekiang province, and the Chinese-held area at the head of Hangchow Bay. Other American, Chinese and foreign refugees, meanwhile, were in

SHANGHAI, Dec. 23. (?)—Japan formed a new autonomous government at captured Nanking today, presumably to replace Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek’s nationalist government. It was only 10 days ago that a similar autonomous government, headed by Chinese, was set up by Japan at Peiping, center of the vast north China region taken by the Japanese army in its latest invasion of China. The Japanese army appeared today to be nowhere near the end of its conquest as it was spreading its reaches over an ever-widening front which threatened to encompass every important coastal city and inestimable territory inland. Foreigners were warned to evacuate Hangchow, Chekiang province capital and seaport, to escape being endangered by an imminent siege by Japanese forces. Three hundred Americans and other foreigners fled from the threat of another Japanese attack at Hankow, Yangtze river valley city. The fore

By The Associated Press, Shanghai, Dec. 23 (Thursday).—Japanese declared today the fall of Hangchow was imminent while thousands of foreign and Chinese refugees fled from Canton, Tsingtao, Hankow and other widely-scattered cities where attacks were expected. A Japanese spokesman said the invading troops were approaching Hangchow, seaport south of Shanghai, and were hopeful that the Chinese would withdraw to prevent destruction of the famous beauty spot and Buddhist Mecca. Foreign sources reported that the Hangchow defenders were offering stiff resistance but that Japanese armored trains had advanced to within sixteen miles of the city along the Shanghai - Hangchow Railway. Reports that the Japanese were massing troops for an attack on Canton, South China metropolis, increased the evacuation of natives. Thousands fled westward into the interior and toward Hongkong. Bias Bay Activities. Un

HENDAYE, Franco-Spanish Frontier, (P), A column of insurgent artillery and troops smashed thru the government siege of the military garrison at Teruel, a radio dispatch reported adding that a counter offensive was being prepared. The message from the Teruel radio station, received at insurgent headquarters at Irun, said the garrison and some of the civil population still were resisting government assaults. Barricaded in a seminary overlooking the ancient Aragon city, insurgent troops had made their stand after a surprise government attack drove them out of the city in a blizzard.

TOKYO, Dec. 23 (P)—Japanese commanders in China have received government orders to respect foreign interests even at the risk of permitting Chinese to escape, it was understood today. The orders, said to have been issued within the last few days, were regarded as a direct result of the government's grave anxiety over angry United States and British protests against Japanese army and navy attacks on American and British gunboats. Reference to the new orders, it was understood, will be made in notes to be sent to the United States and British governments on the attacks on the United States gunboat Panay and the British gunboat Ladybird. The foreign office, it was learned today, has begun drafting a reply to American notes.

1937-04-30.text: RIS, April 30.—France, possibly in collaboration with Great Britain, will help evacuate the harassed civilian population of Bilbao, high government officials indicated today. “You can rest assured all necessary measures to proceed with the evacuation are being taken,” members of the senate foreign affairs commission said. Yvon Delbos, foreign minister, told them. “Civilians should no longer be subjected to the threat of bombardment or capture by Mola’s forces (the insurgent northern army under Gen. Emilio Mola) which it is feared may happen soon,” Delbos added. Great Britain and France also have decided to conduct an investigation into the devastating bombing and machine-gunning of Guernica, sacred city of the Basque, Delbos told the commission. The Guernica inquiry will be conducted by trusted consular agents. It will seek to establish, the foreign minister explained, whether German pla

To Provide Haven London, April 29 (P) -- Britain agreed tonight to provide haven for children of Spanish Bilbao during the siege by civil war insurgents. Home Secretary Sir John Simon announced that the children might be brought to England by the national joint committee for Spanish relief, but without the aid of public funds. He specified a “limited number” of the children but did not say how many. There were authoritative indications tonight that British and French warships might aid the actual evacuation of the more than 300,000 non-combatants within the Basque capital. France wanted first to obtain a pledge of non-interference from Insurgent Generalissimo Francisco Franco. Britain hoped for a temporary truce between government Basques and insurgent troops during the period of evacuation. Situation Acute The Bilbao situation became acute tonight with insurgent capture of Guernica, 20

London, April 30.—(P)—London’s busmen voted today to strike at midnight, The threatened walkout by 145,000 men, which may paralyze the city’s main public transport system on Coronation day, May 12, became a virtual certainty when union delegates decided to instruct their men to quit.

LONDON, April 30.—(UP)—Mrs. Wallis Simpson's application for a final divorce decree was definitely set today for hearing in the divorce court Monday. Mrs. Simpson's application for a decree absolute, which would free her to marry the Duke of Windsor, was among those in today’s “cause” list of the divorce court, to be issued this afternoon as set for hearing Monday:

PARIS, April 30—(P)—France and Great Britain have agreed to aid in evacuation of civilians from Bilbao, in response to urgent appeals of the Basque Loyalist government, the foreign office asserted today. ‘Several thousand,’ it was said, were to be included in the first lot to be sent from the war-torn area and it was assumed that most of them would be small children. Great Britain, the foreign office said, undertook to obtain the consent of the Spanish Nationalist governing Junta to consent to the evacuation and agree not to fire on any Basque, French or British ships used to evacuate the refugees. Announcement Today The foreign office said that the decision to evacuate refugees probably would be announced formally at London late today. At France’s suggestion, Basque Loyalists asked the Central Loyalist government to house refugees in Spain, instead of abroad, so it was expected that the

SOBERTON, Hampshire, England, April 30.—(P)—A Royal Air Force pilot was killed and two others escaped in parachute jumps today from three military planes which crashed in mid-air. One plane flying above the formation nose-dived into the other two. The crash was the 25th fatal Royal Air Force accident this year, and caused the 47th death. There were 54 accidents and 96 deaths for the whole year of 1936.

LONDON, April 30.—A strike by 145,000 busmen at midnight threatened London and its suburbs today. There were approximately 25,000 in the city proper and 120,000 in surrounding counties who announced they would step from buses unless their demands were met by 4 p. m. (11 a. m. EST.) Denied their demand for a half-hour reduction in their eight-hour working day, the men rejected any compromise. Some 25,000 other busmen in counties surrounding London were expected to strike in sympathy.

By United Press LONDON, April 30.—The conference of British miners’ delegates decided unanimously today to strike on May 22. All districts will be asked to turn in their strike notices in time to become effective on that date.

1937-05-17.text: London — () — Unofficial but usually well-informed sources said Friday the British government appeared to have won its quarrel with the Duke of Windsor to keep Wallis Warfield from styling herself “Her Royal Highness” after they are married. British society and persons to whom the distinction between “The Duchess of Windsor” and “Her Royal Highness the Duchess of Windsor” are vital matters cited the highly authoritative “Debrett’s” as conclusive proof that former King Edward VIII could not win. They referred also to the status of Queen Elizabeth herself at the time she married the then Duke of York and contended that only an act of the king could confer a royal title on Mrs. Warfield. Queen Elizabeth, who was the commoner-born Lady Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon, was raised to royal rank by King George V, her father-in-law, by a special announcement after her marriage in 1923. Friday sources maint

LONDON, May 17 (4)—The British press today brought out into the open a controversy of its own over the possibility of a royal recognition of Mrs. Wallis Warfield by means of the formal announcement of her engagement to the Duke of Windsor by King George VI himself. While the Sunday Referee reported the king was ready to extend the royal family's sanction of the match by announcing the betrothal of his brother and the woman for whom Edward gave up his throne, the Express said such a move was impossible. “Ecclesiastical objections” to Mrs. Warfield as a twice-divorced person, the Express said, prevented the king from taking any such action. The Sunday Referee, which has not always been correct in its information concerning the abdicated monarch and his American fiancée, predicted King George would announce his brother's engagement this week. The style with which Mrs. Warfield would be desi

HONG KONG, May 17.—Sixty persons, most of them Japanese, were killed today when the Japanese tender Dojima Maru exploded at Queen's Pier. Ten mutilated bodies were recovered 100 yards from the pier in the harbor at the British Crown Colony here. The tender belonged to the Osaka Shosen Kaisha, Japanese freight and passenger steamship line.

LONDON (#) — Germany is constructing great new fortifications along the Baltic coast, it was disclosed Thursday night, to speed completion of a vast network of defenses at every border. The new line centers about Lübeck Bay north of Hamburg and looks northward toward the Nordic countries. Building of the fortifications was revealed by Germans who related that workers had jammed Travemünde, a popular spa near Hamburg, and rooms were at a premium for that reason. They recounted: The Priwall, a section of Travemünde where there are both sea and land plane facilities, has been designated as a submarine harbor. Fortifications have been erected east and west from Travemünde. A seaplane harbor has been constructed at Schlutup; an airdrome near Alt-Gartz. Coastal batteries have been embedded on the heights overlooking the ley eastward from Travemünde. Summer dwellers at Eckernförde have been ref

BALDWIN STILL LEADS HOT OPPOSITION TO DUKE AND BRIDE BAUIEANANSE Dg AVAOCAY AM | George VI, his coronation just over, today found reason for the uneasy rest of crowned heads in the vexing problem of his prospective sister-in-law, Baltimore-born, twice-divorced Wallis Warfield. In quarters close to the court it was generally held the king himself must settle the question of whether the bride-to-be of the former King Edward is to be fortified with the rank of 'Her Royal Highness' when she and Edward return to move in semi-hostile London court and society circles. King to Act The Sunday Referee predicted the king himself will announce the engagement of the Duke of Windsor and Mrs. Warfield, but even that will not settle the question of her rank. With the duke’s wedding plans—to be announced Tuesday, it was believed King George's decision would be forthcoming this week. In London this contro

INDIANAPOLIS, Ind., May 17—(UP)—Dick Merrill, transatlantic flier, was chosen today as official starter for the 25th annual 500-mile race at Indianapolis Motor Speedway May 31. Merrill made a round-trip hop to England last year with Harry Richman, night club entertainer, and made another round-trip last week in connection with the coronation. T. B. E. Myers, speedway general manager, said Merrill will fly to Indianapolis with a group of New York sports writers. He is a regular transport pilot between New York and Miami, Fla.

Valencia, Spain—(#)—Dr. Juan Negrin, Socialist former minister of the treasury, began Monday an effort to form Spain’s sixth civil war government. President Manuel Azana, called from virtual retirement to find a “win the war” government after Premier Francisco Largo Caballero was forced to resign, selected Dr. Negrin as premier-designate after he had talked with both the treasury minister and with Diego Martinez Barrio, president of congress. Largo Caballero, asked first to try a new government, failed to obtain the support of all parties. Dr. Negrin, the new man of the hour, is 48 years old and a former professor of medicine in the University of Madrid. He is an outstanding man and long an active Socialist. He served several congressional terms and entered the first Largo Caballero cabinet last September as treasury minister.

Bilbao. ()-Fighting hand to hand, Basque loyalists blocked the insurgent advance against Bilbao today on the heights of Biscargi, about ten miles east of here. After hours of intense bombardment of the series of hills held by the enemy, the government troops went over the top to take one of the mountain strongholds at bayonet’s point. They were met by a hail of rifle and machine gun fire and showered with hand grenades as they reached the opposing trenches on the upper slopes. Despite the bitter insurgent resistance, the Basques succeeded in reaching the top of the hill, where they forced back the insurgent defenders after a sanguinary hand to-hand battle.

1937-05-24.text: Monts, France, May 22 (4)—The Duke of Windsor, former British king now in a French castle, found himself entirely surrounded by Americans tonight. First and foremost was his duchess-to-be, Mrs. Wallis Warfield. Then there were Mrs. D. Buchanan Merryman, Mrs. Warfield's “Aunt Bessie” from Washington, D. C.; Mr. and Mrs. Herman L. Rogers of New York, and Mr. and Mrs. Frederick Bate, “personal American friends” of the duke. Bate is London representative of the National Broadcasting Company. At dinner the Duke of Windsor was the only “foreigner” present. An American trailer was parked at the gates of the Chateau de Cande. It harbored Cornelius Vanderbilt Jr. He sought to enter the grounds, but police turned him back. Rogers came to the gate and said they would “talk it over,” however. There was a mystery man. Villagers said he called himself “the senator from West Virginia,” but nobody could

SOUTHAMPTON, England, May 24 — (Pp) — Four thousand little children of the Spanish Basque-lands, safe in England from all gave the memories of a war they did not want, fled in screaming terror today from the thunder of a fleet of British military planes. The children, gathered in a city of 500 tents in the fields six miles from Southampton following their arrival from Bilbao, were wandering, big-eyed, about the camp this morning. It was their first day in a land of strange things and strange people. Suddenly, the rumble of aerial motors echoed over the English countryside. A fleet of Royal Air Force planes, out for a practice 'spin, roared overhead. Bilbao’s nightmare was too new! Expecting the crash of bombs, the sickening whine and thud of machine gun bullets and then—the gaping wrecks of homes—the children ran in blind panic for the tents.

NEW YORK, May 24 (AP).— Sources close to the family of Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh Monday reported that a son was born coronation night, May 12, to Colonel and Mrs. Lindbergh. The report was circulated widely, but lacked direct confirmation. The Lindberghs are at their English home, Longbarn, Sevenoaks, Kent. It was to this pastoral setting that the Lindberghs fled in December of 1935, shortly before Bruno Richard Hauptmann went to New Jersey's electric chair for the murder of baby Charles Augustus.

LONDON, May 24.—(UP)—Great Britain is sounding out the major non-intervention powers on the possibility of a truce in Spain which would permit the withdrawal of foreign volunteers fighting there, Viscount Cranborne, parliamentary secretary of the state for the foreign office, told questioners today in the house of commons. Cranborne said the government is asking the powers whether they would join Britain “with the object of inducing the parties to agree to a cessation of hostilities on all Spanish fronts for a period sufficient to enable the withdrawal of foreign volunteers.” “We feel that only with the greatest difficulty could withdrawal be carried out in the midst of active hostilities,” he said. “The replies of the various governments are still being awaited.” The question arose on resumption of parliament after the whitsun recess.

CLEVELAND, May 24— (INS) The birth of a son to Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh on May 13 was revealed in a letter to Mrs. Charles L. Cutter, 92 years old, grandmother of Mrs. Lindbergh, it was learned today. According to the letter, the baby was born “in England” and both Mrs. Lindbergh and the children were “very well indeed,” the grandmother was informed. Because of her advanced age, she did not talk directly to newspaper men, but issued the announcement through her housekeeper. She said she was permitted to say only that the letter came “from England,” but believed it may have been sent by Colonel Lindbergh himself. Mrs. Cutter is the mother of Mrs. Dwight W. Morrow, Mrs. Lindbergh's mother. She lived in Cleveland Heights. SEVEN OAKS, KENT, England, May 24— (INS) — Cables from the United States telling of the birth of a son brought no formal announcement from the Lindbergh househol

ROME, May 23—(4)—Italy is opposed to any armistice or truce in the Spanish Civil War at this time, a source close to the government said today. This represented authoritative Italian reaction to reports that Great Britain has proposed to the leading European powers an effort to halt fighting in Spain long enough to permit withdrawal of foreign volunteers. Virginio Gayda, Fascist writer who frequently voices official viewpoints, asserted such an armistice would be in effect “direct intervention” which would be all the more undesirable “because it would be exercised while the Spanish Nationalists (insurgents) are preparing to launch a decisive attack on Bilbao.” Other authoritative quarters said the British proposal would disturb the work of the non-intervention committee, which already is discussing the possibility of withdrawing foreign volunteers from Spain. (Well informed quarters in L

Charles A. Lindbergh, said today a baby boy was born to the Lindberghs Coronation night, May 12. Mrs. Charles L. Cutter, grandmother of Mrs. Lindbergh, said news of the new arrival came to her by letter from Mrs. Lindbergh. The letter which was received Saturday did not disclose the name of the child, she said. London, May 13. First reports of a new Lindbergh baby reached the United States embassy today from the Flying Colonel's home near Weald, Kent. But the Lindberghs turned aside all inquiries. His closest friends were unable to reach him by telephone. The reports, however, said Mrs. Lindbergh was in good health. The baby had not been seen by anyone outside the Lindbergh’s home, nor has the birth been registered. This need not be done locally until six weeks after birth and registration at the American consulate is not necessary.
ES Ne LONDON, W.P)—The Evening Standard reported Monday that Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh is in a nursing home in southern England.

1937-12-25.text: SANDRINGHAM, England, Dec. 25.—(#)—King George VI gave the age-old Christmas greeting of "peace and good will" in a broadcast today to the empire, heard by millions throughout the world. Seated before the microphone in his study in Sandringham House, the monarch reverted to the custom of his father, the late George V, who instituted an annual Christmas broadcast. There was none last year in the gloom that followed the abdication of the king's brother, Edward, now Duke of Windsor. Queen Elizabeth, Queen Mother Mary and other members of the royal family sat in an adjoining room as the monarch referred briefly to "this unforgettable year" of his coronation and to "shadows of enmity and fear" throughout the world. Speaking clearly and succinctly for only four minutes, the monarch said: (Continued on Page 5, Col. 2)

Jerusalem. -(/P)- Strong contingents of British troops guarded the Bethlehem pilgrimage today after reports were received that 43 Arabs were killed and more than 20 wounded in a furious two-day battle in the Tiberias region. Only three British casualties were reported in the battle and they suffered wounds. Pilgrims of many creeds and races thronged to the shrines of the Holy City and nearby Bethlehem today to commemorate the birth of a Prince of Peace while police guarded against a feared outbreak of terrorism. Pealing bells summoned Christmas worshippers to masses said by western, Greek and Armenian Christians; 4,000 British troops patrolled the Moab and Judean hills on guard against more terrorists. Heavily reinforced police guarded other areas after unconfirmed reports said a second battle in the Tiberias region had raised the toll of deaths to 33 in two days, Virtual Martial Law. Th

PAIN LAT NAT MNT BLTUL VR, Ri be AN OND Dec. 25.—A plea that the spirit of Christmas prevail to dispel ‘the shadows of enmity and fear’ over parts of the world was broadcast to the British Empire today by King George. His address, carried to the far reaches of the Empire, was rebroadcast by the National and Columbia Broadcasting Systems for the benefit of listeners in the United States. Professing inability to take the place of his father, the late King George, in the annual Christmas message to the Empire, the King expressed his gratitude to his subjects for their love and loyalty during “this unforgettable year now drawing to its end.” King George spoke from a room in Sandringham Palace. “We have promised to try and be worthy of your trust and this is a pledge that we shall always keep,” he said. Text of the King's address follows: “Many of you will remember the Christmas broadcasts of

Hendaye, Franco-Spanish Frontier, Dec. 24.-44%--The Spanish government declared tonight its forces had destroyed the last insurgent defenders of Teruel and hailed the victory as the first in a "final drive" to crush insurrection throughout Spain. But the insurgents, flatly denying the few hundred of their comrades remaining in Teruel had been annihilated, massed reinforcements to recapture the strategic city at the southernmost tip of the Aragon front. An army of 40,000 men commanded by General Miguel Aranda, insurgent chief in southern Aragon, was concentrated northwest of Teruel ready to participate in an encircling movement already started against government troops holding the city, the insurgent high command announced. Heavy snow had hampered movements of General Aranda’s army, but it was said to be ready for action. Government dispatches told of capturing the last insurgent strongho

TOKYO, Dec. 24.—(4#)—The Japanese government tonight placed upon the Japanese navy the brunt of blame for sinking of the United States gunboat Panay, but did not mention the army’s share in the incident. A note to the United States acknowledged Japan's responsibility for naval aircraft bombardment of the Panay and three Standard Oil vessels on the Yangtze river above Nanking on December 12, before Japanese captured China’s capital. The note, approved by Emperor Hirohito and the cabinet, said those responsible had been “duly dealt with according to law” and emphasized Japan's strenuous efforts henceforth to prevent such incidents involving neutral powers in the undeclared Chinese-Japanese war. But it did not specifically refer to the allegation that Japanese troops, in surface boats or from shore, machine-gunned the Panay. This previously had been disputed by Japanese political and army o

SHANGHAI, Dec. 25.—(Saturday)—(AP)—Japanese columns today crossed the Yellow River for a new drive into Shantung province while, in Shanghai, the Japanese command announced the fall of Hangchow, capital of Chekiang province and one of China’s most prosperous cities. For China, Christmas brought no peace on earth as the Japanese legions added rapidly to the thousands of square miles already conquered, carrying out their own concept of assuring the peace of the Far East. Tension Eased at Hangchow For Hangchow, however, there apparently was release from the terrors of siege. The Japanese announced their troops entered the city, for centuries famed as a beauty spot and religious center, at 8 a.m. Friday, pouring in through all its gates. There was no news of fighting. This was taken to mean the Chinese defenders had abandoned resistance and their capitulation spared Hangchow a final air bomb

Cannes, France, Dec. 25.—(P)—The Duke of Windsor practically bought out a floral shop today to celebrate his first Christmas with his bride, the former Wallis Warfield. Rising late after a Christmas eve dinner with a few friends, the duke went to his favorite floral shop and purchased nearly $300 worth of orchids, violets and out-of-season lilacs. With a big smile, he ordered the lot delivered at once to the duchess at the villa of Mr. and Mrs. Herman L. Rogers, where the Windsors are staying. The couple spent a quiet morning exchanging personal gifts.

Shanghai. — (4) - The United States prepared today quickly to reopen its embassy at Nanking, fallen capital of republican China, to safeguard American interests. The United States gunboat Oahu was ordered ready to sail up the Yangtze river to Nanking Tuesday, carrying Consuls John B. Allison and James Espy. Fourteen Americans still are in Nanking. The British and German embassies requested the Oahu also to transport their representatives to Nanking so that their embassies could be reopened without delay. No Change In Status. It was understood there would be no change in the embassy's status, despite Japanese occupation of the city, because the United States recognizes the central government of Generalissimo Chiang Kai-Shek as the only authoritative regime in China. (An international train, meanwhile, reached Hongkong, British crown colony, with 96 Americans among 296 refugees of eight na

1937-01-27.text: PORTSMOUTH, O., Jan. 27--(AP)—With its worst flood in history almost at crest stage, Portsmouth dug in today for the task of caring for refugees and preparing for a quick ‘clean up.’ City council appropriated $200,000 to get rehabilitation work under way as soon as the flood waters of the Ohio and Scioto rivers, which rose past 74.18 feet at 9 A. M., started to recede. Relief officials said it was necessary to evacuate nearly 5,000 of the 35,000 homeless in greater Portsmouth because of a critical sanitation problem. More than 1,500 already have been moved from the area.

BRUSSELS, Belgium, Jan. 26 (P) — Twelve persons were killed today when a Belgian mail plane crashed near Oran, Algeria. The eight passengers and four members of the crew perished when the pilot apparently attempted to land at Oran on a regular return trip from the Belgian Congo, in Central Africa.

HENDAYE, Franco - Spanish Frontier, Jan. 27 (UP) — Gen. Francisco Franco, insurgent generalissimo, has knocked the props from two of Madrid's main pillars of defense, putting the capital in near desperate circumstances, reliable uncensored dispatches said today. They were borne out by a speed-up in evacuation of non-combatants and food rationing in Madrid. Rebel forces succeeded in consolidating their gains at Aranjuez south of Madrid, which now appears definitely cut off from Madrid, just as is El Escorial, on the northwest. Franco's main army is expected to attack between Las Rosas and El Escorial as soon as the weather will permit.

Santander, Spain —(/P)— Despite bombs raining from a government seaplane, the Insurgent warship España Wednesday succeeded in a daring seizure of the Socialist patrol boat Alejandro at the very entrance to this Bay of Biscay harbor. The España’s anti-aircraft guns replied to the attack from the air and kept the bomber at bay until the raid was completed.

- Moscow, Jan. 26. (4)—One of the Bolshevist officials reputed to be responsible for the slaying of Tsar Nicholas and his family in 1918 himself faced the prospect of death. The Soviet government's net for those accused of plotting its downfall, cast ever wider by the testimony of 17 men on trial here as traitors, enmeshed Alexander Georgivich Belaborodoff, former president of the Orensburg Soviet. He was arrested at Rostoff-on-the-Don after M. S. Bugoslavsky, one of the 17 accused as Trotzkyist plotters, implicated him in a plot to overthrow the Soviet regime—an exile at Busk, Siberia, in. Some historians have written that Belaborodoff personally took part in the executions of the Tsar, the Tsarina, their son and four daughters, even cutting up and burning the bodies.

Alex Stein Taken to Moscow to Testify in Conspiracy Case. Moscow, Jan. 26—(U, P.)—Alex Stein, a German engineer, was brought in under guard at the trial of seventeen prominent Bolshevists today to testify that he and other Germans had been engaged in wrecking Soviet machinery. Stein’s appearance coincided with the indications that prosecution of various foreigners might follow the present trial, in which the defendants appear headed for the firing squad. Stein is not a defendant, but was brought in as a special witness. He is a German citizen. Speaking in German, he testified that he was engaged in wrecking with other Germans. They specialized in machinery. He asked permission of Vassily Ulrich, president of the military Collegium of the Supreme Court, who is presiding at the trial, to tell all about the wrecking. Ulrich cautioned him against mentioning names.

MOSCOW, Jan. 27 (P).—Sergei Sedoff, second son of Leon Trotsky, was reported arrested today upon the denunciation of factory workers at Krasnoyarsk, where there was alleged to have been an attempt to poison employees with generator gas. The report was not immediately confirmed officially. It was understood Sedoff had been missing since August.

MADRID, Jan. 27—Socialist troops, resisting Fascist attacks with machine guns and bombs, halted a threatened insurgent advance today in the El Pardo sector, five miles from the capital’s northern gates. The government barricades held firm under vicious Fascist onslaughts which Socialist commanders predicted might be the forerunner of a heavier and more general drive against the besieged city. Two insurgent attacks, the defense junta reported, were repulsed south of Madrid. Fighting around the capital began yesterday with a government artillery bombardment of Fascist fortifications west and north of the city. The enemy assault, with successful resistance from militiamen on the Socialist side of the barricades, followed. Military action, however, was slowed up by fresh rains, and the two sides retired temporarily.

1937-11-18.text: WASHINGTON, Nov. 18. —The United States and Great Britain today prepared to enter into a trade alliance of far-reaching economic and political significance. The two great English-speaking democracies announced simultaneously in Washington and London that a basis has been reached for a reciprocal trade agreement giving most-favored-nation treatment to the commerce between the two countries. The trade pact is regarded as one of the greatest forward steps to smash the barriers blocking world economic recovery. Great Britain is the United States’ largest customer. Political Significance As great as is its economic importance, the world-wide political significance of the tie between the United States and Britain looms even larger. Politically, it is regarded as democracy’s answer to the Fascist alliance concluded between Italy, Germany and Japan at Rome two weeks ago. Coming at the moment whe

LONDON, Great Britain today moved her foreign policy toward two distinct goals—weaken- ing of the Rome-Berlin axis through diplomatic talks in Berlin and strengthening of key position with insurgent Spain. A few hours after Lord Halifax arrived in Berlin for conversations with Chancellor Adolf Hitler on British-German relations, possibly including Germany's colonial demands, a proposal was made in the House of Lords to have the League of Nations consider Germany's demands. Germany Said Dangerous The proposal was made by Lord Allen of Hurtwood, who asserted that Germany was dangerous in her present "psychological mood." Lord Plymouth, undersecretary for foreign affairs, said the government felt there were "serious objections" to such procedure. He pleaded against arguing the colonial question "for obvious reasons," meaning that Halifax might be embarrassed in his forthcoming visit with Hi
WALMER, England, Nov. 17—(—Captain Harry Pearson, 72, who piloted many swimmers across the English Channel and sometimes was called the father of channel swimming, died today.

; BOSTON, Mass., Nov. 16—England is free of much of the labor unrest which we are experiencing. Labor troubles have decreased drastically in recent years. From a peak in 1926, the annual number of workers involved in disputes has dropped 86 per cent. Not only the return of prosperity, but the high degree of unionization, are responsible for this improvement. Total membership in trade unions in England at present is 5,400,000, or nearly one-half of all male industrial workers. Our own figures are roughly 7,000,000 union members. This is about one-fourth of our male industrial workers. Yet, surprisingly enough, union interest in England seems to be on the wane. Labor leaders over there are now trying desperately to stage a “demonstration” as they call it. They recently have had a hard time in getting even small audiences. When I asked one of the leaders the reason for this difficulty, he s

Vatican City, May 17. — (45) Pope Pius XI will elevate five prelates to the college of cardinals in two ceremonial consistories next month. Three will be Italians, one English, and one French. Their elevation will increase to 69 the strength of the college which traditionally is limited to a maximum of 70. The Vatican announced today the following with the named cardinals in a secret session Dec. 1: Archbishops Giuseppe Plazzardo, Vatican undersecretary of state, Ermenegilde Pellegrinetti, nuncio to Yugoslavia, Giovanni Piazza, patriarch of Venice, Arthur Hinsley of Westminster, and Pierre Gerlier of Lyon. The 57-year-old Pope will bestow red hats upon them at a public consistory Dec. 16. The elevation of the archbishop of Westminster will give England her first cardinal since the death of Francis Cardinal Bourne in 1945. With the new members, the college of cardinals will be composed of
STOCKHOLM, Sweden (UP) - The 1937 Nobel prize for literature has been awarded to the French author, Roger Martin Du Gard, it was announced today.

Ostend, Belgium, Nov. 16 (4)—A flaming Belgian airliner crashed today, all but wiping out the ancient grand ducal line of Hesse Bei Rhein. All seven occupants of the long plane were killed—in-cluding five members of the former German royal family which has close blood ties with every reigning house in Europe. The victims: Grand Duke George Donatus von Hesse Bei Rhein, 31, grandson of Queen Victoria. The grand duke’s 26 year old wife, the former Princess Cecile of Greece and Denmark and a first cousin of the Duchess of Kent. Their sons, Prince Ludwig Ernst, 6, and Prince Alexander George, 4. The grand duke’s mother, the dowager Grand Duchess Eleanore von Hesse Bei Rhein, 66. Baron Von Riedessel Zu Eisen-marshall of the grand duke’s court, Herr Martens, German glider expert, and a maid. Three crew members. The news overwhelmed Prince Ludwig von Hesse Bei Rhein, who was waiting in London to

| Shanghai, Nov. 18—(Thursday) | Chinese apparently were making /at least a temporarily successful stand today against Japan’s westward advance. With heavy rains helping them brew: Japanese planes and mobile equipment, the Chinese fought desperate rearguard actions to hold their enemy east of the main defense line between Shanghai and Nanking. _ In the capital, nevertheless, the evacuation of civilians and government bureaus was accelerated by an unofficial warning to the populace to flee the path of the Japanese advance. | Prepare for Attack The Domei (Japanese) news agency said Japan's army in North China had massed three columns along an 180-mile front on the Yellow river preparatory to an attack on Tsinanfu, capital of Shantung Province. Chinese declared the Japanese still were held above the river, which they must cross in the face of strong Chinese defenses to reach the last unconq

1937-08-06.text: LONDON, Aug. 6 (AP)—Lloyds, the British Underwriters, reported from Gibraltar today that an Italian and a British steamer were being bombarded by planes at a spot just off the coast of Algeria near war-torn Spain. The British tanker, British Corporal, flashed an SOS that she was being bombed and then later cancelled it and steamed into Algiers, 30 miles southeast of here. Crew Is Safe. Her crew of 43 were safe and the wireless receiver which she reported smashed was repaired. A few hours later, Lloyds said, the Italian steamer, Mongioia, dispatched an SOS saying she was bombed from the air. The ship was bound from Genoa to New Orleans. The first flash from the Corporal, en route from the Port of Abadan in the Persian Gulf to the Land’s End in England, said “we are being bombed, hurry.” Neither of the reports identified the attackers.

London, Aug. 6 (4)—The Italian steamer Mongicia was missing tonight hours after she and the British tanker British Corporal were mysteriously attacked by unidentified bombing planes in the western Mediterranean. The Mongicia flashed a brief SOS saying she had been attacked. There were no further reports. The British Corporal, after sending an SOS and then retracting it, reached the port of Algiers under her own power and apparently not seriously damaged. None of her crew of 43 was injured. Both ships were attacked almost at the same time and in the same spot off the coast of Algeria. Both Spanish government and insurgent planes are based within striking distance of either ship engaged in Spanish trade. The Mongicia was en route from Genoa to New Orleans, the British Corporal from the Persian Gulf port of Abadan to England with a cargo of gasoline. Both were miles off the coast. Few Air A

(By the Associated Press) War planes of unstated nationality bombed the British tanker British Corporal and the Italian steamer Mongolia today off the coast of Algeria near war-torn Spain. The tanker reached Algiers safely with none of her crew hurt. The Italian ship, bombed a few hours later, flashed an SOS telling of the attack. Neither ship was bound for a Spanish port. Insurgent commanders admitted a powerful government siege force including the rejuvenated Catalan arms—virtually has encircled insurgent General Francisco Franco's upper Aragon stronghold, Huesca. Government troops were reported facing “almost impregnable” insurgent fortifications on three sides of the city and government air squadrons were blasting it from the skies. Communiques from both sides reported demoralization in the other. Insurgents declared General Jose Miaja, commander of government troops in central Spain

ABOARD COAST GUARD CUTTER CHELAN, OFF NEWPORT. (UP). Ranger completed a brilliant defense of the America’s Cup Thursday winning a fourth straight race from Endeavour II and administering to the British sloop the most humiliating defeat in the 86 year history of the yachting series. According to unofficial figures, Ranger Thursday established 4 new America's Cup records for a triangular course, completing the 30 miles in 3 hours, 6 minutes and 55 seconds. The former mark of 3:09:01 was established by the original Endeavour in the second race of the 1934 series. Ranger’s unofficial finishing time was 3:46:55 p.m. Endeavour finished at 3:50:45. Thursday's race was over a triangular course. When the first leg was completed Ranger led by about a mile. Part of this lead came as a present when Endeavour arrived too soon at the starting mark and had to recross the starting line.

| Rome, Aug. 6 (AP).—The Italian government announced today that British and Italian diplomats would meet in Rome for formal conversations to settle differences between the two countries. British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain recently exchanged friendship letters with Premier Mussolini. Rome and London have been at odds since Britain insisted on the imposition of sanctions against Italy during the Italian conquest of Ethiopia. The tension was renewed with the outbreak of the Spanish civil war.

Ty Onited Press) London, Aug. 6. — Owners of the steam tankship British Corporal announced today that the vessel was bombed for an hour this morning by three monoplanes whose identity was not determined. The vessel suffered only slight damage, the owners said, and there were no casualties among the 40 crew members.

LONDON, Aug. 6—(4)—Esther Sebag-Montefiore, a 26-year-old widow, gave up more than a million dollars for love today. She wed Geoffrey Myddleton, 22, a physiologist, despite a clause in the will of her late husband, Arthur, which left her $1,900,000 on the condition she did not remarry. However, the will provided an annuity of $15,000 a year if she did marry again.

LONDON, Aug. 5.—(AP)—Another non-intervention bubble evidently had burst tonight on the eve of a neutrality committee vacation. Despite earlier indications that new compromises had been reached for reviving supposedly dying hope of isolating the Spanish civil war, the irreconcilables on the “hands off Spain” committee had made no concessions. The Earl of Plymouth, British chairman of the 27-power committee, announced that what had been heralded hopefully as a “mystery” meeting tomorrow to break the deadlock merely would be a session to “clarify” the issues and vote adjournment for a holiday. The new spurt of neutrality hopes was based on reports that Russia had modified her opposition to the British compromise plan—simultaneous withdrawal of foreign troops from Spain and recognition of the Spanish insurgents.

1937-03-16.text: WASHINGTON, March 16—The U. S. destroyer Fairfax today rescued the captain and crew of eight of the British four-masted schooner Avon Queen off the coast of San Salvador Island, the navy department was advised by radio. The commander of the Fairfax said he encountered the disabled schooner off the northeast coast of San Salvador Island flying a distress signal. The schooner was in a sinking condition with the main deck awash and the pumps out of order. The Fairfax took off the crew and the sinking vessel was abandoned. San Salvador Island is a small island north of Haiti and east of Cuba in the Atlantic.

Croydon, Eng., March 16, (7) — Officials at Croydon Airport announced receipt of word that an Imperial Airways liner carrying C. F. W. Dod, European manager of the lines, and 2 crew members had crashed near Cologne, Germany, killing all three. The ship left Croydon for Cologne yesterday evening. The other two aboard were the pilot, Capt. G. B. Holmes, who formerly flew in the United States and Canada, and the wireless operator, T. E. Langman.

LONDON, March 16.-(UP)--'Sir Austen Chamberlain, one of England’s most brilliant statesmen and a member of the family which has been a guiding influence in British politics for half a century, died today. Sir Austen was 73. He was a son of the famous Joseph Chamberlain of tariff reform and a half-brother of Neville Chamberlain, the brilliant present chancellor of the exchequer, slated to be next prime minister. - His was a career of climax and anti-climax, the tragedy of a man whose personal power in the house of commons was unequalled but who failed on two distinct occasions to attain the goal of his life —when it was almost within his grasp.

ELY, England—A town crier, ringing his bell of office, ran through the streets of the ancient village of Haddenham near here today, summoning all able-bodied men to report on the river bank to aid in combating flood waters which threatened to overwhelm 100 square miles of the richest farm land in Great Britain. Watches had kept vigil for days on the banks of the Ouse and its tributaries in Cambridgeshire, watching the waters rise from persistent rain and snow. Early today, watchers on Aldreth Causeway, near Haddenham, saw the old West River overflow and burst through Aldreth Causeway which holds back the water from the rich fens (marsh lands) south of Ely. Soon the water flooded a square mile of country to a depth of nine inches. A village constable was summoned and he roused town crier George Chapman, forty. Chapman broke precedent by grabbing his bell and ran through the streets callin

KALGAN, CHAHAR PROVINCE, CHINA, March 16—The Mongol hordes of northern China were reported by missionaries today to have declared their independence from China and proclaimed themselves a new nation—Mongokuo—“similar” to the Japanese-inspired state of Manchoukuo. Wholly unconfirmed reports brought to this last northern outpost of Chinese influence by missionaries from the snow wastes of northern Chahar, said that the irregular troops of the rebellious Mongol prince Teh Wang had established the new state with the assistance of Japanese advisers and military men. The advices caused Kalgan political circles to seethe with uncertainty over the future of all north China, many seeing in the alleged establishment of the puppet state of Mongokuo a threat of possible war between Japan and China. The report said the new nation carved out of northern Chahar province included an area roughly the siz

BERLIN, March 16 (P)—Col. General Hermann Wilhelm Goering, Germany’s number 2 man, made a sensational and unexplained reference in a radio speech today to “those who believe, as a last resort, to overcome Germany through murder and cowardly attempts.” In some quarters the phrases were interpreted as a sensational intimation that a possible attempt on the lives of leading personalities of the Nazi regime might have come to the government's attention. The general, whose functions are virtually those of prime minister, was speaking in commemoration of the second anniversary of Germany’s regained “army equality.” Toward the end of his speech, at a point where the radio transmission was poor, he cried: “May those be forewarned who believe, as a last resort, to overcome Germany through murder and cowardly attempts; here, too, the fervent love of the entire people will constitute the safest ram

HENDAYE, Franco-Spanish Frontier, March 16.—(uncensored)—UP—Gen. Jose Miaja’s international brigade isolated a large body of Italian soldiers and a 600-truck army supply train at Brihuega today, frontier dispatches reported. Loyalist aviation and artillery began an intense bombardment of the town of 5,000 persons, headquarters of Gen. Jose Moscardo, hero of the Alcazar siege and commander of the left column in the nationalist army’s fifth offensive against Madrid. In 24 hours the loyalists drove forward from Trijueque, in the Guadalajara sector northeast of Madrid, to encircle Brihuega and attack it from the rear. Uncensored reports from the scene said the city was almost surrounded, with the army supply train parked in the center of the town. Loyalist aviation repeatedly bombed the food and munition trucks of Gen. Moscardo’s division, destroying many of them, and bringing the advance of

BERLIN, Mar. 16.——Col. General Hermann Wilhelm Goering called down "oe" today upon the heads of those who "believe, perhaps as a last resort, that they can overpower Germany by murder or cowardly assassinations." In a rearmament day speech which some interpreted as an intimation that a possible attempt on the lives of leading personalities had come to the attention of the government, Germany's No. 2 man warned "all" at home again "playing with fire." The reference to a possible attempt at "murder or cowardly assassinations" was not contained in the published version of General Goering’s speech, but the propaganda ministry acknowledged he had said it. The propaganda ministry said the phrase was merely an impulsive outburst against Communists and denied it had any special significance.—— General Goering, who is the air minister, extolled armament as the Reich’s greatest contribution to pea

1937-03-19.text: NEW LONDON, Texas, March 19—(AP)—Laborers ceased digging into the ruins of the London consolidated school this afternoon and wearily said “the job is finished” after 425 bodies had been removed from the pile of debris. Colonel C. E. Parker, national guard commander, said every brick had been turned in the basement of the explosion-rocked structure and that the job of seeking bodies had ended. He said final cleaning up would take only about an hour longer. He said about 425 bodies had been lifted from the pile of steel and brick and added that “there may have been a few more than that.” Wearied oil field laborers who had toiled for nearly 21 hours, some of them during a slashing rainstorm, stopped work in groups and went home to bereaved wives.

London, March 19.—(#)—The last apparent barrier to Mrs. Wallis Simpson's absolute divorce and her marriage to Edward of Windsor was cleared today when a charge of "collusion" was dismissed by the president of the British divorce court. Sir Boyd Merriman, president of the court, directed the charge stricken from the record after the king's proctor informed the court, treating the case "as any other," he had made a careful investigation and failed to find any grounds to prevent the absolute divorce of Mrs. Simpson and Ernest Simpson. His action following the proctor’s surprise move in asking "for instructions" in the case removed all legal obstacles except the technical granting of the final decree April 27th.

TRIPOLI, Libya, March 17 (*)— Premier Mussolini, referring scathingly to British nervousness over Italy's ascendancy in the Mediterranean, told a cheering throng of 100,000 today the Italian empire had been forced to rearm to meet the rearmament threat of others. While the guns of the massed Italian battlefleet boomed in the harbor of the province's capital, Il Duce shouted: “We rearm on sea, in the sky and on land because it is our imperious duty in the face of the armaments of others.” Declaring that such reports disturbed the peace of all peoples, Mussolini said “an alarmist campaign has been evident in the more or less great democratic countries over my trip to Libya. This neuropathic alarmism, this sowing of suspected dangers, does not enhance the cause of peace because it profoundly disturbs relations between peoples.
