LONDON, Oct. 4 U.P—The government has avoided an open break with the duke of Windsor by giving him permission to visit the United States with his Baltimore-born bride, it was understood today. Permission for the visit was given most reluctantly, it was said in quarters close to Buckingham palace, to end the rumors—which here were interpreted almost as threats—that the duke might return to Britain. The public commented today that he and his duchess might settle down in the United States eventually. There seemed some reason for belief that any such decision might win government approval—if for no reason.

ONasV¥ SS 2208 GF S22 2 SALE LONDON, Oct. 4—()—An unidentified submarine tried to torpedo the British destroyer Basilisk, the admiralty said today, in an encounter in the western Mediterranean — the first since inauguration of the patrol plan drafted at Nyon to drive pirate warcraft from the great sea. One torpedo was fired at the Basilisk, which replied by releasing a depth charge. The torpedo missed the destroyer, but whether the depth charge took effect was not known.

LONDON, Oct. 4--(UP)—The British Labor party, in conference at Bournemouth today, unanimously approved a resolution calling for a boycott on Japanese goods and urging the government to put a ban on munitions or financial credits to Japan. As the resolution was passed, Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain had received a letter from the executive committee of the party urging a special session of parliament to consider action in the Chinese-Japanese crisis.

NEW YORK, ()—Reports that the exiled former British monarch, the Duke of Windsor, and his American bride might become part-time residents of the United States were revived today as they planned an American visit. While the terse announcement of their projected trip here gave no hint of their plans beyond a study by Windsor of housing and working conditions in the United States, it renewed speculation that the principals in the most famous romance of this generation might purchase a home in America. It has been reported frequently since their marriage last June that the former Wallis Warfield hoped to spend considerable time near her former home in Baltimore each year. It was taken as a matter of course that “Aunt Bessie,” Mrs. 1D. B. Merryman, who returned last week from Europe, silent about her niece and new husband, had charge of arrangements, but the question “where will they live whi

The Associated Press. LONDON, Oct. 4. — Scores of bleeding, battered demonstrators were in hospitals and jails today after police clashed with a veritable army of anti-Fascist demonstrators bent on stopping a parade of Sir Oswald Mosley’s blackshirts Sunday. Long-smoldering hostility between British Fascists and Leftist factions broke into open street warfare, precipitating one of the wildest disorders in London’s history. Mounted police and bobbies on foot, concentrated in southeast London, charged repeatedly into the mob of anti-Fascists, swinging their batons in an effort to clear the streets of barricades thrown up by nearly 100,000 demonstrators. The streets were strewn with fallen men and women, some knocked unconscious, many with head wounds and other injuries. They lay where they fell until ambulances could get through the turbulent mob to take them away to hospitals. Announce 96

PARIS, (AP) Edward of Windsor announced Sunday night he will bring his American born duchess to her native land “in the near future.” The former king-emperor of the British empire, who renounced his throne for love of the former Wallis Warfield of Baltimore, said he and his bride of four months would visit both the United States and Germany to study housing and working conditions of the two nations. The sudden announcement, made while the duke and duchess were in Paris on a shopping trip, immediately raised speculation concerning the couple's exact plans and the implications of Edward's journey to his wife's homeland. The brief statement merely said, however, the trip would afford new opportunity to study “the well being of the working man” in which his royal highness “has always interested himself.” British circles of Paris, as well as London itself, were plunged by the surprise move in

London, Oct. 3 (A)--The informed Italian press indicated today that Premier Mussolini would turn down the Franco-British invitation to a three-power conference on the Spanish civil war, thus muddling further the tense European situation. Il Duce, in Italy, studied his reply to the note which was designed to lead to withdrawal of thousands of Italian soldiers fighting for Spanish insurgent forces. The polite, but frank, invitation hinted that if Mussolini is not willing to withdraw Italian volunteers from Spain, the French frontier would be thrown open to shipment of munitions to government forces. The only open indication of Premier Mussolini's intentions was contained in an article in his newspaper, Popolo D'Italia, which said Count Dino Grandi, Ambassador to London, had suggested to British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden that such a conference seemed “inopportune.”

1937-11-20.text: Berlin, Nov. 20—(AP)—An official invitation to Baron Konstantin Von Neurath, Germany's foreign minister, to visit England was announced today. No date was set. This was generally considered the one concrete result of the “unofficial” visit to Germany of Viscount Halifax, Britain's lord president of the council, who yesterday spent five hours with Chancellor Adolf Hitler at Berchtesgaden, discussing Anglo-German relations. It was recalled that Von Neurath cancelled a scheduled visit to London last June 21. Germany and Britain then were at odds over the Spanish civil war. It was announced that Lord Halifax would leave for London tomorrow, according to his original schedule.

Berchtesgaden, Germany, Nov. 19—Viscount Halifax, of Britain, and Chancellor Adolf Hitler, of Germany, today exchanged views on Anglo-German relations in a five-hour meeting but kept to themselves any conclusions they may have reached. Despite official secrecy, however, there were indications that few if any, concrete results were achieved by the “unofficial” visit of Britain’s Lord President of the Council to Hitler's picturesque mountain retreat here. The meeting, toward which European Chancellories had been looking for a week, occupied two hours less than the seven originally scheduled and Hitler was understood to have used half the time showing his guest the beauties of the Bavarian winter landscape and his art treasures.

LONDON, Nov. 19.— (U.P) — Russia, alarmed by the threat to her Far Eastern frontier as a result of Japanese victories in China, has informed the Spanish loyalist government that she is withdrawing material support, it was reported tonight. The loyalist regime at Barcelona has been told, it was said, that Russia's role in Spain must be liquidated because of “growing preoccupation” with events in the Far East. ‘Need Men at Home. It is necessary, according to the Russian notification, for the Red army to hold all its pilots, fighting and bombing planes and war materials ready to meet any emergency at home. Withdrawal of Russian support would strip the loyalists of their greatest source of aid, at a crucial moment when Insurgent Generalissimo Francisco Franco is about to launch a large-scale objective on the northern Aragon front with the objective of cutting off Madrid from communication wi

PARIS, .?. Premier Chautemps told the chamber of deputies Friday night a situation of “terrible gravity” had been disclosed by the government's investigation of secret revolutionary societies. Armed mobile guards were stationed about government buildings as police struck at what authorities believed to be a rightist revolutionary committee organized to seize power and apparently capable of waging warfare on a nationwide scale. The radical-socialist premier said the government would ask special legislation to reinforce its swift action against a secret society known as “Les Cagoulards,” “the hooded ones,” thought to be one section of the revolutionary group. The chamber gave the people's front government a 339 to 160 vote of confidence after Chautemps pledged the cabinet to preserve “republican order” at home and defend peace abroad. Getting More Serious. After a conference with Chautemps

SHANGHAI, Nov. 20 (AP)—A Japanese army spokesman declared today that 15 Japanese soldiers under a second lieutenant captured Soochow, keystone of China's “Hindenburg line,” without firing a single shot. The spokesman declared the fall was “one of the most significant captures of an important city in the annals of war.” According to this account there was no real Chinese resistance at Soochow, considered the gate to Nanking, the Chinese capital from which the government withdrew today. The main Japanese force, expecting to be confronted by at least one Chinese division, was amazed to meet only small apparently dazed groups of Chinese soldiers, with loaded rifles and fixed bayonets, lolling about Soochow as the Japanese marched in. None of these even questioned the presence of Japanese troops, he said. The spokesman said the lack of Chinese resistance was due probably to extreme fatigue, o

Shanghai, Nov. 19 (AP) — China's leaders at Nanking debated tonight whether to defend the capital at all costs or, by voluntary withdrawal as the Japanese approached, save it from destruction by Japanese warplanes and guns. Japanese asserted their legions drew closer to Nanking as hammer blows in the center, right and left of China's “Hindenburg line” weakened that defense system some 56 miles west of Shanghai but still from 125 to 150 miles from Nanking. A Japanese army was reported within three miles of Soochow and preparing for an assault on that central strongpoint. Kashing, 35 miles to the southeast, was already in Japanese hands and its defenders in flight. Changhsu, 25 miles to the north, was being encircled by Japanese columns which drove past its walls to the west. In Nanking, Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek and his military associates were understood to favor defense of the city

| SHANGHAI, Nov. 20 — (AP) — Japan’s legions toward Nanking, China's capital, today through three gaps in the main Chinese defenses. Soochow, pivotal strongpoint of China's “Hindenburg” line west of Shanghai, fell to the Japanese after a fierce bombardment. Japanese said the Chinese army was retreating in confusion from the city, 50 miles west of Shanghai and about 125 miles east of Nanking. Both ends of the “Hindenburg” line also had been turned by the Japanese today, the 100th day of hostilities on the Shanghai front. Kashing, 25 miles southeast of Soochow, was in Japanese hands. A third Japanese column had skirted Changshu, 24 miles to the north. Chinese did not deny the fall of Soochow. They said the vital defense center was abandoned after it virtually had been

| Hendaye, Franco-Spanish Frontier, Nov. 19.—()-——-A Spanish government dispatch asserted government artillery today scored direct hits on an insurgent staff headquarters at Fuentes de Ebro, on the Aragon front in northeastern Spain. While government field guns pounded the middle Aragon front, Generalissimo Francisco Franco's insurgent forces sloshed through mud to prepare for their general offensive, which insurgent leaders have declared would begin as soon as the weather turned favorable. One report said Franco was sending some of the Aragon battalions on all sectors, to the Madrid and Almeria fronts, in central and southern Spain, planning to open a general attack on all sectors.

After a series of urgent conferences among leaders of the Nazi government it was announced that Germany would ask that the neutrality control powers—Great Britain, France, Italy and Germany—meet, under the revised control agreement, to undertake pertinent measures. "The German government, at any rate, is not willing to look on idly at the practice shooting by Spanish bolshevist U-boat pirates until in the end they may even score a hit," said the communique. It was recalled that last time a German warship was attacked in Spanish waters, when the battleship Deutschland was bombed by airplanes in the Balearic islands, Fuehrer Adolf Hitler sent a fleet to bombard Almeria and kill some 20 persons.

LONDON. (P. There were indications Friday night Great Britain would grant Spanish insurgent Generalissimo Franco the rights of a belligerent government if he captures Bilbao. The foreign office received Franco's request that Britain accord his government rights and obligations of an independent state as far as hostilities are concerned. There was no official comment, but usually reliable informants said favorable action depended upon Franco's success in the Bilbao campaign. Franco, under belligerent status, could establish a legal blockade of Spanish government ports if his navy is sufficiently strong. He would have the advantages of international law to support military activities. Hitherto, British observers point out, insurgent ships have been considered here to be operating as pirates if they sought to prevent free movement of shipping into Spanish government ports, or interfered wit

London, June 19. (AP)—Don Budge, America’s top ranking tennis star, crushed Henry Wilfred (Bunny) Austin, British Davis Cup ace, 6-1, 6-2, in the final round of the Queens Club tournament today. Budge’s one-sided triumph not only enabled him to retain the title he won a year ago but also established him more firmly than ever as favorite for the All-England championship, starting at Wimbledon on Monday. Budge finished the tournament with the remarkable record of having lost only six games in 12 sets. The crowd of 2,000 sat almost silent in amazement as he made Austin look like a second-rater.

LONDON, June 19 (A Charley): Laughton, asked by the Daily Express about his inclusion in a list of alleged tax avoiders at Washington, said today. “My dear fellow, I don't know anything about the damned thing. It’s been dithering over my head for two years now and I’m so tired of hearing about it. (Dither: to tremble, quake, quiver, shake; also bother, trouble—Ed.)

AIGUES-VIVES, France, June 18 (*)—Gaston Doumergue, 73, former president and twice premier of France, died today in his native village. The elderly statesman had lived in retirement among the vineyards of his countryside since he slipped quietly out of Paris Nov. 15, 1934, at the end of his second term as prime minister. “Papa” Doumergue, as he was known, was the first Protestant to hold that office under the Third Republic. Despite his nickname, Doumergue was a bachelor until he was 67. He was married to Madame Jeanne Grave, a widow, just 12 days before he left the Elysee palace at the end of his initial term in 1931. In February 1934, after the bloody “Stavisky” riots, the aging statesman was called to the service of his country once again to weld all parties except Socialists and Communists into a national government. In November of the same year, however, he resigned the premiership

Rome, June 18.—(/?)—The Giornale D’Italia in a dispatch from Salamanca, Spain, reported today 104 American volunteers to the Spanish government army perished in the sinking of the steamship Cuidad de Barcelona May 30. The Americans were said to be part of a group of 1,000 foreign volunteers, most of whom were reported lost. The dispatch also said 800 airplane motors of American manufacture sank with the vessel.

| Moscow, June 18 (#)— Russia's drive against enemies within was expanded tonight to include those charged with speculation in bread, tampering with the Soviet lumber industry, delaying automobile production and wrecking locomotives. There was no indication of any lessening of the hunt for those accused of adhering to Leon Trotsky, exiled revolutionary leader, or of sabotage and conspiracy plots to overthrow the Soviet Union. Already more than 100 persons have been executed by firing squads. Many thousands are believed to be in jails and labor camps. Denunciations of “wreckers, spies and diversionists” continued to pour into Moscow from Arctic Archangel and the Black and Red deserts of middle Asia, the Taiga or swampy forestlands of the Soviet far east. The latest indications of executions came from middle Asia where seven persons were condemned on charges of wrecking locomotives in the

HENDAYE, June 198.—(AP)—A “black arrow”—part Italian—brigade seized the Sondica airport just outside Bilbao today as insurgent headquarters reported the capture of more territory on the edges of the battered Basque capital. The insurgents said the fleeing Basques fired the hangars and burned an “undetermined number” of airplanes. Casualty losses in the past week of furious fighting were set by the insurgents at 20,000 killed, wounded, captured and deserted. The Basques insisted they still held Mount Archanda, key point of their third line of defense on the east bank of the Nervion river. They asserted they still held the ruins of the Casino and other buildings in Bilbao after a day of bitter fighting. Refugees who made their way here tonight said Bilbao was fortified with barricades of cobblestones and hidden mines for a finish fight.

1937-07-05.text: Paris, July 4 (&) — Two French warships were ordered tonight to speed to the Spanish coast between Bilbao and Santander, where the insurgent cruiser Almirante Cervera today captured the French refugee ship Tregastel. London, July 4 (®)—The British cabinet will meet tomorrow to review the grave international situation created by the deadlock over conflicting schemes for keeping Spain's civil war beyond the Pyrenees. Although some British authorities believed there were indications Italy and Germany might be won to a compromise the tension which had gripped European capitals since Friday was unrelaxed. Friday a meeting of the directing subcommittee of the 27 nations committee to keep the Spanish war isolated adjourned with Europe clearly aligned in two camps—Britain and France, backed by Soviet Russia, against Italy and Germany, supported by Portugal. The British cabinet faces a difficult

ROME-U.P.—Premier Benito Mussolini, fiery leader of more than 41,000,000 Fascists, was reported today to have abandoned all hopes of an understanding with Great Britain and to be preparing actively for a possible war in the Mediterranean within one year. Persons close to Il Duce said the dictator is convinced that England intends to “humble” him as soon as the British rearmament program has been completed.

TOKYO, July 3—Dispatches from Hsinking, capital of the Japanese-inspired state of Manchukuo, said today that Soviet Russia would start withdrawal of troops and gunboats from Amur river islands this afternoon. Recall of the forces under an agreement reached between the Japanese ambassador to Moscow and the Soviet foreign office further eased war tension arising from a clash between Soviet gunboats and Japanese-Manchukuoan forces last Wednesday. The dispatches said 20 Russian patrol boats were being withdrawn from the Sennufu and Bolshoi islands in the Amur river in addition to troops. The Japanese army in Manchukuo, in a statement from Hsinking hailed the peaceful settlement of the dispute but warned that further “illegal acts” against Manchukuoan territory by the Soviets would not be tolerated. Actual Russian evacuation, however, apparently was awaited by Japanese army leaders before the

TOKYO, July 4.—(AP)—Complete evacuation of Soviet land and naval forces from disputed islands in the Amur river was reported in dispatches reaching Tokyo today, ending a five-day Russo-Japanese war scare. Headquarters of Japan’s Manchurian army at Hsinking reported Russia had withdrawn all her troops and river gunboats from the immediate vicinity of Sennufu and Bolshoi islands, where Russian and Japanese forces clashed Wednesday with numerous Russian casualties. The Russians began efforts to salvage two of their gunboats, one of which was sunk and the other beached and badly damaged by Japanese-Manchoukuo artillery Wednesday. Japanese authorities here and in Hsinking asserted the Russian evacuation of the islands, about 75 miles southeast of Blagoveschensk, provided only temporary appeasement of a situation in which continued friction is to be expected. Botwood, Nfld., July 5 (GP) Ready for an experimental flight across the Atlantic, Capt. Harold E. Gray, master of the Pan-American Clipper III, said today he planned to start the big flying boat on its eastward crossing at 4 p.m., E.K.S.T. 'We'll be flying on a weather map,' he said, 'and the map at present indicates nearly ideal conditions for observations: clear weather on both sides of the ocean and everything from sunshine to snow and fog in between.' Gray and his six-man crew, which includes a steward, did not appear worried by the prospects of storms on their 1,995-mile (CQ) hope to Foynes, Irish Free State.

SEARCY, Ark. June 5 (UP)— Two persons were injured, one seriously, when they were struck by a train today at Bald Knob, two miles northeast of here. The injured were Wilbur Bell, 25, of Wynne, Ark., and his wife, 26. Bell received a fractured leg, shoulder injuries and numerous scalp lacerations. His condition was not believed critical. Mrs. Bell was reported near death this afternoon by physicians. Her skull was fractured and she received several cuts and bruises. First reports said Bell and his wife were walking on the Missouri Pacific railway track early today and were hit by the "Sunshine Special," running from Memphis to Little Rock.

WASHINGTON. (UP). The treasury has sketched a legislative program to seal “loopholes” in the revenue laws, officials disclosed. They added the suggestions will be laid before the senate-house committee on tax evasion and avoidance whenever the committee is ready to receive it. The committee will decide Tuesday whether to continue hearings in its tax investigation or to begin drafting legislation at once. Treasury tax officials and attorneys already have explained to the committee a series of alleged tax avoidance devices, sprinkling their testimony with the names of leaders in finance, business and society. Authorities disclosed one major proposal to increase tax.

Earle, Pennsylvania’s “New Deal” governor, told a rain-drenched throng of cheering steel strikers and coal miners today that the state's attorney general on Wednesday “to see if we can't force an election.” The governor told the crowd, estimated at 7,500 by Sheriff Michael J. Boyle: “You don’t need acts of violence when you have Franklin Delano Roosevelt in Washington, a liberal congress and a governor like me.” Posea One Question Gov. Earle’s comment on “forcing an election” referred to the claims by John L. Lewis’ C.I.O. leaders that the union would win if collective bargaining elections were held in the plants of steel companies along the seven-state steel strike front. 1937-08-03.text: ROME. (%). Benito Mussolini has assured British Premier Chamberlain of his friendship in a personally signed letter. The letter was presented to Chamberlain by Count Dino Grandi, Italian ambassador to London.

LONDON (#) — An exchange of personal messages of friendship between the heads of the British and Italian governments was believed Monday night to have opened a new phase of Anglo-Italian relations, possibly removing one of Europe's most dangerous friction points. A letter from Premier Benito Mussolini to Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain was delivered Monday to complete the exchange. Relations between Italy and Britain have been cool in recent years, at times badly strained, because of the conflict of interests in the Mediterranean and the Red Sea and a series of diplomatic issues. British officials expressed belief this might be ended now.

London, Aug. 3, (®)—King George VI flew from Windsor Castle to Southwold, Suffolk, today in the royal family’s new red and blue monoplane for his first flight since he became king last December. The 115 mile flight was made in 35 minutes. The king did not take the controls himself. The plane was flown by Wing Commander E. F. H. Fielden, whose post as captain of the king’s flight was created by King Edward VIII before he gave up the throne to George. The twin-engined plane circled over the royal lodge at Windsor where the king had been spending the weekend with his family before heading for the boys’ camp which the king organized when he was Duke of York. Some 400 boys chosen from factories and schools are given holidays at the camp by the sea.

Newport, R. I, Aug. 2.—(AP)—Ranger, Harold S. Vanderbilt’s “Galloping Ghost” of the sailing seas, handed T. O. M. Sopwith’s Endeavor II a record-smashing drubbing today of such proportions that the British challenger for the America’s Cup promptly took “time out” before resuming what now looks like a hopeless pursuit of the fastest “J” sloop this country ever sent to the yachting wars. After trailing his American rival across the finish line of a 30-mile triangular course by 18 minutes, 82 seconds, approximately three miles, thereby sustaining his second straight defeat by a margin even more crushing than was witnessed Saturday, Sopwith immediately requested and received permission from the New York Yacht Club's race committee for a day’s postponement. The third race thus will be set back to Wednesday while the Briton seeks some means of getting better results from a boat that tonight ap

Newport, R.I., Aug. 3—A one-day halt in the yachting battle for the America’s cup was called today in the wake of a second rout of the British challenger, Endeavour II., by Harold S. Vanderbilt's defending sloop, Ranger. Both yachts were taken to the Herreshoff yard at Bristol for inspection after T. O. M. Sopwith, thoroughly trounced by Vanderbilt in the two races already held, asked for a postponement of today's scheduled race.

Bristol, R. I., Aug. 3, (P) — An examination of the hull of Tom Sopwith’s British Cup challenger Endeavour II in drydock here today disclosed no apparent damage or trouble to the sloop. Sopwith said he was “just looking over” the challenger and probably would not do anything to her. Painters were touching up the bottom of Ranger, also drydocked for examination.

HENDAYE, Franco - Spanish frontier, Aug. 2.——()—Insurgent artillery opened a bombardment of Madrid's outer defenses today after driving a spearhead into Spanish government lines west of the capital. Battles were fought on three other fronts. Generalissimo Francisco Franco's troops pressed hard against government defenses in eastern and southern Spain. On the northwestern front, insurgents reported defeating an attempt to break their lines east of Oviedo, in Asturias. Government forces had about 1,000 troops in the rout attack, the insurgent reports. At Cuero, troops numbering 8,000 rushed against insurgent lines, only to be caught in a crossfire of rifle and machine gun bullets. “Two hundred bodies were left dangling in barbed wire entanglements when the attackers retired,” the advices said. R. by any means” in a denunciation of the wrecking of the Russian consulate at Tientsin. While he and his Baltimore-born duchess—surrounded by 70 trunks in their nine-room suite at the Hotel Meurice—puzzled over where to go now, his spokesman made non-committal replies to scores of rumors. (By The Associated Press) PARIS, Nov. 6. — The Duke of Windsor decided tonight to drop his survey of world working conditions until the storm raised by American labor criticism on his trip to the United States subsided. After a day of indecision during which Windsor considered an immediate trip to Soviet Russia to balance his tour of Nazi Germany and prove to the world he plays no politics, persons close to him said he and his duchess would remain in Paris a week before leaving for a rest. Hopes To Pave Way Friends said the duke hoped to pave the way for his postponed study of American labor conditions with possible trips to Russia, Scandinavia and Europe's “neutral countries” after the “misconceptions” over his motives had been cleared. Rome, Nov. 6.— (4) —Fascists warned the world tonight that the military forces of Italy, Germany and Japan were prepared to back the tri-power anti-communist pact signed today. They intimated that the brief agreement, which makes Italy a charter member of the German-Japanese anti-bolshevist front, binds the three powers to a "collaboration" which goes beyond even the fight on communism. The note specified such an "exchange of views" would be within the framework of the nine-power treaty under which the Brussels conference was convoked. Neither the site of the possible meeting nor the participating nations were designated, however, leaving the door open to Japan to express her wishes. onangnal, NOV. /—(ounday)—(/#P)—The vanguard of a Japanese flying column driving north from Hangchow bay was reported today to be within 25 miles of Shanghai. Refugees streaming from Sung-kiang, 22 miles southwest of Shanghai, informed Red Cross ambulance drivers the column had split into several units, with an advance body reaching a rice ferry on the Whangpoo river, three miles from Sunkfang, at dawn. While warships heavily bombarded a number of ports along the bay, from which the Japanese launched their thrust suddenly yesterday, the warplanes invaded the rich silk, cotton and rice region between the bay and Shanghai. BRUSSELS, Nov. 6 (UP).—The United States today defeated an attempt to let the Far Eastern peace conference lapse into oblivion after the delegates of 19 nations, discouraged by the new German-Italian-Japanese alliance, sent a note to Japan offering their services as mediators. Norman H. Davis, America’s “roving ambassador,” battled almost single-handedly to keep the conference in session after dispatch of the note, which rejected Japan's contention that the signatories and adherents of the nine-power Washington treaty are without authority to “interfere” in her war in China. The Tokyo government was asked whether it would establish contact with the conference and enter into peace conversations. MOSCOW, Nov. 6—(4)—The communist international defied a triple alliance of Germany, Italy and Japan tonight on the eve of the 20th anniversary of the Bolshevist rise to power in Russia. The Comintern, international communist organization centering in Moscow, warned the three powers their workers, inspired by 20 years of socialism in Russia, would use the next war for a revolution against capitalism. A defiant Comintern manifesto was issued as an estimated 1,099,000 Russians made ready to parade through Red Square tomorrow before Joseph Stalin. SHANGHAI Nov. 6. (Sunday) — Two divisions of China's crack combat troops were rushed to the Sun-gvin sector today to protect the vital Shanghai-Nanking communication line from a Japanese flying column thrusting inland from the south. The Chinese were reported making good progress against the invaders and the immediate threat to the Chinese right flank at Shanghai was believed to have been averted. Strike At Flank The new Japanese column sweeping in from the seacoast south of Shanghai struck at the Chinese flank. A Japanese spokesman said the column, newly landed from transports and fighting “every inch of the way,” pushed the Chinese lines back 18 miles to the south bank of the Whangpoo river. May 28—(AP)—Friends of the Duke of Windsor said today they had received a telephone message direct from Edward which informed them that he had lost his fight to obtain for Wallis Warfield the title: “Her Royal Highness.” An important announcement affecting the whole issue of the titles which the duke and his future wife will bear was expected shortly. London — Great Britain smoothly switched governments today and Stanley Baldwin, “saviour of the monarchy,” left the prime ministry to return to his favorite avocation of raising pigs. The 69-year-old statesman handed over one of the world’s biggest jobs to conservative Arthur Neville Chamberlain, his right hand man who is only one year his junior. “Honest Stan” Baldwin quit with his political prestige at its peak. Although he was virtually unknown to the general public 16 years ago, probably no other prime minister in 100 years has retired amid such acclaim—chiefly because of his handling of the abdication crisis last December. Drives to Palace Months of preparation for the change from Baldwin to Chamberlain made the momentous event: (Continued on Page 15, Col. 2)

London—Stanley Baldwin resigned as prime minister today, Neville Chamberlain succeeding him, and the British cabinet underwent an extensive reorganization. It was mostly a reshuffling of cabinet posts. Although several new faces appeared, there was little change in the complexion of the government and the policies of the Baldwin regime were expected to be continued under Chamberlain. The biggest surprise was a shift in the war and navy ministries, in the midst of the government's huge re-armament program which undoubtedly will be continued. The post of air and defense coordinator was left unchanged. Baldwin, the country squire who has guided the country through a critical period, retired to the House of Lords as an earl and was also created a Knight of the Garter, an extraordinary honor. His wife was made a Dame Grand Cross of the British Empire. Capt. Anthony Eden was re-appointed forei

Monts, France, May 28.—(7)—An associate of the Duke of Windsor disclosed today that Edward and Mrs. Wallis Warfield were planning to visit the United States as a “second honeymoon.” Under arrangements which the abdicated British king and his bride-to-be are considering, the associate said, their stay in the United States would be brief and part of a trip around the world. Edward and the woman for whom he renounced his empire were said to have selected tentatively either October or November for the trip to America, after spending their “first honeymoon” in Austria. Herman L. Rogers, spokesman for Windsor and Mrs. Warfield, acknowledged they might go on a world cruise and visit the United States, but added “not in the immediate future.”

Aberdeen, Scotland, May 28—(UP)—Prof. Alfred Adler, world famous psychologist, collapsed in the street today and died in an ambulance on his way to the hospital. Prof. Adler was taking his customary after-breakfast stroll in Union Street, Aberdeen’s main thoroughfare. Tonight he was to have delivered the last of a series of lectures on psychopathology at Aberdeen University. Dr. Adler, who reputedly coined the expression, “inferiority complex,” had not complained of being ill, his secretary said, but recently he had been working hard and it was believed he might have overtaxed himself. Dr. Alfred Adler ranked with Sigmund Freud as one of the world’s great psychologists. Born the son of a rather poor Jewish father in an outer district of Vienna on Feb. 7, 1870, Adler became a living example of his theory of “over-compensation,” the innate faculty not only to overcome shortcomings of human

LONDON, May 28 —(—King George VI today formally forbade Mrs. Wallis Warfield to use the title “Her Royal Highness” when she becomes the bride of his brother, the Duke of Windsor. CALL HER “YOUR GRACE” The London Gazette, official court organ, announced that King George has decreed that the Duke of Windsor, the former King Edward VIII, shall lose the title of “His Royal Highness,” but that his wife and their descendants, if any, shall not hold that title. Earlier today the duke, at the Chateau de Cande, Monts, France, telephoned friends in London that he had been informed his brother had decided against him in his insistence that royal status be given his wife. The Gazette announced that letters patent had been issued dated May 27 defining the application of the title of “Royal Highness.” FOLLOW OLD RULE After Mrs. Warfield becomes the Duchess of Windsor on June 3, she will be addressed a

Valencia — The apartments of Milton Wells, United States consul, were damaged and shaken today during a terrific air raid on the temporary loyalist capital. Many were killed and wounded in the raid. A British ship in the harbor was damaged and the Paraguayan legation was wrecked. An unofficial check showed 42 persons killed ashore, 67 gravely wounded, 45 others less seriously injured, and at least 30 buildings wrecked. Three bombs fell within ten yards of Wells’ apartment and another apartment occupied by United States embassy and consular employees, shattering the windows. Two other apartment houses were blown to the ground by the explosion, killing or wounding 40 sleeping occupants. It was the first of approximately 100 explosive and incendiary bombs dropped on the sleeping city by six rebel planes which flew over the harbor and city.

LONDON, May 28 (UP) -- Stanley Baldwin, “savior of the monarchy,” retired today as Great Britain's prime minister after historic service and was succeeded by Arthur Neville Chamberlain, his chancellor of the exchequer. King George VI conferred on Baldwin the highest distinction within the gift of the crown—a Knighthood of the Garter—tonight after the smoothly managed switch of governments. The king received the new national government, still a coalition administration, in a special audience at Buckingham Palace after the change-over from “Honest Stan,” the king-maker, to cool, ef-

1937-07-12.text: | WALTON HEATH, Eng., July 12 ca cea Cotton, British open champion, took a two up lead over Denny Shute of the United States at the half way mark of their 72-hole $2,500 “world championship” match here today. One up through 31 holes, Shute's driver played him false and cost him the 32, 33 and 34th holes, and only by sinking a 12-foot putt on the last green was he able to save himself from losing another.

HONOLULU, UP). The American freighter Golden Bear lost one crew member, but by heroic measures rescued 750 persons from imminent disaster when two great volcanic eruptions destroyed the town of Rabaul, New Britain, New Guinea, May 29. Capt. E. M. Olsen of the Golden Bear described the cataclysm and rescue upon arrival of the Matson line freighter. Risking envelopment of his ship and all hands in the lava flow, Olsen said his men made their way ashore to lead 750 persons, mostly women and children, out of the doomed city. Victor A. Costner, the Golden Bear’s radioman, disappeared, Olsen said, as crew members groped their way ashore in pitch darkness, through downpours of volcanic ashes and pumice. Olsen expressed belief Costner walked off the wharf in the darkness, but Rabaul’s harbor had a deep scum of ashes and pumice on its surface. Olsen said more than 250 persons perished under the s

LONDON, July 12.—A conference between Britain and the United States on the situation in China was mentioned as a possibility today by Captain Anthony Eden, foreign secretary. Lieutenant Commander L. R. Fletcher asked Eden in Commons: "Has the foreign secretary considered entering into consultations with the United States government regarding these incidents?" "This kind of consideration is very present in my mind," Eden replied. Previously, the secretary mentioned the possibility of harmful effect on British and other foreign interests.

HONOLULU, July 12.—The volcano which erupted in the harbor of Rabaul, New Britain Island, killed 262 persons, including one American, and rained destruction on the town, Capt E. M. Olsen of the Matson freighter Golden Bear said when he arrived here today. The Golden Bear was lying at the dock in Rabaul when the volcano on Vulean Island erupted, May 29. “Within thirty minutes after the eruption started the entire area was in darkness,” Captain Olsen said. “Fine ashes and pumice dust sifted down onto the harbor and town. There was a suffocating sulphurous smell from the volcano and molten lava flowed down its sides.” The lone American lost was Victor M. Costner, radioman on the Golden Bear. He disappeared after the crew fled ashore and was not seen again.

LONDON (UP)—Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden indicated Britain’s solidarity with France today in discussing the Spanish Non-Intervention problem in the House of Commons. France has just notified the Non-Intervention committee that she will withdraw tomorrow the facilities hitherto afforded to neu- (Turn to Peace 129—No. 8.)

PARIS, July 14, 1942. Andre Charles Corbin, French minister at London, notified the British foreign office today that France will withdraw tomorrow the facilities accorded neutral observers on the French-Spanish frontier. The control, which has been exercised by 155 neutral agents since April 19, will end at noon tomorrow, Corbin advised the British government. France's own border patrol men, who have orders to keep munitions, men and other contraband from Spain, will remain on duty pending further developments—specifically whether the powers arrange effective control of the Spanish coasts and the Spanish-Portuguese frontier. When the government's intention to suspend its control plan was announced Saturday, it was intimated that the suspension might be revoked if a compromise was agreed on before tomorrow. Today however, the announcement of suspension was not qualified.

MOSCOW (U.P.)—Three Russian air heroes sped over the Arctic Sea on their way to the United States today, seeking to reach San Francisco or Los Angeles and break the world airplane distance record of 5,657 miles. They started from Schelkovo Airport, 20 miles from Moscow, at 7:25 p.m., Sunday (EST) intended to fly over the North Pole and down through Canada as did their three fellow aviators who landed near Vancouver, Washington, three weeks ago. The plane is an ANT-25-1, sister ship to that which made the previous flight. In the plane were Michael Gromov, Russia’s star test pilot; Maj. Andre Yumashev of the Red Army and Sergei Danilile. They hoped to land in California Wednesday, and thus set a new world distance record to supplant that made by Maurice Rossi and Paul Codos of France from New York to Syria in 1933. Only a few officials and other onlookers witnessed the takeoff. There was a

1937-09-05.text: London, Sept. 4.—(#)—European diplomats, facing the League of Nations assembly and a conference of Mediterranean powers next week, today were engaged in the most intense activity since German troops marched back into the Rhineland 18 months ago. The foremost question before them, an outgrowth of the Spanish war, was protection of merchant shipping and warships in the Mediterranean against the recent series of 'piratical' attacks by unidentified submarines and airplanes. Italy Suspected. The finger of suspicion in the Mediterranean crisis pointed at Italy. This was due largely to Premier Benito Mussolini's friendly exchange with insurgent Generalissimo Francisco Franco after the latter’s recent capture of Santander, and Il Duce’s expressed determination to keep bolshevism out of the Mediterranean. The French foreign office announced invitations of the Mediterranean conference would be iss

SHANGHAI, Sept. 5. (Sunday) (AP) — Ten Japanese warplanes carried the undeclared war with China into a year area of Shanghai today, a heavy bombardment hitting the west station of the Shanghai-Hankow railroad. The station is near the British-defended sector of the international settlement. Damage was heavy and casualties were believed to have been many. Earlier, Japan's bristling naval guns and bombing planes pushed the battle for supremacy in China 600 miles into the southland—and lost the first major encounter. Three Japanese warships steamed into the southern port of Amoy Friday, above them several squadrons of warplanes, and began firing on Chinese forts. The defenders answered with artillery fire, and battle roared throughout the day. By nightfall, Chinese reports said, one Japanese warship was disabled and had to be towed away by her companions; the aerial bombardment caused no ser

LONDON, Sept. 4.—Great Britain, backed by the most powerful naval alliance since the World War, moved tonight toward a showdown in the Mediterranean which may provoke the most serious crisis in Anglo-Italian relations since the Ethiopian war. British warships were sent to the Mediterranean to exterminate submarine "pirates" and Britain created a French proposal for a conference next week at Geneva to plan a concerted "war on piracy." Italy was plainly worried by the situation, which has aligned five naval powers — Britain, France, Turkey, Greece and Russia — into a bloc which may begin to assert its area of naval influence. Italy is seeking, through every diplomatic channel, an invitation to the conference. The British fleet, on "a destroyer," has ordered the sternest measures to clear the Mediterranean of illegal activities. Additional warships and the French fleet were instructed to at

SHANGHAI, Sunday, Sept. 5.—(UP)— Enraged Chinese fighting to expel a quarter of a million Japanese invaders from their homeland received indirect assistance today from four of the world’s greatest powers—Soviet Russia, Britain, the United States, and France. Russia cooperated in the completion of a direct air line from Nanking to Moscow, opening a reliable route for fleets of Soviet airplanes which were reported flying to the assistance of the Chinese air force. The three other great powers joined in an effort to force Japanese warships out of vital areas in the spreading Shanghai battle zone.

SHANGHAI, Sept. 5.—(Sunday)—(P)—More than 100 civilians were killed or wounded today by Japanese aerial bombs rained on the ravaged city from ten warplanes that attacked the west station of the Hubei-Dal Hanechow railway. TOKYO, Sept. 5—(Sunday)—(P)—Japan today extended its naval blockade of the Chinese coast to include new waters through which Chinese shipping is forbidden to ply off the war-torn continent. The foreign office announced extension of the blockade effective at noon Sunday (10 p.m. EST Saturday.) The peaceful commerce of third powers will be treated “with due respect,” the foreign office said. He said Japan must make impossible “recurrence of such calamitous hostilities as at present” and readjust relations with China so Japan could put into effect her policy of “cooperation” between Japan, her protectorate, Manchukuo, and China. —With bombs and steel Japan today flung back her answer to the demand of three foreign powers that Chinese and Japanese forces cease fighting near the international settlement, where the lives of thousands of Americans and other foreigners have been endangered by two days of steady bombing. ASK WITHDRAWAL The Japanese war planes took to the air at dawn and began unloading bombs within a stone's throw of the settlement proper — 12 hours after the United States, Great Britain and France had formally asked withdrawal of her war fleet and troops from the settlement area. Desperately pressed by an enraged Chinese army that hammered back the lines of well-dressed Japanese troops to the banks of the Whang-poo, and harried by a new menace from Soviet Russia — the threat of war planes coming into China over a new air route from Moscow — the Japanese military command spurned the tri-power proposal

ABOARD YACHT INDIAN OFF RHODE ISLAND, ()—President Roosevelt declared Saturday night that “both sides have made mistakes” in recent employer-worker conflicts and urged the use of “sanity and reason” in adjusting labor disputes. “The conference table must eventually take the place of the strike,” he said, in a Labor Day statement made public as he cruised aboard the yacht Potomac in Long Island Sound. It was his first formal statement on the subject since the wave of strikes started sweeping over the country nearly eight months ago, and the first comment of any kind he had made since his Washington press conference statement at the peak of the steel strike, inferentially attacking extremists in industry and labor unions. It followed a radio speech Friday night by John L. Lewis, head of the Committee for Industrial Organization, caustically criticizing the president for his attitude in the

There was no great anxiety, however, although it was considered possible the pair might have been forced down somewhere in Ireland. RECORD UNBROKEN When 3:32 P.M. passed without the fliers’ arrival, they lost a chance to beat the Newfoundland-Croydon record of 13 hours and 17 minutes set by Captain Jimmy Mollison last October. Weather conditions were fair around the Irish coast, but fog and rain were reported between there and London. Croydon officials said they received a garbled message which they were sure came from Merrill at 3:25 P.M. (9:25 A.M. EST). London—(?)—Americans pouring into London today for the start of coronation week can’t help but feel at home despite the fog and rain that settled down normally after unusual London sunshine. The theme colors of the decorations are red, white and blue, against a riot of purple, yellow, green, orange, and what have you. Fourteen liners, headed by the Queen Mary with 2,000 passengers, brought reinforcements into London, mostly from America, totaling between 7,000 and 8,000. Rudy Vallee, hopping between night clubs and cabarets, was seasick a couple of days on the way over. They tossed a blighter who booed him at the Holborn Empire, a vaudeville house, right into the street. There will be 58 microphones in Westminster Abbey alone, one on each arm of the thrones of both the king and queen. London, May 9.—Undaunted by a cold, drizzling rain, throngs estimated at nearly 1,000,000 persons fought and jammed their way into the streets between Buckingham Palace and Westminster Abbey early this morning to watch the final rehearsal of the coronation procession. It was the show for the masses, the chance for those who cannot witness Wednesday's brilliant spectacle to get an idea of what the progress of King George VI and Queen Elizabeth to their coronation will be like. The outpouring was the largest crowd in London since the funeral of King George V, 16 months ago, a vast assortment of shivering, bedraggled but happy human beings who cheered wildly at the sight of the empty gilded coach of state and the various mounted military contingents. It provided an excellent preview of the throngs that will swarm. (Continued on Page &)

LONDON, May 10—(U P)—Coronation week opened today with showers and a hus strike and a determination of millions of people to celebrate fittingly, come what might, the biggest set event on the British calendar. Representatives of an empire that covers one-fourth the world, envoys from 53 world nations, tourists from nearly as many and the visitors from the British provinces joined Londoners in defying the weather to do its worst, and lending their own color to an occasion which makes plain as nothing else does that kings may come and go, but the kingdom goes on forever. Celebrations will reach their climax Wednesday when King George VI is crowned at Westminster Abbey, along with his consort Queen Elizabeth. But today the empire capital had been turned over to the celebrants and there was little to be seen of the city’s normal bustling attention to business. Princes and princesses, Indian

- London, May 10. ()—Sir Stafford Cripps, Laborite member of parliament, in a bitter outburst in a political speech at Stockton today, characterized the coronation planned for King George VI as “bunkum and bunting.” The ceremony, the Labor party leader declared, was “simply being run as a political stunt by the Conservative party.”

New York, May 9.—(#)— Dick Merrill and Jack Lambie, on a nonstop flight to London, pointed their monoplane into the blackness covering the north Atlantic at 10:15 p.m., Eastern Standard time, tonight, after a swift cruise up the coast. Six hours and 40 minutes out of Floyd Bennett airport, they had covered 1,155 miles, part of it through a driving rain. Their last message was terse, and made no mention of the rain which had been reported a few minutes earlier after leaving Sidney, N. S. It came from 20 miles south of St. Johns, Newfoundland, and was ‘just leaving land.’ Speed High An hour earlier the fliers had flashed back ‘over the Sidney, N. S., airport at 4,000 feet—everything O. K.,’ Merrill and his co-pilot, Jack Lambie, radioed Eastern Airlines. The heavily loaded plane had flown 802 miles from New York, at an average speed of 173.14 miles an hour. Making their first ocean flight

Croydon, England, May 10.— His third trans-Atlantic flight behind him, Henry T. ‘Dick’ Merrill, crack pilot of the Eastern Airlines, landed his speedy Lockheed monoplane at Croydon airdrome this afternoon, after an interrupted crossing from Floyd Bennett Field, New York. Merrill brought his silver plane to earth at this landing field at 6:38 p. m. (12:38 EST), 21 hours and two minutes after leaving New York. Accompanied by John S. Lambie, his regular co-pilot on the Miami to New York run of the Eastern Airlines, Merrill landed first at the Royal Air Force Airdrome near North Weald, Essex. This landing was made at 6:10 p. m. (12:10 p. m. EST). The fliers left at 6:22 p. m. (12:22 p. m. EST) for Croydon. Merrill and Lambie hoped to fly back across the Atlantic immediately after the coronation. Before leaving New York, Merrill expressed the hope of being home again by Thursday. The landing

MONTS, France, May 10,—(U.P)— Mrs. Wallis Warfield Simpson discarded the name of her divorced husband today and legally became Wallis Warfield, a name she will keep only briefly until she becomes the Duchess of Windsor. The change was made by British deed poll. Her London lawyers made the application four days ago and notified her today that it had been granted.

1937-10-16.text: LONDON, Oct. 16 — Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden tonight demanded swift and honest action to end the danger that Spain may bring Europe to war. The foreign secretary made the demand at an obscure political rally in Llandudno, Wales on the eve of the nonintervention sub-committee meeting in London called to seek agreement on withdrawal of foreign volunteers from Spain. Eden declared Britain and France stood shoulder to shoulder to ensure that the nonintervention committee’s efforts will be successful and added that any nation which obstructed the committee’s work would have to suffer French and British displeasure. That Britain has not intervened in Spain with soldiers, he said, does not mean that Britain is indifferent to the fate of Spain. “A clear distinction must be made between nonintervention in what is purely a Spanish affair and nonintervention where British interests are at stake

WASHINGTON, Oct. 16.—Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh has accepted a renewal of his commission in the American Army Air Corps Reserve. This action, which became known at the War Department today, was believed to set definitely at rest reports that the noted aviator, now residing in England, may relinquish his American citizenship to become a British subject.

Bangor, Me. Oct. 15. (#)—Al Brady’s body went into a bleak grave today, unmourned, unattended, unmarked. The Indiana gang leader, killed with his chief aide, Clarence Lee Shaffer, Jr., in a federal machine gun coup here Columbus Day, was buried in an isolated section of Mount Hope cemetery. Only brief funeral services by a minister whose name officials declined to reveal preceded removal of the body from an undertaking parlor to the “city property” section of the cemetery, set aside for unknown or unclaimed bodies.

Jerusalem, Oct. 15 (4) — The shadowy movements of the Grand Mufti of Jerusalem, only member of the Arab higher committee not deported or banished as morally responsible for Palestine's long unrest, heightened fear tonight of new terrorism in the Holy Land. The British military clamped down a nightfall curfew and also threatened martial law. The latest disturbances included the ambush killing of two British constables in a skirmish with an Arab band near Bethlehem and other casualties within 48 hours. Four Arabs have been killed and 12 Jews injured. The disturbances were a repetition of outbreaks which have flared since the British invoked tight military control of the Holy Land in a renewed effort to stamp out terrorism and conflict between the Jews and Arabs.

—The bodies of nearly 200 American and British volunteers were found by agents of the non-Intervention committee along the Franco-Spanish frontier during the summer, Col. C.D. O. Lunn, a Danish officer, said today. Col. Lunn, commander of the International border guard, said. What most of those found dead apparently became lost in the mountains and wandered until they collapsed from exhaustion. “Some fell from cliffs into crevasses,” he said. Many of the bodies were attacked by wolves, only a few bones and clothing remaining. All were in such a state they were unrecognizable.” The American and British casualties were only a part of a larger number of volunteers found dead, the total of which Lunn did not estimate.

SHANGHAI, Oct. 15 (U.P) - Chinese reports from Canton said today that 18 British warships, including an aircraft carrier and a submarine were concentrated off Hong Kong. The Chinese Central News Agency also reported from Canton that ten Japanese planes bombed Tsengchen, 30 miles east of Canton, killing or wounding more than 200 civilians. The planes also bombed Taishan, 70 miles southwest of Canton, inflicting more than 30 casualties. The agency said the planes destroyed more than 200 yards of the Canton-Kowloon railroad, in which there are heavy British investments.

TOKYO (#) — Kohei Goshi, financial expert of the newspaper Yomiuri Shinbun, painted a dismal picture today of Japan’s foreign money problems. “IF both American and British money markets refused financing to Japan,” Goshi declared, “it would be a more serious situation than mere political or economic sanctions.” A recent survey by the Associated Press disclosed that numerous representatives of American firms here have been ordered to discontinue credit selling and to make cash sales only. Goshi declared that Japan has found financing of her trade increasingly difficult in New York and London. “The sharp decline in Japan’s public bonds on foreign markets clearly shows the extent to which foreign nations doubt the soundness of Japan's economy,” he said. “As American banks are hesitant, exports to Japan are weakening and turning gradually from credit selling toward cash selling.” Discussing

TOKYO, Oct. 18.—()—Sir Robert Craigie, British ambassador to Tokyo, today delivered to the foreign office a note protesting against the aerial attack last Tuesday of British motorcars on the highway between Nanking and Shanghai. He talked with Koki Hirota, Japanese minister of foreign affairs.

1937-01-12.text: LONDON, Jan. 12.—(#)—Four persons were drowned and 20 others were missing today after the Finnish motorship Johanna Thorden sank off the Orkney Islands in an ocean storm. The ship of 3,228 tons was en route to Gothenburg. It was not known whether she struck a reef or broke up on the rocks. Eight survivors in a lifeboat landed at South Ronaldsay, one of the Orkney Islands where four bodies were washed up. The missing persons were reported to be in a lifeboat on the sea.

Paris, Jan. 11.—(4#)—Official France gave Spain’s insurgent dictator-designate ‘a few days’ to rid Spanish Morocco of any German tinge tonight. Meanwhile, French troops drilled in the French Moroccan zone; French and British warships made the eastern Mediterranean a point of convergence; French officials said the general staff, with a combined land, air and sea maneuver, could occupy Spanish Morocco in 26 hours, if need be. LONDON, Jan. 12—4}—Five men were dismissed from service in two British naval yards today after a two-year investigation of suspected sabotage and leakage of confidential information. The Devonport dismissals resulted from discovery of “certain documents” in the workboxes of four employees, it was said. Detectives had been called in to investigate damage to the submarine L-54 at Devonport in April, 1936. Another case which received official attention was the discovery of pieces of metal in the machinery of the Griffin, Britain's newest destroyer.

LONDON, Jan. 12, (AP)—Great Britain turned down a Soviet request today for the use of her fleet to protect neutral shipping from Spain's insurgent warships while the European neutrality sub-committee studied a demand for the impounding of Spanish government gold. It was explained the British intervention agreement that would do away with activities of insurgent patrol boats now trying to blockade Spanish government ports. A report on an estimated $500,000,000 in Bank of Spain gold deposited abroad in the names of individuals was before the sub-committee. Italy wants this gold impounded by neutral powers until the civil war is over.

PARIS, Jan. 12—Fuehrer Adolf Hitler wants France to invite Dr. Hjalmar Schacht, his most eminent authority on economics and finance, to Paris to engage in political, economic and financial conversations, it was said authoritatively today. Andre François-Poncet, ambassador to Germany, arrived today and conveyed to Foreign Minister Yvon Delbos an expression of Hitler's desire that Schacht be invited here. The ambassador reported also on his exchange of assurance with Hitler on Spanish Morocco yesterday, which brought a sudden end to the dangerous situation caused by France's fears of German infiltration. Important as Hitler's wish for a visit here by Schacht seemed, French authorities did not seem to be eager for such a visit unless the German government was prepared to give France political guarantees such as negotiations for an arms limitation agreement. Paris—()—In a sudden breaking of the acute tension which has bound Europe since before the Christmas holidays, France and Germany were reported Tuesday to be negotiating a vast accord in “full and lasting settlement” of their difficulties. Ambassadors of both countries returned to their capitals bearing dispatches which, diplomatic circles said, signalled overtures for a broad economic and political agreement. It was a sudden and welcome lifting of the war clouds that had become increasingly darker since France and Britain stiffened their demands on Germany against volunteer aid to insurgents in the Spanish civil war and reported Nazi infiltration in Spanish Morocco. The first break came in Berlin where Reich Chancellor Adolf Hitler and French Ambassador Andre Francois-Poncet exchanged mutual assurances of territorial integrity for Spain and her territories, including Spanish Morocco. Madrid, Jan. 12. — (7) — Government forces launched a sudden offensive on the Madrid front today and apparently turned the tide in the latest fascist threat against the beleaguered capital. Despite the socialists’ rebound from last week's pressure by Gen. Francisco Franco’s insurgents, streams of refugees fled out of the opposite side of Madrid. Their flight to safety crude the war zone complied with the defense Junta’s decree ordering evacuation of the civil population. The insurgent drive against the western edge of the city was reported stopped by a socialist counter-offensive which extended along the El Escorial road. Government artillery pounded incessantly at insurgent concentrations throughout the area. A war bulletin said a fascist attack also was frustrated in the Guadalajara front northeast of Madrid. The compulsory evacuation order stood, however. About 2,500 women, children,

MADRID (UP) -- Loyalist defenders, erecting new fortifications, feared today that the next general attack on the capital might bring into play the wide use of gas. It was said unofficially that tear gas was employed extensively during the latter part of the insurgents' seven-day offensive last week. Loyalist officers expressed concern lest the use of tear gas might not presage the use of deadlier, toxic gases. Government reports listed 4,000 insurgent casualties in last week's offensive, of which 1,000 were killed. Of those killed, loyalist reports said, the majority were Germans. A blanket of mist which enveloped Madrid yesterday gave the capital a day of peace and tranquility, broken only by occasional artillery fire from the city and a few answering insurgent shots. 1937-08-09.text: LONDON, (P)— Possible French objections to a practical working agreement between Great Britain and Italy arose today as diplomats began preparing Britain's case for the Rome friendship talks scheduled to start at the end of September. Diplomats were compelled to keep in mind constantly that a four-power western pact to replace the abandoned Locarno — reliably reported as a possible outcome of the growing friendliness — would raise a storm of protest in a People's Front France bound by a pact with Russia. On the other hand, it was felt likely that France, which has been following the British lead in most matters of foreign policy through traditional fear of Germany, would realize that, in the long run, she would stand to benefit as much as Britain by settling accounts with Italy. Foreign office experts, therefore, have set themselves with enthusiasm to the task of preparing the groundwork

Dunkirk, France, Aug. 8--(@-- Six hundred passengers aboard the Belgian channel steamer Princess Marie Jose were landed safely today after the ship collided with the British eteamer Clan MacNeil off Dunkirk. Four injured passengers were taken to a hospital. The Marie Jose was en route to Dover from Ostend when she was struck forward by the Clan MacNeil's prow and rapidly took water. Tugs, guided by radio, reached the vessel and guided her to a canal lock where passengers were taken off.

Hongkong, Aug. 9.—-(Monday)—(/P)—Edward S. Smith, formerly of Los Angeles, Calif., pilot of a Chinese airliner which made a forced landing at sea, was taken to a hospital today with internal injuries after he and seven other survivors were brought ashore. The survivors arrived aboard the British destroyer Thracian after being picked up by a Chinese junk, transferred to a customs cruiser and later to the Thracian in heavy seas last night. The six Chinese passengers, one of whom was injured, and E. M. Walsh, an American aviator employed by the Canton government, told a graphic story of the accident. The airliner, a twin-engined (Sikorsky) amphibian belonging to the China National Aviation company, ran into difficulties off Chilang point, 85 miles northeast of here. HONGKONG (/) — Three members of the crew of a Chinese airliner forced down at sea in a heavy fog were missing today as eight survivors, including two Americans, were brought to Hongkong aboard the British destroyer Thracian. The plane’s pilot, Edward S. Smith, formerly of Los Angeles, Calif., was taken to a hospital suffering severe bruises and an injured hand. The other American aboard, E. M. Walsh, an aviator employed by the Canton government, was not injured.

The member of the house foreign affairs committee declared he would introduce a resolution for a congressional investigation to determine whether such an agreement was negotiated when Walter Runge- man, president of the Britain Board of Trade, visited here last January. Asserting the general staff allegedly had recommended withdrawal of American troops from China ‘a number of times,” Tinkham said: “The American people have a right to know whether or not his failure to act in this matter is because of an agreement or understanding between the United States and Great Britain that the United States will support and fortify British policies in the Far East,” Plot Al

Flags of foreign nations were hoisted on flagstaffs and British authorities had huge union jacks, including some as large as four tennis courts, painted on roads and open spaces about the British concessions. London— (INS) —“Shoot down without warning” any airplanes attacking British ships on the high seas, was the drastic order given to all British warships Monday. This command, it was learned, was issued to ships of the Mediterranean fleet in consequence of the bombing on Friday of the English tanker British Corporal. Similar instructions, it was understood, were issued to the French navy.

Despite this threat, the weary diplomats stationed in London as representatives of the principal European powers headed for the day’s discussions in an atmosphere more optimistic than any since the Spanish war broke out 15 months ago. Three factors presaged eventual harmony among the nine powers represented—with the possible exception of Russia: 1. British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain's virtual assurance that Britain was determined not to go to war. 2. | LONDON, Oct. 22.— (7) — King George VI officially closed today a historic parliamentary session — which his brother, now the Duke of Windsor, had opened last Nov. 3 — with a message reflecting “distress” at air and sea attacks on Chinese noncombatants, The king’s message proroguing parliament was read to assembled commons and lords by Lord Chancellor Hailsham. It detailed the government's “persistence” in efforts to isolate warring Spain and noted “with satisfaction the strengthening of all three of my defense forces.” On Tuesday the king comes in person to the house of lords to open the new parliament session, and it was thought he would himself read the opening speech from the throne. Encouraging the Chinese-Japanese conflict by failure to stand by the League of Nations, the Prime Minister declared: “Pending rejuvenation of the league x x x we have got to find practical means for restoring peace in the world.” Earlier in the debate, Sir Archibald said, “We have been successful in obtaining that cooperation of the United States which is one of the dearest objects in the foreign policy of members of all parts of the house.” “I said, let us not fail to seize the opportunities given us—this glorious opportunity of lining up with the United States to defend those ideals of peace and justice which are common to our two countri

London, Oct. 21 (4?)—The fall of Gijon to Spanish insurgents tonight thrust Europe's non-intervention machinery into a race to withdraw foreign "volunteers" from Spain before Insurgent Generalissimo Francisco Franco's legions threaten a complete conquest. British Foreign Office experts labored to perfect details of the withdrawal scheme based on yesterday's Italo-German compromise in time for tomorrow’s meeting of the nine-power non-intervention sub-committee. It is proposed that a commission go to Spain to determine the manner of removing volunteers from the Spanish civil war—in which Italy has semi-officially admitted at least 40,000 Black-shirt troops are fighting with Franco. That Europe's tension over the Spanish crisis had slackened was indicated by Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden who, addressing the fall opening of the House of Commons, thanked Italy for her "eleventh hour" but "ve

LONDON—Soviet Russia was reported today to have slowed up the deliberations of the Spanish non-intervention powers by insisting on proportionate withdrawal of foreign volunteers instead of an equal withdrawal from both sides in Spain. Britain and France previously had agreed to the Italian demand for equal withdrawal but Russia held to the theory that more foreigners are fighting with the Nationalists than with the Loyalists and that therefore the withdrawal should be in ratio to the number of fighting on each side.

But, even while they talked, it appeared Father Time himself might solve the problem—that the next few months might see a decisive end of the civil conflict. He set up a Fascist grand council to govern it, with himself as its all-powerful head. Dublin, Irish Free State, Oct. 22, (PF) — Americans today won more than half of the tickets drawn from the Irish Hospital Sweepstakes’ whirling drums of chance, Out of 600 tickets drawn up to luncheon recess, Americans won 329. Forty horses were drawn. There were 54 more horses, with 15 tickets on each, to be drawn this afternoon.

LONDON, Oct. 22.—Fuehrer Adolf Hitler and Premier Benito Mussolini are seeking some compromise basis on which to bring the Spanish war to a close, it was reported in diplomatic circles here today. The reports were based on the fact that Joachim von Ribbentrop, German ambassador to London, traveled to Rome today. Aides explained the trip as purely personal but diplomats The diplomatic circles said that following the diplomatic victory within the non-intervention committee and the fall of Gijon, Mussolini suggested to Hitler that foreign volunteers be withdrawn gradually and that Gen. 1937-04-10.text: LONDON. (41) The Japanese monoplane Divine Wind landed at Croydon airdrome at 9:26 a.m., ec, 8. t., completing a record breaking 9,800 mile flight from Tokyo in a little more than 94 hours. The plane landed at Athens and Rome and flew over Paris on the last laps of the trip. By their brilliant flight, Pilot Masaaki Linuma, only 26 years old, and Kenji Tsukagoshi, 38, wireless operator, crowned with success one of Japan's first bids for international flying honors, in a Japanese made plane.
LONDON. — The London Midland and Scottish Railway plans to run 130 excursion trains, bringing 65,000 passengers from the provinces to London, during Coronation Week, it is announced.

MADRID, April 10—(4)—The second day of the government's major counter-offensive to break the insurgent grip in Madrid province brought terrific combat today at the very doors of the city. While 3,000 of Gen. Francisco Franco's men were reported isolated by a machine gun trap in University City, the northwestern suburb, the government opened a deafening artillery and aerial strafing of the whole array of siege lines. A once placid lake in the Casa De Campo sector, across the river from University City was the center of a raging inferno of gunfire and exploding grenades and dynamite. Hundreds of lordly pines on the once green slopes were blasted out by their roots by artillery fire. Every house was an army fortification. From Madrid to the east, watchers occasionally could see camouflaged tanks and armored cars darting through the trees. Periodic bursts of flame followed by columns of blue

ROME, April 10 (AP)—Marshal Italo Balbo became commander-in-chief of Italy’s armed forces in North Africa today in a cabinet decree establishing a new ministry of “Italian Africa” and guaranteeing the “traditional right” of natives of Libya. The cabinet created four new African provinces in Libya—Tripoli, Masurata, Bengasi and Derna, approved expenditure of 103,000,000 lire ($5,668,000) for colonial development and gave Libyans minor posts in the territorial government. Discussion of new population measures in Italy proper, which may include increased taxes on bachelors and childless husbands, was postponed until next Tuesday. The new colonial ministry will absorb the present ministry of colonies, headed at present by Alessandro Lessona.

MADRID, April 10.—(UP)—Rebels were beaten back with heavy losses when they went “over the top” at dawn today in efforts to halt the loyalist offensive. The rebels counterattacked after a “zero hour” lull in the loyalist battle to break the siege of Madrid which began yesterday. Insurgent troops went in waves in the El Pardo sector north of Madrid but were thrown back. The engagement was brief and decisive. The loyalists held their newly won positions in the great park and passed on in eleven other sectors to the south and west. Aviation and artillery units cooperated with the infantry. They flew over Casa de Campo and then bombed Monte Garabita. The government artillery went into action on the Casa de Campo sector replying to an intensive rebel artillery fire from the salient across the Manzanares river. TORONTO Ont., April 9.—(Canadian Press)—General Motors officials decided tonight to resume partial operations at the Oshawa plant tomorrow in what Premier Mitchell Hepburn predicted would be a showdown in the strike inspired by the John L. Lewis labor organization. The parts department at Oshawa will be opened under government protection, if necessary, the premier said. Determined to guard against any disorder and vigorously opposed to the Lewis committee for industrial organization, the premier concentrated mounted and provincial police here—35 miles from Oshawa and ready for a dash to that city at a moment's notice. As there were indications the strike might spread to other industries, four representatives of the Oshawa local of the United Automobile Workers of America union, which is affiliated with the CIO, came here to confer with Hepburn. BRUSSELS, Belgium, April 10.—(#)——Belgium's political temper neared the fever point today on the eve of a bitter “one seat” election that may determine whether the little nation will swing from traditional democracy to Fascism. The 42-year-old American-educated premier, Paul Van Zeeland, will contest on Sunday youthful Leon De Grelle, militant leader of the Rexists, party of the extreme right, for a seat in the Chamber of Representatives. (It is a bye-election involving only the one seat, De Grelle forced it by having one of his deputies resign, Van Zeeland accepted the challenge.) King Leopold, although ostensibly neutral, was known to favor Van Zeeland. And Van Zeeland was conceded the best chance. The premier's cause was further enhanced today by a denunciation of “Rexism” as a danger to the church by the Catholic Archbishop of Malines. Police were forced to protect Rexist Senator Cou

OSHAWA, Ont., April 10. (UP)— Angry pickets, shouting “We'll skin you when you come out,” permitted approximately 100 employees to enter the strike-bound plant of the General Motors Corporation of Canada today. The United Automobile Workers union massed 1,000 pickets around the plant when employees arrived to resume operations in the parts and service department—a non-production unit. Most of the returning workers were employed in the plant's offices, but about 20 were non-union men on their way to the parts department. They drew the verbal fire of the strikers. Despite these threats, the pickets appeared in good humor. 1937-06-10.text: London, June 7—The price of bar gold was pegged at $34.72 a fine ounce on the London market today in an effort to stem the flow of the precious metal to the United States. The new price was an advance of 98 cents to the ounce. The new price cut the profit which exporters of bullion stood to make by shipment to the United States. At today’s price for the pound sterling shippers of the yellow metal stood to profit about five cents an ounce, compared with around 14 cents Saturday. The narrowing of the margin between the London price and the government-fixed price of $35 an ounce in New York made shipment less profitable and tended to discourage selling on the London market. London sales today were 262 bars, valued at about $3,636,000, as compared with 465 bars valued at about $6,434,000 Saturday.
