LONDON— (U.P) --The slander suit of Ernest A. Simpson against Mrs. Joan Sutherland has been settled out of court, possibly with an apology or monetary damages or both, and will be formally closed in court, Friday. Whether Mrs. Sutherland, whom Simpson accused of insinuating that he was “well paid” to permit the Duchess of Windsor to divorce him, will appear in court was not known.

London, ~ (P) ~ Ernest Aldrich Simpson's slander action against Mrs. Joan Sutherland will be settled in court tomorrow, it was indicated today. The case officially was scheduled for “mention” before Lord Chief Justice Hewart in the king's bench division. This was interpreted to mean that counsel will explain that the remarks on which the slander action is based resulted from misinformation, apologies will be tendered, and the case settled. Simpson's writ was based on remarks Mrs. Sutherland, wife of Lieut. Col. A. H. Sutherland, was alleged to have made at a west end restaurant anent the Simpson divorce case.

CASTLE GANDOLFO, Italy, June 9 (#)—Pope Pius XI personally declared today he would continue the ‘bitter fight for German Catholics ‘no matter what becomes of us” and lamented the “menacing” conditions within Nazi Germany. The pope's pronouncement, made to a group of Bavarian Catholic pilgrims, was interpreted as an indirect reply to the last German note which virtually broke off diplomatic relations between the Holy See and Germany. The pope said conditions in Germany were “so grave, so menacing and so dolorous” for Catholicism that “they cause one to weep.” The papal statement allayed rumors the Vatican, because of representations from the Italian government, soon would modify its policy toward Germany. Italy and Germany have a cooperative understanding in international affairs. In a pre-Easter encyclical the pope accused the Nazis of violating the German-Vatican concordat which reserve

- MARIENWERDER, East Prussia, June 9.—(AP)—Reichsfuehrer Adolf Hitler is scheduled to address 600 of his oldest and trusted followers on Polish frontier problems here on June 19. Dramatically he has chosen for his important party conference this town of 14,000 inhabitants which borders on the free state of Danzig, once Polish and once German and governed since the World War under League of Nations supervision. He will speak in the medieval castle of Marienburg, once the seat of the Teutonic knights who conquered little Danzig six centuries ago (and who later suffered crushing defeat at the hands of a Polish king.) The setting will be a symbolic reminder of the Nazi theory that national socialism is a crusade as was that of the knights of old, and that Nazis are members of an order. PERPIGNAN, French - Spanish Frontier, June 10.—Indalecio Prieto, strong man of the loyalist government, promised today that he would save Bilbao by organizing a general offensive of loyalist forces. Such an offensive has long been a loyalist dream. Prieto said the reality was near. ‘Loyalist superiority in manpower has not been questioned. But the nationalists have been admittedly superior in equipment, direction and trained personnel. Prieto, in a statement to the United Press today, asserted the loyalists soon will command an army of 500,000 men, every one of whom will have had military training. Prieto, a moderate Socialist leader, took office May 18 in a reorganized loyalist cabinet as minister of national defense. Under him were merged for the first time the ministries of war, navy, air and munitions. A brilliant record as air and marine minister, which included credit for the Itali

Halle, Germany, June 10 (4)—Five freight handlers were known today to have been killed and many others of the 80 on duty were reported missing in a mysterious fire which swept the railroad yards. Explosions after explosions spread the blaze. A number of the handlers and clerks were injured in the fire which broke out last night and destroyed 30 freight cars.

VIENNA, June 10 (INS).-—Rumors that Josef Stalin, Soviet dictator, is desperately ill cropped up again today when the Vienna leftist newspaper De Stunde reported that Dr. Hans Eppinger, famous internal cancer specialist, had been twice called to Moscow to see Stalin. “The professor has gone east,” was all that his office would say, confirming, at least, his absence.

LONDON, June 22 (#)—The registration of the birth of Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh’s infant son disclosed today he had been named Land Morrow Lindbergh. The document, filed with the registrar of births and deaths of Marylebone Borough, confirmed that the boy was born May 12 at the fashionable London clinic nursing home in Devonshire Place. The birth of Colonel Lindbergh's third son was not known until a relative of the family in the United States made public portions of a letter she had received announcing the arrival. Even then the details were not disclosed.

London, June 22. ()—Sir John Simon, the British chancellor of the exchequer, announced to the House of Commons today that Great Britain does not intend to reopen war debt discussions with the United States in connection with pending proposals for an Anglo-American trade agreement.

LONDON, June 22.—(P)—The new son of Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh was named today. He was registered at Marylebone town hall as Land Morrow Lindbergh. The Land is a family name of Lindbergh’s mother, Mrs. Evangeline Lindbergh, and the Morrow is for Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh's family.

Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden told the House of Commons that Great Britain had no intention of joining Germany, Italy and France in a mass warship review off the Spanish government capital of Valencia — something Germany wants to “impress” the Spaniards that they must stay away from foreign warships. Members of the House cheered Eden as he went on to declare that the British government feels the principal source of trouble in Spain is the presence of foreign fighters, and that the government wants these fighters removed immediately. Simla, India, June 20.--(AP)--Sixteen members of a German Himalayan expedition have been killed by an avalanche, the British political agent at Gilgit, northern Kashmir, reported today. Seven Germans and nine Gurkha porters were overwhelmed in a huge slide, the agent reported. They were members of an expedition that reached India early in May to attempt the ascent of Mount Nanga Parbat, 26,629-foot peak in the western Himalayas. The British agent left Gilgit for the scene of the disaster, presumably on or near Mount Parbat. The expedition's leader, Dr. Karl Win, professor of geography at Munich University, escaped. Mount Nanga Parbat, highest peak in the British Empire, has defied all attempts to reach its summit. This is the second German expedition to come to disaster in trying to conquer Nanga Parbat. LONDON, June 22.—Great Britain will refuse to participate in any naval demonstration on the Spanish coast as the Germans sought as a warning to the Spanish government, Foreign Secretary Eden told Parliament today. He made the announcement after an excited report circulated that Germany presented France and Britain a virtual ultimatum for stringent punishment to the Spanish government for purported torpedo attack on the cruiser Leipzig.

| £0KyO, Jan. 23.———(A)——Japan's Parliamentary political parties overthrew the cabinet of Premier Koki Hirota today, forcing the government to resign under their bitter attacks against the army. The premier, unable to reach a compromise between the angry military leaders and the political parties, presented the cabinet's mass resignation to the emperor, after a final session of his ministers. It was the first time in Japan's parliamentary history the lower house had succeeded in wrecking the government which always before had resorted to dissolution and a general election when the diet’s opposition became too strong. Whether or not it will be a true victory for the political leaders depends, observers said, on the membership of the succeeding cabinet which the militarists are striving to capture.

The Soviet government placed Karl Radek, bearded man of letters, and 16 of his accused eco-plotters on trial for their lives in what was a gay ballroom in the Russia of the Tsars. America’s new ambassador, Joseph E. Davies, listened avidly. Reading of the startling indictment showed complete admissions of guilt allegedly had been obtained from all 17 defendants. They were accused of conspiring with the exiled Leon Trotsky, now in Mexico, to give the Ukraine to Germany and the Soviet maritime and Amur provinces to Japan in order to obtain foreign aid in overthrowing the regime of Joseph Stalin. FLORENCE, Italy, Jan. 23.— Crown Prince Michael of Rumania underwent an emergency operation for appendicitis today and was reported in a grave condition. His father, King Carol, was called to his bedside. Reliable sources said Michael had a relapse early this afternoon and that his temperature rose suddenly.

Tokyo—The cabinet resigned today as the result of an angry dispute between army and political leaders. Premier Koki Hirota went at once to the imperial palace and submitted the resignations of the ministers. The emperor accepted the resignations informally, asking Premier Hirota and his associates to remain at their posts until a new cabinet was named. Acceptance of the resignations was informal because technically they will not become effective until a new cabinet is named. Parliamentary leaders decided upon resignation as the alternative to dissolution of parliament, demanded by Gen. Count Hisaichi Terauchi, war minister, as spokesman for army leaders.

MADRID, Jan. 23.—Insurgent artillery bombarded the American-owned telephone building and the Grand Via shortly before noon today, scoring ten direct hits on Madrid's only skyscraper and killing an estimated twenty persons. The fourth floor of the telephone building, operated by a subsidiary of the International Telephone & Telegraph Co., was in flames as I write this dispatch 50 feet away. Ten rebel shells smashed their way through the building from the third to the eleventh floors, wrecking telephone switchboards, control boards and lines. The screaming shells tore through the dining room and press room on the fifth floor where the American newspaper correspondents have been telephoning their reports on the siege of Madrid for the last two months. The first rebel shell came hurtling in while I was crossing the Grand Via, Madrid’s Broadway, and missed me by about 20 feet. The bombardment

Paris, Jan. 23—Premier Blum will ask Adolf Hitler to halt Germany's “feverish armament program” as the first agreement for economic assistance from France, authoritative sources said today. The Socialist premier will make his request tomorrow in an address at Lyons, when he will disclose pending plans for a Franco-German political and economic agreement. Flanked by 16 cabinet ministers, Blum will lay down five suggestions for stabilizing the troubled European situation which, informed sources predicted, may be answered by Hitler at the German Reichstag session six days later. The proposals were expected to include: 1, cessation of the Nazi rearmament program; 2, adoption of a “conciliatory” attitude toward Europe’s political problem as the price of French economic help; 3, immediate publication of national defense budgets; 4, publicity for arms programs followed by limitation and eventua

Moscow—A strange tale of international intrigue in which the exiled Leon Trotsky was accused of seeking the military aid of Germany, Poland and Japan to overthrow the Soviet government was told today at the trial of 17 former government officials, all prominent. The defendants, accused of aiding Trotsky's plotting all pleaded guilty and apparently were headed for the firing squad. The many allegations included a plan to give Sakhalin Island to Japan for its oil supplies in event of war with the United States, and to aid Germany’s conquest of the Danube countries and the Balkans. As in previous trials, the defendants seemed almost to boast of their guilt as they shouted their sins through microphones.

1937-11-02.text: LONDON, Nov. 2. (#)—Mediterranean tension was heightened today by reports that Spain's insurgents were throwing a tight air and naval blockade along the entire Eastern Spanish coast to cut the Valencia government off from outside help by way of the high seas. Insurgent Generalissimo Francisco Franco's strategy sharply increased the danger of international complications in the Mediterranean. He was believed planning to rely largely on planes based on the Balearic island Mallorca to rule shipping lanes and cut off Valencia and Barcelona from food and munitions. Franco's naval commander, Vice-Admiral Francisco Moreno Fernández at Palma, Mallorca, had 35 ships at his command to build the sea blockade. Three were sighted off Valencia last night.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 2 (AP)—British Ambassador Sir Ronald Lindsay conferred with Sumner Welles, acting secretary of state, today on arrangements for the forthcoming visit of the Duke and Duchess of Windsor. Although the envoy said afterward that plans still are subject to change in accordance with the wishes of the royal visitors, it was learned they planned a 36-hour stay in Washington. During this time they will be received by President Roosevelt. The British Ambassador and Lady Lindsay will be the first representatives of Britain to entertain Edward, England's abdicated monarch. They will entertain the Duke and Duchess at dinner Nov. 12.

LONDON. (GP). Foreign Secretary Eden Monday promised Great Britain would go “as far as the United States in measures to end the Chinese-Japanese war and warned European dictators Britain never would “stand and deliver at anyone’s command.” Without mentioning Italy by name, Eden’s blunt declaration before the House of Commons tossed back Premier Mussolini’s demand for restoration of German colonies and scored Mussolini's and Reichsführer Hitler’s diplomacy in hard-hitting phrases. Just before leaving for the Brussels conference on the far eastern conflict, Eden declared Britain would “in this difficult far eastern situation go as far as the United States in full agreement with them—not rushing in front but not being left behind.” He said, “I feel I ought to make it quite plain the initiative for holding the conference in Brussels never came from us at all but from the United States govern

LONDON, Nov. 2—(U.P)—Great Britain's patience with “certain governments” appeared today to be approaching exhaustion. An amazed House of Commons voted, 364 to 142, its confidence in the government’s foreign policy after Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden warned that Britain was not disposed to accept meekly from abroad, dictatorial directions regarding her foreign policies. “We offer our cooperation to all, but we accept dictation from none,” Eden declared amid the loudest cheers that have greeted a government speech in Commons in recent years. The foreign secretary roused the members to feverish excitement with a stern reprimand directed at Premier Mussolini of Italy, who had said in a Fascist “birthday” speech in Rome that lasting European peace depended upon restoration of Germany’s colonies in Africa, lost after the World War. NEW YORK, Nov. 1--(AP)--Charley Bedaux, wealthy emissary-without-portfolio for the Duke of Windsor, arrived tonight to make ready for the forthcoming American visit of the abdicated British monarch and his American-born wife, the former Wallis Warfield. Bedaux, who will help chart a public relations path for the royal couple, didn’t bring the news so many had been waiting for—just what points in the United States they would visit. That, he said by ship-to-shore telephone as the liner Europa pushed up New York Harbor, would be announced by the duke himself. Thus, the social side of the trip apparently was undecided, 10 days before the scheduled arrival of the royal couple on November 11, and the country’s leading hostesses were left guessing. WASHINGTON, Nov. 2 Gp — British Ambassador Ronald Lindsay and Lady Lindsay will entertain the Duke and Duchess of Windsor at an embassy dinner the evening of November 12, the embassy announced today.

SHANGHAI, Nov. 2.— (INS) —While British troops fired angrily at a Japanese airplane, French troops swung dramatically into action on the Chinese front today, rushing to the aid of Chinese refugees threatened by the Japanese. The French moved out of the French concession in the international settlement and took control of Nanyang University near the concession boundary. Japanese officers, claiming that the university housed a Chinese military detachment, had threatened to launch an assault against it. This plan was apparently balked by the French action. The French flag was hoisted over the university. The action was taken in response to appeals to neutral forces by the university president. The French took charge of many refugees. At the same time British troops in the international settlement sent volleys of shot against Japanese airplanes soaring above them.

London, Nov. 2—Great Britain was reported by an informed source tonight to be on the verge of reaching a trade agreement with Insurgent Spain. Under the terms, which the informant said would be announced at an appropriate moment, commercial missions and consular offices would be established in both countries. The informant said he did not believe, however, that the agreement would constitute diplomatic recognition, even de facto, of Francisco Franco's government as it was a "purely commercial affair" and would affect only consuls. Full de jure recognition would involve an exchange of ambassadors. The agreement would not permit an insurgent mission to approach the British foreign office officially, the informant said. The arrangement would compare, it was stated, to that existing between Britain and Soviet Russia before the two countries established diplomatic relations. Franco's missions

1937-01-01.text: cs today as Europe greeted 1937. Diplomatic circles saw the possibility of definite achievement of the strict non-intervention in the Spanish civil war for which they labored so fruitlessly in 1936. Indications from Rome and Berlin led them to believe Europe's two great fascist powers would give priority to the problem of foreign volunteers in the peninsula. Other countries already have expressed adherence in principle to the new Franco-British “hands off” demands. Ready For War Romans faced the new year with an army of 1,000,000 men ready for the call to arms but despite the tension, jubilant Romans paved the city’s ancient streets with broken glass and crockery in a celebration almost as old as Rome itself. For days old household utensils have been gathered in piles and at the last stroke of midnight’s twelve they were hurled from house windows to the avenues below in a symbolic shatte

LONDON, Dec. 31.—(4—The 15-year struggle of the sea powers to limit war fleets by treaty died tonight. For its eulogy there were plans for bigger ships and bigger guns from sea to sea. The Washington and London treaties of 1922 and 1930, respectively, by which the nations sought to curb the size of naval forces, expired with the old year. In their place was a two-thirds unratified treaty among the United States, France and Great Britain, which provides a limit for the size of individual men o' war, but put no curb on numbers. All Nations Building. Every one of the old treaty nations, America, Britain, France, Italy, Japan is ready to build more, bigger, faster warships. In the same race are Soviet Russia and rearmed Germany, bitter enemies from every political standpoint. Great Britain paced the rest tonight. With everything arranged to lay the keels for two 35,000-ton capital ships on N

LONDON, Jan. 1 (AP)—The preliminary draft of a proposed plan to block arms shipments to both sides in the Spanish civil war was forwarded to the Fascist and Socialist governments today by the international non-intervention committee. Details of the proposal, approved by the committee December 23, were not disclosed. The Spanish governments at Burgos and Valencia were asked to discuss the suggestion, broadly designed to prevent foreign shipments of armaments to the opposing sides in the domestic conflict. Replies were expected in time for consideration at the next session of the neutrality group January 5. LONDON, Jan. 1 (UP)—Italy will insist on financial neutrality, suppression of propaganda and strict and immediate enforcement of restrictive measures on migration as conditions to an agreement prohibiting participation of foreign volunteers in the Spanish revolution. The latest official

LONDON (UP)——British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden prepared Friday to send immediately to General Francisco Franco and Premier Francisco Largo Caballero an outline of a plan for controlling and supervising non-intervention in Spain's civil war. It was expected that the communications would go out before night to the Spanish insurgent leader and the loyalist premier, in order to speed up action on the program. Eden will request that they accept or reject the plan within 10 days after receipt. It was recalled that early in December Eden on behalf of the non-intervention committee similarly forwarded a communication to Valencia and Burgos.

LONDON, Jan. 1.— (4) — Lloyd's advices from Gibraltar today said the British steamer Etrib, bound from Haifa for Liverpool, was fired upon and forced to stop by an insurgent Spanish trawler 124 miles off Europa Point. The trawler's commander was said to have demanded the Etrib’s ports of departure and destination, as well as the ship's papers. The captain refused to submit the papers and after further questioning was permitted to proceed.

LONDON. (UP), King George VI pushed thoughts of the abdicated Edward VIII into the background in a New Year's greeting to the empire: His message: “In succeeding to the throne I follow a father (George V) who had won for himself an abiding place in the hearts of his peoples, and a brother whose brilliant qualities gave promise of another historic reign—a reign cut short in circumstances upon which, from their very sadness, none of us would wish to dwell.”

LONDON, Jan. 1.—(UP)—Italy will insist on financial neutrality, suppression of propaganda and strict and immediate enforcement of restrictive measures on migration as conditions to an agreement prohibiting participation of foreign volunteers in the Spanish revolution, the latest official Italian expression on the question revealed today. The Italian viewpoint was set forth in a note which Ambassador Dino Grandi handed Lord Plymouth, chairman of the international non-intervention committee. The statement was accepted as forecasting the nature of Italy's forthcoming replies directly to Britain and France in answer to their latest neutrality proposals.

Madrid, Friday, Jan. 1.—(.--War ushered in the new year for the besieged Madrid today as 12 Fascist insurgent shells fell in the center of the city on the stroke of midnight. Militiamen in the Puerto del Sol showed their disdain as the shells exploded while they were eating the traditional 12 lucky grapes to herald 1987. With each explosion, the militia women cried: “Long live the republic.” The artillery shelling was renewed yesterday after Fascist warplanes circled over the capital without dropping bombs. There were no major changes in positions of defenders or the besieging Fascists. (Avila reports said ferocious fire, loosed by Socialist militiamen, had attacked Fascist troops near Villa Verde, but that the insurgents finally drove them back.)

1937-12-30.text: LONDON, Dec. 30 (4)—Japan, in a note to Britain made public today, declared Japanese attacks on the Gunboat Ladybird and other British ships in Chinese waters were a mistake. But to insure against further incidents Japan has dealt properly with responsible military and naval officers on the ground that they failed to take full precautions. New orders have been given to Japanese forces, the note said, for the greatest possible care that attacks shall not be made upon the lives and property of British or other nationals. The note was similar in content to the Japanese explanation of bombing by Japanese planes of the American Gunboat Panay and three Standard Oil vessels. The British foreign office released the explanation, in reply to British protests against such incidents, without any comment to indicate whether it was satisfactory. A British seaman was killed and two wounded on Dec. 13 w

LONDON, Dec. 30 (UP).—Japan, in a note to Great Britain regarding an attack on the gunboat Ladybird, gave assurances similar to those she offered regarding an attack on the United States gunboat Panay, publication of the text disclosed today. The Ladybird was attacked by Japanese artillery in the Yangtze river above Nanking on December 2, the same day as the airplane attack which sank the Panay. (A Tokyo dispatch to the United Press said the foreign office there released the “essentials” of the note to Great Britain tonight). Japan's note said that though the Ladybird attack was due entirely to a mistake, the Japanese government, to insure against possible similar mistakes “have dealt properly according to law with the commanding officer and other officers concerned.

(International News Service) LONDON, Dec. 30—Great Britain plans to join the United States in increasing naval strength next year, International News Service learned today. The admiralty has decided to urge the cabinet to approve construction of a 23,000-ton aircraft carrier and four new 8,000-ton cruisers equipped with six-inch guns. These will be in addition to more than 100 warships now under construction or on order. Bolster Strength. In another attempt to bolster naval strength as speedily as possible in view of the menacing international situation, the admiralty also has decided to move for stepping up existing schedules. The admiralty hopes to advance by six months at least completion of a number of battleships now under construction, with the likelihood the King George and Prince of Wales will be launched in 1939 instead of 1940 as originally planned. PARIS, Dec. 30—A new outbreak of strikes in the rich mining region of northern France intensified the turbulent labor situation today after firm government steps brought quick settlement of the public service tie-up in Paris. A thousand coal miners at Anzin quit work this morning in protest against discharge of three miners. This stoppage aroused official concern lest the strike spread among all of the 16,000 miners employed by the Anzin company. Local government officials sought to negotiate a settlement. Premier Camille Chautemps' threat to call striking public service workers, most of whom are army reservists, to the colors, caused prompt submission to his demands for settlement of the Paris strike. Six hundred sailors at Rouen whose recent walkout tied up 36 ships, continued on strike. The agreement to call off the Paris service strike came in the early hours of the morning after lab

[BY ASSOCIATED PRESS] Shanghai—Japanese armies met stiff Chinese resistance today on Shantung province fronts outside Peinetes, the dynamite-rocked slain China seaport from which a number of Americans were in flight. Japanese sources themselves sent word of fierce fighting some 100 miles west of Tsingtao, between the railroad centers of Weihsien and Tsingchow. South of Tsinan, the conquered provincial capital, warfare on the outskirts of Taian gave China’s sacred mountain, Tai Shan, a baptism of fire. The United States gunboat Sacramento docked in Shanghai and disembarked first American civilian refugees from the threatened port 400 miles to the north. Twenty-five Americans, with a number of nurses and dependents, made the trip. More on Way Another contingent of American Tsingtao refugees headed for Shanghai on the steamer Shuntien. The United States cruiser Marblehead and destroyer Pope

Shanghai, Dec. 29. (4)—Acute tension gripped Tsingtao today as Chinese, apparently resigned to loss of the rich north China port, spread devastation to leave the Japanese nothing but ashes. A series of explosions late last night rocked the city as Chinese soldiers blew up telegraph, cable and radio offices, creating fear the Chinese “broken tile” policy might mean greater destruction before the expected Japanese entry. Ships Stand By The United States cruiser Marblehead and destroyer Pope moved close to shore, ready to evacuate Americans in case of sudden cruiser lay near to take off Britons. With the United States gunboat Sacramento already at sea bound for Shanghai with 45 American refugees, 159 Americans remained in Tsingtao and 13 others in its environs. Eleven Americans still were at Tsinan, Shantung province about 200 miles west of Tsingtao, which Japan's forces already had occupie

CAIRO, Dec. 30.—(#)—Egypt was plunged today into the greatest political crisis of young King Farouk's 20-month reign when he dismissed Premier Mustapha Nahas Pasha and appointed Mohamed Mahmoud to form a new government. Mahmoud, 55 years old, Oxford educated and premier in 1928 and 1929, immediately started drafting a new cabinet, then decided to dissolve parliament and hold elections within two months. The long feud between the palace and the government of the Wafdist (Nationalist) premier already had resulted in a strike of 10,000 government railway workers in Cairo. Police were on the alert to forestall threatened disorders. It was understood that preparations had been made to move British troops to Egypt from Palestine in event of an emergency—ostensibly to protect British interests.

SHANGHAI, Dec. 30. (U.P)—Japanese opened a terrific aerial attack on Canton today while Chinese continued sabotage in Tsingtao and assassins' bullets killed Loh Peh-Hong, wealthy pro-Japanese merchant of Shanghai. The air raid on Canton was the most severe in many months and apparently was aimed at the Chinese arsenal, possibly foreshadowing the long-anticipated offensive against the southern seaport, with its adjacent vast foreign interests. Foreigners expressed grave perturbation over developments. Eight Japanese war planes participated in the raid. For 45 minutes they dropped tons of explosives on the suburban districts of the city. It was the most severe air assault since Sept. 8 but Chinese sources claimed that the damage was slight. The assassination of Loh, Chinese Catholic leader who had been mentioned for the post of mayor and presumably was acceptable to the Japanese, caused a

1937-01-08.text: (By Associated Press) Great Britain and France drove toward localizing Spain’s war today, spurred by reports of German invasion of Morocco, threatening Gibraltar and the Colonial border. There’s a sought a practical plan to keep foreign arms and men from the civil conflict. France announced she will never permit Germany to gain a foothold in Spanish Morocco, saying she would ask a consultation of neutrality powers to stop foreign intervention in Spain. Belgium demanded indemnity for Baron Jacques Deborchgrave, diplomat allegedly executed outside of Madrid. Germany announced the turning over of two seized Spanish government ships to insurgents because a demand for the return of cargo and passengers of a captured German freighter were ignored. Mexico opened ports for reshipment of United States arms to Spain, announcing war supplies will be permitted through this country “if the license is

Germany and Italy, in a sweeping proposal to ban non-intervention in the Spanish civil war yesterday (Thursday), suggested ejection from Spain of all non-Spanish fighters. Both Germany and Italy in notes to France and Great Britain agreed in principle to French and British pleas for a ban on the flow of foreign volunteers into Spain. Reservations were made by both nations, however, Germany's chief proviso was that all interested powers agree on effective supervision to halt intervention. France, meanwhile, disclosed she will concentrate 34 warships and a number of submarines near Spain within two weeks. Although officials said the movements were part of annual maneuvers, they pointed out the vessels would be in 'a strategic position' in relation to Spain. French frontier authorities reported volunteers from many countries were proceeding across the southern border of France to aid the Sp

LONDON, Jan. 8—The British cabinet held an emergency session today in the midst of growing European tension over Spain, based on the question of German and Italian military aid and the alleged German penetration of Spanish Morocco. The latter question has aroused France, fearful that, if Germany gets a foothold in Morocco, France will be confronted in the Mediterranean by a powerful fascist neighbor, with attendant disturbance of the delicate balance of power in the inland sea.

BERLIN, Jan. 7 (P)—Germany proposed Thursday that all foreign participants be ejected from the Spanish civil war, “including political agitators”—a note apparently directed at communists. Acting with Italy, the German government informed France and Britain that she is willing to accept on her own conditions the plea that foreign volunteer enlistments to Spain be stopped, But, the German note said, the Nazi government felt an embargo now “would profit only the Bolshevist side in Spain, which obviously is already sufficiently filled out with foreign volunteers.” Inferring criticism of Britain and France, the German note contended the Nazis were among the first to urge prevention of volunteer enlistments last summer, but that Britain and France were unwilling. Now, Germany suggested, if Britain and France have changed viewpoints, it must be asked seriously “whether the proposed embargo at t

LONDON, Jan. 5 (AP) — Britain will concentrate 90 warships in near Spanish waters the Admiralty announced Friday night after a hurried cabinet session heard reports of German military activity in Spanish Morocco. Dispatch of the naval units coincides with regular naval maneuvers in the Mediterranean area, the Admiralty said, but the fleets would be ready for action if needed. The British home fleet leaves Portsmouth and other English ports January 18. The Mediterranean fleet is moving about to relieve comrades in and near Spanish ports, where 18 war craft have been on constant duty. The battleships Nelson and Rodney, of 33,900 and 38,000 tons, will lead the home fleet southward and remain in the Eastern Mediterranean or off the West African coast. The home fleet consists of 49 units, that of the Mediterranean 41.

. By Vatted Press Spanish civil war developments: BERLIN — German reprisals expected as ultimatum to Spanish loyalists on seized steamer Palos expires. LONDON — British home fleet ordered to Mediterranean, where 105 warships will be concentrated; French fleet also going south but Paris insists the movement is not connected with Spain. PARIS — German activity in Spanish Morocco arouses grave concern. MADRID — Furious battle in progress for possession of capital. PERPIGNAN — Two rebel warships bombarded towns just on Spanish side of French border in northeastern Spain. LONDON, Jan. 8 — The British home fleet has received orders to sail for the Mediterranean for “combined maneuvers” with the Mediterranean fleet which will put 105 British fighting ships within reach of the Spanish war zone. It was described as a routine business, but with the government increasingly anxious over the Spanish
LONDON, Jan. 5.—An armed Spanish insurgent trawler seized an unidentified Russian steamer bound westward in the Straits of Gibraltar and conducted her to Ceuta, Spanish Morocco, Lloyd's reported.

LONDON, Jan. 8.—()—British cabinet ministers met today in a hurriedly-called special session to consider both German military activities across the straits from Gibraltar and the non-intervention problem in Spain itself. Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden called the conference after a night discussion with the prime minister, Stanley Baldwin will see King George VI at Sandringham over the week-end and acquaint him with the international developments.

1937-01-17.text: By The Associated Press LONDON — Film actress Ann Harding, who fled America to keep the custody of her daughter and incidentally pick up a bit of movie money in England, has found romance as well—with an American. The golden-haired former wife of Harry Bannister will wed shy Werner Janssen, brilliant orchestra conductor and composer who fought his way up from New York’s west side cabarets to the podium of the New York Philharmonic. Miss Harding indicated the wedding would be soon but would not say when or where. Miss Harding is 34. Janssen 37.

MADRID, Jan. 15.—Soldiers confessed today that they had eaten Willie, the wart hog, an aged inmate of the Madrid zoo. It took a machine gun to kill him, the soldiers said, but after they picked out the bullets, added some parsley and a little seasoning, he made a succulent meal.

CANNES, France, Jan. 16 (4).— A sudden dash of the Duke of Windsor to the woman for whom he sacrificed his throne would be no surprise to most Riviera folk, repeated and emphatic statements to the contrary notwithstanding. Why, people of Cannes ask, should two persons who showed a disregard of conventionalism to the extent of shaking an empire, now become so scrupulous on the score? Some fine day, they predict almost unanimously, the duke, bored with the loneliness of his Austrian castle, will rush to her, final decree or no final decree.

OSLO, Norway, Jan. 16.—Police today seized the passport of the “mystery woman” who attempted to collect the $37,000 Nobel peace prize awarded to the German pacifist, Karl von Ossietzky. The woman, supposedly a German, who gave the name of Mrs. Alexandra Kreutzberger, was confined to her hotel where she refused to see anyone. She said she was secretary to a Dr. Kurt Wannow, of Berlin, and was acting at his instructions. “I don't know Ossietzky or his wife personally and am only acting on orders,” she declared. A section of the Norwegian press charged her action was an attempt by Nazi authorities to seize the Nobel prize money. Ossietzky, released from a Nazi concentration camp shortly before he received the prize, long has been in disfavor of the Nazi party. Diplomatic protests of the award were made by Germany at the time it was voted. It was understood the bank to which the Nobel commit

MADRID, Jan. 16.~The capital’s defenders contended today that they had checked a rebel mass attack in which Gen. Francisco Franco threw the whole weight of his army against the loyalist defenses on the west and northwest of the city. Newspapers appeared with huge black headlines about the failure of the attack. The rattle of shells and bullets lessened during the day as a cold, wet blanket of fog re-enveloped the capital. There was Uae y MARR, GEASECRANL SPRUPRPEEE YL AU YY OS batteries, interrupted by one spasmodic burst from rebel batteries. After 10 hours of continuous fighting, accompanied by an incessant roar of the heaviest artillery on both sides, the Government lines still held. Wave after wave of attacking insurgent troops were turned back with heavy losses as the Loyalist artillery hammered away at their lines of communications to prevent replacements from coming up. Possibility of reviving Premier Mussolini's four-power peace agreement of 1933 was said in reliable quarters tonight to have been discussed by Il Duce and Colonel-General Hermann Wilhelm Goering of Germany. The Italian premier and Reichsführer Hitler's chief aide were represented as seeking primarily an alliance against communism and as considering whether the bloc formed under Mussolini's pact—Great Britain, France, Italy and Germany—might not be recreated. (The treaty signed by representatives of the four countries at Rome July 15, 1933, was designed to guarantee peace in Europe for ten years, aid in reduction of armaments and lead to bettering of economic conditions. (The bloc split apart when Italy invaded Ethiopia late in 1935. The pact specified that signatories should maintain and respect the territorial integrity and political independence of League of Nations members. Ethiopia w

TACOMA, Wash., Jan. 16—(/)— Search for the “hide-out” of Charles Mattson's kidnap-slayer and a mill watchman’s report he heard what he believed was a child's scream on the night of January 6 topped developments today in the wide-spread hunt for the murderer. The 10-year-old boy’s badly beaten nude body was found in the snow about seven miles southwest of Everett last Monday. The watchman, whose name was withheld, told officers he had thought little of the cries at the time, assuming they were from a child at play. State and Everett police and the sheriff denied reports of a “pick up” order for the son of an Everett resident whose hobbies were knife-throwing and dissecting animals. The man’s parents live on the Everett east side and the son has, as his “den,” a shack in the bay front brushland near Everett, about five miles from the place where the Tacoma kidnap victim's body was found. (By Associated Press) Detroit, Jan. 16 — Michigan's National Guard troops remained on duty in the automotive strike zone at Flint today as plans went forward for the opening of peace negotiations between General Motors and union representatives and the evacuation of sit-down strikers in company plants. Orders for partial demobilization of troops were rescinded suddenly; more than 600 of them were about to board a train for home when instructions to remain were received. The 2300 troops, Mayor Harold E. Bradshaw said, will remain during Sunday and Monday. The Mayor, who conferred with Gov. Frank Murphy before the new orders were issued, insisted that neither he nor the governor anticipated a renewal of last Monday's violence, but that he recommended retention of the soldiers over the weekend during which the “sit-down” strikers in two Fisher Body plants at Flint are to vacate.

1937-05-29.text: LONDON, (?), King-maker Stanley Baldwin stepped from the British premiership into private life Friday, victorious to the last in his fight to keep Wallis Warfield from official membership in the British royal family, and with the duties of government given safely into the hands of his chancellor of the exchequer, Arthur Neville Chamberlain. The 69 year old “honest Stan,” who kept Mrs. Warfield from becoming queen by marriage to Edward VIII in the battle over constitutional rights of a monarch last December, appeared also to have prevented the American-born woman from becoming “her royal highness” when she marries Edward in France on June 3. Friends of the now duke of Windsor said they had received a telephone message direct from him that he had lost the fight to win the royal rank for his bride-to-be. A “letters patent” King George VI was expected shortly to announce the status of titles

SANDWICH, England, May 29 (UP).-Robert Sweeny Jr, an American who lives in London, won the British amateur golf championship today, defeating Lionel Munn of County Cork, Ireland, 3 and 2, in the 36-hole final match. The 25-year-old stock broker who has lived in London since he was 16, led virtually all the way over the Irish veteran who is twice Sweeny’s age.

LONDON, May 28 ()—A decree of King George VI published to-night recorded an overwhelming defeat for the Duke of Windsor in his fight to make his bride-to-be, American-born Wallis Warfield, “Her Royal Highness.” The king specifically forbade the future duchess to use the royal title after her marriage June 3. More than that, his decree showed that the Duke himself, since his abdication as king last December, has not enjoyed royal status until yesterday. From yesterday he became “his royal highness” only by special dispensation of the brother who succeeded him on the throne. It was disclosed such action by the king was necessary because the Duke actually had forfeited his royal status when he abdicated and renounced all rights of succession to the throne for himself and his heirs. King’s Decision in Court Organ The king’s decision—or that of the British government—was published in an annou

of OREN Oe eee 68 8 New London, Texas, May 29— Diplomas were sent today to the families who lost 24 senior sons and daughters in the New London school blast which killed hundreds last March. The explosion was ignored last night as the 50 surviving seniors were graduated. They were counseled to forget the wounds of the past and think for the future.

LONDON, May 28.— UP — Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain, taking over leadership of the government from Stanley Baldwin, tonight reshuffled two important cabinet posts responsible for spending the bulk of Britain's $37,500,000,000 rearmament fund. In an unexplained move, a few hours after he was called to Buckingham Palace to receive the seal of the premiership from King George VI, Chamberlain turned the Baldwin cabinet inside out. Only 16 of the 28 major cabinet portfolios remained in the same hands when he was through. He removed Alfred Duff Cooper from the post of secretary of war and made him first lord of the admiralty, succeeding Sir Samuel Hoare, who became home secretary. Leslie Hore-Belisha, secretary of transport, became secretary of war. The other two defense posts—air and co-ordinated defense—remained unchanged.

MOTS, France, May 28—(A’)—The duke of Windsor and his bride-to-be met the British government’s refusal to rank her as “Her Royal Highness” with outward silence tonight, But there must have been anguish at the unexpected decision. Mrs. Warfield, it was reliably said, already had had “H. R. H.” and coronets embroidered on some articles of her trousseau. The duke’s friends had thought the matter settled in victory for him and Mrs. Warfield after a stiff fight. The duke’s spokesman had announced Mrs. Warfield would bear the title “Her Royal Highness.” Windsor’s friends expressed hope that Neville Chamberlain, Baldwin's successor as Prime Minister, would show a more friendly attitude. They said efforts already have been made to soften the government's policies toward the ex-king, especially that of keeping him “isolated.” The duke of Kent, Edward's favorite brother, is anxious to attend the w

London, May 29—(#)—Italy and Germany accused the Spanish government today of bombing Italian and German naval vessels participating in the neutral patrol of Mediterranean waters east of Spain, and thus complicating international effort to halt the civil strife. Soviet Russia, meanwhile, gave assent in principle to British proposals for a truce in the Spanish hostilities but made the reservation that the insurgents first must withdraw all foreign troops and cease war activity. The truce proposal has been virtually shelved for the time being, however. The Italian representatives on the 27-nation non-intervention committee presented charges that six seamen were killed and seven wounded when a Spanish government plane bombed the Italian auxiliary ship Barletta off Mallorca. The German government announced that the commander of German naval forces in Spanish waters had warned the Valencia gov

MONTS, France. (UP). Members of the household at the Chateau de Cande said that the duke of Windsor long ago discounted the British court and government decision that Mrs. Wallis Warfield must be content to rank, after their marriage, as an ordinary duchess. His only uncertainty, it was said, was the manner in which the decision to make him a “royal highness” and Mrs. Warfield, as his wife, a less illustrious “her grace,” would be published. Gossip in the household was that Queen Elizabeth might have had a role in the decision to publish the decision in the official London Gazette. It was gossiped that the queen disliked Mrs. Warfield, that the duchess of Gloucester was neutral and that the duchess of Kent was in Mrs. Warfield’s favor. The duchesses are wives of the king’s—and the duke’s—brothers. It was said that the decision not to make Mrs. Warfield a “royal highness” was no surprise

1937-09-20.text: GENEVA, Sept. 20.—(UP)— Great Britain, admittedly anxious over the international situation from Spain to China, made sweeping gestures today for United States, German and Italian aid in putting the world on the road toward better times. The world assembly of the league had just delivered a smashing blow to the Loyalist Spanish government by rejecting its candidacy for re-election to the league council, or governing body, when Anthony Eden, British foreign secretary, addressed the assembly. Armed To Hilt He warned the world that Britain is re-arming to the hilt, and will continue to do so as long as peace is threatened. He said that Britain now is building 450,000 tons of warships, to cost $660,000,000. ‘But he went on with his appeals for a world effort to better conditions by what he said was the only means—removing fear and raising standards of living. He centered on the United States,

LONDON (#) — Italy reasserted Sunday her flat demand for equality in the Nyon “anti-pirate” patrol of the Mediterranean as Great Britain and France attempted to ease the increasing tension in that sea, sorely troubled by the Spanish civil war. However, in moving for alleviation of the crisis Britain and France displayed no intention of yielding in the slightest degree their dominant role in the Mediterranean patrol scheme. Foreign Minister Count Galeazzo Ciano replied to the request of the British and French governments for clarification of Italy’s demand for full parity. This was hailed in Rome as an indication that France and Britain were making the first move to break the diplomatic impasse to obtain Italian participation. But informed sources in London said the situation was unchanged. One authority put it thus: “It is not a question of Britain and France backing down on the plan, bu

Newport, R.I., Sept. 20—(UP)—A rolling sea today held the fate of the British Racing Sloop Endeavour and her crew of 20, missing since last Monday when the trim craft lost her convoy in a raging storm 200 miles off Nantucket Light. As several coast guard vessels, searching for the craft for the fifth day, swept a wide area south of Nova Scotia, T. O. M. Sopwith, former owner of the sloop, sent word to Tollesbury, England, where seven members of the crew lived, not to worry, that “she’ll come in in two or three weeks.”

London, Sept. 19.—(AP)—Spokesmen of the United States and seven other countries pledged themselves tonight to strive for peace through economic cooperation in a world where “cravings and quarrels threaten to bring about human catastrophe at any moment.” On a worldwide radio (Columbia) hookup, representatives of the United States, Canada, France, Great Britain, Austria, Czechoslovakia, Belgium and Colombia urged broader international trade to prevent warfare. Hard to Conceive Peace The symposium was sponsored by the National Peace Conference. Secretary of State Cordell Hull, speaking from New York, said it is “difficult” to talk of peace when bombs are exploding and desperate armies are marching.” He declared, however, that through enlarged international trade there can come “an equilib- (Continued on Page 2)

BOSTON. |.P. Anxious watchers on two sides of the Atlantic pinned chief hope for the safety of the British racing sloop Endeavour with 20 men on the possibility the trim craft might have continued to England after losing her convoy in a hurricane nearly a week ago. While coast guard vessels for the fourth day searched the rolling seas south of Nova Scotia without a trace of Endeavour, shipping was warned of a disturbance over Quebec causing fresh to strong southwest winds, shifting to northwest, and small craft warnings were posted from Delaware to Maine. Just before the warnings went up, the Endeavour’s convoy, the 180-foot motor yacht Viva II, sailed from Newport, R.I., for England, planning to search for the sloop on the way. Viva lost Endeavour last Monday night when a nine-inch hawser rope parted in a 100-mile gale. At that time the vessels were 200 miles off Nantucket lightship. Vi

Britain offered, before the League assembly at Geneva today to negotiate a trade agreement with the United States, to listen to suggestions Italy might have on the Mediterranean pirate patrol problem, and in Germany's favor to discuss reduction of colonial tariffs. Anthony Eden, British foreign secretary, in making the offers said also that Britain though rearming is still ready for a disarmament agreement. Other developments in the Mediterranean problem: GENEVA.—League assembly in smashing blow at Loyalist Spanish government rejects Spain's candidacy for re-election to council, ROME.—Italy moves to break deadlock on Mediterranean; makes "practical observations" to Britain and France. LONDON.—British and French fleet movements in Mediterranean reach wartime proportions.

Hendaye, Franco-British Frontier, Sept. 19.—(#)—Asturians sprang out of their rugged strongholds today and delivered a furious surprise attack on the insurgent line along the valley of the Sella river, east of Gijon. Military dispatches to the state it was the heaviest battle to date in the insurgent campaign to wipe out the small government-held area about Gijon. Both sides suffered heavy losses. The insurgents, who compose the coastal column driving westward toward besieged Gijon, were thrown back by the sudden infantry attack. Finally reinforced, they fought back to their original positions. Fighting continued during the night. Brest, France, Sept. 19.—(/P)—The captain of the Spanish government submarine C-4 and three members of his crew were arrested at Bordeaux today after attempting to seize another Spanish government submarine, the C-2, which had just finished repairs in Brest. Au

CANTERBURY CLUB, Cleveland, Sept. 20.~(UP)—Ralph Guldahl, of Chicago, today defeated Horton Smith, Missouri-reared Chicagoan, in their 18-hole playoff for the Western open golf championship. He finished with a 72, four strokes better than Smith’s 76. The two players each shot 288 at the end of the regulation 72-hole tournament yesterday. The victory gave Guldahl his second consecutive Western open title. He won the championship at Davenport, Ia., last year, when he shot a 274 to come within one stroke of equalling Tommy Armour’s record of 273.

1937-01-07.text: LONDON, Jan. 6.—(4)—Great Britain ordered a mass movement of 172,000 tons of warships in the Mediterranean today after requesting Germany and Italy to answer by Saturday her proposal to ban volunteers from the Spanish civil war. Four of the British navy’s largest fighting ships prepared to steam between Gibraltar and Malta in naval maneuvers described by the admiralty as “routine” but interpreted as “significant” in the tense Spanish crisis. The Italian reply to the British suggestion to halt the flow of foreign volunteers into Spain was expected to be ready for transmission today or tomorrow. The German answer, it was learned, also would be ready today but would not reach London until Thursday or Friday. Simultaneously receipt of the answers tomorrow, it was said, would not be surprising.

By The Associated Press Germany and Italy, the Fascist powers of Europe, answered French and British pleas that they stop sending volunteers to Spain in conciliatory, yet reserved, notes tonight. Both replies, delivered in Berlin and in Rome, were said to agree in principle that volunteers should not go from other countries to fight with the Spanish government or the insurgents. Informed sources indicated they made their acceptance conditional, however, upon the formulation of a broad non-intervention plan which would bar both direct and indirect forms of foreign aid in Spain. Their replies were delivered while French officials—following the lead of Great Britain—announced that warships and a number of submarines would be concentrated in Spain within two weeks, “in case they are needed in connection with the Spanish crisis.” Britain already has 172,000 tons of naval craft near the coast

Ominous war clouds gathered over Europe last night in the storm of dispute over aid to belligerents of the Spanish civil war. Britain speeded more warships to Spanish waters. France held troops ready for a possible dash to the Spanish border. Both nations appeared ready to act unless Germany and Italy agree to stop intervening in the Iberian Peninsula. There was talk of a coastal blockade to halt the flow of arms and men to Socialist defenders and Fascist attackers. Indications were Italy and Germany would temporize in replies to the Franco-British plea to halt volunteer enlistments, and the answers were expected soon. Britain itself was troubled by news a contingent of her own Nationals would enlist with the Spanish Socialist. Berlin made known Nazi warships would continue to patrol the Spanish coast but without further reprisals for loss of the freighter Palos’ cargo to Bilbao Basques.

LONDON, Jan. 7 (AP).—Great Britain, with a warning eye on her mighty fleet massing in Spanish waters, looked to Germany and Italy today for a “constructive” answer to demands for non-intervention on the Spanish civil war. Observers pointed out British men-of-war were moving toward Spain in sufficient numbers to enforce a blockade of the peninsula, should such action become necessary. The British position to enforce isolation of Spain's “little world war” was considered in informed circles to be strengthened through American action to bar shipments of armaments to both sides of the civil conflict. LONDON, Jan. 7—(4)—An earthquake, estimated from seismograph needle movement to be almost as forceful as the quake in the Indian Quetta region in which 26,000 persons were killed in May 1935, was registered in London today. Experts said the needles moved between six and seven inches. The earthquake was estimated to have occurred approximately 4,770 miles away, apparently either in Central Asia or the West Indies.

VIENNA, Jan. 7—(UP)—Edward VII, Duke of Windsor, and Alfonso XIII, former king of Spain, lunched together today at a Vienna hotel, and conversed at length, reminiscing on their lives since they left their thrones. Fellow monarchs in exile, the duke because he left his British throne for love of Mrs. Wallis Simpson, one-time Baltimore society woman, Alfonso, because his people forced him from the throne in 1931, provided a colorful contrast. Edward is blonde and even more nervous since his abdication, at 42, so that he might marry as he liked; Alfonso, at 50, swarthy and suave, head of the ancient Bourbon House.

ROME, Jan. 7 (U.P)—Italy, in a memorandum to the French and British governments, offered today to withdraw all support from the nationalists in the Spanish civil war provided other nations withdrew all support of the loyalists, it was said authoritatively. The note was delivered last night, in memorandum form, and was expected to be published to- (Continued on Page 2, Column 1)

BERLIN, Jan. 7 (UP)—Germany, in a polite but critical note to Britain and France, expressed conditional readiness tonight to support any moves to halt the flow of foreign “volunteer” troops into Spain. The German reply included four points. In the first it picked flaws both in the substance and method of the Franco-British proposals for the withdrawal of foreign troops. It criticized the direct Franco-British appeal to Germany and Italy instead of going through the international non-intervention committee in London, declaring that it would be more consistent to abandon the committee altogether if the powers insist on making such direct appeals.

1937-12-27.text: LONDON, Dec. 26.—(UP)—Citizens of London poked wary heads out of doors today and heard strange tales of the worst Christmas fog since 1904. The grimy curtain of “pea soup,” lifting slowly in most sections, left a trail of dignified police bowled over by motorists, charred debris where firemen fought fires they could not see and millions of raw throats. Probably the most nettled victim of all was Goalkeeper Bartram of the Chariton soccer team, who stuck doggedly to his post not knowing the game had been called off until after the other players had left the field. A searching party finally found him. The fog made a crazy patchwork over the celebrating city, but sooner or later every section was blanketed. Merrymakers reckless enough to start out for parties wandered miles from their goals. From telephone booth oases in the desert of grey darkness they called for directions from their anxio

JERUSALEM, Dec. 26.—(4’)}—Rain-soaked British troops closed in from three directions today on a band of Arab terrorists responsible for three days of bloody Christmas fighting in the hills of Galilee. The official casualty list showed 30 known dead in the three days of guerrilla warfare although unofficial estimates put the toll as high as 50. British Lieutenant M. W. Mountain and Private J. S. Creasey were killed and three British soldiers were wounded. The other 28 known dead were Arabs. The remnant of the terrorist gang—about 200 strong—was pushing desperately toward the closely guarded Transjordan frontier. To entrap them, all roads were closed to private traffic throughout almost the whole northern district. Troops also were searching each village they entered. British native police were guarding the Lebanese and Syrian borders as well, co-operating with the 8,000 regulars of the Br

LONDON, Dec 27 (#)—Violet, dowager duchess of Rutland, mother of the ninth duke of Rutland and mother-in-law of Alfred Duff Cooper, first lord of the admiralty, died today following an appendicitis operation. She was about 75 years old.

Shanghai, Dec. 27, (UP) — New, grave international complications were threatened today when Japanese authorities announced a series of drastic regulations aimed against any person, Chinese or foreign, who commits offenses against Japanese forces in China. A few hours after the regulations were announced a Japanese army spokesman complained that someone had thrown three hand grenades at a Japanese military launch in Soochow creek, bordering the British defense sector of the international settlement. Soldier Wounded. One of the bombs exploded, the spokesman said, and slightly wounded a Japanese soldier. Announcement of the regulations was a new development. They apply to all territory occupied by the Japanese, in other parts of China as well as in Shanghai, and the spokesman who announced them said that foreigners would be subject to them. The death penalty is provided if "offenses" under

WINDSOR, Ont., Dec. 27. (47)—Weston W. Fletcher, 28, for whom several thousand persons in the United States and Canada offered blood transfusions in a fight against a streptococcus viridans infection, died at 5:40 a.m. today in Grace Hospital. Offers from blood donors poured into the hospital after the victim's mother issued an appeal a month ago. The requirements that the donor have type four blood and have recovered from streptococcus viridans excluded all but a handful of the volunteers. It was reported Fletcher had five transfusions.

Hendaye, Franco-Spanish Frontier, Dec. 27. (P)—Insurgent troops and civilians held out in two flaming citadels today against Spanish government attackers in control of the rest of the ancient Aragon city of Teruel. Government advices said the massive Teruel seminary and the Bank of Spain, both on fire, still housed a defiant group of Italian officers, German officers and Spanish sympathizers of insurgent Generalissimo Francisco Franco. The attacking forces had tightened their grip on the strategic city 135 miles east of Madrid by successfully storming the civil guard barracks, leaving only the two strongholds to be conquered. Beleaguered remnants of the insurgent garrison fought to prolong the siege in the hope shock troops under General Miguel Aranda could hammer through government lines to relieve them. Communiques of the two factions and dispatches from the front gave little indicatio

- HENDAYE (P) - Spanish loyalists asserted Monday that two small groups of buildings in which the remnants of a rebel garrison held out at Teruel were aflame and that all the defenders seemed doomed. There were persistent reports from loyalist centers that several high Spanish fascist leaders were trapped in the building and that one reason for the desperate defense, and refusal of invitations to surrender was that the leaders knew they faced execution if captured. It was said that men in the buildings included fascists responsible for the execution of many loyalists. Reports said also that among rebels already made prisoner were several high Spanish fascists and that these men would be tried by the special revolutionary tribunal as responsible for death orders against loyalists. Loyalist reports indicated the possibility that there was dissension among the remaining defenders. It was as

(By the Associated Press) Shanghai, Dec. 27—(Monday)— The capture of Tsinan, capital of Shantung province, by a Japanese army was reported today in dispatches. Japanese forces, crossing the turbulent Yellow River at several points in western Shantung, were pressing inward into the heart of the province. South of Shanghai another Japanese army extended its conquests into Chekiang province. Hangchow, the provincial capital, fell to invaders Christmas Eve. Communications Broken The report of Tsinan’s fall came by way of Hankow, one of China’s temporary capitals, and was confirmed by dispatches from Tsingtao, Shantung’s chief port. Tsingtao previously had reported its communications with Tsinan had been ruptured. If Tsinan has been captured it would be the seventh Chinese provincial capital to fall to the Japanese, in addition to Nanking, the national capital. The others are Paoting, Hebei;

1937-06-18.text: WASHINGTON, June 18. (AP)—Elmer L. Irey, treasury tax investigator, told congressional investigators today Charles Laughton, the actor, had “effected substantial reductions” in taxes by turning over his Hollywood earnings to a British corporation. A short time before the treasury investigator laid before the committee the names of a group of prominent capitalists who, he asserted, escaped American taxes by forming foreign corporations. Irey said Laughton, described as an English citizen, set up a holding company in England and contracted with it to pay him a $20,000 salary in 1935. At the same time, he said, Laughton handed over to the company all his earnings for that year from American moving picture activities. These totaled, he said, $190,280. He added that the entire arrangement “may be perfectly legal.” But it is just another illustration, he said, of methods used to get around Ame
