SHANGHAI, Nov. 22 (#)—The possibility of a new Japanese-British incident developed here today when Japanese naval authorities prevented the British steamer Kaying from unloading rice originating at Saigon, French Indo-China, pending investigation of the cargo’s status. The Japanese said their understanding was that the cargo, imported under a military permit, was not paying duty and that the consignee was the Central Trust of China, a Chinese government agency.

1937-08-18.text: LONDON, Aug. 18.—()—Britain moved sternly today to protect her “arterial road” through the Mediterranean with what was described as a “shoot-to-sink” order against submarines that molest British merchantmen. The dramatic order crackled from the admiralty radio to units of the Mediterranean fleet and to the naval bases at Gibraltar and Malta. It was interpreted in London as sure indication that British patience was near the breaking point, as the result of an increasing series of air and sea attacks reported in sections of the Mediterranean far from Spanish waters. Of eight ships reporting attacks since August 6, only one was of British registry, however. This was the oil tanker British Corporal and it was said to have been the target of a bomb and a machine gun attack by planes—not a submarine.

| LONDON, (P)—Great Britain may propose that she, the United States and France assume responsibility for safeguarding Chinese and Japanese interests at Shanghai in order to spare the city, it was reported today. It was said the government already had issued orders for diplomatic representatives to sound out reaction to the idea at Washington, Paris, Tokyo and Nanking. The plan was discussed at yesterday's cabinet meeting, it was understood. Any such offer would be contingent upon the removal of Chinese and Japanese troops and bluejackets, and an engagement to respect the neutrality of the international settlement. The Daily Mail reported today the cabinet considered sending more troops to Shanghai. British officials are convinced a war between China and Japan is inevitable and see a Japanese victory as almost certain. But there is a conviction that unless Japan delivers the death blow wi

(By the Associated Press) London, Aug. 17.—The British admiralty today ordered the empire’s men o'war to counter-attack any submarine attacking a British merchantman. The admiralty issued the orders upon instructions from the cabinet, which expressed its perturbation at the increasing number of attacks upon shipping in the Mediterranean. “We Will Take Action” “This promiscuous sinking of ships is getting a bit steep,” an admiralty spokesman said. “We are simply telling the world we will take action.” He said the decision was limited to Spanish troubles. “That's flat,” the spokesman declared. “If one of our ships is attacked without warning, we will sink whoever did it. That’s it in a nutshell.” Spanish Ship Sunk The latest Mediterranean incident was the sinking of the Spanish ship, Ciudad de Cadiz, yesterday reportedly by a submarine outside Dardenelles. NEW YORK, Aug. 17 (The immigration service did today what Mrs. Esther Worman has not been able to do for seven years—locate her missing husband, Augustus. Worman was at Bills Island on a charge of illegally entering the United States in 1930 from England by way of Canada. He was arrested in a downtown rooming house and was held for a hearing which may mean his deportation. If he is deported to England, Mrs. Worman will be glad, because she is going to be deported too, not from New York, but from Galveston. She was discovered, nude on a freighter last week, a stowaway. Mrs. Worman made a 20-day voyage in the hold of the freighter where stifling heat, she said, made clothes not only unnecessary but unbearable. That was why she was nude when they found her, the woman explained.

Mounting with horrified speed in the Sino-Japanese war today, 5000 Japanese were reported slain in the battle over Nankow Pass and many more lives lost as shelling in Shanghai continued relentlessly for its sixth day. Led by the United States and Britain, western powers launched moves to stem the slaughter. Developments: 1. Chinese scuttled six Japanese cargo ships in Shanghai port. While Japanese warships and artillery concentrated fire on Shanghai's electric and water stations, and aircraft of both nations continued bombardments. Shanghai, Aug. 18.—(AP)—Chinese snipers’ bullets three times imperilled Americans today while the Dollar liner McKinley evacuated 294 American women and children refugees off Shanghai today. Near panic broke out on the tender carrying the refugees to the President McKinley when Chinese snipers, evidently mistaking the craft for a Japanese vessel despite waving American flags, peppered it with rifle fire. Passengers on deck flopped to their stomachs, not daring to stand long enough to race for protection below. Twice, shore snipers opened fire on the tender. Once Chinese bullets whistled over the President McKinley’s decks and through her rigging when riflemen along the shore began peppering the river full of Japanese destroyers. The first fright came when bombs from Japanese warplanes fell dangerously close to the liner itself in the Yangtze river, although Captain Bryant had ordered hug

CANNES, France, Aug. 18. (U.P)—The mayor of Cannes, Pierre Nouveau, said today that John A. Roosevelt, son of President Roosevelt, had hurled a glass of champagne in his face during the annual “Battle of Flowers” festival. The mayor said the incident occurred Sunday in the presence of the prefect general and many distinguished visitors who occupied a stand in front of the fashionable Carlton Hotel. He said that President's 20-year-old son, touring Europe with a classmate during his vacation from Harvard University, threw the champagne when he presented Roosevelt with a bouquet of flowers in behalf of this Riviera resort. One of young Roosevelt's friends threw the bouquet into a gutter. Mayor Nouveau did not know whether Roosevelt threw the champagne purposely or in a carnival spirit. Not wishing to create a scandal, the mayor said he left the hotel without commenting, or complaining. Man

1937-08-12.text: Tunis, Tunisia—(F)—A Spanish government ship of about 6,000 tons today was reported torpedoed and sunk off Cape Bon, 60 miles from here, with the loss of 12 of her 40 crew members. Lloyds reported the ship was the tank motor vessel Campeador. The master of the British ship Dido, nearby, said three of the crew were picked up near the vessel last night. He described it then as “blazing furiously.” The Campeador, of Santander, carried a cargo of benzine.

Shanghai, China, Aug. 13. Friday,— Virtual martial law prevailed today throughout Shanghai, international settlement, the French concession and the native city. Britain mobilized a regiment at Hong Kong crown colony in South China for possible transport to this war threatened city of 3,500,000 people, and was reported to have appealed to the United States to send a regiment of infantry from the Philippines to re-enforce more than 1,000 United States marines permanently stationed here. American volunteers faced steel helmeted Japanese blue jackets landed from the Japanese third fleet which stood off the city along the roads of the international concession. A rumor was circulated that the Japanese had delivered an “ultimatum” to Chinese Mayor O. K. Yui threatening “drastic action” unless Chinese armed forces which killed two Japanese navy men earlier in the week were withdrawn twelve miles

LOS ANGELES, Aug. 12. (UP) —Freddie Bartholomew’s aunt charged today that the boy was smuggled out of England at the age of 10 in violation of that country’s child labor law to become a movie star in Hollywood. She blamed Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer studio for plotting the act which her and the boy out as “ho! visitors. to America,” and entered them into this country on visitors’ passports. LOS ANGELES, Ave, 12. (P)—Freddie Bartholomew, juvenile film star was brought to the United States in violation of British child labor laws, his aunt and guardian, Miss Myllcent Bartholomew, asserted in an affidavit on file today. Miss Bartholomew, who threatens to take Freddie back to England unless Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer raises his $1,100 a week film salary to $3,000, said a representative of the studio engineered his entrance into the United States on a visitor’s passport in 1934. The affidavit denied M-G-M now has a valid contract for the 13-year-old star's services.

Nanking, China, Aug. 12.— (AP)— Reliable reports late tonight said American, British, French and German ambassadors had dispatched both a joint communication to the Chinese and Japanese governments, expressing hope that foreign lives and property in Shanghai would be kept from danger. A statement was expected shortly from the Chinese government. Chinese officials, openly fearful of a repetition of the 1932 Sino-Japanese hostilities within Shanghai, were thrown into a scramble of war preparations by the lightning changes at Shanghai. Officials reiterated that Nanking could not agree to withdraw its forces from Shanghai, however much it deplored the consequences. Instead, heavy Chinese troop movements toward the city completely disrupted train service. Telegraph and telephone communications with Shanghai were so overburdened that even Chinese government messages required about 30 hours for

OGDEN, Utah, Aug. 12.—(UP)—Six-year-old Arthur Koch, German boy who speaks no English, passed through here as “First Class Freight” today, a baggage tag tied around his throat directing trainmen to give him transportation to San Francisco. The boy started his solitary journey at Hartford, Conn., and has been routed through according to the directions on his “Bill of Lading”. He will visit his mother, Mrs. Victor George Eliot in San Francisco.

Shanghai, Aug. 12, — (AP)— Ranks of Japanese bluejackets moved into battle position in Shanghai to face an unstemmed torrent of Chinese regulars tonight and the garrisons of the United States and three other nations mobilized “for the worst.” A “peace” conference intended to ease the crisis in the panic-stricken city ended in failure. Backed by 21 warships at Shanghai’s wharves, Japanese naval forces, estimated to number between 5000 and 8000, moved into the same positions they occupied during 1932's Chinese-Japanese hostilities. They deployed along the fringe of the Japanese portion of the international settlement and roads extending northward. Chinese central government troops streaming into the city answered to no authority but the army. Civilian authorities would not try to stop them. Each force indicated it was not planning to attack, but the situation needed only a spark to touch o

MOSCOW, Aug. 2. — (AP) — Sigismund Levaneffsky, the Soviet union's most famous flier, took off today for a transpolar flight to New York. Unlike two previous, successful Russian flights to North America over the roof of the world, this will not aim for the Pacific coast and will not be non-stop. Levaneffsky and five members of his crew took off at six-thirteen p. m. with stops scheduled at Fairbanks, Alaska; Edmonton, Alberta, and — possibly — Chicago.

1937-12-21.text: SHANGHAI, DEC. 20. (AP).-A Japanese military official today issued a report on the sinking of the United States gunboat Panay which contradicted virtually every statement previously made by American naval officers and British, Italian and American survivors. The report by Major General Kumakichi Harada purported to be "the sum total of staff officers’ investigation" of the bombing of the Panay and three Standard Oil Company vessels December 12. In conflict with the story of survivors, Harada’s statement: 1. Denied that Japanese army boats had fired on the Panay as it was sinking. 2. Asserted the gunboat was moving at the time of the incident when officially it had been reported anchored for more than two hours in the Yangtze river 27 miles above Nanking. Because the statement was at such variance with previously reported facts, one of the correspondents present at the interview asked whe

LONDON, (®). Lloyds announced the United States liner City of Hamburg had wirelessed that she was sinking after a collision ten miles east of Terschelling, The Netherlands. The City of Hamburg is owned by the Baltimore Mail Steamship company and is an 8,424 ton vessel. The steamer later wirelessed it was trying to make port under its own power, though heavily damaged. BALTIMORE. J. H. Threadgill, traffic manager of the Baltimore Mail line, said the company’s sinking liner City of Hamburg had a passenger list of “not more than four or five and a crew of 75.”

London, Dec. 21, — Persistent reports were heard today that Russia was strengthening her Far East air and sea forces on a large scale. Latest advices said Russia was moving part of the Black Sea fleet to Vladivostok. The battleship Lieutenant Schmidt, not listed in the navy roster, and the armored cruiser Red Ukraine, accompanied by destroyers and 20 submarines, were reported to have been ordered from Sebastopol. Detachments of the air force from Moscow and Kiev also were reported to have been sent to the Far East. Russia has been anxious to keep its Black Sea fleet at full strength because of the Mediterranean tension over Spain, but in any case she could safely detach large forces of submarines from western waters because she has one of the strongest submarine fleets in the world, with 149 built or under construction.

LONDON, Dec. 21 (AP)—Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain told the House of Commons today that “no attempt has ever been made by Japan for peaceful settlement” of her war on China. “It is time now for the Japanese government to show it is not unmindful of the rights and interests of foreigners and that their assurances and apologies meant something more than words,” the premier declared. Concerning the entire foreign situation, he said Great Britain's “definite objective” is the “settlement of the grievances of the world without war.”

LOUISVILLE, Ky., Dec. 20—Final honors were paid today to Robert W. Bingham by his state and nation and the British Empire to which he was accredited as ambassador. The body of the North Carolinian who adopted Louisville as his home 40 years ago was brought back today from Baltimore, Md., where death claimed him Saturday night, accompanied by representatives of President Roosevelt, the diplomatic service and Great Britain. A detachment of the 5th and 13th U.S. Cavalry from Fort Knox escorted the funeral cortege from the train to Calvary Episcopal Church, where services were held at noon with burial in Cavehill Cemetery here. The death of Bingham aroused speculation today that President Roosevelt might immediately appoint Joseph P. Kennedy as his successor at London. It was recalled that Bingham had planned to retire soon and that Mr. Roosevelt had talked with Kennedy about the London post

London, Dec. 20. (#)—Great Britain emphasized her grave view of the Far Eastern crisis tonight by naming a new ambassador to China. Sir Archibald Knatchbull-Hugessen, who was wounded last August when Japanese planes machine-gunned his plane, will be transferred. The Foreign Office announced Sir Archibald, a veteran diplomat who has been ambassador to Baghdad since 1935, would take over the China post "as soon as possible." The announcement said that "recent events in the Far East" made it essential Britain should be represented in China "by a diplomat of ambassadorial rank and that arrangements to such an end should be made with the least possible delay." The sudden decision—considered by political circles to reflect the serious view the government took of an increasingly grave situation—came as the cabinet was reconsidering six capital warships to reinforce its China fleet on advice fro

shipping just before the annexation of Manchukuo. House of Commons gathered today for foreign affairs debate, with a group of its members advocating a mighty patrol of Chinese waters by combined fleets of American, British and French warships. At a session of the group on the eve of today's discussion the view was expressed that a lumping of the naval forces of the three nations in the Far East would tend to check "Japan's aim to dominate China to the complete exclusion of foreign interests." This view was expected to be urged formally during the debate and the House anticipated a caucus statement from Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain and Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden on the government's reaction to disturbing developments in the Orient. The government already had emphasized its grave view of the Far Eastern crisis by naming a new ambassador to China to replace Sir Hugh Montgomery Kan

Shanghai, Dec. 21.—(Tuesday)—(AP) — Three hundred American and British women and children attempting to flee war threats in central China today were turned back by a military boom obstructing passage down the Yangtze river. The refugee-laden British Steamer Woosung was unable to pass a new obstruction at Matung, more than 100 miles up the Yangtze from Nanking, and turned back toward war-menaced Hankow. Foreign officials in Hankow, one of China's three temporary capitals, were attempting to arrange evacuation of the refugees on an international train to Canton, southern metropolis, before Japan's war machine launches an expected attack in central China. The British cruiser Capetown, part of the Woosung's convoy, was able, however, to clear the river boom and reached Wuhu. It was not known whether the cruiser could pass other military obstructions in the Yangtze, including the partly destr

1937-03-10.text: BOSTON, Mass. March 10:UP — The British freighter “Laila,” built only six months ago at a cost of $1,500,000, was destroyed within an hour today by a general alarm fire, believed to have started by a spark from its funnel. Explosions continued to rock the fire-blackened hulk and it seemed in danger of sinking. Two firemen were injured. The pier was charred, a fireboat was crippled and the waterfront property menaced. The army of firemen mustered by five alarms battled the flaming boat from land and sea.

GEORGETOWN, British Guiana, March 9—(VP)—Exhausted and worn, J. G. Le Van, American psychologist and explorer, reached Georgetown today, ending almost a month’s struggle to find his way out of the desolate grassy savannas after superstitious porters, frightened by his scientific research, deserted him. Le Van's porters, fearing he was pekenaima, or evil spirit, fled in terror when he dug up the skeletons of warriors killed in battle 300 years ago. Alone in the trackless grasslands, Le Van let his horse pick its way to a small inland village where he was cared for temporarily. When he reached Georgetown, he had lost 30 pounds.

Boston, March 10 -P;—The table of approaching labor conferences on wage and hour demands sounded outside the gates of New England’s humming textile mills today as John L. Lewis's committee for industrial organization turned its organizing drive east. In Lawrence, Lowell, Fall River Mass, and Manchester, N. H. organizers predicted their union soon would drive for a 35-hour week and wage increases—but not until membership rolls were longer. A lush field awaited the C. T. O- 91,566 cotton mill employees. As estimated by the National Association of Cotton Manufacturers, Workers’ meetings were scheduled with greater frequency throughout the area, and organizers of the United Textile Workers of America and the Federation of Woolen and Worsted Workers became more active as the organization drive was thrown into gear by the C. I. O. at Washington. The textile picture by cities: Lawrence, Mass.—2

ARCACHON, France, March 9— (®)—Officers of two British destroyers said tonight that as late as this morning the Spanish government's munition ship Mar Cantabrico was afloat and moving under her own power, the war prize of insurgent captors. They confirmed earlier reports that the freighter, which carried rich shipments of war supplies from New York and Vera Cruz, Mexico, consigned to the Madrid regime, had not been sunk in the Bay of Biscay. The accounts given by officers of the destroyers Echo and Eclipse, which sped out into the bay yesterday in the belief the Mar Cantabrico’s distress signals came from a British liner, contradicted the report the commander of the Echo sent the London admiralty last night. The British officers said they believe there were two United States citizens aboard the Mar Cantabrico. They were said to be aircraft experts taken along from Vera Cruz when the frei

| ARCACHON, France, March 9.-- the only uncaptured survivor of the Spanish Nationalist freighter Mar Cantabrico, torpedoed, shelled and seized by the rebel cruiser Canarias, yesterday, arrived here today and reported that the ship instead of sinking had been towed to port again as a prize of war, His story added a new twist to the fantastic sea incident which became a highlight of the Spanish civil war. The ship was reported loaded with a $2,700,000 cargo of planes, machine guns, and other war supplies from the United States, The survivor, Pablo Juan Boo, was landed by the French trawler which picked him up from the water as he tried to escape from the crippled ship. He said the freighter caught fire, but the flames were brought under control and the freighter was towed by the cruiser to the rebel port of San Sebastian. Other reports growing out of the incident are to the effect the ship

Spanish government troops northeast of Madrid fell back today before an insurgent force which government commanders said consisted of “15,000 Italians and Spaniards.” The insurgent headquarters at Avila reported the advancing army had shattered government opposition along the Guadalajara-Zaragoza highway and reached a point less than 50 miles from Madrid, moving up 15 miles. Government accounts, admitting Madrid’s soldiers had yielded somewhat in heavy fighting against a mechanized insurgent army, did not give the distance of the insurgent force from Madrid. The mystery of the Spanish munitions transport Mar Cantabrico still was not cleared up, as reports at Arcachon, France, said she had been conveyed to an insurgent port by the insurgent cruiser which shelled her in the Bay of Biscay. Previous accounts had said the ship sank. A French steamer, the Djbel Antar, reported she was bombed b

Madrid, Mar. 10—Reinforced government troops were reported by their commanders to be yielding slowly today to an army of 15,000 Italians and Spaniards driving southwest towards Madrid through Guadalajara province. The defense forces held recently to their positions along the Aragon highway against terrific insurgent fire and, in two undisclosed sectors of the new front, were reported withstanding the attacks. They found themselves battling against heavily armored, mechanized infantry using tanks, airplanes and—until now unseen in this war—machine guns mounted on swift, highly mobile motorcycles. Government commanders expressed belief Gen. Francisco Franco, insurgent commander, now had disclosed his strategy in the first phase of a long-expected offensive against the beleaguered capital. Gen. Jose Miaja, government commander in central Spain, prepared to meet the onslaught on at least thr

ARCACHON, France, March 10 (4) The munitions transport Mar Cantabrico was reported today to have been saved from destruction and convoyed as a prize of war to an insurgent Spanish port for the salvage of her $2,700,000 cargo of American-made munitions. First reported sunk in the stormy Bay of Biscay Monday when she attempted to slip past the insurgent blockade, the mystery vessel was said to have been able to leave the scene of ambush under her own power with the shell-ignited blaze in her No. 2 hold under control.

1937-03-25.text: LONDON, March 24-KAP— An angry clash in which the Italian and Russian members almost came to blows gave the European neutrality committee’s long-sought ban on foreign intervention in Spain an inauspicious send-off tonight. In a tumultuous meeting, delegates of the 27 nations comprising the committee settled the last details of a land and sea cordon around Spain which Europe hoped would isolate the civil war and help preserve the continent's peace. Appointment of 16 key administrators to supervise the international patrols left only the last step, the date for the scheme to become fully operative, to be decided. The swift action of the “hands off Spain” committee, however, failed to allay fear that speeches yesterday by Premier Benito Mussolini and Count Dino Grandi, Italian ambassador to London, presaged new Italian efforts to help the Spanish insurgents. The session was thrown into an u

London, March 25—(AP)—Great Britain backed up forceful action by France today to halt any further landing of Italian soldiers in Spain, agreeing, if necessary, to a warship blockade of the war-torn peninsula. An accord by the two powers, through Foreign Minister Yvon Delbos of France and the British ambassador to France, Sir George Simsall Clerk, was disclosed today. They agreed, with full knowledge of other European powers within the non-intervention committee, on "all points" of a program to make non-intervention completely effective and decided it was imperative to prevent, even by force, any further Italian reinforcements. British sources pointed out that the agreement was interpreted to mean that Britain was ready to discuss stringent measures presently but had made no decision actually to dispatch warships against any Italian incursions in event fresh troops left Italy to aid the i

Washington, Mar. 25—(#)—Justice Sutherland became today the fourth member of the Supreme Court to reach the age of 75. The bearded jurist, a native of England, was the first member of the court since 1794 to be born on foreign soil. He was brought to this country at the age of 15 months. A former Republican senator from Utah, he was appointed an associate justice by President Harding in 1922. Sutherland is one of the justices who have voted most consistently against Roosevelt administration laws. He has sided with the administration in four cases and against it in 13. He has written four of the opinions deciding New Deal litigation. Chief Justice Hughes, who will be 75 on April 11, has written five.

LONDON, March 25—UPI—Hope of finding the 71-year-old Duchess of Kent alive was all but abandoned today, the third day after she took off from Woburn Abbey on a short solo flight. Searchers leaned to a belief her plane had been forced down in the North Sea somewhere off Lincolnshire.

Paris, March 25—(4)—France rallied her European allies about her today in a move to erect a naval blockade against the possibility of Italy waging an undeclared war against the republican government in Spain. Great Britain, a foreign office spokesman declared, has pledged aid to France in blocking Italian landings if more troops were dispatched to the war-torn peninsula. Fearing that Premier Mussolini of Italy might scrap the London non-intervention agreement to isolate the civil conflict, France assured herself of the support of her own central European allies should she feel action necessary, by a series of extraordinary diplomatic conferences. Raises Grave Crisis Diplomatic circles considered France's stern attitude against any break in the international neutrality lineup had raised the gravest crisis in troubled Europe since Germany gave assurances of her peaceful intentions in the f

New London, Tex. - () - Officials voiced assurance today the heating system will be ascertained safe before grade school children return to classes Monday at the London consolidated school, where a blast killed 455 last Thursday. Yesterday the board voted to rebuild the school as quickly as possible. The few surviving high school students will study in the gymnasium and auditorium of the grade school.

LONDON, March 25.—(7)—George Black, the English producer who "doesn't want any strip tease dancers here," fled into hiding today from Diane Raye, the American dancer who wants to demonstrate undressing to British audiences. "I said Miss Raye determinedly, 'I have been looking for Mr. Black all day to get this crazy report about my act being banned straightened out. And I shall go on trying. 'I shall appear on the stage Monday or there will be fireworks. Justice is not being done to English audiences when someone tries to make out they are too prudish to like my act.' Anyway, Miss Raye pointed out, 'my act is not vulgarity but art.' It is at this point that Black has declared doubts. Black took a preview look at Diane's Broadway specialty and, with the startled gasp, 'it's too hot for England,' fled. He had imported Diane from Manhattan for a new show to open Monday without having seen he

LONDON—(UP)—France has proposed to Great Britain a four-power naval control plan to keep volunteers and war munitions out of Spain, it was said authoritatively today. The Italian, German, British and French navies would be authorized to turn back vessels flying the flag of any of the 27 nations signatory to the international non-intervention agreement which might be carrying men or munitions for the civil war combatants. Yvon Delbos, French Foreign Minister, outlined the new plan yesterday to Sir George Clerk, retiring British Ambassador. From this conference, and a conference between Delbos and the German Ambassador, came the news from Paris that France was ready to ask for coercive action to keep Italian volunteers from Spain. This, coupled with the belief that Italy must send such volunteers in view of the reported severe defeat of Italians on the Madrid front, caused the gravest anxi

1937-09-16.text: ONDAROIN, Sept. 1d. — DPrilain and France, disregarding Italy's objections to the accord of Nyon, mustered the most powerful naval and air armadas set in motion since the World War today to begin their hunt for pirate submarines in the Mediterranean. British and French warships already were patrolling the main Mediterranean sea lanes, without waiting for their own reinforcements from other seas. Totals More Than 150 It was estimated the units already on patrol in the Mediterranean and the additional vessels under orders to speed there would bring the Anglo-French armada up to more than 150 warships, powerfully supported by aircraft. The reinforcements were pouring into the Mediterranean from Britain's home fleet and France's Atlantic bases to crush the submarine piracy which has proved the most menacing to world peace of all the offshoots of the Spanish Civil War. Next Move Brings Questi

BOSTON, Sept 15—(4)—The coast guard tonight ordered two cutters out to search for the British yacht Endeavor I, after its convoy, the motor yacht Viva II limped into port at Newport, R. I., and reported her tow line to the racing sloop had parted in a gale of hurricane force 200 miles out in the Atlantic. Captain Wallace Grist, master of the Viva, telephoned to coast guard headquarters here, describing the Endeavor’s plight. “The seas were too heavy for the Endeavor to make any headway, and we didn’t see her after the tow line parted because of the thick weather,” he told friends in Newport. “The Endeavor may have drifted north towards Nova Scotia. We didn’t hear her radio, which apparently was out of commission.” “The wind reached a velocity of a little more than 100 miles an hour and we on the Viva were in tough shape ourselves.

By The Associated Press BOSTON — Two crack coast guard cutters, the Cayuga and Chelan, today sped to a spot 200 miles east of Nantucket in search of Endeavor, an English racing yacht which parted from her convoy's tow line in a gale Monday night. The yacht was en route to England.

Waits for Others to Act The Italian attitude as disclosed by various reliable sources today was that Il Duce had stated his minimum demands and was waiting to see if the other fellow wished to discuss them. Italy, in a sharp note to France and Britain, sponsors of the Nyon conference, protested Tuesday at the minor assignment under the Nyon accord which would restrict Italy’s part in the anti-piracy campaign to policing only the Tyrrhenian Sea off her western coast. Chicago, Ill. (7?)—A new kind of lung disease resembling tuberculosis which attacks only farmers was reported today to the international congress of radiology. An English physician, Dr. Richard Fawcitt, of Ulverston, declared that the ailment, which is caused by breathing mold from hay and grain into the lungs is similar to silicosis in the lungs of miners. The latter disease is produced by breathing fine dust. Apparently, he added, many farmers in the United States and other countries of the world have the disease but it has heretofore been diagnosed as tuberculosis or asthma. It is definitely an occupational disease which appears in epidemic form whenever moldy hay or grain carrying the fungi of the mold is harvested.

London, Sept. 16—Italian demands for Mediterranean equality were snared in a tense diplomatic impasse today while Anglo-French naval activity reached virtual wartime pitch. Deadlocked over who should make the first move on Italy's protest that the international anti-piracy patrol put her in a back seat, Britain and France rushed a mighty concentration of war vessels and war planes on Italy's "mare nostrum"—our sea. The first contingent of destroyers to reinforce the vast Anglo-French piracy patrol sped from England toward Europe's trouble-fraught "backward." The five long narrow fighting craft carried triple loads of depth charges and a full supply of torpedoes with which, if necessary, to blast belligerent submarines out of Mediterranean trade routes. The munitions cargoes were reminiscent of World War days when Britain battled to prevent German U-boats from cutting off her food supply.

LONDON, Sept. 16—Lloyd's reported from Gibraltar today that the Danish Steamer Tula, out of Antwerp for Alexandria, Egypt, had been halted in the straits of Gibraltar by an armed trawler and taken to Ceuta, Morocco.

Washington, Sept. 16, (UF)~ President Roosevelt arranged today to canvass the European international situation with American ambassadors to England and Germany. The President needs 18-minute appointment before noon with William H. Dodd, U.S. diplomatic representative to Berlin, and one of 10 minutes later with Robert W. Bingham, ambassador to Great Britain. Both Dodd and Bingham will return shortly to their posts abroad.

1937-04-13.text: London, April 13—(#)—British labor leaders moved today to force the government to lift the insurgent Spanish blockade of the port of Bilbao and convoy supply ships to the beleaguered Basque capital. Major Clement Attlee, leader of the opposition, declared he would ask for a formal vote of censure against the cabinet of Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin in the House of Commons tomorrow. Such action would throw wide open the whole question of the Spanish war and non-intervention efforts. Attlee’s motion, laid against the compromise position announced by Baldwin yesterday, will demand the government tolerate no interference with British shipping. Albert V. Alexander, former first lord of the admiralty, joined Attlee in the move to condemn the policy of withdrawing protection (continued on page three)

London, April 12,—(/)—Great Britain, determined to avoid an “incident,” compromised today in assuring her merchantmen protection against the Spanish insurgent sea blockade outside territorial waters in the Bay of Biscay. Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin incurred the wrath of the labor opposition in the House of Commons when he declared the government's policy: To protect the Union Jack up to the three-mile limit off northern Spain but no further. Although an armada of British men-of-war, among them the H. M. S. Hood, one of the world’s mightiest vessels, was posted outside the insurgent-besieged city of Bilbao, Baldwin asserted they could not protect cargo vessels actually entering the port. “Does not the government's position amount to a blockade of Bil.

LONDON, April 13, (P)—Labor party leaders, constituting the official opposition, have decided to move a vote of censure against the government tomorrow for its attitude on the Bilbao blockade, it was learned today. Regardless of the censure motion—whose defeat was assured—a bitter political fight seemed certain against the decision to recognize the Spanish Nationalist blockade of Bilbao as a “special situation.” Conservatives, discussing the problem outside the House of Commons, called the government's decision “a wise gesture of cautious neutrality.” Labor men used such terms as “cowardly surrender.” There were reports in political circles that the government was influenced not only by diplomatic caution but by strong pressure from navy chieftains.

ST. JEAN DE LUZ, Franco-Spanish Frontier. April 13. — The tightening of the insurgent warship blockade, after Great Britain's withdrawal of protection from her merchantmen within Spanish waters, threatened today to force the surrender of Bilbao to the encircling insurgent armies. Latest developments were: 1—Insurgents launched a counter-offensive in the university city sector of Madrid, seeking to bolster their shaky positions. 2—From Seville, the rebel high command claimed the government has lost 12,000 men in recent fighting, 5,000 of whom were killed. “Live, Let Live” 3—British foreign secretary enunciated a “live and let live” policy, declaring against intervention in the affairs of others but moving to protect British ships on the high seas from Spanish rebel interference. 4—Reports in Paris diplomatic circles said rebel blockade of Bilbao was engineered by insurgents’ German advisory staff. 5—Insurgent communique at Salamanca claimed loyalists were mowed down with huge losses when trapped between rebel and governm

OSHAWA, Ont. (UPR) Hugh Thompson, of the committee for industrial organization, today warned the General Motors Corporation not to attempt to meet English demands for automobiles with shipments from plants in the United States. The C.L.O. organizer, directing the strike here of nearly 3,000 employees of the General Motors Corporation of Canada, said that "if one car is shipped from the United States there will be that many more cars available." His statement was in an announcement: Carmichael, vice president and general manager of the Canadian company, that automobiles required immediately for the English trade would have to be supplied. (Continued On Page Four)

Oshawa, Ont., April 13.—(P—A move by Canada’s minister of labor to mediate the Oshawa strike pivoted today upon consent by General Motors of Canada, Ltd. Meanwhile, other developments added fuel to the already heated controversy of international scope: Hugh Thompson, John L. Lewis’ right hand man in the Oshawa strike, asserted the U. S. Supreme Court decision on the Wagner Act would cast the United Automobile Workers’ union in the role of sole bargaining agent for General Motors workers here and in the United States. Premier Mitchell Hepburn of Ontario accused Lewis of trying to become “economic and political dictator” of both the United States and Canada and declared that, if he came to Canada and sponsored any overt act, or if any of his aides should do so, they would be jailed “for a good, long time and there wouldn't be any bail.” Thompson announced a drive for membership would be st

Berlin—(?)—The German police Tuesday placed an absolute 60-day ban on Jewish meetings of any sort, with the exception of worship at synagogues. No explanation was offered. Police declined to divulge the reason for the action even to the leaders of Jewish organizations.

1937-10-11.text: LONDON, OCT. 11. (AP).--France weighed the possibility today of throwing open her Pyrenees frontier to allow arms and volunteers to teach the Valencia government to break the stalemate in the Anglo-French-Italian Mediterranean crisis. This step was considered as a possible counter-blow to Italy's polite but stern refusal of the Franco-British invitation to discuss withdrawal of thousands of Italian volunteers from the Spanish civil war. Paris and London maintained close touch, deliberating on the next move in the delicate situation. Premier Mussolini was reported planning to hurl thousands more of Italian soldiers into the Spanish war in the hope of clinching a speedy insurgent victory. Such reports were flatly denied by Italian officials, however.

LONDON, Oct. 10.—(#) — French statesmen assumed command of Anglo-French strategy today in the effort to bring Italy into a round table conference on removal of volunteers from the Spanish civil war. Spurred by the terse declaration of Foreign Minister Yvon Delbos—“We must act!”—experts of the foreign office in Paris worked at framing a plan acceptable to Britain for the next move to counter Italy's rejection of an invitation to a three-power conference, Italy Declined. The Italian government, in notes delivered at Rome yesterday to British and French envoys, firmly declined to join with Britain and France in a conference to talk over the “volunteers” issue. Italy declared such discussions could be carried on in the London non-intervention committee of 27 European nations. She added she would not take part in any conference to which Germany was not invited, French Officials found the pres

MUNICH, Oct. 11 (4P)—Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh arrived here today at 11:55 a.m. from Frankfort on the Main where they spent last night after a flight from England. They were welcomed by Baron Von Koeppelle, of the German air ministry, and Major Truman Smith, the military attaché of the United States embassy.

| LONDON, Gel, 11—(UP)—Belief hardened in London and Paris today that unless Britain and France stood together and took immediate measures to restore balance in the Spanish War, they would have to take much stronger action later. Two developments showed clearly the anxiety France and Britain share as the result of Italy's refusal to discuss with them the withdrawal of foreign volunteers from the Spanish Civil War: 1. The French general staff was again reported in diplomatic quarters to have told Premier Camille Chautemps that it would not accept responsibility for the national defense if large scale foreign intervention in Spain leading to a Nationalist victory were permitted. 2. NEW YORK, Nov. 10.—(AP)—Leading security and commodity exchanges in the United States and Canada will be closed tomorrow, November 11, in commemoration of Armistice Day. Livestock markets will remain open. Principal foreign markets will be closed with the exception of London and Liverpool which will operate as usual.

PARIS, Oct. 31 (UP)— France has notified Great Britain that she will not open her frontier to Spain, or take other retaliatory action against Italy, without the approval of the British government, it was understood today. But at the same time, it was said, the government notified Britain that France was firmly decided to liberate herself from her non-intervention pledges unless Italy promised: (1) To send no more troops to Spain; (2) To withdraw those now in Spain coincident with the withdrawal of other volunteers in the Civil War. Thus the situation was that France was giving further time for Italian reflection but apparently was determined to open her Spanish frontier, to permit arms and men to reach the loyalists through French territory, unless Italy consented to negotiations on volunteers. French leaders hold that actually the Spanish non-intervention agreement has broken down as th

Liverpool, Eng., Oct. 11 (UP)—Sir Oswald Mosley, British fascist leader, was suffering from concussion of the brain today, the result of an attack made on him as he was about to address a crowd of 8,000 at a meeting yesterday. Mosley had just climbed on top of a truck from which he was to address the crowd by means of a loud speaker. It developed that most of those in the crowd were anti-fascists. Before Mosley could say a word, there was a shower of stones and he fell unconscious. Twenty persons were injured in the general fight which followed. Mounted police rode into the crowd, arrested many and formed a cordon about the truck so the meeting could continue. Mosley was taken to hospital where he was found to be suffering from a puncture wound in the skull. What was called a minor operation was performed on him, and physicians said there was no reason for anxiety.

So serious was the situation regarded that it was understood no decision at all on British action would be taken before the cabinet as a whole had reviewed possibilities at its regular meeting Wednesday. Analysis of the Italian note refusing the British-French "invitation" to discuss volunteer withdrawal left no doubt among British and French leaders that Mussolini’s rejection was a definite one. Any suggestions he had made or might make for consideration of the question with Germany included, or to refer it to the Spanish non-intervention committee, seemed unlikely to change this view. It was felt that the note meant Mussolini was determined to keep his "volunteers" in Spain and that he would send more if he saw fit. 1937-04-03.text: London, April 2 (#)---Eight persons died and 40 were injured today when a crowded suburban train crashed into another atop a 60-foot viaduct. A passenger dragged himself from the twisted debris in time to flag a third train. The accident occurred when an electric train from Coulsdon ripped away the rear, wooden coach of a train which had halted just outside Battersea Park. Seven of the dead were in the rear coach. An eighth passenger died in a hospital tonight. Another car was tossed to the edge of the Longhedge viaduct which spans the mainline of the Southern railway. A third was knocked across a live rail and burst into flames. The current was cut and the fire extinguished. Rescue workers used ladders to reach the viaduct and worked in driving rain to pull the dead and injured from the wreckage.

Madrid, April 3—(4?)—Fifteen thousand Insurgent soldiers, described in government reports as mostly Italian, were reported facing today possibly the greatest mass slaughter of the civil war in a military trap on the Cordoba front. The Insurgent force, already having retreated more than 15 miles after an unsuccessful siege of Pozoblanco, a mineral land stronghold of the Madrid-Valencia government, was said to have been caught more than 20 miles northwest of Cordoba City, its principal base of supplies. Government capture of the town of Villaharta yesterday placed Madrid's jubilant “Milicianos” in a position to dominate the only main road connecting Cordoba with the mass of Gen. Gonzalo Queipo De Llano's men. Occupation of the road would isolate and subject them to concerted thrusts of government cavalry, tanks, infantry and planes. Loyalist and insurgents jockeyed for position on widely scattered fronts today with the current advantage slightly on the side of the government forces in Spain's civil war. Italian troops seemed unable to withstand the attacks of the onrushing loyalists in south central Spain and suffered their third defeat in less than a fortnight. German soldiers were mentioned in insignificant fighting reports. Dispatches from the loyalists at Madrid claimed that 10,000 Italians and Germans had been cut off from the Spanish base at Cordoba on the southern fronts. The insurgent forces there, with these thousands of foreign "mercenaries," seemed to be unable to stem men fighting for their lives and their country and the loyalists captured three strategic towns and bombed Cordoba in the southern offensive. ROUEN, France, April 3—(4)—The Journal De Rouen said today it was reliably informed the Duke of Windsor and Mrs. Wallis Warfield Simpson would be married at the Chateau De Saint Saens, near Rouen, which is owned by the Duke of Westminster. The newspaper said the Chateau was selected as the wedding site because Queen Mother Mary planned to attend the ceremony and wished to avoid a long trip to Austria or a more distant point in France.

(By The Associated Press) MADRID, Apr. 3—Continued smashing government successes along a wide and strategically important front in Cordoba province were described last night in dispatches from the southern battlefield.

Bilbao, Spain, April 3 (4).—The Government Basques fought their way to the top of the 4,600 foot mountain peak today in what their commanders asserted was a successful attempt to halt the insurgent drive on Bilbao from the south. They occupied the summit Lacruz, highest of the Cantabrian peaks which surround Bilbao and which insurgents must surmount before starting the downhill advance of the northern autonomous capital.

Washington, April 3,—UP—An imminent showdown on curtailing the Roosevelt court bill hearings may bring the first test of strength in the closely divided Senate judiciary committee. Supporters of the measure, becoming restive after four weeks of testimony, hinted today at an attempt to end the hearings soon. Senator McGill, Democrat, Kansas, one of the members still uncommitted, also said he believed the testimony should be brought to a quick close. Pursues Delay Policy. Chairman Ashurst, Democrat, Arizona, still was pursuing his policy of “delay, hesitation and postponement,” arguing that the longer the hearings lasted the better the bill’s chances. He had agreed to let opponents continue to run the hearings throughout next week and the following Monday. The remainder of the week after next was reserved for administration witnesses. Any attempt to curtail the hearings will be resisted by

| NEW YORK, April 3 (P).—The city of Norfolk advised Radio Marine today that the German steamer Borkum was in distress in mid-Atlantic and that two steamers were speeding to her assistance. The City of Norfolk, a coastwise steamer, wirelessly at 3:53 a.m. (EST), that the German steamer gave her position as 40.02 degrees longitude and 35.21 degrees latitude. Her steering gear was out of commission, she reported, tadio Marine said the steamer Colombie, about 200 miles away, and the British steamer Tamaroa, 60 miles away, had responded to the SOS of the distressed ship. Messages from the City of Norfolk said apparently the radio aboard the German steamer was not working properly, as she kept repeating distress signals. Radio Marine corporation reported at 7:45 a.m. (EST) that the Borkum was still sending distress signals because its receiving equipment was out of order and the operator had

1937-02-20.text: LONDON, Feb. 20. (?)—The nations of Europe clamped an embargo on fighting men for Spain today to halt the menace of “the little world war” of civil conflict converting the continent into its battle field. Even while they timed their stringent measures—long term jail sentences in some cases—to take effect at midnight tonight, 27 nations were pledged to impose a workable war blockade by land and sea around the peninsula by March 6. See Objections Overcome Portugal alone of the members of the international non-intervention committee remained to be converted entirely, but informed observers felt her objections to foreign observers on her soil would be overcome over the week-end. This last stumbling block was expected to be met by a compromise allowing British inspectors to see that Portugal keeps her pledge not to send arms or guns to her war-torn neighbor. The Italian ban on volunteers, ann

LONDON, Feb. 19.—Twenty-six European nations—with Portugal’s help apparently assured—tonight virtually completed plans to encircle war-ravaged Spain with prying eyes, vigilant to halt men and munitions at midnight Saturday. Only details of the coastal naval patrol and the Anglo-Portuguese agreement for stationing of frontier guards remained to be ironed out by international negotiations, nearing the end of months of bickering and deadlock. A ring of warships and border guards, to isolate Spain from foreign assistance, was the neutrality committee’s final solution of the Spanish problem. Foreign observers within her realm, Portugal at first asserted, would reflect upon her national honor, although neither France nor Great Britain demurred at the stationing of observers along the Pyrenees and at Gibraltar. Britain, however, persuaded Portugal to accept tentatively a compromise providing th

NEW YORK, Feb. 20 — (7) — The long promised nuptials of Mary Pickford and Buddy Rogers probably will take place next month in England, the prospective bridegroom said today just before he sailed on the Isle De France to fulfill a moving picture contract in London.

LONDON. Feb. 20.—(UP)—Germany, Italy and Portugal enacted laws today to forbid volunteers entering the Spanish civil war, and all was ready for a general ban effective at midnight tonight. French mobile guards and other units already were at their stations along the Spanish frontier to stop the flow there, principally to the Loyalists. The German, Italian and Portuguese bans include enlistment, departure or transit of volunteers for the war, under heavy penalty. In addition, Portugal decreed that all of its citizens who have enlisted in the Spanish armies must return home within a month.

Le Bourget, France, Feb. 20.-The Duke and Duchess of Kent arrived here today by plane from London. They were reported to have arranged to leave by train tonight for Vienna where they will visit the Duke of Windsor.

ROME, Feb. 20 (4)—Marshall Graziani, viceroy of Ethiopia, was slightly wounded by a hand grenade, an official communique announced today, when rebellious natives at Addis Ababa attempted to assassinate him as he presented them with gifts. Many others, including the Abuna Coptic Cyril, bishop of Ethiopia, were gravely wounded, the announcement said, when the natives hurled the grenades during a huge celebration of the birth of Prince Vittorio Emanuel, future emperor of Ethiopia.

Bombay, India, Feb. 24.—U™—Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh landed here at 1 p.m. (2 a.m. central standard time) today after being unreported for 48 hours on an aerial jaunt over India. Little concern had been felt for the flying colonel and his wife, whose insistence on absolute privacy has previously caused them to be reported lost, although a widespread unofficial search failed to penetrate their mysterious two-day disappearance.

Shanghai—(AP)—About 200 men, identified by authorities as Italian civilians and sailors from an Italian man-of-war at anchor here, stormed a motion picture theater today and routed the audience with gunfire, ammonia bombs and clubs. They slugged two Russian film projection operators showing a Russian-made picture dealing with the Italian conquest of Ethiopia and seized the film. One suffered a broken arm, the other a gash on the head. Before Chinese police, British settlement authorities, Japanese Marines and Italian officials arrived at the Isis theater, on the border of the international settlement, the mob had wrecked the interior of the place and fled.

1937-04-17.text: LONDON, April 16 (#)—Final details were arranged today for the international naval blockade of Spain upon which hangs Europe’s hopes of isolating the civil war. When the vessels of Great Britain, France, Italy and Germany start their patrol at midnight Monday, April 19, they will seek to prevent further foreign arms and men entering Spain. Proposals for the recall of volunteers already in action in Spain, informed sources said, will not be brought before the full non-intervention committee until the effectiveness of the blockade has been proved. Vessels flying the United States flag, as well as ships of all other non-member nations, will be subjected to examination, and their governments will be notified. Member nations are bound to bar arms and men, which the committee has embargoed, in their ships and they will be under close surveillance. Enforcement of the embargo, at an annual cost

SAN FRANCISCO, April 16 Lord Marley, British laborite today advised Americans to stay away from the coronation of King George VI. Marley, former lord-in-waiting to King George V, said he didn’t want to see his American friends “generally exploited.” In San Francisco to help the Jewish National Welfare Fund drive, Marley told an interviewer he opposed the “general commercialization” of the coronation May 12 and the attempt to make a profit. He asserted the fanfare attending George VI's accession was being counted upon to offset popular sympathy for the Duke of Windsor. “The government feared there might be a falling off in popular support of the coronation,” he explained. “So they adopted a plan of having more soldiers, more military bands, bigger and better decorations, and now a general commercialization of the whole coronation and an attempt to make a profit, with which I am myself ent

London, April 17—(#)—The Earl of Londesborough, one of the best dressed men in England, died of pneumonia today in a nursing home. He was 42 years old. He was prominent in turf, football and greyhound racing circles, and a darling of Bond street. An American list, in 1933, placed him at the top of the world’s best dressed men.

— London, April 17. (AP):—The birth of a son to Countess Russell, wife of Bertrand Russell, the 64-year-old writer, was announced today. Countess Russell, 27, former secretary to the philosopher-author, was named correspondent by Earl Russell's second wife, Dora, when she divorced him in 1934. Russell is widely known for his advocacy of "companionate marriage." In her divorce suit, Russell's second wife disclosed that the earl and countess had signed a document in 1933 absolving each other of all indiscretions committed prior to that time. She charged, however, that Russell had been guilty of immoral conduct subsequent to the agreement and was granted a decree on that ground. Russell did not contest the suit. In January 1936, Russell married the present countess, Miss Patricia Helen Spence.

| London (UP)—A pamphlet entitled ‘Catching Thieves on Paper’ which gives hints to police officers on how to make use of the information gathered by the Criminal Records Office, has been issued by Scotland Yard.

PERPIGNAN, France, (UP) — John Tylus, 23, of Yorkville, O., today faced a 20-day prison sentence and expulsion from France after his conviction on a charge of attempting to cross the frontier as a Spanish civil war volunteer. Four British subjects, convicted with Tylus, drew the same sentences for violating France's non-intervention agreement.

Berlin, Apr. 17. - 'The killing of a Nazi organizer in Argentina aroused German press and officialdom today to a burst of excitement. Rudolph Hess, Reichsführer Adolf Hitler's deputy for party affairs, immediately cabled the Argentine section of the party deep sympathy for the “dastardly murder” of Josef Riedel, 37, leader of the Villa Ballester group of the Argentine section of Nazi foreign organization. Konstantin Von Neurath, foreign minister, instructed the German ambassador at Buenos Aires to offer condolences to Riedel’s widow and followers. A similar cable from Wilhelm Bohle, chief of the Nazi foreign organization, ordered four days of party mourning for Riedel. Bohle issued a manifesto praising the South American organizer as a “loyal Nazi who died in fulfillment of his duty.” He expressed grief that the slaying was in Argentina “with which Germany has for many years been on the

Oshawa, Ont., April 16.—(?—Homer Marti, president of the United Automobile Workers, said Friday night the union would charge the Ford Motor company with violation of the Wagner labor disputes act. The former Baptist minister who now leads the auto division of John L. Lewis’ committee for industrial organization said the La Follette senate committee investigating civil liberties violations also would be asked to look at the relations between Henry Ford and his employees. “We will have Henry Ford definitely on the run by Monday,” Martin said, refusing to elaborate on the nature of the charges he said the union would file with the national labor relations board. 1937-10-19.text: LONDON, Oct. 19 (#)—Germany’s Chancellor Hitler was expected today to send special instructions from his Bavarian retreat which may mean success or failure for European powers trying to agree on a formula for withdrawal of foreign soldiery from Spain. The Reichschancellor’s attitude—hitherto only a backdrop for Premier Mussolini of Italy in these vital talks—was projected to the forefront when Hitler's ambassador to London, Joachim Von Ribbentrop, made an unexpected, semi-secret flight to Germany to obtain der Führer’s views. (A Munich dispatch said the envoy arrived there last evening and immediately proceeded to Berchtesgaden to report to Hitler.) The departure from England of the Nazi representative in the London negotiations was not known generally until it was disclosed he had reached Germany. It was doubtful whether he would return here in time for resumption of the non-interventio

LONDON. Oct. 18.—P)—Great Britain and France drafted a plan of joint action today for tomorrow's ‘crucial non-intervention meeting over which Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden himself will preside in an effort to drive through an agreement to withdraw foreign volunteers from Spain's civil war. Eden conferred with Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain and French Ambassador Charles Corbin on Franco-British policy for the international committee meeting. A semi-official assertion from Rome that only 40,000 Italian troops were fighting with the Spanish insurgent armies projected a new element of strife into the negotiations. British and French authorities have expressed belief there are at least 100,000 Italians serving under Insurgent Generalissimo Francisco Franco and have urged a “token” withdrawal on that basis as a guarantee of good faith. The Spanish embassy, commenting on the Rome report, s

London—Joseph Bruce Ismay, 74, British shipowner and former chairman of the White Star Line, died here yesterday. Ismay was one of the survivors of the Titanic disaster in 1912 and was the target of bitter criticism because, as head of the line, he had left the vessel safely in one of the lifeboats. His conduct was investigated by the United States Senate and the British Board of Trade and he was exonerated in both instances. He resigned as chairman and managing director of the White Star Line the following year.

London—4 U.P.—Soviet Russia rejected a French proposal Tuesday night for solution of the Spanish non-intervention problem. The rejection was made by Ivan Maiski, Soviet ambassador, at a meeting of nine powers represented on the "Chairman‘s Sub-Committee" of the International Non-Intervention Committee of 27 nations. The French plan dealt with "symbolic" withdrawal of foreign volunteers from each side in Spain, dispatch of a committee to supervise the withdrawal, and a study of granting belligerent rights to each side.

London, Oct. 19.—Armed with fresh instructions, delegates of nine European powers began today the crucial business stage of negotiations on withdrawal of foreign volunteers from the Spanish civil war. Delegates were pessimistic. But French sources, usually well-informed, reported that France was ready to make a new concession to Italy—to propose that an equal number of volunteers be withdrawn from the Spanish Nationalist and Spanish Loyalist armies as a symbol of good faith. So far France has insisted firmly that any withdrawal, even symbolic, must be in proportion to the number of volunteers fighting for the respective combatants. Today's meeting was a resumption of one Saturday of the “chairman’s sub-committee” of the Spanish non-intervention committee. Represented were Britain, France and Russia, all insistent that all foreign volunteers must be withdrawn; Germany, Italy and Portugal,

London, (4)—Gen. Charles G. Dawes, Chicago financier, expressed his opinion today that the current break in the Wall Street market does not denote a rapidly approaching major depression. The performance of business in post depressions, Gen. Dawes said, indicated a business recession should be expected, but that it should not last long. The former vice-president based his predictions upon a study of conditions between 1899 and 1902, which he said more or less paralleled current trends. He recalled days at the turn of the century when the stock market fell rapidly, but general business did not follow the downturn with the same degree of severity. The market was jolted hard in 1901 when Northern Pacific stock was cornered, he said, but the jolt did not hit business so hard. Gen. Dawes added that economists still regard that period as one of prosperity for general business. Many of the most

JERUSALEM, (UP), Heavy casualties were inflicted on a large band of Syrians attempting to cross the Palestine frontier Monday, unconfirmed reports said, as the government of British mandated Palestine retaliated for recent outrages. Military sappers, army engineer units, blew up homes of Arabs involved in raiding a derailed train Friday, the reports stated, and at the same time blasted two houses in Lydda in punishment for the burning of new airport buildings there Saturday. Strong guard detachments patrolled many holy land districts to prevent further violence. Kilted Scottish soldiery deployed over the Hebron countryside southwest of Jerusalem Monday night in pursuit of Arabs who had raided a police arsenal almost under the noses of native constables. A company of the famous Black Watch, newly rushed to Palestine to cope with the renewed state of terror in the Holy Land arising from Ar

London, Oct. 19 oP—Nine powers pledged officially to non-intervention in the Spanish civil war plunged again today into the controversial problem of withdrawing foreign volunteers from the conflict. While Ambassador Joachim Von Ribbentrop, Germany's representative, was at home conferring with Chancellor Hitler, the Soviet delegate, Ivan M. Maisky, was reported under instructions from Moscow not to give in either to the Fascists or Nazis. Ribbentrop, who hurried to Germany by air yesterday, presumably to obtain new instructions from Hitler, had not returned to London but the German charge d'affaires Dr. Ernest Wormain, was present to represent his government. Hitler's attitude toward withdrawal of volunteers was expected to be transmitted to the non-intervention subcommittees by Ribbentrop upon his return.

1937-07-27.text: WIMBLEDON, Eng., July 27—(AP)—Sorrel-topped Don Budge, undefeated this year, whipped Henry Wilfred (Bunny) Austin today, 8-6, 3-6, 6-4, 6-3 as the United States completed its rout of Great Britain’s Davis Cup forces and regained the international tennis trophy for the first time since 1927. Budge’s victory came after 21-year-old Frankie Parker of Milwaukee had clinched the cup with an astonishing straight set triumph over Charles Edgar Hare, 6-2, 6-4, 6-2, thus making the final score four victories for the United States against one for Great Britain's unsuccessful cup defenders.

LONDON, (UP)—Twelve convicts were killed today when 300 convicted murderers mutinied in a 3,800 foot deep prison salt mine at Targu-Ocna, Roumania, an Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Bucharest reported. The convicts attacked guards in the depths of the mine with picks, hammers and shovels. Four guards were injured seriously and several were hurt slightly as they fired on the rioters. As soon as they became aware of the outbreak, prison authorities on the surface cut off the mine's electric light and water supplies. Thirst became unbearable in the salt diggings and the mutineers soon commandeered elevators and came to the surface. As they reached the surface, guards seized each group and herded them into the prison.

HOLLYWOOD, July 27. — So little is left of Freddie Bartholomew's $1,190 weekly salary after lawyers, tax collectors, relatives and agents take their shares that his aunt and guardian, Miss Millicent Bartholomew, said today she was considering taking him back to England, ending his motion picture career. Miss Bartholomew has been trying to negotiate a $2,500 weekly contract for the curly-haired little actor and failing that, she plans to restore him to private life in his native land, away from the lawsuits and publicity of the movie colony, "where he can grow up like a normal boy." She took him away today on his first vacation in ten months. "Everybody has been after his money," she said. "Unless his future can be better assured I don't think there is any reason for him to continue in Hollywood. There has been no happiness for either of us. I am planning to take him back to England where

London, July 26.—(AP)—The Duchess of Kent and her two small children escaped unharmed tonight from a collision in which the royal automobile's windows were smashed and its side was crushed. En route to their summer cottage, “Bloody Point House” in Sandwich, the party was traveling downhill in Kent when the car collided with another.
London, July 27—(UP)— Lloyd's reported today the capture, presumably by insurgents, of the 2,539-ton British steamer Mirupanu, which was bound from Rotterdam for the Spanish government port of Gijon.

London, July 26. -(P) — The principal European powers striving to keep alive the principle of nonintervention in the Spanish civil war, broke one deadlock today but appeared to be running into another. Possible Russian refusal to accord belligerent rights to the insurgent regime in Spain was the new obstacle. Ivan Malsky, Soviet ambassador, started a long, wrangling meeting of the nonintervention subcommittee with this statement: “Under no circumstances will I accept granting belligerent rights to Franco (Gen. Francisco Franco, the insurgent leader).” After the meeting Malsky said his statement did not necessarily bind his government. Authoritative observers said that if Moscow did stand by it, however, it would dynamite the whole nonintervention scheme. The subcommittee, the directing group of the 27-nations committee seeking to isolate the Spanish war, resolved an earlier deadlock, whi

LONDON () — Britain's legislators debated the realities of war defense for London today while her diplomats started from scratch again on the British plan to keep the Spanish war in Spain. The nine-power non-intervention sub-committee called for the views of 27 nations, the full membership of the neutrality group, on Anthony Eden's controversial scheme to isolate the Spanish conflict. Meanwhile, critics of the British government's defense plans went to their benches in the House of Commons prepared for oratorical visualization of air raids they believe would be directed at London in event of general European war. Many members of Parliament regard this, the southeast corner of England, as “the most tempting target in the world.” After hearing Defense Minister Sir Thomas Inskip outline his work in coordination of military and protective measures, such proposals as these were expected: Orga

LONDON (UP) — The leading shipbreakers and scrap metal merchants of the world have opened negotiations to form an international scrap metal ring, it is reported here. The European war scares and rearmament programs have vastly increased the demand and price of scrap metal.

1937-02-09.text: LONDON, Feb. 9 (P)---German Ambassador Joachim Von Ribbentrop raised his hand in the Nazi salute to King George VI again today——at the new monarch’s first levee. Ignoring the furore last week over his first such salute, he stretched his arm out when he presented 18 members of his staff in the beautiful throne room of St. James’ Palace, but his subordinates did not follow his example. The salute passed almost unnoticed. The ambassadors were presented to the king in order of their seniority and Von Ribbentrop, a recent appointee, was among the last.

VIENNA, Feb. 8—(AP)— The Duke of Windsor played the role of guide to his sister, Mary, and her husband today while an authoritative source said he was less inclined to rush his marriage to Wallis Warfield Simpson than he had been last week. A friend close to the British royal family declared that after several talks with his sister, the princess royal, who came here yesterday, the former king was considering making less haste in his wedding plans and might decide on a civil marriage in Hungary. A reliable source said Friday Edward intended to marry Mrs. Simpson April 27—the day her divorce from Ernest Aldrich Simpson is likely to become final—in Vienna or at the Enzesfeld castle of his now absent host, the Baron Eugene de Rothschild. Today he was represented as feeling that if only a civil marriage is held, it might be in Hungary, because the Hungarian attitude toward marriage and divorc

WASHINGTON, Feb. 9 (AP).-— Speaker Bankhead, Democrat, Alabama, wiped tears from his eyes last night at the curtain speech of his actress-daughter, Tallulah. The New York and London stage star spoke after the seventh curtain call accorded her performance in “Reflected Glory,” presented here after a Broadway run. “ I hate to step out of character,” she began. “It’s disillusioning, I know. But you have been so very gracious. “ I imagine you all understand” — she gestured to her father's box — “that I’ve been terribly nervous. I’ve been playing this play for seven months, but I’ll remember tonight as one of the happiest of my life — with humble gratitude.” She tossed a kiss to her “daddy” and disappeared. The speaker of the house removed his spectacles and brushed away a tear. It was the first time the graying legislator, who used to play Romeo to her little-girl Juliet, had seen his daught

LONDON (UP) — The House of Commons cheered today when Walter Runciman, president of the Board of Trade, in reporting on his recent conversations with President Roosevelt and Secretary of State Cordell Hull, said "we hope that the results of our conversations will facilitate economic cooperation between the United States and ourselves." He added that both sides are exploring the possibility of a trade pact.

By JORN DE GANDT (Copyright, 1937, by United Press.) OUTSIDE MALAGA — National leaders closed Malaga to all but military men today as their troops completed the mopping up of their conquest, Spain’s great south coast port. Newspaper correspondents, at first permitted to enter the city with the nationalist vanguards that poured in from half a dozen columns, were sent to the outskirts. It was announced that as a first step nationalist authorities formed three tribunals, with a total of 13 judges, to investigate allegations that loyalists assassinated right wing adherents during their tenure of the city.
