The other dominoes in order are Barcelona, Valencia and Madrid; and when the toppling starts, the strategists say, the actual fighting will be over in two months and the war, cleaned up before the end of its second year. It is now in its 17th month, Ranged in the bitter cold of the Aragon front between Huesca and Zaragoza a quarter of a million of Franco's insurgent soldiers are ready for a push at the first domino, Lerida, and the civil struggle is stirring again to a climax. Lerida lies in the line of Franco's impending march toward Barcelona, S

LONDON, Dec. 6—(#)—The course of the last six months of the Spanish civil war has convinced the insurgents their victory over the Republican government is but a matter of time. Germany and Italy have supplied open aid; most of Spain’s raw materials have fallen into insurgent hands; Generalissimo Francisco Franco has in place a quarter of a million men for the northeastern area he hopes will end the war. Six months ago the questions were: Which side will win? Is the civil war the start of a world conflict? Today, insurgents ask only: How much longer will it take Franco and his seasoned army of 750,000 to complete the insurgent conquest? Half a year ago the issue still hung in the balance. The insurgents were staggered by the overwhelming defeat of the Italian legions at Guadalajara in March just as Madrid seemed at Franco’s mercy; the government seemed impregnable in the northern province

SHANGHAI, Dec. 6 (AP)—Twelve Japanese consular police raided a Chinese operated, British registered hotel in the Shanghai International Settlement today without notifying settlement authorities or obtaining their permission. The Japanese police, armed with rifles and pistols, dashed from the Hongkew section of Shanghai to Nanking road, ignoring traffic signals. They entered the hotel and arrested four Chinese, one of them a woman. Japanese military authorities questioned the prisoners for an hour and then released them.

1937-09-25.text: Washington, Sept. 25.— State Department officials feared today that Japan had given her answer—with bombs—to foreign protests of aerial attacks on Chinese civilian areas. Continuation of bombing raids on Chinese cities, in defiance of American and British protests, was considered a more direct method than the use of words in expressing Japan’s determination to continue her attempt to subdue China. Japanese activities appeared to have placed squarely before the State Department the necessity of deciding what, if any, further action will be taken by this government to restore peace in the undeclared Japanese-Chinese war. For the present, until Japan formally replies to the United States’ bombing protest, the State Department was not expected to take further definitive action. But officials made no attempt to disguise their fear that they will be forced to make a decision on future policy s

London, Sept. 24. (4)—British insurance companies tonight raised their insurance rate on the Yacht Endeavor I, missing at sea for eleven days, to 40 percent. In effect they were wagering only 3 to 2 that she would turn up safe. The British challenger in the 1934 race for the America’s cup disappeared Sept. 13 in a violent storm off Nantucket Lightship when she snapped her tow line. A report to Lloyds yesterday that she had been sighted off the Azores proved false. Under the new rates insurance companies holding policies on the yacht must pay $40 for every $100 reinsurance if they wish to spread their possible loss. A thorough investigation by Lloyds uncovered no evidence of the Endeavor’s whereabouts or of the cause of the radio report yesterday that she had been located near the Azores.

Shanghai, Sep. 9 (Ar) (Saturday) — Japanese air bombers renewed their raids on Nanking, China’s capital, today. Chinese asserted the city’s strong anti-aircraft defenses shot down four of a fleet of 36 planes that roared over Nanking before noon, ending the capital's respite from the Japanese aerial campaign to destroy it. There were no immediate reports of casualties or damages. A Japanese air fleet penetrated the heart of China yesterday to bomb the Wuhan cities, Hankow, Wuchang and Hanyang, where estimates of the dead ranged between 100 and 200 and of wounded between 200 and 500. Nearly all the victims were non-combatants, many of them women and children stricken when the raiders bombed and machine-gunned Wuchang, on the south end of the great Yangtze river. Foreigners Periled American and British gunboats were endangered as bombs fell near their berths in the river, but as far as cou

MADRID, Sept. 25 (4?)-—Government officials uprooting what was described as a vast counter-revolutionary movement to overthrow the Madrid-Valencia regime declared today its ramifications reached directly into the Chilean embassy. They asserted the general staff headquarters for the civil and military conspiracy was located there. A Chilean businessman, identified as Manuel Asencio Zuria, and two men said to be employees of the Argentine embassy were among the 200 persons already under arrest in this besieged metropolis. Asencio Zuria, accused as the chief of one of four groups comprising the counter-revolutionists, was said to have had 1,650 men at his command, ready to strike at the rear of government troops defending Madrid upon a junction of the insurgent operations on the Madrid front. The sudden drawing of the government net was reported to have brought capture of the conspiracy lea

Munich, Germany, Sept. 24 (AP)—The duce of fascism and the fuehrer of nazism will meet tomorrow for the second time in their historic careers to toast the common ideals of their political creeds and perhaps to address to the world a joint appeal for peace. Adolf Hitler, chancellor of Germany and leader of his nation, already is here to be host in the dramatic meeting in this city of national socialism, now in dress with flowers, flags and under the vigilant eyes of thousands of crack German guardsmen. Speeds Over Austria Benito Mussolini, duce of fascist Italy, sped across Austria by special train for the rendezvous and for a five-day triumphal tour of Germany. The two had met once before, briefly, at Venice in 1934. What they will do at the second meeting and of what they will talk were the great questions in the minds of European statesmen tonight. Would Form Pact Diplomats gathering h

Hendaye, Franco-Spanish frontier, Sept. 25. (Pi)—Spanish government artillery hurled a terrific bombardment into insurgent Oviedo in northern Spain today. The government troops apparently sought to force surrender by the Oviedo garrison, under siege for 14 months, before insurgent reinforcements can reach the city. An insurgent column is moving swiftly toward Oviedo, and today was reported less than 25 miles to the south of the Asturian capital. As government guns unleashed their thunder, Asturian troops fell back before an insurgent advance toward Lena, 20 miles south of Oviedo. Insurgent advices said 400 shells fell into Oviedo in a two-hour bombardment adding further destruction to havoc wrought in the grueling siege that started almost with the opening of the civil war. The advance on Lena, effected by the insurgent column moving down out of the Cantabrian mountains, was aimed at rel

MADRID, Sept. 24. — (# -- The Spanish central government tonight disclosed the arrest of more than 200 persons accused of directing a “great plot” designed to overthrow the government. A communique said the plot centered at Madrid. Officials said about 5,000 men planned to attack government forces from the rear in a combined civilian and military uprising. Another 2,509 persons, they stated, were to seize public buildings in Madrid. A number of officers, soldiers and civilians were said to be implicated as ringleaders. Many were reported under arrest. Punishment to the “full extent of the law” will be meted out to those guilty of plotting against the government, the communique said. General Jose Miaja, commander of central government forces, announced exposure of the plot. He declared it was unquestionably the most important counter-revolutionary discovery by military agents since the ou

Alexandria, Egypt, Sept. 25. (7) Between 30 and 40 persons were reported killed or injured today when a procession of 80,000 workmen, celebrating their loyalty to the new Egyptian king, Farouk I, became panicky in trying to force a way into a narrow street. They piled up and were trampled underfoot by the surging procession in a street near Ras El Tin palace.

1937-10-30.text: London, Oct. 29. —(AP)— The greatest indignation was manifest in British official circles today over the killing of three royal Ulster riflemen in Shanghai — the latest on a lengthening list of British casualties attributed to Japanese gunfire. The fact that killings occurred so soon after a British sentry was machine gunned to death Sunday at a British defense post in Shanghai, increased the bitterness, informed persons said, although formal comment was withheld pending an official report on the incident. Ink was scarcely dry on the Japanese apology and offer of compensation for Sunday’s shooting. The House of Commons adjourned for the weekend before news of the shooting became known in London. On the basis of past attacks on British lives and property, many members have demanded the imposition of a trade boycott on Japan as a means of reprisal. Tom Williams, a laborite, urged the appli

* TOKYO, Oct. 30—(U. P.)—The ‘council on the current situation,’ comprised of leaders of the Seiyukai political party and other important personages, tonight unanimously adopted a resolution favoring a movement to sever diplomatic relations with Great Britain. The resolution blamed the British government for complicating international relations in connection with the Chinese situation, it branded the British attitude ‘greatly regrettable.’ The council charged that since the outset of the ‘incident’ with China, the British have assisted the Chinese in their anti-Japanese actions, Terming alleged British assistance to the Chinese an ‘improper third-power attitude,’ the council resolution additionally charged Britain with being responsible for the convocation of the Nine-Power Conference at Brussels Nov. 3, thereby ‘fostering international intervention.’ The council warned that unless Brita

SHANGHAI, Oct. 30—()—The Japanese navy today gave China's “Lost Battalion” in Chapei until tomorrow to surrender and warned American and British defense units and residents of nearby sections in the International Settlement to take precautions. Unless the Chinese give up their warehouse stronghold just across Soochow creek from the American defense positions, the Japanese said they would blast them out, Rear Admiral Tadao Honda, Japanese naval attache, officially declared Japanese patience was exhausted with the “more or less heroic stand” of the “do-or-die” unit of the crack 88th division. He warned all residents living in the International Settlement near the sector and the American and British defense units in close proximity to take precautions to avert possible casualties and damage. Plans Not Detailed Rear Admiral Honda did not disclose exactly when the Japanese planned to take act

SHANGHAI, Oct. 29 (2) — Three British soldiers were killed and three seriously wounded Friday night as Japanese bombardments west of Shanghai brought deadly peril to Americans and other foreigners. British military headquarters said the men, members of the Royal Ulster Rifles, were hit during a two-hour shelling by Japanese artillery of the Hungjao area west of Shanghai, to which Chinese forces had retreated from the old front north of the city. Vigorous Protest Lodged British authorities protested vigorously to Admiral Kiyoshi Hasegawa, commanding Japanese naval forces at Shanghai. Anglo-Japanese relations, already bitter over the killing Sunday of another member of the Ulster Rifles by fire from a Japanese plane, became more tense. Seven Chinese noncombatants were killed or wounded by the same shells that hit the Britishers. Other Japanese projectiles exploded in the French concession,

London, Oct. 29—(@—The sub-committee on nonintervention ended another bitter five-hour session Friday night with a deadlock between communist Russia and the nazi-fascist front of Germany, Italy and Portugal blocking agreement on Great Britain's plan to withdraw foreign volunteers from Spain. The plan was accepted in its entirety by Britain, France, Belgium, Czechoslovakia, and Sweden at Friday's session, Russia accepted it with reservations on the granting of belligerent rights to the Spanish warring parties. Germany, Italy and Portugal accepted without reservations, but on condition of unanimity. The deadlock was on the question of unanimity. The plan envisages, besides the withdrawal of foreign soldiers from the Spanish armies, the granting of belligerent rights and restoration of land and sea supervision to ensure nonintervention. Ivan M. Maisky, Soviet ambassador, abstained from voti

LONDON, Oct. 29.—A warning that drastic action against Japan as the result of the killing of two British soldiers in Shanghai would mean war was sounded in the House of Commons this afternoon as news of the latest outrage on the Far Eastern battlefront reached London.— Word of the killings reached and shocked officialdom just as the house assembled to resume debate on the foreign situation. Richard Thomas Asland, liberal, demanded that the British delegation to the forthcoming nine-power conference on Japanese aggression proceed to Brussels fully prepared to make a forthright demand for a trade boycott against Japan “supported, if necessary, by force.” “That Means War” Horrified cries of “that means war” rang out from government benches as Asland made his demand. Members of the government sought to appease and mollify the liberal demand for drastic measures in an effort to forestall a fi

LONDON, Oct 30—Lord Louis Mountbatten, a cousin of King George, today disclosed two mysterious night-time raids within a week on his luxurious apartment. On the second intrusion, Thursday night, the marauder escaped over rooftops after waking Lord Mountbatten’s 19-year-old daughter, Patricia, by turning his flashlight into her room from a porch. Nothing was stolen on that occasion nor on Sunday when the intruder entered the nursery and ransacked several rooms. Lord Mountbatten disclosed details through his Secretary in a statement which termed “ridiculous” rumor that the intruders were “either foreign spies or intended kidnappers.” He expressed belief the raids were the work of a “cat burglar.”

| SHANGHAI, Oct. 30.—(U.P.)—The Domei (Japanese) news agency reported today that Japanese spokesmen charged Chinese guns were responsible for the deaths of three British soldiers. The spokesmen denied emphatically that Japanese guns were responsible, the agency said. Evacuation Starts. SHANGHAI, Oct. 31.—(Sunday)—UPI—One hundred and fifty “dare-to-die” Chinese troops who for three days defied overwhelming Japanese attackers, early today started evacuating.

1937-04-23.text: Bilbao, Spain, April 23—Three British food ships, running an attempted insurgent blockade, under partial protection of British men of war, steamed into besieged Bilbao today to the cheers of famished Basques and the crash of six insurgent air raids. Government and insurgent pilots engaged in deadly sky fights high over the Basque capital while the cargo boats, loaded with 6,100 tons of provisions, docked in the broad Nervion river. Defies Threats The food freighters Macgregor, Hamsterly and Stanbrook defied threats from the insurgent cruiser Almirante Cervera and armed trawler Galerna, outside the three mile limit under the protecting guns of H. M. S. Hood, the largest battleship and a flotilla of British destroyers. The Basque trawler Bizkaya then convoyed the food fleet into Bilbao’s port inside the three mile limit, in which official British protection has been forbidden. Dropped Bomb

Los Angeles, Apr. 22 (AP).-Mrs. Violet Wells Norton testified today she is convinced that Clark Gable, screen idol, is the 'Frank Billings' she named as the unwed father of her daughter. The plump, 47-year-old English woman made the accusation in a crowded federal courtroom. Only a few minutes earlier, she had scrutinized the actor at close range after having had him recalled a third time as a witness—this time for herself. She is on trial charged with having named Gable the father of Gwendoline Norton, 13, and of trying to extract money from him.

Bilbao, Spain —(P)— A fleet of three British food ships, under the protection of British men-of-war and the barking guns of Basque shore batteries, ran a gauntlet of insurgent fire today to break through the blockade of Bilbao with desperately needed supplies. Frantically cheering crowds of Basques lined the docks to greet the sturdy merchantmen as they came into view down the lower reaches of the broad Nervion river that has made the Basque capital the first seaport of Spain. Crammed into their holds were 6,100 tons of foodstuffs for the starving population of the city swollen to almost 400,000 by the steady influx of refugees from the surrounding country. Defy Rebel Shells The three cargo vessels, the MacGregor, the Hamsterley and the Stanbrook, captained by veteran British seadogs, defied the shells of the insurgent fleet during the night and docked just after 8 a.m. (2 a.m. CST). Jus

LONDON — (U.P.) — The Duke of Windsor, thoroughly angry after months of critical and intimate discussion on his life in British publications, has demanded the withdrawal of the newest best seller about him. The senior partner of the Duke's solicitors, Allen and Overy, told the United Press that they had demanded that the leading publishing firm of William Heinemann, Ltd., publisher of "Coronation Commentary" by Geoffrey Dennis, withdraw the book from circulation and publish a suitable apology on the ground that it libels the duke. In the event that the demand is refused, the spokesman said a writ for libel would be issued. The book was published April 12. It was merciless in its criticism of the duke who is bound to silence by his position. In Dennis’ book were such things as this: “He left his land with kingly dignity and repaired to the more welcome company of rich American Jewesses...

Quebec, April 23—44)—(Canadian Press)—Judge Laetare Roy today quashed an 11-months’ old warrant for the arrest of Ann Harding, which Miss Harding's former husband, Harry Bannister, obtained in an unsuccessful attempt to keep the actress from taking her 9-year-old daughter to England last May. Bannister charged Miss Harding with abducting the child, but her attorneys, desiring to nullify the warrant before the actress returns from England, said she had California court permission to take the child abroad. Miss Harding is now Mrs. Werner Janssen.

Los Angeles, April 22,—-(#)—Mrs. Violet Wells Norton declared Thursday she is convinced that Clark Gable, screen idol, is the “Frank Billings” whose mistress she was in England and who she declares is the unwed father of her daughter. The 47-year-old Englishwoman, on trial charged with having named Gable the father of Gwendoline Norton, 13, and of trying to extract money from him, made the declaration when she was cross-examined by Federal Prosecutor John Powell. "I am still convinced that he (Gable) is one and the same man,” she said. Powell asked her if she might be mistaken in thus identifying the film hero. “Not unless there is a living double of Frank Billings,” said Mrs. Norton. Before she was placed in the witness chair, the court gave her permission to approach Gable and view him at close quarters. This was while Gable was on the stand as a defense witness. She looked him over an

(By Associated Press) Lewiston, Me., April 23—Dr. Howard Myer, New England regional labor director, announced today he expected manufacturers in the Lewiston-Auburn shoe area affected by a four-weeks strike would agree to a conference with workers’ representatives soon. While C. I. O. leaders awaited arraignment in superior court on indictments charging conspiracy to injure the business of manufacturers and to prevent workers from returning to their shops, Powers Hapgood, C. I. O. secretary for New England, asserted he was optimistic an agreement might be reached within a few days. Ten organizers and three strikers later were held in total bail of $26,000 on the superior court indictment. Judge Arthur Chapman continued the cases until later in the day when C. I. O. attorneys said the bail would be furnished. Sidney Grant, attorney for the C. I. O., was notified upon entering court that h

London, Apr. 22 (#).—Actors in Britain's biggest one-day show—the coronation of King George VI—went through two more rehearsals today, to make sure nothing will be forgotten May 12. Dignitaries of the church and state at Westminster Abbey concentrated on proper timing of each act. They carried cardboard replicas of crown, sword and sceptre in practice processions and stopwatches checked the times to and from the altar. The Archbishop of Canterbury, the Dean of Westminster, and the Lord Mayor of London participated in the morning rehearsal. The Duke of Gloucester, and the Duke and Duchess of Kent attended the second tryout this afternoon. From now on until coronation time, there will be many rehearsals and a secret dress rehearsal will be held May 10.

1937-08-08.text: LONDON, AUG. 7. (AP)—Great Britain dispatched a strong note today to Spanish insurgent authorities at Palma, Mallorca, protesting yesterday's “mystery” plane attack on the British tanker Corporal. The protest followed a report from the British consul general at Algeciras that the machine gun and bomb attack “probably” was executed by “anti-government” aircraft. Three monoplanes of unidentified nationality dove at the British Corporal in the Mediterranean, 30 miles northwest of Algeciras, sprayed the decks with machine gun fire and dropped bombs close to the vessel. The same planes were believed responsible for a similar attack on the Italian steamer Mongolia and a machine-gun onslaught against a French cargo boat, the Djebel Amour. Palma is an insurgent naval and air base on one of the Balearic islands about 150 miles east of Valencia in the Mediterranean, within easy flying distance of

| LONDON, Aug. 6 --UP---Great Britain may buy the once proud liner Leviathan for scrap metal to use in its rearmament program now proceeding at an urgent rate, it was understood today. It was reported further that the admiralty might ask for five more giant battleships in next year's program--to be added to five already budgeted. A representative of a British firm is due at New York Monday on the liner Queen Mary, now the French Normandie’s rival for the Atlantic blue ribbon which the Leviathan once claimed, to negotiate for the United States liner, it was understood.

The Spanish situation took a graver international turn today after aerial attacks on a British ship, two French ships and an Italian ship in the Mediterranean. British ships have been fired on before, but in Spanish territorial waters and Britain has accepted the situation. In this instance, however, the ship apparently was on the high seas, 40 miles west of Algiers. Britain protested strongly to the Insurgents, having been advised by the consul general at Algiers that the attacking planes apparently were Insurgent. Italian Ship Hit Three planes dropped about 40 bombs and then turned machine gun fire on the ship. There were no direct hits, however. The Italian ship, Montgioia, was hit and it was reported the master had died of a lung wound. The non-intervention plan for control of Spain had virtually collapsed and the Loyalist coast was open to the running of arms and munitions to aid th

| London, Aug. 7.—A hint of possible retaliatory action was given by the German embassy today after cancellation by the government of permits of three German newspaper correspondents to reside in Britain. The correspondents were Werner von Crome, chief London correspondent of the Berlin Lokalanzeiger; Herr Wrede, a colleague of von Crome, and Wolf von Langen, London representative of the Orafreachschar News Agency. Permits of women secretaries of von Crome and von Langen also were revoked. All concerned but von Crome have left London. A German embassy official said today in discussing the incident: “Details of the expulsion have been forwarded to Berlin, where future action will be decided. It is not known whether retaliatory action will be taken against British correspondents in Berlin.” Usually reliable sources reported that the men were suspected of espionage, but von Crome said he wa

LONDON, Aug. 7—The British home office's order compelling three German newspaper correspondents to leave England tonight appeared likely to open a prolonged Anglo-German controversy. Two of the three already have left for Germany. As Berlin dispatches told of German official threats of retaliation, there were indications the embassy here was preparing for some action in the matter. Confer With Ambassador Two members of the embassy staff traveled by airplane to Renfrew, in Scotland, where the ambassador, Joachim von Ribbentrop, is on vacation. The correspondents’ plight was understood to be the subject of a conference. The home office declined, without explanation, to renew the labor permits of the German writers and they were given two weeks to wind up their personal affairs and leave the country. The one remaining in London was Werner Crome, chief correspondent here of the Berliner Loka

LONDON. (4). Great Britain, convinced that Spanish insurgent airplanes were responsible, added to her long series of protests to the regime of Gen. Francisco Franco with another against the air attack Friday on the tanker British Corporal. Merchantmen of Italy and France also were targets for three unidentified planes in an area about 30 miles off the Algerian coast, and the captain of the Italian steamer, Franco Solari, died of wounds. But Italian officials, evidently assuming that Spanish government planes made the attacks, took no action, although they expressed keen indignation. The British and Italian vessels were not harmed. Britain's protest, a note to insurgent authorities at Palma, Mallorca, was made after her consul general at Algiers reported the bomb and machine gun attack “probably was the work of anti-government aircraft.” Aboard the Italian vessel, the Mongioia, not only w

ALGIERS, Algeria, Aug. 7.—(INS)—Escorts for ships of all major foreign powers venturing into Mediterranean waters were ordered Saturday as the result of mystery attacks on merchantmen of Britain, Italy and France. Maritime powers ordered ships not to leave port unless they were under escort as far as the open sea. Authorities of the three major Mediterranean powers meanwhile sought to place responsibility for the strange bomb attacks on the British Corporal, English tanker, the Italian freighter Mongioia, and the French steamer Djebel Amour. LONDON, Aug. 7.—(INS)—The British Government drafted a strong protest to the Nationalist junta in Spain Saturday over the bombing of the British tanker British Corporal, one of three foreign ships attacked in the Mediterranean Friday. The Admiralty issued a statement declaring the markings of three planes which attacked the British Corporal "indicate

| SHANGHAI, Aug. 7—(AP)— Japanese and Chinese diplomats tonight expressed hope that formal, declared war between their countries can be averted, but war fears still gripped central China and in the north formidable armies moved toward fresh collisions. Hasty withdrawals of thousands of Japanese from widely separated parts of China reached a climax when the Japanese navy, under instructions from Tokyo, ordered complete abandonment of the Japanese concession at Hankow, great port and industrial center of the middle Yangtze valley. Orders were issued for all Japanese in Hankow, including 400 marines and volunteers, to be aboard ships on the Yangtze river by noon Sunday, when it was expected the Japanese would abandon completely the concession which has been center of their trade in central China for a generation. Jap Ships to Leave Even five Japanese naval vessels lying in the river were ex

1937-03-28.text: A second distress call within four hours turned the big liner Empress of Canada, off her course to go to the rescue. At the same time several Japanese freighters began a race to the volunteers’ side. In the van of the rescue ships the British freighter Fresno City neared the scene in a 240-mile run she started when the Volunteer sent her first call for help at 12:30 a. m. (PST). A second call for help at 4 a. m. to the Empress of Canada said: “The Fresno City is coming to my assistance. Water is gaining fast. Request you come also.” The Empress of Canada was 638 miles from the Volunteer. The various messages indicated the Volunteer’s crew of about 40 ‘See Freighter In, Page 2, Col. 1D

NEW LONDON, Tex., March —(P)— Bereaved families of London’s school explosion will return to the wrecked building tomorrow to seek consolation in the resurrection. Easter memorial services at the very doorstep of the structure, ruined by a gas explosion 10 days ago, will supplant services planned prior to the disaster. Surrounded by the ruins, survivors and families will assemble to pay tribute to 455 students and teachers killed in the blast. Gov. James V. Allred, speaking from Austin, will read a message from President Roosevelt at the opening of the program at 2 p.m. Sympathy of 8,000,000 school children throughout the nation is to be expressed in a nine-foot floral cross of thousands of red carnations on a field of white.

WASHINGTON, March 27 (#) - The state department announced today that James W. Gerard, wartime ambassador to Germany, will head the delegation representing the United States at the coronation of King George VI in London, on May 12. General John J. Pershing and Admiral Hugh Rodman, retired, will be the other delegates. Curtis Bok, of Philadelphia, has been designated secretary of the mission and Colonel James L. Collings and Commander Frank E. Beatty will act as aides to General Pershing and Admiral Rodman.

MADRID, March 27 (AP)—Government troops clung to positions on the Pozoblanco front tonight after, their commanders said, they had withstood an insurgent charge in which hundreds of the attackers were killed. Correspondents with the insurgent army said the insurgents, driving across the western part of the Sierra Morenas, smashed successfully against government lines and won control of the mountain watershed. Dispatches to Madrid related the government militiamen had held the ground they gained in the last two days, offensive, in the face of a severe onslaught by insurgent tanks and airplanes. Gen. Jose Miaja, the government commander who has sent his men in hard attacks at the enemy since he took complete charge in central Spain recently, had a new column moving westward toward Alirla, which is some 50 miles west of Madrid.

VALENCIA, Spain. (UP)—The rebels, hard pressed in the Pozoblanco region, 160 miles south of Madrid, struck back yesterday with a counter offensive. Advices reaching here said the offensive collapsed and the rebel forces, reported to include 10,000 Italians, were driven back with losses. A newspaper report from a reliable source said that Italy is planning to send 100,000 troops to Spain and arms are being assembled to equip them. The tide of war has moved back and forth during the past two days with the loyalists claiming to have held their gains.

VIENNA. (%, The duke of Windsor cut his servant problem down by practically two-thirds Saturday night, preparatory to moving to the Austrian Tyrol. That will save him quite a bit of money from what he has been spending while living at rambling Enzesfeld castle. One of the duke's seventeen servants who asked to be taken along from Enzesfeld said an adjutant told him he was “sorry, his royal highness must economize.” He will get along with only six servants at his new quarters at the modest appleback at St. Wolfgang in the picturesque Tyrol. Three of them, including the chef and his favorite castle kitchen equipment, will be taken from the group of 17 that has served Windsor at Enzesfeld. He arranged tentatively to read part of the Easter service Sunday in the Anglican church at Vienna, where his participation in Christmas services caused some British criticism.

PERPIGNAN France, March 27. Claiming they were going to Spain as “tourists,” a group of 13 Americans and five Canadians were jailed tonight for further questioning by French authorities as “suspected volunteers” to the Spanish government army. Officials said the Americans had passports stamped “not valid for travel in Spain.” They were led by an American who said he was Joe Ballet, 30, of Cleveland, O.

BERLIN, March 97.—(#)—The Nazi-edited Zwölf Uhr Blatt came out in a special edition for measures to “reform” the European press by curtailing its freedom, but tonight responsible observers were beginning to think the campaign was a flash in the pan. The newspaper, publishing contributions from twenty European editors and an editorial believed penned by Propaganda Minister Paul Joseph Goebbels, attacked “International press terror” and declared: “Freedom of the press is, in reality, defended only by reactionaries of a past epoch.” However, other newspapers failed to take up the cry. It was recalled that although some Nazis long have clamored for a general European “gag rule,” international newspapermen have been admonished directly only to be truthful and have been told that treatment of news must be a matter of “personal discipline.” Witheim Weiss, head of the German confederation, was t

1937-11-17.text: London, Nov. 17.—(4#)—Grand Duke Ludwig Von Hesse Bei Rhein, second cousin to Britain’s King George, was married today to Miss Margaret Campbell Geddes in a private ceremony cloaked with the tragedy of an air crash that killed nearly all the bridegroom’s family. After the ceremony at St. Peter’s church in Eton Square, the mourning newlyweds started their honeymoon with a trip to Ostend, Belgium, to claim the bodies of the Duke’s mother, brother and his brother’s wife and sons and take them to the family seat at Darmstadt, Germany. They were among 11 persons killed yesterday when a London-bound airliner crashed in flames near Ostend in a fog, as they were en route to London for the wedding. The plane hit a chimney. The Duke and Duchess of Kent and German Ambassador Joachim Von Ribbentrop headed the wedding guest list. The ceremony had been set for Saturday but was moved forward because of

Vatican City — (?)— Pope Pius will create five new cardinals at a Consistory December 13. There will be three Italians, one English and one French. The Vatican announced the following are to be named: Archbishops Giuseppe Pizzardo, Vatican undersecretary of state; Ermenegildo Pellegrinetti, nuncio to Yugoslavia; Giovanni Piazza, patriarch to Venice; Arthur Hinsley of Westminster Cathedral in London; and Pierre Gerlier of Lyon. The five will receive red hats at a public consistory three days after the secret session. The announcement was regarded as evidence the Pontiff believes his health “will stand the strain of the elaborate ceremonies involved.

LONDON, Nov. 17--Grand Duke Ludwig of Hesse and Miss Margaret Campbell Geddes, daughter of Sir Auckland Geddes, were married today at St. Peter's Church, Eaton Square. It was a quiet, poignant service at this church where most of England's fashionable weddings are solemnized, for the ceremony was held in an atmosphere of deep tragedy. Every member but one of the duke’s immediate family — his elder brother, Grand Duke George; his sister-in-law, Grand Duchess Cecile; his mother Dowager Grand Duchess Elenore and his little nephews, Princes Ludwig and Aldenbach who were to have been pages—were killed at Ostend yesterday in the crash of a Belgian air liner in which they were flying here. They were on the way to the wedding, which was to have been held Saturday in a setting brilliant to match the status of a German royal grand ducal family. Instead, the ceremony was put ahead today—so that the

LONDON, Nov. 15 (2?) — Soviet Russia, in an unexpected move, tonight removed a major obstacle to withdrawal of foreign volunteers from Spain. She modified her opposition to granting belligerent rights to the warring Spanish factions and accepted a general plan approved by other nonintervention powers for removing foreign soldiers from the civil war. With the exception of Russia, the other nations had agreed to extend belligerent rights to the Spanish government and the insurgents when "substantial progress" had been made in getting alien volunteers out of Spain. Russia had insisted such rights should not be granted until all volunteers had been withdrawn. Ivan Maisky, Soviet representative on the non-intervention committee, said Russia would leave interpretation of "substantial withdrawal" until the question should be considered by the committee.

BERLIN (UP) — Viscount Halifax, lord president of the council in the British cabinet, arrived today for a series of ‘private’ talks with German leaders intended to assure the peaceable cooperation which British and German governments alike have long sought. Viscount Halifax arrived by train this morning and was met at the station by Sir Neville Henderson, the British ambassador, and Vicco Karl Von Buelow-Schwante, chief of proceeded to be the ambassador's guest during his visit. Ostensibly Lord Halifax's visit is a private one, to attend the international hunting exhibition here, and there was no arrangement for a formal reception. It is admitted now, however, the talks he intends to have with Fuehrer Adolf Hitler and other leaders in the next few days are of major diplomatic moment, Because of the delicacy of the international situation, and particularly because of the ‘Berlin-Rome axis

LONDON, Nov. 17 (U.P)—His bride of a few hours in tears and wearing mourning, Grand Duke Ludwig of Hesse started for Ostend today on a sad honeymoon—to claim the bodies of his entire immediate family, who perished there in a flaming airplane. The grand duke and his bride, Miss Margaret Campbell Geddes, daughter of Sir Auckland Geddes, were married today at St. Peter’s Church in Eaton Square. It was a strange wedding. Rejoicing was replaced by sorrow and the wedding gowns with somber black. The grand duke and duchess left immediately afterward for Belgium, where the duke will supervise the removal of the bodies of his mother, elder brother, sister-in-law and two young nephews for burial.

. BERLIN, (AP).—Viscount Halifax arrived in Berlin from London today on a visit which was expected to include discussion of Germany’s colonial aspirations with Chancellor Adolf Hitler. Halifax was greeted at the station by the British embassy staff and Vice Karl von Bülow-Schwanen of the German foreign office.

BOSTON, Nov. 17.—- (P) Charles Cox, 26-year-old English man, weighed anchor today aboard the 37-foot Ketch Namo, ready for a 50,000-mile, three-year cruise around the world. Cox, skipper-owner, and his two companions, John Gagnon, 19, and Everett Macdonald, 22 Shelburne, N. S., fisherman, plan to touch New York, sail down the Atlantic to Florida, through the Panama Canal to New Zealand, Australia, Africa and finally to England, where Cox plans to visit with his family at Sussex.

1937-08-05.text: Aboard Coast Guard Cutter Argo, off Newport, R. I., Aug. 5—Gaining her lead on a record ten-mile windward leg and holding it safe over the rest of the 30-mile triangular course, Harold S. Vanderbilt's sleek, snub-nosed Ranger today led T. O. M. Sopwith’s Endeavour II, the British challenger, across the finish line by approximately half a mile to score her fourth and deciding victory in defense of the America’s Cup.

London, Aug. 4.—A report that Premier Benito Mussolini tried recently to obtain from Fuehrer Adolf Hitler a declaration of support in event of an attack by Great Britain but failed was published today by the conservative Daily Telegraph. The story was advanced as a report to which foreign diplomatic circles attached importance. If true, it would explain the apparently urgent haste with which Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain last week wrote a personal letter to Mussolini, seeking better relations. There had been no satisfactory explanation of this letter, or of Mussolini’s reply. According to the report, Mussolini about six weeks ago wrote a personal letter to Hitler. In it, the story is, he expressed the view that Britain was preparing to attack Italy by means of direct action to check Italian aspirations in the Mediterranean. (Continued on Page Five)

London, Aug. 5. Pi—The captain of the Netherlands steamer Maas-kerk ordered his passengers into the lifeboats today after the steamer struck Brenton Rock off Cape Palmas, West Africa, radio messages to Lloyd's reported. The number of passengers was not known here. The 4,452-ton ship hit the rock at 10:42 a.m. G. M. T. (4:24 a. m Central Standard time) and the boats were ordered lowered about four hours later. The pumps could not halt the rising water.

PEIPING—(UP)—Foreign powers already affronted by incidents in which photographers of the United States and other nations have been molested by Japanese troops, issued a warning to Japan today. The United States, British, French and Italian embassies cautioned Japan that she must comply with the Boxer protocol, guaranteeing the maintenance of communications between Peiping and Tientsin. There was increasing fear among foreigners that their nationals may be endangered in the fighting between Chinese and Japanese which threatens to become general. Americans and others have been advised to seek safety in foreign concessions and other concentration points. Peiping, the ancient capital, was made uneasy by continued Japanese demonstrations of military strength. A Japanese column of 250 trucks, 35 tanks and a battery of four big field guns paraded through the city on its way to Tungchow, 15 mile

LONDON, Aug. 5. (U.P.) — Great Britain has embarked fully on a forceful diplomatic program of peace consolidation and intends to start the business phase of the program early this autumn, it was understood today. It was expected that both Baron Constantin von Neurath and Count Galeazzo Ciano, the German and Italian foreign ministers, would be in London in September and the possibility was foreseen that before this meeting Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden might see Ciano at Rome. Indications were that the British program had been prepared carefully for deliberate progressive action that might, if it succeeded, find Britain, France, Germany and Italy bound by a Western European peace-preservation agreement. A prime factor will be Britain's $7,500,000,000 arms program, now well advanced. French and admiralty reports are that Great Britain will have 664,000 tons of warships building by the end

By the eB Press. Shanghai, Aug. 5.—(Thursday)— Hurried evacuation of Japanese noncombatants from a vast area of China caused fear today that Japan’s week-old undeclared war in North China might spread deeper than had been expected. Japanese reports disclosed that withdrawals of Japanese nationals were being effected with increasing rapidity and were drawing Japanese residents even from China’s interior. At the same time, authorities in Nanking were said to fear for the safety of 8,000 Chinese nationals in Japan and to have considered evacuating them. Japs Move Southward. The theater of war shifted definitely to the south, apparently toward an impending clash between both nations' main forces. Two Japanese columns penetrated steadily southward to strike at the central Chinese government’s first-line defense. Japanese commanders reported virtually no opposition. Inpouring reinforcements, a

Madrid, Aug. 4 —(P)— General Jose Miaja, commander of Spanish government central armies, told The Associated Press today that insurgents had lost more than 20,000 men and suffered complete upset of their summer campaign in the government’s month-old offensive outside Madrid. During the drive, he said, 2,000 insurgents were taken prisoners. “The operations were of great importance," the government military leader explained. “You cannot measure the results merely by the number of kilometers we sliced from the enemy’s territory. At first glance it may appear no more than the capture of a few towns. “But in reality, we have broken many threads of the enemy's schemes.” Miaja described the advance into insurgent territory west of Madrid as a “real triumph” because “we were able to concentrate many thousands of men without the enemy's knowledge.”

Cristobal, Canal Zone, Aug. 4.—UP—The navy said tonight that the Pan-American-Grace airliner which crashed with 14 persons in the sea off Panama struck the water with terrific force, tearing the ship into scattered fragments. The violent impact strewed pieces over a wide area, only the plane’s steel frame staying intact, and probably pinning bodies of passengers and crew members inside the shattered fuselage, the navy said. Relinquishing search for the bodies, a navy spokesman said it probably would recall two submarines and two destroyers from the scene of the disaster tomorrow. No more planes will be sent out. Evidence of Explosion (The navy department in Washington disclosed there was evidence of an explosion aboard the craft at the time of the crash. A dispatch from the naval commandant in the Canal zone reported evidences of fire on recovered parts of the wreckage.) It was feared th

1937-11-27.text: The United States and Britain have told Japan of their concern over any Japanese attempt to interfere with the integrity of the Chinese maritime customs. Secretary Hull announced in Washington today that Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo had conveyed the American government’s formal representations on this subject to Japan. The British ambassador to Japan was instructed to leave the Tokyo government “in no doubt whatsoever” that Britain insisted it must be consulted on any changes the Japanese conquerors of Shanghai contemplated in customs and communications matters there. Secretary Hull emphasized that although the powers were in close contact on the Chinese customs question, their representatives at Tokyo did not constitute joint action. LONDON, NOV. 27. (AP). The greatest fog in many years curtained half of England today, choking transportation and endangering pedestrians and motorists for a third day. Weather officials said the “block out” was one of the worst on record and predicted it would continue over the weekend. At least ten deaths have been attributed to the murk. Trains and buses ran behind schedule or quit running altogether. Shipping on the lower Thames was halted. Pedestrians formed hand to hand chains to guide themselves on London's sidewalks behind leaders carrying torches and blazing newspapers. Three persons fell into reservoirs and a river while groping in the darkness. The three men in the crew of a German plane were killed last night when the craft crashed in taking off from fog cloaked Croydon airdrome. Four motorists were killed early yesterday in a crash in a London suburb and several persons were

LONDON, Nov. 27. (4?)—Britain's ambassador to Tokyo, Sir Robert L. Craigie, today was instructed to make it clear to the Japanese government that Britain insists on her right to be consulted on any arrangement the Japanese may make regarding Chinese maritime customs. It was understood in informed quarters that the United States and France were taking similar action. It was also understood that Craigie was instructed to reserve the right to be consulted about any change the Japanese contemplate in regard to postal, wireless and telegraph services in the Shanghai area. (Britain and other powers are interested in the fate of the Chinese maritime customs because a large part of its revenue is pledged for service of China's foreign debt.)

LONDON, Nov. 27.—The British government made formal representations to Japan today over Japanese threats to seize all Chinese government property and functions, particularly the customs service in greater Shanghai. Sir Robert Craigie, British ambassador to Japan, was expected to inform officials in Tokyo of this government's concern over the growing aggressiveness of the Japanese military forces in the Shanghai area.

JERUSALEM, Nov. 27—(UP)—Shiek Forham el Sadi, 70-year-old Moslem leader, one of those responsible for recent terrorism, was hanged today. He was the first man condemned by the new British military court established November 18 after the worst outbreak of Jewish-Arab acts of terrorism since the rioting of 1929 when two hundred persons were killed. The military court here began its second case, the trials of two or three Arabs arrested with the Sheik in a raid by British military forces in Mozar, north Palestine, last Sunday. The military courts are functioning under a decree providing the death penalty for possession of firearms, sabotage, intimidation and terrorism.

London, Eng. (INS) — Great Britain, it was learned today, is prepared to consider the return to Germany of some of her lost colonies but at a price and upon certain conditions. The price is Germany’s return to a rehashed League of Nations and her participation in a western European peace settlement. The conditions are that she administer the colonies under a League of Nations mandate and guarantee the political freedom and interests of the inhabitants of the restored colonies. It was learned that French Premier Camille Chautemps when he meets Premier Chamberlain next week will inform the latter that France is now prepared to join Britain in granting colony concessions to Germany as part of a European peace settlement.

The British ambassador in Tokyo was instructed to leave the Japanese government "in no doubt whatsoever" that Britain insisted its rights be consulted concerning any changes Japan contemplated regarding the Chinese maritime customs and Chinese communications facilities in the conquered Shanghai area. Britain, the United States and other foreign powers are interested in the Chinese customs because their revenues are largely pledged for payment of foreign loans. SHANGHAI, Nov. 27 (1) Japanese authorities today began assuming control and supervision of all former functions of the Chinese government in Shanghai's international settlement and French concession. A Japanese embassy spokesman made clear that his government considers it has a right to take over all authority and agencies of the Chinese government and intends to exercise its rights immediately. Japan will establish “control and close supervision,” he said, of China's communications system, including the radio administration which has working agreements with the American Commercial Pacific Cable, Radio Corporation of America and Mackay Radio. A wireless report to the United States cruiser Augusta, in Shanghai harbor, told of the arrival of United States Ambassador Nelson T. 1937-01-26.text: Heartened makers of neutrality pushed ahead today to formulate a working scheme for leaving Spain alone. Italo-German agreement to join a general embargo of foreign volunteers to the warring peninsula paved the way for a practical plan to keep both men and guns from Spain. The London neutrality committee was called to meet Thursday to accomplish that purpose and to let Spain's Socialist government and its Fascist Insurgents fight it out by themselves. For months major European exponents of the two philosophies have made it a “little world war” by their help on one side or the other. Italian and German “volunteers” and armaments have been on the side of the Insurgents; Russians, Frenchmen, and men of many nations have fought in defense of the government. LONDON, Jan. 26—King George VI sent a message to the House of Commons today, asking for legislation to provide for a regency in case of his illness or absence from the country. Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin presented the message to the Speaker. The King’s message also asked legislation to include provision for accession to the throne during infancy, meaning Princess Elizabeth, the heir presumptive, before she is

MOSCOW, Jan. 26 (AP)—Alexander Stein, German mining engineer, testified today at the trial of 17 confessed Trotskyist plotters he engaged in Siberian sabotage to help “Germany recover her former power” in the Soviet Union. The 55-year-old engineer, first foreign witness, declared through an interpreter he received his instructions from another German named Flesser who told him: “Germany had to recover her former power so Germans in the Soviet Union had to engage in wreckage so as to increase German strength and give her a free hand.” Stein’s testimony followed a heated debate between Prosecutor Andrey Vishinsky and Vasily Ulrich, the presiding judge, over mention of a “certain foreign official.” Stein said his wrecking activities were centered in the coal mines near Anjer but “later I was reprimanded for insufficient wrecking.” At least 100 communists, foreign observers estimated, have b

TOKYO—(AP)—The army, standing virtually alone, Monday night loomed as a formidable barrier to the formation of a cabinet by Gen. Kazushige Ugaki, former governor-general of Korea. Ugaki, although a retired general and four times minister of war, was opposed by the present high command because of his moderate leanings, his friendly relations with political parties and because as minister he reduced the standing army by two divisions. The army, although isolated in its opposition to a Ugaki cabinet, could block it. The law requires that a general or lieutenant-general on the active list be minister of war. The generals therefore could prevent formation of any ministry they disliked by refusing to permit any of their number to assume the war portfolio.

Cincinnati, Jan. 26—Rising in muddy, slow-rising torrents, the Ohio river’s flood waters today spread over an area of more than a million acres, taking a toll of at least 111 known dead, driving 550,000 from their homes and leaving many thousands more marooned in precarious straits. Whole towns and villages showed only rooftops. Property damage was estimated far in excess of $10,000,000—and on every side from city officials and army engineers came the warning: “The worst is yet to come.” Flood Exodus Wholesale evacuation of flooded towns in Tennessee, Kentucky, southwestern Missouri, Arkansas and Mississippi signaled the greatest mass flood exodus in history. DETROIT, Jan. 26.—(#)—Police and pickets clashed again today in the weeks-old General Motors strike, five persons being hurt as union men sought to prevent office workers from entering the Cadillac unit of the corporation here. The clash followed closely upon a disturbance last night at Anderson, Ind., in which three persons were hurt. The Cadillac unit is one of those in which a sit-down strike recently was called by the United Automobile Workers of America. It was not one of the plants the corporation planned to reopen tomorrow, however. One woman and four men hurt in the melee at the Cadillac plant were removed by union representatives for private treatment. From the union sound truck there came the announcement: “Tomorrow we will have a real picket line and nobody will get in.” The General Motors strike extended from coast to coast today for the first time as the corporation complete

MIAMI, Jan. 26. (AP)—A three-way investigation was pushed today into the disaster which brought death by drowning to 17 passengers of a bus crossing the Everglades. The bus carried 30 passengers, the driver, and a Negro porter bound for Florida’s west coast. Investigators agreed that some mechanical failure caused the accident yesterday. The company blamed either a tire blow-out or a snapped front spring shackle. M. R. Evans of Red Oak, Iowa, was recovering from shock and exposure. First report listed Evans among those drowned. He is a retired farmer who left Red Oak Jan. 1 to spend the winter in Florida. Unmarried, he owns two farms and some town property at Red Oak. Also on the trip was another Red Oak man, Ed Scheerbarth, who was not listed as a passenger on the bus. Evans was suffering from shock and was taken to a Miami hospital.

(By The Associated Press) DEAD—At least 132 in 11 states: Kentucky 44 (including estimate of 12 in reformatory riot in which one official said toll might reach 45); Ohio, 13; Missouri, 13; West Virginia, 9; Tennessee, 23; Indiana, 6; Arkansas, 18; Illinois, 3; Mississippi, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, 1 each. Homeless, at least 550,000. Weather Outlook—Rain or snow in Ohio and Tennessee valleys, clearing skies in Pennsylvania flood region, rain or snow in parts of Indiana, Illinois and Missouri. Relief Measures—President Roosevelt designates $790,000,000 proposed work relief appropriation as available for flood succor. Red Cross seeks $10,000,000 in public contributions. 1937-01-21.text: (By the Associated Press) Air and ground battles broke with new violence on the Madrid and Malaga fronts of warring Spain today, Neutrality efforts stood stock still. But Italy and Germany will inform Great Britain shortly, it was learned, that foreign financial aid and propaganda must be eliminated from Spain along with foreign volunteers. The League of Nations council met at Geneva to discuss both the need of Germany for raw materials and Spanish government protests against alleged Italo-German violation of its sovereignty. Fascist and socialist airplanes fought a machine gun battle over Madrid. Fascist insurgents struck back at the socialist government ground forces for an almost-successful attack on the “Hill of Angels” south of Madrid. Insurgent planes bombed southern Malaga, on the sea, laying the groundwork for assault by storm. Socialist defenders of Malaga and reinforced insurge

Hollywood, Jan. 21.—Charles (Buddy) Rogers, the actor-musician, will make Mary Pickford his bride next March in London, Hollywood wags informed today. Friends said the couple has decided on an English wedding, though Rogers only admits that the ceremony will not take place before he sails from New York February 27. The handsome Kansan has contracted for a role in a British-made film. Miss Pickford is scheduled to follow him eastward on March 15.

LONDON, Jan. 21 ()—Moderating weather promised Northern Europe relief today from wind and blizzards which caused at least 45 deaths and scattered wrecked shipping along its coasts. Damage on land and sea was widespread. Craft in Atlantic waters and along the Scandinavian coast bore the brunt of the stormy seas and gale-driven snows. Rescuers searched for bodies from the wrecked Finnish steamer Savonmaa which foundered near Kristiansand, Norway, with a loss of 20 lives, and for the bodies of the captain and 24 members of the crew of the German naval experimental ship Welle which went down with all hands off the coast of the German state of Holstein.

ENZESFELD, Austria — (UP) — The Duke of Windsor, unperturbed by a collision between his automobile and another on an icy Vienna street, took the wheel from his shaken chauffeur last night and drove the car back to Enzesfeld. The duke had attended a cocktail party at the British embassy in Vienna. The streets were icy and on the return journey the duke’s car and another driven by a merchant, skidded into each other. The duke alighted to find that a mud guard of his car was smashed and the radiator damaged. He noticed that the nerves of his own chauffeur were upset so he took the wheel.

HOLLYWOOD, Jan. 21 (UP)—A spring wedding in London today appeared probable for Mary Pickford and Buddy Rogers. Rogers will sail from New York February 27 to fill a picture engagement, and he admitted that Miss Pickford intended to sail March 15. Rogers refuses to discuss the probable wedding date, but insisted there would be no marriage before he leaves. He intends to return here in May.

LONDON, Jan. 20.—14—Winter, tightening an icy grip over Europe today, left many villages snowbound and was believed to have caused at least 49 deaths in gale-lashed seas. ‘Twenty-five persons drowned when a German ship sank in a heavy blizzard. ‘Twenty others were lost from the Finnish CAMEL Savonnia off Norway's southern coast. Two French fishing boats, each with three men aboard, were believed to have foundered near the French port of Saint Malo in the English Channel. Many Northern European regions were snowbound, but statesmen arriving at Geneva for a League of Nations council found fair weather. Huge waves pounded the coasts of Britain and France along the English Channel and the Atlantic. - BAYONNE, Spain, Jan. 21— Fourteen thousand persons have been executed since the beginning of the Spanish civil war by rebel Rightists in the province of Navarra, which is the northeast corner of Spain bordering in part on the Bay of Biscay, according to reports issued today by Basque authorities at Bayonne. The Basque national government in northern Spain is in sympathy with the loyal Leftist cause.

Bombay, India—4—Mohandas K. Gandhi, aged leader of the Indian nationalist movement, created widespread surprise today by publicly disowning the title of “Mahatma,” maintaining he had no right to the honor. The title of Mahatma means high-minded or great-souled and has been applied to Gandhi for so long it had come to be considered almost a synonym for his name.

1937-12-20.text: LOUISVILLE, Ky. Dec. 20. The body of Robert Worth Bingham was en route today to Louisville where he gained prominence as a newspaper publisher before he was named ambassador to Great Britain. After arrival the body will lie in state for two hours at the City Hall. Funeral services will be conducted at noon by Bishop Emeritus Charles E. Woodcock at the Calvary Episcopal Church. Private burial services will be held at Cavehill Cemetery. Bingham, who was 66, died at Johns Hopkins Hospital at Baltimore Saturday night from Hodgkin's disease, an ailment affecting the lymph system of the body. Earlier in the week he underwent an operation and hospital authorities announced he suffered from inflammation of the abdomen. Aboard the funeral train, scheduled to arrive at 9:35 a.m., were members of his family. White House Secretary Marvin T. McIntyre, who will represent President Roosevelt at the fun

Louisville, Ky.—(#)—A special railway car bore the body of Robert Worth Bingham home to Louisville today for burial at the scene where he achieved fame as a newspaper publisher before becoming United States ambassador to Great Britain. The department of war sent four troops of dismounted cavalry from Fort Knox, Ky., to act as an escort of honor for the 66-year-old envoy at the private burial in Cave Hill cemetery this afternoon. Operations of Bingham’s newspapers, the Louisville Courier-Journal and Times, were adjusted to permit employees to meet the train on its arrival or view the body as it lay in state at Calvary Episcopal church before funeral services at noon. Aboard the special car with the body, along with members of the ambassador’s family who were with him when he died in Baltimore late Saturday, were representatives of the United States and Great Britain. (By the ASSOCIATED Press) London, Dec. 20--The scope of a new world naval armaments race was disclosed today by the publication of the 1937 edition of the authoritative yearbook, “Jane's Fighting Ships.” An editor's foreword declared: “In the 12 months that elapsed since the 1936 edition appeared there has been ‘no abatement in the flood of orders for new warships. In the whole world ‘there is scarcely a naval power of any importance which has not felt impelled to join in the common impulse to bring its fleet up to date.” The book cited the big warship building activities of Great Britain, the United States, France, Italy, Russia, Japan and Germany. It added: “Thus all seven of the principal powers now are committed to a policy of building capital ships, a sufficient commentary on the enthusiasm showed in uniformed quarters for substitution of cheaper weapons, such as torpedo boats, subm

Washington, 4—The death of Ambassador Robert W. Bingham aroused speculation today that President Roosevelt might immediately appoint Joseph P. Kennedy as his successor at London. It was recalled that Bingham had planned to retire soon and that Mr. Roosevelt had talked with Kennedy about the London post. A week ago Kennedy, now chairman of the maritime commission, visited the Baltimore hospital where Bingham died Saturday night. Presumably he discussed with the ambassador the problems he might face as envoy to London.

Washington, Dec. 18 (4?)—Ready Senate approval of the expected appointment of Joseph P. Kennedy as Ambassador to London seemed in prospect tonight, although there were some Senators who thought him more valuable at home than abroad. Members of the foreign relations committee, commending the choice, said the Administration would lose a valuable business advisor, but took the view that the question of where Kennedy would be most effective was one for him and the President to decide. "Kennedy is an excellent man anywhere you put him," commented Senator Pope (D., Idaho), a committee member. "He has been one of our best men on financial problems, but I think he also would make an excellent ambassador if the President wants him in London."

LONDON, Dec. 20 (P) — Fog and ice disrupted traffic in the British Isles today and a channel gale caused the liner Queen Mary to skip a call at Plymouth. The ship, due to land with 300 passengers and 2,300 bags of Christmas mail, proceeded directly to Cherbourg and Southampton. Visibility was reduced to a few yards in London and central England areas, grounding early morning planes and delaying trains and motorists.

LONDON, England, Dec. 2 (UP)—Japan fully accepts in principle her liability to make full compensation for casualties of British soldiers and sailors in China, Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden told the House of Commons today.

LONDON. (U.P) -- Great Britain, the United States and France have made representations to Japan suggesting creation of a safety zone at Hankow, present seat of the Chinese government and foreign embassy staffs, it was learned today.

1937-05-14.text: FLIERS RETURN OVER OCEAN BOSTON, May 14—()—Swooping to the ground momentarily in order to get their bearings after successfully completing a flight from London, Dick Merrill and Jack Lambie today landed at the naval air base at Squantum, near Boston, and almost immediately took off again for New York. They expected to reach Floyd Bennett Field, New York, in about an hour. The Squantum air base, Merrill said, was the first land they had seen since 7 a. m. (Central Standard Time), when they were over Newfoundland.

LONDON, May 14 (AP)—Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin warned the opening session of Britain's imperial conference today, “the international situation is difficult and even threatening.” He was elected by the statesmen-delegates to preside over their deliberations to evolve a coordinated stand on such vital empire questions as defense and communication, foreign policy, trade and migration. “The responsibility rests upon us,” said Baldwin, “to see that our deliberations not only are of service to ourselves but also may help in some measure toward solution of those international problems which are perplexing the world. Armament Race “It will be our task to examine causes of the present national unrest, to exchange views upon them and to consider whether there is any contribution which we, cooperating together, could make to their diminution or removal.”

LONDON. (UP) The future ranking of Wallis Warfield as duchess of Windsor apparently has been definitely fixed, informed persons disclosed, by changing the duke's Order of the Garter banner to a position behind that of his three younger brothers. That would make the future duchess of Windsor eighth lady of the realm. She would rank below Queen Elizabeth; the queen mother, Mary; Princess Elizabeth, the heiress presumptive; Princess Margaret Rose, the king's second child; the princess royal, sister of the king, the duchess of Gloucester, wife of the third Windsor. | QUINCY, Mass, May 14 (UP)— Henry T. (Dick) Merrill landed his monoplane at the Squantum Naval Reserve air base at 2:40 p.m. (RDT) today. Merrill, accompanied by his co-pilot, John S. Lambie, brought back pictures of the coronation from England for American newspapers. He and Lambie flew to England last week in 21 hours and 30 minutes. At 2:40 p.m. the flyers had been in the air 22 hours and 27 minutes, beating the time of the only other flight of comparable distance from England to the United States, that of Captain James A. Mollison and his wife, Amy, in 1933 by 16 hours and 24 minutes.

New York —(WUP)— Henry T. "Dick" Merrill, the only person who ever made two round trip flights across the Atlantic, set his Lockheed-Electra monoplane down on Floyd Bennett field today after a 190-mile hop from Quincy, Mass., where he had landed after a flight from Southport, England, because of fog. He landed at 2:36 p.m. (CST). The total elapsed time since the takeoff from England was computed unofficially at 24 hours and 23 minutes, making it the fastest westward flight ever made despite the time lost at Quincy and in groping through the fog. At 12:40 p.m., when Merrill and John S. Lambie, his copilot, landed at Quincy, they had been in the air 22 hours and 27 minutes. Their time there was 16 hours and 24 minutes better than that of the only other England-to-America flight of comparable distance—made by Capt. James A. Mollison and his wife, Amy, in 1933. Former King Edward's demand that Wallis Warfield become “her royal highness” when she marries him was said to have caused a dispute with the government that may endanger his hope of returning some day to England. The government was willing that Mrs. Warfield be known as the duchess of Windsor. But it drew the line at the three little words which would rank her with the duchess of Kent and the duchess of Gloucester, wives of Edward's and King George's younger brothers. There were reports also that some members of the royal family opposed the designation. Edward was said to be insistent on coupling the title of “her royal highness, the duchess of Windsor.” A source close to the government revealed the cause of the struggle while the empire sought to forget the previous crisis of Edward's abdication in adulation of the newly crowned George and his Scottish Queen Elizabeth. Boston, May 14.—Findings a “hole” in the clouds after spanning the Atlantic on the return flight from London, Dick Merrill and Jack Lambie today brought their plane down at the naval air base at Squantum, near Boston. Merrill kept his motors warm after landing and prepared for an almost immediate take-off with Floyd Bennett field, New York, his final destination. Naval officers at the base timed the pilot at 2:40 p. m. daylight time on his landing. Merrill and Lambie cruised about for some time before landing, seeking a rift in the “low ceiling” that would enable them to make a safe landing. The break in the flight near Boston was unexpected, however, as reports had been received from him shortly before indicating he was nearing New York. In fact, a throng awaited at Floyd Bennett field in expectation of a momentary appearance of the man who has twice completed round trip flights across

London, May 14.—Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin opened an imperial conference—a veritable British League of Nations—today on the keynote of a national defense program which would free the mother country from the menace of attack. Nearing the end of a long political career, speaking not with the fiery eloquence of a dictator but the quiet firmness of a man addressing friends, Baldwin faced delegates representing countries peopled by 425,000,000 British subjects and at the outset of his opening speech showed what was uppermost in British minds. He referred to ‘“the ruinous race of armament”’ and continued: “With so many of the most powerful nations of the world expanding their armed forces, we in this country have decided that it is our duty to put our own defenses in order at a cost the magnitude of which you know. (That is, $7,500,000,000). “We deplore the necessity but we have no choice.

1937-12-15.text: LONDON, Dec. 15.—(AP)—Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden informed Commons today that Great Britain is seeking definite action by Japan to guard against recurrence of attacks on British shipping. He said the Japanese government realizes the recurrence of such incidents in the Far East must impair relations between the two countries. The note being dispatched today would define the British government’s attitude “toward the whole series of incidents, emphasizing the seriousness of the situation thus created and requirements which, in their judgment, flow from it,” Eden said. SHANGHAI. (Wednesday). American and British gunboats steamed down the Yangtze Wednesday and reported by wireless that all foreign survivors of the Panay bombing were safe on board and were being brought to Shanghai. Four newspapermen on the ships sent messages saying the entire band was suffering from shock and exposure and in addition a number of survivors suffered from wounds. "It was a miracle any escaped" both the bombing and the Chinese-Japanese fighting near Hohsien, where the refugees landed, the message said. The gunboats reported no additional casualties. One of the four slain foreigners was unidentified but believed to be a Panay seaman. Seventeen were listed as wounded. HONG KONG, Dec. 15 @P— Japanese war planes bombed Shumehun, the border of British leased territory, at 3:10 p. m. today.

LONDON, Dec. 15, — Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden, emphasizing the seriousness of the situation in the Orient, informed the House of Commons today that the British Government had sent a note to Japan, defining the British Government's attitude towards the whole series of incidents affecting British lives and property in China. The note to which Eden referred was approved by a full cabinet meeting.

Informed sources said they expected it would be approved at a regular meeting of the cabinet tomorrow morning and dispatched immediately. Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain and Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden conferred tonight at 10 Downing Street. Political circles believed Britain would send a note similar to that sent by the United States over the bombardment Sunday of the gunboat Panay and three Standard Oil vessels. 1937-06-25.text: London, June 25 (A) - Great Britain and France have decided to use their own warships to fill the gap in the “hands off Spain” sea patrol which was created by Italo-German withdrawal, it was learned tonight. This decision became known after a bitter full dress debate in the House of Commons in which Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain and Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden insisted Britain would push the principle of non-intervention in Spain through a 27-power European agreement. They asked Britain to “keep cool,” over the protests of liberals like David Lloyd George, who cried that Italy and Germany had made the non-intervention idea a “farce” and suggested it might be a good idea to scrap it. Eden took occasion to say that Soviet Russia, too, had sent “very large” quantities of arms to help government Spain. Germany and Italy are on the insurgent side.
