German and Italian warships patrolled the coasts of Spain on their own initiative today, their commanders acting in apparent concert. Italian vessels were under orders to strike back immediately at any "attack" from the Spanish government. The German battle fleet, about to be reinforced by the pocket battleship Graf Spee, was told to "protect German interests." "Uneasy fear still pervaded Britain that the joint Italian-German withdrawal from the non-intervention patrol intended to isolate the Spanish war was the forerunner of an attack against government Spain as "punishment" for an alleged attempt to torpedo the German cruiser Leipzig. The German cruiser Koln arrived unexpectedly at Gibraltar, but the whereabouts of the rest of the German fleet went unreported. Reports from Tangier, Morocco, said Italian and German warships had sailed from there. From Paris, meantime, came word that Fra

LONDON, June 25.—(UP)—The government informed the House of Commons today that there is grave danger of war in Europe, but that with patience and caution, Britain may avert it. Dramatic Speech Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain made a dramatic speech that to the startled members of Commons struck a parallel to the historic speech of Sir Edward Grey late in July of 1914, on the eve of the World War when he warned of the danger ahead. The most notable portion of his speech, perhaps, as regards events of the moment, was his dismissal of the alleged Loyalist submarine attack on the German cruiser Leipzig with the statement that there was a possibility that the Leipzig's officers were mistaken in their assertion that torpedoes were fired on the ship. Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden, joining in the debate, said: "There rests on the government the appalling responsibility to take no step to provo

LONDON, (P)—Great Britain and France have warned Germany that any belligerent action against Loyalist Spain would be regarded with the greatest gravity, it was reported today. It was asserted that the warning covered any aggression against the Loyalist fleet or any blockade of the Loyalist coast. The warning was understood to have been sent through Sir Neville Henderson, Ambassador at Berlin. Authoritative sources said that Baron Constantin Von Neurath, German foreign minister, informed Henderson that Germany intended to confine its present action to withdrawal from neutrality patrol work, and hence the warning was unnecessary. Evidences increased of the tension as the result of Germany’s and Italy’s withdrawal from the International Neutrality control plan—a withdrawal, however, which left powerfully reinforced Fascist-Nazi fleets within striking distance of the Loyalist coast ready for

LONDON. (CP). The British government and especially its foreign secretary, Anthony Eden, worked vigorously to allay Europe’s latest war scare and to distract attention from a convergence of the powers’ warships toward the Spanish danger zone. While Germany sent more naval craft into the Mediterranean, France maneuvered fighting ships between Algeria and Sardinia and Italian warships patrolled Spanish coasts, the British admiralty directing the largest fleet of all, remained silent. It declined to disclose the dispositions of Britain’s naval strength around Spain, while its spokesmen discounted the reported massing of German and Italian fleets in the Mediterranean. Eden told the House of Commons reports of German naval movements “should be received with great reserve.” Nevertheless there remained much uneasiness over the possibility of independent action by Italy and Germany against the S

LONDON, June 25.—Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain, in his first speech on foreign affairs as head of the reorganized government, urged the country to calm today and said that though war was an ever-present danger, he believed it might be stopped. “The government's policy is to maintain the peace of Europe and confine the Spanish civil war to Spain,” he said at the outset of his speech, and in concluding he said earnestly. “In high mountains a sudden exclamation may start an avalanche. That is the position in which we find ourselves today. I believe that, although the snow may be perilously poised it has not yet begun to move. If we can exercise patience, caution and self-restraint we may yet be able to save the peace of Europe.” Members read into his words an admission that peace was gravely threatened and that it was up to Great Britain, with its new £7,590,000,000 rearmament program

By Associated Press Britain's prime minister, Neville Chamberlain, promised the House of Commons today he would do everything in his power to keep the Spanish civil war from bursting into a general conflict. He urged Great Britain to “keep cool.” He advocated renewed efforts to withdraw all foreign fighters from Spain and filling in of the gap in the neutrality patrol of Spanish shores that resulted from German and Italian withdrawal. Warships Take Stations While Chamberlain opened a Commons debate, German and Italian warships were strung along Britain's “empire life line” in the Mediterranean, near Spain's bloody shores. The sea power of Britain and France was well represented there, too. (?)—Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden stepped into a bitter Commons debate over the Spanish crisis Friday to declare that Soviet Russia, as well as Germany and Italy, had sent “very large” shipments of arms into Spain. Eden joined the present premier, Neville Chamberlain, in urging a “keep cool” attitude toward Italo-German withdrawal from the Spanish neutrality patrol. With Chamberlain he stressed that the outlook is “not hopeless”; that Italy and Germany still may stay with the 25 other nations who are pledged to keep their hands out of the Spanish civil war. Chamberlain promised the House of Commons Friday he would do everything in his power to keep the Spanish civil war from bursting into a general conflict. 1937-06-06.text: By The Associated Press LONDON—Further diplomatic wooing of Germany and Italy tonight was seen necessary before the two may be won back into the group of non-intervention-in-Spain nations. Both nations responded to the British proposal outlining a basis for their return to cooperation with the European "hands-off Spain" committee following their withdrawal Monday after warships of both were bombed by Spanish government warplanes. It was reported unofficially both Rome and Berlin balked at the British suggestion the commanders of the international patrol should consult before any reprisals be taken in event of a patrol vessel being attacked. British officials reserved comment but it was understood strong hopes were held here Hitler and Premier Mussolini would fall into line after further negotiations. France’s reply also is being studied. Paris was understood to be concerned over what som

Great Britain's diplomats strove yesterday to salvage the international agreement for neutrality in the Spanish civil war, but prospects for immediate success appeared dim. Both Germany and Italy were reported to have balked at one point in the British proposal to bring them back into the nonintervention committee after their withdrawal last Monday. It was understood they could not see eye to eye with Britain’s foreign secretary, Anthony Eden, on a stipulation which would require consultation among commanders of international patrol vessels before reprisal could be taken in case a patrol ship were attacked. Some Agreement Points on which the two nations were said to agree with Britain called for establishment of zones of security for neutral warships in Spanish waters and reciprocal undertakings not to indulge in further provocation.

ROME, June 5.—Italy was understood tonight to have balked at one of the three points in the Brivisi proposal to draw Italy and Germany back into cooperation with the European "hands-off-Spain" committee. Informed sources said the Italian comment on the British plan was received by Sir Eric Drummond, British ambassador to Rome, from Count Galeazzo Ciano, Italy’s foreign minister. Agrees To First Two Points It was understood Count Ciano expressed agreement on the first two points of the proposal—dealing with the establishment of extended zones of security for warships at the international patrol around Spain and reciprocal undertakings not to indulge in further provocation. Informed sources said the foreign minister expressed reserve, however, on the third point which would require consultations among the commanders of the international patrol naval forces before any reprisals be undertake

ARLINGTON, Eng. June 5. (U.P)—Dresses were torn from screaming girls who fought today for admittance to St. Paul's Church where the Rev. Robert Anderson Jardine, the “poor man’s parson” who married the Duke and Duchess of Windsor, performed the same service for a young Yorkshire couple. Police reserves were called to restore order while the round-shouldered vicar, who defied the Church of England hierarchy to give the Duke of Windsor “a Christian marriage,” pleaded with the crowd to be calm. Five hundred managed to get inside the church—its largest congregation in years—before police closed the doors. Hundreds stood outside. The street was blocked. Those unable to enter the church sought vantage points in shop windows and on the tops of automobiles. The bridal couple—Georgia Gamble, a coach painter, and Doris Haylett, slim and pretty—were nervous and embarrassed.

TOKYO, June 5— (AP) — Thousands of Japanese children, many weeping bitterly, took part today in solemn Buddhist funeral ceremonies for the “departed spirits” of some 12,000 dolls which have “died” in the past year. While the children stood in front of long tables on which the shattered remains of their dolls lay, Buddhist abbots and priests chanted sutras and burned incense and a chorus of small girls sang the “Song of the Dolls” as a requiem. The scene was the children’s doll hospital. The sincerely mourned departed were dolls the hospital had found beyond repair and which therefore were considered to have “died.” The service is an annual affair based on the Buddhist belief that even inanimate things contain “seeds of life” and are capable of attaining perfect Buddhahood.

: BERLIN, June 5. (UP)—Col. Gen. Hermann W. Goering, who is Adolf Hitler's right-hand man, told a Nazi audience tonight that whenever Germany's sovereignty is insulted “then the blood must flow.” Goering, addressing a mass meeting in the Thietrich Fekart open air theater, referred to the bombing of the Nazi “pocket battleship” Deutschland by loyalist airplanes at Iviza a week ago and Germany's reprisal—the destruction of Almeria, Spain, by four German warships. “If anyone thought that Germany could be insulted with impunity the latest events have shown that we are again masters,” Goering, who is commander in chief of the German air force, asserted. “When blood has been spilled it cannot be corrected with but only with blood. Then, the blood must flow.” Goering’s was in celebration of the anniversary of the founding of the reich air defense league. He revealed, during his address that Ger

MOSCOW, June 5—(AP)—The Soviet government's recently intensified drive to rid the country of persons it believes to be foreign spies or wreckers was disclosed today to have turned against Japanese and German consulates. Diplomatic sources said the foreign commissariat had "suggested" the closing of several of the seven Japanese and seven German consular offices in the Soviet Union but that both countries had resisted such action. Pravda, organ of the communist party, sounded the keynote of the anti-spy campaign with this editorial blast: "The detection and destruction of all Japanese and German spies has become the important business of the day." The government's campaign of expulsion against foreigners it considers enemies of the regime continued with vigor. During May hundreds of aliens, including some Americans, were compelled to leave. Authorities have indicated July 1 has been set a

Youngstown, Ohio, June 5.—Republic Steel Corp. fought in two courts today to free its plants from the grip of strikers, and the steel workers organizing committee countered with an avowal "pickets will no longer permit their lines to be broken, cost what it may." "Sinister and bloody things are in the offing in Youngstown," declared the SWOC's Chairman Philip Murray as Republic obtained a court order directing pickets to permit access to its Warren and Niles plant plans and to give up "clubs... and other weapons." In Chicago, scene of the strike fighting fatal to seven men last Sunday, Mayor Edward J. Kelly directed Republic to remove by Monday night the men encamped in its plant there. He said building and health regulations were being violated. Republic Corporation offices in Cleveland sent another telegram to Washington post office office over the name of Board Chairman Tom Girdler de

1937-10-15.text: London, Oct. 15—Britain and France, determined to make no more major concessions to Italy, planned procedure today for a show-down with Premier Mussolini on the question of withdrawing his armies from Spain. The climax of 15 months of effort to confine the civil war to Spain will come when the nine nations sub-committee of the London non-intervention committee meets tomorrow in an attempt to agree on a plan to remove thousands of foreigners fighting in Spain. France’s patience with Mussolini's delaying tactics was plainly at an end. The British were among reserved but the London-Paris allies stood agreed to speedy counter measures to restore “the balance in Spain” if the sub-committee deliberations proved fruitless. The fact that the British and French general staffs were discussing steps to be taken in case the diplomatic talks fail showed the seriousness with which Paris and London vie

Jerusalem, Oct. 15—(#)—Guerilla bands of Arabs struck new terror in the Holy Land today and two young British policemen fell in a pre-dawn ambush on the Bethlehem road. Constables Norman Harrison and Austin Malia were added to the list of dead which already included four Arabs. Twelve Jews were injured in the last two days. Authorities were expected to declare a nightly curfew and possibly proclaim martial law unless British military moves brought order. The old quarters of Jerusalem were blanketed with military detachments. All civilians were being searched for weapons. The two constables were shot to death in a spectacular skirmish with a large band of armed Arabs near Bethlehem. Before dawn authorities learned of the concentration of an armed gang on the main road to Bethlehem near Colomon’s pool and rushed four carloads of police to the scene.

Terrorism in the Holy Land, reaching an acute stage with the ambush slaying of two British constables, centered diplomatic attention on another of the world’s trouble spots today. Unrest In Palestine As the British government was concentrating on prevention of the Spanish civil war spreading to a European conflagration, the latest Arab unrest came from the mandated Palestine territory. The 27-power non-intervention sub-committee meets at London tomorrow to try again to agree on a plan for withdrawal of foreigners in Spain. For Settlement Orient reports from sections where Japanese and Chinese soldiers are fighting fiercely in Shanghai and along a wide front in North China, gave no hope of any immediate settlement. The fall of Gijon, last government-held seaport in northwest Spain is believed imminent. Vatican Denies VATICAN CITY. (4)—Assertions of private Vatican sources that instruction

LONDON, (#). French foreign office officials said Thursday night France is considering joint direct action with Great Britain if a non-intervention subcommittee fails to obtain withdrawal of Italian volunteers from Spanish insurgent armies. France stood ready to protect her Mediterranean trade routes after agreeing to go along with Britain in giving the nine power subcommittee a quick chance to obtain withdrawal of the troops. The committee is to meet here Saturday morning. French sources were pessimistic on the outcome of the meeting where the Spanish question is to be discussed on il duce’s chosen ground. British spokesmen were only moderately hopeful. Official sources in Paris said France and Britain agreed to demand immediate “symbolic” withdrawal of some foreign troops from Spain as the price for their return to the nonintervention committee table. They asserted the two powers will

SHANGHAI, Oct. 15—(UP)— Chinese reports from Canton said today that 18 British warships, including an aircraft carrier and a submarine, were concentrated off Hong Kong. The Chinese Central News Agency also reported from Canton that ten Japanese planes bombed Tsengchen, 30 miles east of Canton, killing or wounding more than 200 civilians. The planes also bombed Taishan, 70 miles southwest of Canton, inflicting more than 30 casualties. The Agency said the planes destroyed more than 200 yards of the Canton-Kowloon railroad, in which there are heavy British investments. By JOHN R. MORRIS SHANGHAI, Oct. 15—(UP)— The battle of Shanghai, which entered a temporary lull today after yesterday's furious Chinese offensive, has caused damage estimated by foreign sources today of approximately one billion dollars. This was approximately double the damage of the 1932 siege and in addition 80 percent of

7 PARIS, Oct. 15.—France and Italy may make mutual concessions of importance in an effort to prevent a final break over the problem of foreign volunteers in the Spanish civil war, it was reported today. A situation that seemed almost hopeless and led France and Great Britain to consider the advisability of a peaceful, symbolic occupation of the fortified island of Minorca in the Balearics group was brightened by the following reports: 1—That France, as a final concession to Premier Benito Mussolini, might agree to recognize the Spanish nationalists as belligerents coincident with the actual start of withdrawal of volunteers from Spain. 2—That Mussolini himself had decided, on his own initiative, to withdraw 5000 of his troops from Spain soon. The second report was accompanied by the assertion that as the result of any Italian withdrawal of men, for whatever reason, the powers might be ex

DUISBURG, Germany, Oct. 15. The Duke of Windsor spent 90 minutes today crawling around in the coal pits of the Friedrich Heinrich mine on his survey of labor conditions under the Nazi regime. Some 5,000 German miners cheered as the former British monarch, wearing regulation miners’ overalls, went down into the pits. The Duchess of Windsor remained at Essen. “I hope you photographers won't shoot me before I have had a chance to clean up. I’ve never been so black in my life.” Officials said Windsor walked and crawled over two miles underground. No visitor, they said, had ever asked so many questions indicating such an expert knowledge of the mining industry as the Duke.

JERUSALEM, Oct. 15.—Twenty-four hours of bloodshed, the outgrowth of Great Britain’s Palestine partition proposal, were climaxed tonight with the enforcement of drastic curfew regulations. After a day of violent disorder including ambushing, a train derailment and a bus bombing in which at least seven persons were killed including two British constables and more than a score were wounded, authorities decreed the curfew.

1937-04-24.text: BILBAO, Spain, (4?)—The Basque government rushed food to its hungry defenders today with mounting hope that the supplies brought by British blockade runners would avert capitulation to Gen. Emilio Mola's fierce insurgent offensive. While the mountainous Durango front, about 20 miles southeast of the capital, echoed machine gun, rifle and artillery fire, 400,000 inhabitants of Bilbao were jubilant, feeling the starvation hold of the insurgents by land and sea had been broken. The first supplies brought to the refugee-swollen capital yesterday went to hospitals and to troops fighting desperately to hold the El Orrio line, less than six miles from Durango. The blockade runners came just in time. Bread was completely lacking on the eve of their arrival. Civil Rule Restored MADRID, (4%) —Civil rule was restored to Madrid today after nine months of martial law in the besieged city. Gen. Jose M

BRUSSELS, April 24—Belgium was released today from her promise to fight for France or Great Britain if either were the victim of aggression. Two documents, releasing the Nation from her mutual assistance obligations under the nullified Locarno Treaty, were signed at the Foreign Office by Paul Spaak, the Belgian Foreign Minister, and the British and French ambassadors, Sir Robert Clive and Jules Laroque. Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden of Great Britain was scheduled to arrive from London by plane tomorrow for further discussion of Belgium's status in the changing Romanan waters.

Lendon, April 23. — Suppression of a book that charged, in one passage, that Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin was disturbed by "muddling and meddling" in his relations with the then King Edward was demanded today by the Duke of Windsor's attorney. The book is "Coronation Commentary." Chapters recounting the reign and abdication of Edward drew from his attorney, A. G. Allen, the assertion that "action will certainly follow unless the publication is withdrawn." "Coronation Commentary" refers to reports that Baldwin had grievances against the king in addition to the king's love for Wallis Warfield Simpson. The book said they included: "Things said and done in his infatuation; his lover's prodigality; the shrill king's rage against those who denied her to him; things left undone in his infatuation: duty neglected; papers held up; papers curiously and Neo-Kaliserishly annotated; no sound unders

LONDON. (AP) Great Britain joined the lengthening list of European nations who would like a world conference to adjust economic barriers to trade—if somebody else would take the first step. The government indicated, too, its hope to discuss World War debts with the United States, but debate in the House of Commons produced only a reiteration of the familiar British stand—willingness to pay when the time is ripe. Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin told Commons the government was ready to enter a world "mutual understanding" conference such as Adolf Hitler suggested this week that President Roosevelt might call. Britain would enter, however, only if prior investigation showed the conference was likely to succeed and only if there were sufficient advance preparation. Baldwin thus placed Britain alongside France, Italy, Austria, Russia, Belgium, Germany and the Scandinavian countries, all of whi

LONDON, Saturday, April 24.—(U.P) A representative of the Duke of Windsor's solicitors, Allen and Overy, said today that libel writs will be issued against William Heinemann, Ltd., Monday morning unless the publisher withdraws the book "Coronation Commentary" from the market. The Heinemann company also must publish an apology because of the book's discussion of intimate details of Edward's life and for its criticism of him, the representative said. Angered by the attacks on his life and friends, Edward asked his solicitors to take action. The book contained such passages as this: "He left his land with kingly dignity and repaired to the more welcome company of rich American Jewesses.... He was a tragic, broken man, but off to the sun and white snow (he went) with full trunks and full pockets... . Until his marriage (to Mrs. Wallis Simpson) was mounted they had no notion how to get rid of

GIBRALTAR, April 24.—The rebel warship Canovas del Castillo today ordered the British freighter Seven Seas Sound to halt in the straits but the freighter ignored the warning and proceeded at full speed to Gibraltar. The Spanish rebel warship followed the British cargo boat into the harbor here. It turned back and steamed out to sea again when the British port launch appeared. The freighter Seven Seas Sound is a sister ship of the Seven Seas Spray, the British ship which earlier in the week ran the rebel blockade and was the first to carry food to the famished inhabitants at Bilbao, loyalist port in northern Spain.

MADRID, April 28—(U?)—Shrapnel from insurgent shells splattered death and injury in downtown Madrid for the twelfth successive day of bombardment today, causing at least a dozen casualties. One man was killed on Gran Via, the capital’s “Broadway,” and four persons were carried away in commandeered passenger automobiles and an ambulance to emergency hospitals. More than 250 persons have been killed and hundreds injured in the attacks. As on previous days, many of the shells ploughed into the Gran Via area, Subway station stairways and basements quickly filled with refugees.

SPF 4880 SSO OM 2 AO Berlin, Apr. 24.—Helmuth Hirsch, young German son of a naturalized American, told United States consular authorities in Poletzensee prison today he had no hope of escaping the headman’s ax for an alleged act which might have involved an attempt on the life of Adolf Hitler. Hirsch has been sentenced to die. The United States government interested itself in his case yesterday, when it became established he held American citizenship through the naturalization of his father. The state's attorney who prosecuted the case, Dr. Volk, declined to divulge the exact nature of the alleged offense except to state that Hirsch had violated the explosives act. (Trials on such treasonable charges are conducted secretly). In informed circles, however, it was an open secret that Hirsch was accused of intending to use explosives for an attempt on “a very high government official”—presum

1937-05-25.text: (By Richard D. McMillan, United Press Staff Correspondent) Monts, France — (WP) — King George VI telephoned his elder brother, the Duke of Windsor, today and informed him regretfully that he is compelled to ban the attendance of British official guests at the wedding of the duke to Mrs. Wallis Warfield. The duke, who gave up the throne for the American woman he loves, succeeded in hiding his anger at what was described by his friends as “the final blow of Edward's enemies.” Members of the household staff gave assurance that King George, forced into his position by governmental and other pressure in Britain, did his best to console his brother. The day toward which the ex-king has looked forward to with so much happiness will be marred by the absence of some of the closest friends of his youth and manhood. The music room where the ceremony will be performed, regarded hitherto as too small

London, May 25—(AP)—Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh, trapped in the tangle of coronation day traffic, barely arrived at a London hospital before her third son was born May 1, it was disclosed today. The Lindberghs, hurrying from their Kent home to the fashionable maternity hospital, were forced to make a wide detour because most of central London was closed for the royal procession. The birth of a son to the flier and the former Anne Morrow was made known only yesterday to United States embassy officials. After announcing the birth, Col. Lindbergh retreated into silence, determined to ensure the privacy of his wife and 13-day-old son. The mother and baby now are convalescing, apparently incognito, (continued on page eight)

LONDON, May 25. UP—A new perambulator arrived at the residence of Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh at Weald, Kent, today, awaiting the arrival of the baby boy born to Mrs. Lindbergh last week. It was reported at Weald that Col. and Mrs. Lindbergh would return to their home, Long Barn, soon. The Daily Express reported that Mrs. Lindbergh was at the London Clinic, in the Devonshire Place medical district here, with her seven pound boy. Lindbergh was reported to have visited the clinic daily since the baby was born, sometimes with his son, Jon, now nearly five years old.

LONDON, May 25 —(®)— Col. Charles A. Lindbergh established a protective veil of silence today about his wife and their new-born son, whose birth on the night of May 12 was disclosed only yesterday by the famous flier to American embassy officials. After his disclosure, Lindbergh retreated into hiding from even his closest friends who wished to extend congratulations. Frequent visits of Lindbergh to a fashionable Mayfair nursing home within the last few weeks stood as the only clue to the whereabouts of Mrs. Lindbergh and their third son. It was generally understood that the former Anne Morrow had given birth to the boy there and one report said she had been entered under the name of “Mrs. Charles” at the fashionable London clinic at Devonshire Place. Sources close to the family said today it was likely the child would be the namesake of his maternal grandfather, the late Dwight W. Morrow

Bayonne, France, May 25.—(AP)—Spanish Insurgent Generalissimo Francisco Franco today broadcast a rejection of Great Britain’s plea for an armistice in the civil war and withdrawal of foreign volunteers from Spain, In a note broadcast from insurgent headquarters at Salamanca, Franco instead demanded “unconditional surrender or war without quarter.”

NORTH STONEHAM, Eng. (UP). Four thousand Spanish child refugees from Bilbao began a new life in a tented city here, safe in England until the civil war shall end and they again may return to their homeland. They were brought to Southampton by the Spanish government liner Habana Sunday night and transferred to the tent community here Monday. Some were tearful and homesick. All were terrified for a time by maneuvers of British airplanes which they thought were Spanish insurgent planes, the same that had bombed their Basqueland homes and caused their transfer to this haven here. Nurses, teachers, interpreters, and cooks worked through the morning to calm them. Finally, all were bathed and clothed, despite kicks and screaming, bewildered protests. The last two arrivals were 10-year-old Dolores Vasques and her 12-year-old brother, Heranz. They were found hiding in a lifeboat on the Habana. Cr

New York, May 25, (P)—The Pan American Airways flying boat Bermuda Clipper left Port Washington, Long Island, today for Bermuda for the first of a series of survey flights before establishment of a regular passenger service. About the same time a British Imperial Airways boat, the Cavalier, took off from Hamilton Harbor, Bermuda, for Port Washington on a similar survey flight. The air distance is 783 miles and the ships, which have a cruising speed of 160 miles an hour, are expected to reach their destinations in something over five hours. Passenger service probably will start next month.

London, Eng. (INS) —Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh are considering the name “Dwight” for their seven pound son, born on May 13. This was the name of Mrs. Lindbergh's father, the late U. S. Senator, Dwight Morrow. No definite decision has yet been reached, however. Col. and Mrs. Lindbergh still have more than a month before they have to register the name. The infant is reported to be particularly healthy with no post natal complications.

1937-02-18.text: YOKOSUKA, Japan, Feb. 18, (P). —Vice Admiral Yashutaro Iwashita, chief of staff of the combined Japanese fleet and a delegate to the London Naval Conference, died of jaundice today. He was 61 years old.

LONDON, Feb. 11—Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, appealed to commons today to approve Great Britain's $7,500,000,000 defense program as a bulwark for the world’s peace. Chamberlain, opening a two-day parliamentary debate on the formidable five-year armaments program entailing unprecedented peacetime expenditures, was believed to be virtually assured of a favorable vote. To Restrict Objections Opposition spokesmen, authoritative sources predicted, would restrict their objections to mere formalities because of near-unanimity on the necessity of rebuilding the empire’s defenses quickly to avert potential menaces to European peace. Britain's little man, the average citizen who pays the nation’s taxes, will be hard hit in any event by the $7,500,000,000 armaments bill. Just how hard hit, however, he will not know until the revenue program in Chamberlain's budget is announced

WASHINGTON (INS) — Great Britain’s decision to expend $7,500,000,000 on its war machine during the next five years today appeared likely to involve the United States and other major powers in a naval armaments race. “This country is committed to the principle of having a navy ‘second to none,’” said Admiral William D. Leahy, chief of naval operations. “It is fair to presume that if any other naval power expands its navy considerably this government will find it necessary to expand accordingly.” His expression followed announcement in London that the British navy, under the vast rearmament program, will be increased in 1937 by three 35,000 ton battleships, seven cruisers and two aircraft carriers. Britain already has laid keels for two battleships which will be matched by the United States with two 35,000 ton capital ships to cost $50,000,000 each. The keels will be laid this summer. The

Washington, Feb. 18—()—The navy high command studied British building plans today to determine if three new battleships would be required to keep the United States navy second to none. "It is a fair presumption," said navy’s ranking officer, Admiral William D. Leahy, "that if any other power expands its fleet, the United States may find it necessary to do likewise." Britain's rearmament program announced yesterday included three new battleships. If they are intended only as replacements for outworn vessels, officers said, the United States might hold its own without additional new construction. "It must be noted," said Leahy, "that the British thus far have actually done no more than we have or plan to do in battleship construction." The keels of two new battleships were laid in England a few weeks ago. The American navy plans to begin construction of two battleships on July 1. The prese

VIENNA, Feb. 18.—(INS)—With the Duke of Windsor reported by informed quarters to be pressing for a financial settlement, Walter Monckton, his attorney, arrived here from London today. Three other representatives of the Royal family and British Government are expected tomorrow when the former king's rumored need for money will be straightened out. The duke will confer with Monckton today at the British Legation here.

(By the Associated Press) Goderich, Ont., Feb. 18—In the well-ordered farm household of Mr. and Mrs. James Masse, the birth of their 21st child caused scarcely a ripple today. Mrs. Masse is 43, her husband, 46. Having looked at their new sister, to be christened Martha, these children marched dutifully to school: Cecilia, 13, Louis, 12, Ivan, 11, Juliette and Antoninette, twins, 10, Archie, 9, Leo, 1. Marie, 20, Yvonne, 18, and Joan, 15, did their chores, which include baking 40 loaves of bread a week, churning 20 pounds of butter and even milking six cows daily. Alphonse, 17, did the outside chores on the 150-acre farm while Papa Masse worked on the highway. Toddling about the house were Michael, 5, Priscilla, 4, and Peter, 3, who were allowed into their mother’s room for a moment to see the baby and 15-month-old Monica. Maurice, 26, is the eldest of the 21 and lives away from home, as

Madrid, Feb. 18 (Thursday) —(/P)—Ten persons were killed and more than 70 wounded in the Vallecas district alone as insurgent air raiders bombed Madrid and its environs twice last night. (Vallecas is on the southeastern edge of the Spanish capital.) The second bombing came shortly after the first air raid on Madrid since Jan. 6, A dozen bombs were dropped. Pending a complete check-up, it was believed most of them had fallen on the outskirts. Red Offensive The raid followed a day in which besieged defenders of the capital struck back at insurgent armies in two violent offensive waves, determined to hold communication arteries on the Jarama front, southeast of the city. The dual push signalized the closing hours of the seventh month of the Spanish civil war, They struck first in the southern Jarama sector. Three hours later another column began moving against La Maranosa, in the central Ja

MADRID, Feb. 18.—(U.R)—The Loyalist offensive in the Jarama river sector south of Madrid, which has been under way since dawn yesterday, was reported today in official dispatches as "steadily advancing" in the regions of La Maranosa and San Martín De La Vega. Insurgent threats against a detour road near Perales were removed when enemy troops had to be withdrawn to defend their positions at La Maranosa, Loyalists said. The insurgent losses in yesterday's fighting were placed at 800 in government reports. Important Loyalist gains were reported in the Usera Carabanchel sector, just outside Madrid on the south, as the battle progressed. Meanwhile, an enemy attack on Queen's Hill, further south, was repulsed, dispatches said.

1937-02-06.text: London, Feb. 6—(P)— The Duke of Windsor’s sister, the Princess Royal Mary, received last minute advice before her departure today for Enzesfeld on a secret mission to help the abdicated monarch solve his financial problems. Princess Mary, accompanied by her husband, the Earl of Harewood, also was believed to have been entrusted by the government with the delicate mission of putting the duke’s exile on a more stable and even quieter basis. Edward was described in authoritative reports from Enzesfeld as anxious to complete the financial settlement—either from the national treasury or the royal income—as he plans to wed Mrs. Wallis Simpson April 27, the day it is now expected her divorce will become final. Government officials, it was said, were anxious to wind up the final phases of the abdication so not even a hint of “the king across the waters” would be raised during the coronation cele

Fighting today to keep Cordoba; socialist government troops fought to keep Malaga; non-interventionists in London sought to keep out of Spain. Russian insistence - supported by France - that the Soviets be permitted to participate in an International patrol of the warring Siberian peninsula, threatened somewhat a fresh start next Tuesday on non-intervention negotiations. A Spanish socialist minister agreed conditionally to the neutrality plan. The negotiations want to set a deadline for the influx of foreign volunteers and complete a scheme for naval supervision of other Spanish imports. Meanwhile: Screened by cavalry and rumbling tanks signalled overhead by ground strafing planes, the Spanish socialist government's troops tried to snatch the rich, inland provincial capital, of Cordoba from their fascist foes while the insurgents laid siege to the government Mediterranean stronghold: Mal

Rome, Feb. 6.—(4)—Vittorio Mussolini, eldest son of Il Duce, and his boyhood sweetheart, Orsola Buvoli, were married today in the Mussolini parish church. Premier Mussolini and his wife, members of the Mussolini and Buvoli families and a few friends, several hundred in all, attended the wedding in St. Joseph’s church. The couple will spend their honeymoon in Italy and then go to the United States, where Vittorio, with ambitions to become an Italian motion picture producer, will study the film industry.

MOSCOW, Feb. 6. (P) — The greatest party purge since 1927 — when the names of Leon Trotsky and hundreds of his followers were scratched off the Communist roster — now is in full swing, reports from throughout Russia indicated today. Hundreds of influential citizens already have been arrested and charged with participating in the so-called “Trotskyist wrecking conspiracy,” these advices showed. Soviet industrial workers have demanded quick prosecution and the death sentence for Alexander Georgivich Belaborodoff, alleged Trotskyist sabotage agent and one of the former Urals Soviet officials held responsible for the summary executions of Czar Nicholas and his family in 1928. Belaborodoff, former president of the Orenburg Soviet, and dozens of other alleged Trotskyist leaders were arrested several weeks ago at Rostov-on-the-Don. Workers in the Rosa Luxembourg tobacco factory charged the pris

ROME.—Lieut. Vittorio Mussolini, 21-year-old aviator and son of Premier Benito Mussolini, married Miss Orsala Buyeu, 23, blonde and pretty, at the small modern parish church of St. Joseph adjoining the premier’s villa today. They planned to leave after a wedding luncheon for the north to spend their honeymoon in the lake region and at Venice, then return to live with the premier at his Villa Colonia. Vittorio had hoped to go to the United States to study the motion picture business, but this plan seemed doomed. Premier Mussolini, with Vittorio and the younger son, Bruno, arrived at the church at 11:05 a.m. (5:05 a.m. EST) and the wedding ceremony was started five minutes later. For more than an hour before the ceremony, thousands of picked black-shirted Fascist militiamen and hundreds of Balilla, the Junior Fascists, stood guard in the vicinity while thousands of spectators packed the st

BERLIN, Feb. 6—(/P)—President Roosevelt's move for United States judicial reform excited universal comment and bannerlines in the German press today. The comment was generally favorable to the plan and the American President was pictured as champion of vigorous leadership against “outworn” methods of government.

Seville, Feb. 6—Opening flood gates of immense mountainside reservoirs, loyalist forces today halted the rebel advances on the seaport of Malaga, with a wall of ice water. The deluge roared down on the narrow coastal plain northeast of Marbella, breaking the insurgents' march after they had swarmed through three villages.

MNOWS NOTHING Of Wedding. CANNES, France, (AP).—Hermaz Rogers, Mrs. Wallis Simpson’s Riviera host, said today he knew nothing about reports that April 2 had been set for her wedding to former King Edward VIII.

1937-12-06.text: ENGLEWOOD, N. J., Dec. 6.—Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh were back in their native land today after an absence of nearly two years. The purpose of their visit—it was presumed to be a visit because they had left their children in England—and its length were known only to themselves and they were not telling. Even their whereabouts had been left a matter for speculation by Lindbergh's strict regimen of secrecy, but there was a great deal of evidence to indicate that they were voluntary prisoners behind the high iron fence of the closely-guarded estate of Mrs. Lindbergh's mother, Mrs. Dwight W. Morrow. This was denied, however, by Mrs. Morrow’s secretary. The Lindberghs returned to the United States on the liner President Harding. Only a vice-president of the United States Lines knew when they engaged passage, the captain of the vessel did not know of his distinguished passenger unti

Commander of the British gunboat Ladybird and two other Britishers were wounded and several hundred Chinese killed or wounded today when Japanese airmen bombed the waterfront and shipping at Wuhu, Yangtze river port 60 miles south, southwest of here. Two British steamers, the Tuckwo and Tatung, were hit. The Tuckwo was set afire and was believed to be a total loss. The Tatung's captain and his wife, both British, were wounded and their steamer was beached. Captain Wounded Lieutenant Commander Harry Douglas Barlow of the Ladybird, although suffering from shrapnel wounds, maneuvered his vessel alongside a hulk—old ship moored offshore to assist landings—belonging to the British Butterfield and Swire Company and towed it away before it was set afire. The 3,770-ton Tuckwo, in flames, drifted against a hulk belonging to the Jardine, Matheson Company, which then also burned. (In Shanghai offic

NEW YORK, Dec. 6.—-(7)— The mighty steamship Leviathan was headed for the junkyards today to provide scrap iron for British armament after the United States Lines refused to sell her to Japanese interests. Basil Harris, a vice-president who announced sale of “Old Levi” to Metal Industries, Ltd., of London, for “more than $800,000,” said offers of Japanese interests which have outbid British and Italian firms in the world’s metal markets were rejected. “We did not consider it advisable at this time to consider an offer from Japan,” he said. “I don't think we could have obtained permission to let that ship go to Japan had we wanted to,” he added. The Leviathan, which carried 200,000 doughboys to France, will have one last fling of the glory it knew briefly before the World War. The 23-year-old liner, once speed queen of the Atlantic, will sail to England under her own power. A week will be

London, Dec. 6—England wondered today whether a British-Belgian royal romance was being unfolded. Unexpected, private visits to England of Belgium's King Leopold III, Queen-Mother Elizabeth and Prince Charles, the king’s bachelor brother, had most Englishmen puzzled and guessing. There were official denials of rumors that the Belgian king's visit to the duke of Portland's Welbeck Abbey estate indicated a romantic attachment for the duke’s 21-year-old granddaughter, Lady Anne Cavendish-Bentinck. Baron Capelle, the king's secretary, described the rumors as “childish fairy tales.” The baron explained that Queen Elizabeth had planned for some time to visit the duke and duchess of Portland, and that the king, “having several days free,” had decided to accompany her. The duke was a friend of the late King Albert of Belgium. He commented on Prince Charles’ unexpected arrival in London yesterday

By The Associated Press LONDON—One passenger and one member of the crew were killed yesterday when the Imperial Airways flying boat Cygnus, en route from India to London, crashed in the outer harbor of Brindisi, on the Southeastern Italian coast, with 13 persons aboard. The eleven rescued, including Air Marshal Sir John Sulman, a government director of Imperial Airways, all were injured. The dead were a steward named Stappani and a Captain MacDonald. The Cygnus, one of the latest type 20-ton Empire flying boats, had landed at Brindisi Saturday night. She crashed at 9 a.m. and sank in the outer harbor after taking off. The cause was not determined. Sir John, who was returning from a tour of Imperial Airways’ Far East services, received a cut on the shoulder. One of the passengers suffered a leg fracture. Other passengers and members of the crew were slightly injured. A sister ship of the

LONDON, Dec. 6—(UP)—The bombing of three British ships by Japanese planes at Wuhu, closely following other friction-producing incidents, brought Anglo-Japanese relations to a point of tenseness today unequaled since the start of the far eastern conflict. The bombings, marked by the wounding of a British naval commander, were expected to touch off a barrage of questions on developments in the far east in parliament. Although the government’s policy is to play for time until the rearmament program nears completion in April, the possibility of a more serious “provocative act” was not considered unlikely in view of developments of the last 48 hours. These included: 1. The bombing of three plainly marked British ships, including H. M. S. Ladybird and the wounding of Lieut. Comdr. H. D. Barlow at the Yangtze river port of Wuhu. 2. The threat that the British crown colony of Hongkong will be br
| LONDON. Dec. 6.—(U.2—London society circles heard rumors today that the Duke of Windsor is planning a brief visit home for Christmas when the whole royal family will be gathered at Sandringham

(By the Associated Press) Traffic accidents took a toll of eight lives in the state over Saturday and Sunday. Seven of the victims were Milwaukeeans. The dead: Mrs. Genevieve Wetterling, 38, of Milwaukee. Sam Brumac, 40, of Milwaukee. Edward Seelen, 50, of Milwaukee. Julius Hansen, 74, of Milwaukee. Joseph Karl, 65, of Milwaukee. Frank Balzer, 26, of Milwaukee. Monroe Goldman, 23, of Milwaukee. Frank Siegwarth, 40, of Wilson township, Sheboygan county. Skull Fracture Fatal Mrs. Wetterling, wife of Frank Wetterling, president of the sausage manufacturing concern which bears his name, died Sunday in a Janesville hospital of a skull fracture suffered Saturday night when the car driven by her husband skidded on the icy pavement between Whitewater and Richmond, struck a tree and turned over. Wetterling was uninjured. Brumac was killed instantly in an auto collision early Sunday on Highway 41

1937-08-25.text: Southampton, Eng., Aug. 25 (AP) — The Pan-American Clipper reached here from France today, completing her first experimental flight from the United States by way of the Azores and Lisbon, Portugal, the projected southerly air lane for commercial flying of the North Atlantic.
Nanking, Aug. 25—A British proposal for cessation of hostilities in the Shanghai area is acceptable to China in principle if Japan also accepts, it was announced unofficially today.

yy the DE EBMRAND (Copyright, 1937, By United Press) Shanghai, China, Aug. 25.—(U.P.)—Japan, determined to smash organized military resistance throughout all China, was officially announced tonight to have declared a blockade of more than 700 miles of the Chinese coast against Chinese shipping from Swatow in the south to the north bank of the Yangtze river, north of Shanghai. Simultaneously the Japanese prepared to bring their total strength in China up to 250,000 men equipped with all the most modern machines of war. Meantime, the great Nipponese military machine here roared into action on four major fronts along a line of more than 1,000 miles against Chinese armies estimated to total 750,000. An unprecedented battle was underway at Shanghai, Fighting in North China In north China two Japanese columns converged on five Chinese divisions trapped between the Nankow pass and Kalgan on the

HENDAYE Franco-Spanish Frontier, Aug. 24, (j)—An insurgent Navarrese brigade took the strategic city of Torrelavega tonight without firing a shot, thus severing the last westward route of escape from government held Santander on the northern Spanish coast. Capture of Torrelavega, situated near the coast some 20 miles southwest of Santander, gave the insurgents control of the important Santander-Oviedo highway and, in effect, dismembered the narrow strip of coastal territory the government has been trying to defend. Insurgent radio reports said tonight the Italian “Black Arrow” column occupied the port of Laredo, 95 miles east of Santander.

Berlin, Aug. 24.— (-P) —The Nazi party high command started a campaign against Rotary clubs in Germany today because the clubs are “not anti-Semitic." Walter Buch, chief justice of the party court, struck the first blow at the organizations in a statement circulated throughout the nation. Buch declared the “essential principles” of German Rotary clubs run counter to national socialism. ‘Rotary is not anti-Semitic, and it is ruled by an international organization conceived in America,” he explained. Jews, he said, have been “camouflaging” themselves behind the doors of the organization, which failed to climb on the Nazi bandwagon in 1933. After ordering all Nazi party members belonging to Rotary to resign from the business men’s organization by Dec. 31 or become liable for “penalties,” Buch called on German officials to force government employees and regular army officers to give up Rotar

(By Associated Press) With Insurgents Attacking Santander, Aug. 25—One hundred thousand insurgent soldiers held Santander in a trap today. The city’s defense forces, 50,000 or more Spanish government troops, were cut off from all retreat with their backs to the Bay of Biscay. Advance patrols of General Franco’s conquering legions were within five miles of the provincial capital. Five columns welded into a solid semi-circular ring moved toward the city from other directions ready for a final push through its gates. What little aviation facilities the defenders had on this front had gone and defense artillery started pulling out days ago. Madrid, Aug. 25—Insurgent batteries began bombarding Madrid again last night, firing several hundred shells into the center of this besieged and war-ravaged city. It was the first time in 18 days the old capital city had been shelled. The crash of artille

Shanghai iP (Thursday) — Unconfirmed reports early today said Japanese troops had entered and searched the Soviet consulate here. This consulate, adjacent to Japan’s own consulate, was closed last week when war engulfed the area.

SHANGHAI, Aug. 25.—Japanese troops, opening a general offensive, stormed in on Shanghai today along three roads north of the city and landed two new armies to the south. All day there was fierce hand to hand fighting on five fronts in the vicinity of the city and all reports indicated the Chinese were resisting stoutly. By midafternoon the horizon beyond the metropolitan area was ringed with flames from the villages where Japanese and Chinese troops were fighting. Chinese army headquarters asserted that headquarters eyewitnesses saw Chinese artillery sink two Japanese destroyers which were shelling the Chinese lines inland from Woosung, down the river. Japanese denied the assertion. Neutral sources were unable to confirm it. Foreign military and civil authorities reported the Chinese had begun a general retreat from the Yangtzepoo section at the east end of Shanghai and danger of a rush

1937-05-30.text: London, May 29—(4)—The British government’s action in denying Mrs. Wallis Warfield the courtesy title of “Her Royal Highness” stirred a controversy today similar to that of last December when the Duke of Windsor quit the throne for romance. While some rejoiced in a decision that meant they never would have to curtsey to the duke’s bride, others thought it was “shabby treatment” and looked to the new premier, Neville Chamberlain, to relax the “isolation” policy of his predecessor, Stanley Baldwin. Observers agreed that while King George promulgated the decree forbidding his brother’s future wife to use the title, apparently it was a result of one of the last acts of Baldwin who waged the battle that ended in Edward’s abdication. The announcement, as last night in the Gazette, The king has been pleased by letters patent under the great seal of the realm bearing the date May 27, 1937, to de

LONDON, May 29.—(U.P)—King George's decree according the Duke of Windsor the title “royal highness” has shoved both the duke and Mrs. Wallis Warfield, his wife-to-be, definitely out of British royal life, it was understood today. First the decree specifically excluded Mrs. Warfield and any children born of the union to the title. But more important, the view was taken in usually well informed quarters that actually both king and government in the decree meant to make it plain that the duke himself—now officially an “outsider”—was given the title only as a courtesy for services rendered. Authoritative information was obtained that both the outgoing government of Stanley Baldwin and the new government of Neville Chamberlain assumed full responsibility. It was said also that under the decree Mrs. Warfield, as the duke’s wife, would not even rank after the royal duchesses but at the bottom o

LONDON, May 29 (UP) — The United Press was informed tonight by an unimpeachable source that King George VI fought a bitter but losing battle against former Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin in an effort to obtain the title “Her Royal Highness” for Mrs. Wallis Warfield. The king pledged his brother before Edward VIII's abdication that he would intervene personally to obtain the coveted H.R.H. letters before her name. He did his best to fulfill that pledge. It was only after members of the royal family, high dignitaries of the church and a powerful group in parliament had joined with Baldwin that the king was forced to relent. He told the enemies of his brother that he was bound “as a brotherly act” to fulfill his pledge. The duke’s enemies, however, were adamant.

Castle Gandolfo, Italy, May 29— (AP)—Pope Pius sent to German Catholics today a special blessing “in the midst of the very grave events” in the Third Reich—the intense controversy between the Nazi state and the church over widespread “immorality” trials of Catholic priests and lay brothers. Thus the Holy Father sought to fortify the church in Germany against a fierce attack by Dr. Paul Joseph Goebbels, Nazi minister of propaganda, on the Catholic clergy at home and abroad. Goebbels delivered the attack before 20,900 ardent Nazis in Berlin's Deutschland Halle last night. It was his reply to George Cardinal Mundelein of Chicago, who accused Germany's government of foisting atrocity propaganda on the world in the Nazi-publicized “immorality” trials. The Pope, who will be 80 years old on Monday, sent an encyclical to Germany before Easter in which he accused the Hitler government of breaking

VALENCIA, Spain. May 28--(AP)—The German cruiser Admira! Scheer was attacked by two loyalist planes near Ibiza in the Balearic Islands after the warship allegedly had fired on the planes. It was announced officially tonight. The planes dropped four bombs which started a fire aboard the vessel, the announcement said. The Admira! Scheer, one of Germany's prize 10,090-ton “pocket battleships,” was sent to Spanish waters to join the international patrol aimed at preventing violations of the non-intervention agreement. The bombing of the ship coincided with a German warning that retaliatory measures would be taken if loyalist planes persisted in molesting German ships. BARCELONA, Spain, May 29. —(UR)—The Catalonian capital was subjected today to the most terrific aerial bombardment it has suffered during the war. Estimates of casualties showed 115 dead and 159 wounded. The raid was conducted

Barcelona, Spain, May 29—(2)—Seven heavy insurgent air raiders scattered bombs over a wide area of Barcelona today, killing at least 70 persons and wounding more than 100 others. (This dispatch was delayed 15 hours, apparently by censors in Barcelona, the Catalan provincial capital.) The armada of twin-motored planes, evidently sent from an insurgent base on the Island of Mallorca, thundered over the sleeping city about 3:30 a.m. Valencia, capital of the main government to the south, was attacked at almost the same hour yesterday, with many killed. Several apartment buildings were wrecked, victims were buried under the debris. The attack lasted only about 10 minutes. Anti-aircraft defenses were impotent. The batteries speedily went into action but the bombers dove at them and machine-gunned their emplacements. The planes, believed by some observers to be the same insurgent fleet that cau

Berlin, May 29.—(4)—The oratorical attack of Joseph Paul Goebbels, minister of propaganda, on the Catholic Church was believed today possibly to foreshadow a Nazi move establishing a “regenerated” German Catholic Church completely severed from the authority of the Vatican. Millions of Germans were stirred to intense speculation by Dr. Goebbels’ speech, broadcast throughout the Reich last night, which threatened widespread expulsion of the Catholic clergy and accused the clergy of a “general decadence of morals.” The fact that Reichsfuehrer Adolf Hitler’s personal mouthpiece, Voelkischer Beobachter, prominently displayed Goebbels’ quotation of Napoleon concerning suppression of monasteries gave weight to rumors that drastic measures were not far off. The concluding words of the Nazi minister’s unprecedented attack were studied closely for a clue to national socialism’s next move in its bi

MONS, France, May 29—The Duke of Windsor was reported to be in a temper and “ready to fight” the decree of his brother-successor which barred Wallis Warfield from the title of “her royal highness.” He was described as “mad and sore!” and the source at the Chateau de Cande said it was impossible to predict what action Edward might be contemplating. It was said the former British monarch who abdicated when Britain refused the Baltimore divorcee as queen, at first would not believe London dispatches telling of the decision. Convinced finally of their truth, the slim, blond Edward who will wed Mrs. Warfield at Cande next Thursday, then declined to consider the decree—or the decision of the British government behind it—as final. It was indicated he might take action to reopen the question, which he had thought settled in his favor before the civil marriage ceremony next week but the procedure

1937-10-28.text: London, Oct. 27 (Py) - Britain dispatched the mighty battle cruiser Hood to Mallorca today to keep an eye on the strategic Balearic islands. The move came as Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden tried to keep the non-intervention sub-committee on the road to removal of foreign volunteers from Spain. The Hood, world’s largest warship, sailed from Gibraltar to relieve the cruiser Despatch, Britain thus will have her highest ranking admiral in the western Mediterranean in constant touch with the islands which lie on the Anglo-French trade lanes. Mallorca, largest of the islands, has been in the hands of Spanish insurgent Generalissimo Francisco Franco for a year and it has been reported an Italian air base already is well established there. A reported Italian threat to dominate the whole Balearic group has made a potentially dangerous offshoot of the Spanish civil war. East of Mallorca lies the o

LONDON—Russia withdrew, in part, today from the activities of the 27-power non-intervention committee, announcing she would no longer support the Spanish control scheme. Following a conference with Anthony Eden, British foreign minister, last night, Ivan Maiski, Soviet ambassador, sent a note to Lord Plymouth, notifying the committee that Russia would not contribute further funds to the non-intervention board or the control scheme. It was pointed out, however, that the action does not imply Russia's withdrawal from the non-intervention committee, membership in which is "quite independent of her commitments to the board and the control scheme." Great Britain and France strove today to break Soviet Russia’s resistance to a plan for withdrawal of foreign “volunteers” from the Spanish civil war while strengthening their fleets in the Mediterranean in event a compromise is not reached. Secret

SHANGHAI — A Japanese tank fired point blank today on a British infantry detachment of which Brigadier A. P. D. Telfer-Smollett, British army commander in chief, was a member. Brigadier Telfer-Smollett was inspecting British defense lines on the West Side of Shanghai, just outside the International Settlement, this morning. The attack brought international tension near to the breaking point, British infantrymen and United States marines alike were on the very edge of savage fighting between Japanese, seeking to isolate Shanghai, and the defending Chinese. Both Americans and Britons had orders to fire at discretion in self-defense. A Japanese tank nosed cautiously halfway across the highway bridge over Soochow Creek in order to attack Chinese “dare or die” men fortified inside a factory. The tank crew saw men of the British Royal Ulster Rifles helping half a dozen terrorized Chinese refug

LONDON, Oct. 28.—(U.P.)—The birth of sextuplets, all boys, to an Indian woman on the northwest frontier, was reported in a letter received by Major General E. D. Giles, from Lieut. Dur Khan, an officer of a British regiment in India. Lieut. Khan wrote that his cousin's wife had given birth to the boys, all of whom were doing well.

LONDON, Oct. 28.—The diplomatic reporter of the Evening News said today Soviet Russia had abandoned its cooperation with the Spanish non-intervention committee. The writer said Ivan Maisky, Soviet ambassador, had notified Lord Plymouth, British chairman of the committee, that Russia no longer would contribute funds to the non-intervention board or share the costs of the Spanish control scheme. Russia is opposed to a French-British plan for equal withdrawal of foreign volunteers by both sides in Spain. Diplomatic quarters suggested that the situation here may have prompted Britain to send the mighty battle cruiser Hood to Majorca and a French warning that warships would fire upon any aggressor, regardless of nationality, attacking French shipping in the Mediterranean.

WASHINGTON (P) — The Washington Post said in a copyrighted story today that Harold Sims, attache of the British embassy, and Mrs. Sims will be hosts to the Duke and Duchess of Windsor during their visit to the capital next month. Mr. and Mrs. Sims, the paper said, are having a large suite prepared for the couple at a fashionable (Wardman Park) hotel. The Post said invitations have gone out for a dinner to be given by Mr. and Mrs. Sims in honor of the former English King and his American-born bride, but it quoted Mrs. Sims as saying she knew “nothing about it.”

LONDON, Oct. 28.—(UP) Great Britain and France strove today to break Soviet Russia's resistance to a plan for withdrawal of foreign "volunteers" from the Spanish civil war while strengthening their fleets in the Mediterranean in event compromise is not reached. Russia announced through Ambassador Ivan Maisky that she will resist any attempt by Italy and Germany to drive her from the international non-intervention committee and indicated that she still opposed any withdrawal of "volunteers" which would involve the granting of belligerent rights to the nationalists. Diplomatic quarters suggested that the situation here may have prompted Britain to send the mighty battle cruiser Hood—the largest in the world—to Majorca and a French warning that warships would fire upon any aggressor, regardless of nationality, attacking French shipping in the Mediterranean. British Foreign Secretary Anthony

LONDON, Oct. 28 (AP).—Diana Wilson, tall English actress for two decades a figure of the English stage, died today of pneumonia. She was 40. She appeared in America after the World War with Isadora Duncan. One of her last engagements here was in the British version of “Anything Goes.”

1937-01-15.text: WASHINGTON, Jan. 15 Wib— President Roosevelt's invitation to Sir Walter Runciman, member of the British cabinet, to spend the Jan. 23 week-end at the White House caused speculation today whether he intended to discuss with his guest a possible Anglo-American trade treaty. Runciman is aboard the liner California, due at New York Monday, on what he described on leaving England as a purely private trip. Disclosure of the unusual White House invitation led to belief that the President had in mind discussion of some vital matter.

Rome, Jan. 15. (UP) The inclusion of Britain and possibly France in a common Halo-German alliance against communism is the primary object of the talks here between Premier Mussolini and Col.-Gen. Hermann Wilhelm Goering, Germany's air minister, as informed sources said last night. This informant said Count Galeazzo Ciano, Italian foreign minister, had prepared the ground for such a project in half a dozen conferences last week with Sir Eric Drummond, British ambassador. Premier Mussolini and General Goering, this authority asserted, are now outlining possible bases for a tri-power cooperation against communism. The initial objective of such an arrangement, it was stated, would be a common line of action in the Spanish civil war. The ultimate objective would be to oppose any communist disturbance of the status quo anywhere in Europe. Diplomatic authorities said France would not necessaril

LONDON, Jan. 14.—(#)—Great Britain announced today perfection of a gas mask which can be used by babies—latest symbol of the completeness with which the government is tackling the problem of home defense. Huge expenditures for navy and air armaments will put Britain in a powerful position to combat enemies anywhere by 1939. But before that the twin problems of protection against air raids and guaranteed food supplies at home are being pushed to immediate solution. Geoffrey Lloyd, undersecretary in the home office, who disclosed recently that 30,000,000 gas masks would be distributed free throughout England in 1937, announced the baby mask development. During the World War, although Britain came within a fortnight of exhausting food supplies, there were comparatively few air-raid casualties. Development of airplanes and long-range bombers, officials emphasized today, now would permit dest

London, Jan. 14 (#)—President Eamon de Valera of the Irish Free State, one of the British Empire's most outspoken political opponents, dropped in unexpectedly today ostensibly to make peace. On his way home from Zurich, Switzerland, where he underwent treatment for eye trouble, De Valera did not catch the first train out of London, as he usually does. Instead, he received Malcolm MacDonald, British Dominions Secretary, at his hotel. The two talked for three hours. Tonight they met again.

| LONDON, Jan. 10.-The engagement of Lord Ashley, former husband of Mrs. Douglas Fairbanks, to Mlle. Francoise Souilier of Paris, was announced today. Lord Ashley was granted a divorce decree nisi from Lady Ashley, a former musical comedy actress, in 1934, in an undefended suit which named Fairbanks, then the husband of Mary Pickford, as co-respondent. Dissolution of the Pickford-Fairbanks marriage became absolute 2 January, 1926.

LONDON, Jan. 15 (2)--Italy formally notified Great Britain today she would conform to the 1936 naval treaty between Britain, the United States and France by mounting maximum armament of 15 inches on her capital ships. The treaty provides a 14-inch limitation providing Japan and Italy agree, Japan has until April 1 to announce whether she will accept the restriction. She was said to have the matter under “active consideration.” Authorities declined to comment on reports from Washington that the new United States battleships might mount 16-inch guns.

ROME, Jan. 14. (UP) — Premier Benito Mussolini and General Hermann Goering decided today that Italy and Germany would agree “in principle” to Britain’s suggestion for stopping the flow of “volunteers” to Spain. But, pending an agreement among all the great European powers to cease aiding either side, the “fascist bloc” will continue pouring men into Spain. They hope that General Francisco Franco may capture Madrid before the non-intervention pact becomes effective. Mussolini and his guest also agreed on a secret commercial understanding. Italian lard and pork will be exchanged for German metals to aid Italy’s rearmament program. The agreement also is expected to cover German cooperation with Italy in developing Ethiopia’s economic resources. LONDON, Jan. 14. (U.P)—British statesmen believed tonight that the Mussolini-Goering conversations in Rome may end foreign intervention in Spain's c

Paris, Jan. 15.—(AP)—The French Chamber of Deputies responded tonight to Premier Leon Blum's plea to show a “will for peace” by unanimously voting him power to ban volunteers from Spain. The vote was 591 to 9. Blum has promised to apply the power only in conjunction with like action of other nations including Britain, Germany, and Italy. The quick vote followed on his declaration the volunteer question had become one of “saving Europe from war.”

1937-09-08.text: (Copyright 1937 by United Press) Shanghai, Sept. 8 (UP)—Japan defied Britain, France and the United States today to enforce their demand that she remove her warships and troops from the immediate vicinity of the Shanghai international settlement. Instead of withdrawing she continued the ferocious attack which is spreading death and ruin throughout the Shanghai area and most of north China. At Sunkiang, near Shanghai, a Japanese airplane bombed the Shanghai-Hangchow passenger train, packed with Chinese refugees from Nanking. A Chinese spokesman estimated that 300 refugees were killed and 400 injured in the wreckage of five coaches. No Troops Aboard. The Chinese said there were no Chinese troops on the train or even in the vicinity of Sunkiang. Bombardment of ships, airplanes and artillery continued all day and into the night close to the international settlement in Shanghai and in the are

(Copyright, 1937, United Press) London, Sept. 8.—Pirate submarines, renewing their bold attacks on merchant ships, added fresh danger today to a Mediterranean crisis that now involved every great power in Europe. The cabinet, its members more anxious than they had been since the Ethiopian crisis of 1935, met to give Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden his final instructions for the anti-submarine conference to be held at Byron, Switzerland, Friday. These instructions, worked out in agreement with France, were that whether Italy and Germany attend the conference or not, whether other nations cooperate or not, Great Britain and France propose to inaugurate a formal plan of naval operations to clear the Mediterranean seas of the “pirate” submarines. With anger mounting here, in Paris, in Rome and in Moscow, there were incidents, either susceptible of trouble. It was reported by Lloyd's {Continue

; United Press Correspondent Shanghai, Sept. 8, — Japan rejected today the British-French-United States demand for withdrawal of her warships and troops from the immediate vicinity of the Shanghai international settlement. Announcement of Japan’s defiance came shortly after the momentous news that China's Communist army of 100,000 or more veteran troops had thrown away its red banners and come to the government’s aid in its extremity. A Japanese embassy spokesman, in announcing Japan's reply to the powers, said Japan was unable to comply with the demands, because such action would imply abandonment of the protection of Japanese life and property in the settlement. The Japanese note proposed withdrawal of Chinese troops from the entire Poctung and Wantag areas on each side of the river close to the settlement, saying that removal from a limited section would not meet the purpose of assuri

London, Sept. 7.—Grim French and British determination tonight kept alive a 12-power anti-piracy conference despite an Italo-Russian breach which jeopardized settlement of European peace problems in the near future. The meeting to check Mediterranean pirate attacks—outgrowth of the Spanish war—and to preserve freedom of the seas must go on Friday, with or without angry Italy's participation, France and Great Britain decided. To back their stand, the two powers felt they had fleets strong enough to suppress marauders. Italy May Send Delegates. High Italian sources indicated, however, that Premier Mussolini may send representatives to the conference at Nyon, Switzerland, despite rage at Russia's note accusing Italy of sinking two Soviet merchantmen. Italy curtly rebuffed Russia with a denial of the charge. A Rome official, who said Italy still was considering the conference invitation in a

+ London, Sept. 7—(#)—Britain has assured Italy, the Daily Mail said tonight, that Russia will not be allowed to transform the forthcoming conference on Mediterranean piracy into a “trial with Italy in the dock.” This assurance, reliable sources believed, likely would result in Italy’s decision to attend the conference—which Russia will attend with the argument that Italian warships are responsible for the sinking of merchant ships in the great sea. Britain, said the Daily Mail, is understood to have assured Italy that no political questions would be raised at the conference beginning Friday. Only technical questions involving the elimination of piracy would be considered. Clash Likely Therefore, said the Mail, “the Soviet nation would not be allowed to put into practice its scheme to transform the conference into a trial with Italy in the dock.” The possibility of bitter clashes between

LONDON, Sept. 7.—(#) — The British tanker Harpa, 3,000 tons, was attacked tonight by “an unidentified battleship” off the coast of North Africa, a Lloyd’s agent reported from Tunis. The Harpa was en route from Port Said, Egypt, to Tunis. The message said a torpedo missed the vessel. The ship managed to reach La Goulette and will sail up a short canal to Tunis later.
