The report brands alcoholism as a disease and its treatment as “a major scientific problem.” Its authors are Dr. Merrtli Moore, associate in psychiatry, Harvard Medical school, and Miss Mildred G. Gray, research fellow in neurology, Harvard Medical school. To date the study has recorded these facts: Alcoholics account for 1-20 of the total of all admissions to the hospital, forming one of the largest groups for which it has

Moscow, Sept. 7. — Russia tonight accepted the British-French invitation to the Mediterranean “piracy” conference, again charged Italy with responsibility for attacks on merchant shipping, and asked pointedly why Germany was invited—contending that the Nazi state is not directly concerned with Mediterranean problems. Russia asked also that the Spanish Madrid-Valencia government be invited as a Mediterranean power which is one of the victims of “pirate warships.” The Soviet note was handed to the French and British embassies tonight. The request for explanation of why Germany was invited asserted that only powers “directly connected in the Mediterranean basis” were supposed to be represented. The Russian note, following close on yesterday's representations charging Italy with sinking two Soviet ships in the eastern Mediterranean, said: “The government of the Union of Socialist Soviet Repu

1937-01-29.text: LONDON—(AP)—The Winter's most violent gales roared across western Europe from Scandinavia to Gibraltar yesterday, swelling the roster of storm dead to at least 56. Heavy rains caused threats of serious floods. Portugal was hard hit as the storm, described by meteorologists as the worst in 50 years, wrecked the harbor of Leixões. Toll of the tempest included 28 trawlers, three sailing vessels, a steamer, a motor vessel and numerous smaller craft in European waters. Two trawlers were believed to have carried 46 men to their deaths in the North Sea Wednesday after distress signals flashed. Neither the French trawler Liretta with 30 men aboard nor the British Amethyst was believed to have kept afloat in the gale and heavy seas.

LONDON, Jan. 29. — (UP) — Sir Percival Phillips, 59, famous American-born war correspondent, died today. Sir Percival, who last visited the United States on the maiden voyage of the liner Queen Mary in May, 1936, was the son of a Brownsville, Pa. country doctor. He was one of the most remarkable journalistic careers in Great Britain, if not the world. For 40 years he had had a “ringside seat” to wars, revolutions, earthquakes and disasters. Armed with a bulletproof typewriter case, he covered in swift sequence the Spanish-American war, the Russo-Japanese war and the various Balkan

BILBAO, SPAIN, Jan. 29.—(2P)—A ship believed to have flown British colors sank near here today, the result, it was reported, of striking an explosive mine. The vessel was believed to have been of about 4,000 tons. A quantity of wreckage had been sighted. (Bilbao, Bay of Biscay seaport is capital of the Basque autonomous government which is allied with Spanish Valencia government). Authorities here announced that "mysterious gunfire" within insurgent lines in the Mount Ascensior sector near Eibar led them to suppose insurgent forces were fighting among themselves. They reported heavy rifle and machine gun fire.

LONDON, Jan. 28—()—Canadian legislation for unemployment insurance, minimum wages, limitation of working hours and regulation of marketing was declared unconstitutional today. The ruling came from the judicial committee of the Privy Council, highest judicial body in the empire. The committee upheld measures to regulate some trade practices and to help indebted farmers. The legislation was adopted by the Canadian Parliament in 1934 and 1935, when the conservative government of Premier R. B. Bennett was in office. Only two of the laws, however, have been put into effect—that to aid farm debtors, which was upheld, and that giving farmers the right to combine in regulating production and marketing of their products, which was declared invalid.

'LONDON, Jan. 29 (4)—Terrific winds left England and France helpless today against a paralyzing blizzard and floods which had cost at least 57 lives at sea. Fears mounted for another 100 persons aboard the 4,855-ton Brazilian liner Santos, unheard from since reporting she was disabled and drifting close to the rocky Berlengas islands off the coast of Portugal. Flooded roads along the border of England and Scotland froze solid, isolating communities from overland travel. Treacherous seas, whipped by a hurricane in the North Atlantic, pounded the Scottish east coast and tied up virtually all shipping. At Lossiemouth, Scotland, mountainous waves endangered the whole harbor entrance. Blizzards borne on the driving winds piled up huge drifts in the south of England, marooning scores of motorists all night in some areas. Rain-swollen rivers in southern France inundated low-lying farms and road

MOSCOW, Jan. 29 —- (4) —Karl Radek, once Russia's foremost newspaper commentator and now on trial for his life with 16 other confessed conspirators, defiantly predicted today “we shall pay for our crimes with our heads.” In varying moments of anger and abjection, Radek admitted treasonable acts against the Soviet Government of Joseph Stalin but classed his crime as “political, nothing else.” “I admit the treason,” he shouted. “I do not defend myself. There are no extenuating circumstances.” His “final words,” directed at the judges of the Military Collegium of the Supreme Court before they were to retire to consider a verdict, contrasted sharply with the dignified pleas for mercy from another defendant, Gregory Sokolnikov, former ambassador to Great Britain.

By Associated Press. MOSCOW, Jan. 26—The military collegium of the Russian supreme court retired tonight to consider the verdict against 17 confessed conspirators in the plot to overthrow the government. Karl Radek, the newspaper commentator and one of the defendants, predicted the death sentence.

| TOKYO, Jan. 29 (P)—Kazushige Ugaki, his determined efforts to form a cabinet blocked by the army, informed Emperor Hirohito today he was unable to form a government and resigned the premiership. | As the retired general officer left the Imperial Palace, he scathingly denounced the army for having brought the nation to the crossroads of fascism or constitutionalism. Ugaki, hailed as one of Japan's most brilliant administrators, apologized to the Emperor for his lifelong association with the army and dramatically announced resignation of his title of general “as an expression of my sorrow and disappointment at these conditions.” Informed quarters considered, however, the sudden development in Japan’s week-old constitutional crisis might be preliminary to Ugaki's formation of an anti-military cabinet to purge the army of its extremist elements. Authoritative sources understood the Emperor

1937-06-12.text: LONDON, (AP).—Great Britain announced officially tonight the conclusion of a four power agreement guaranteeing the safety of foreign warships participating in the neutrality patrol off Spain and the return of Germany and Italy to the European non-intervention fold. All four powers whose warships formed the international fleet agreed not to take retaliatory action before consulting among themselves in the event any of their vessels are attacked.

| London, June 11. (4 y—Ernest Aldrich Simpson swore under voluntary oath in King’s court today that he was paid neither by money nor other consideration to permit the former Wallis Warfield to divorce him without contest. The ship’s broker acted to spike gossip to that effect, accepted an apology through her attorney by a British society woman who had discussed the divorce at a luncheon party, and thereupon withdrew a slander action against her. Mrs. Joan Sutherland, Simpson's attorney told the court, had repeated “irresponsible gossip” to the effect that “a sum of money had been accepted by Simpson as price for his silence.” His client, Attorney H. J. Wallington continued, wished to repudiate that rumor under oath. Wallington asked Simpson if there was any truth in the rumor he had been paid for not obstructing the divorce of Mrs. Simpson, now Duchess of Windsor and wife of the former

London, England, June 12.—LP— Great Britain and most of Europe were in the grip of an early summer heat wave today. The thermometer registered 72 in London at midnight, equalling the highest temperature for that hour in 67 years and causing widespread discomfort. Many Londoners spent the night in their gardens.

LONDON, June 12, (U.P) - At the Infants’ hospital in Vincent square, Dr. David Levi operated for pyloric stenosis (internal obstruction) on a baby weighing only three pounds—claimed to be the smallest child ever to undergo an operation.

- LONDON (P)—Four power conversations to facilitate the return of Germany and Italy to the “hands off Spain” scheme Friday night were reported to have resulted in “good progress. British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden and the French, German and Italian ambassadors discussed the problem today and will meet again Saturday. A British spokesman said there were “no points of disagreement” among the conferees, and fear that French support of Russia’s protest against exclusion from the conversations might hinder action was dispelled. A French foreign office spokesman said in Paris that a new non-intervention agreement guaranteeing the safety of patrol ships in Spanish waters was virtually complete. He added that Germany and Italy may return to the patrol as early as Saturday.

Moscow—()—Eight of the Soviet Union’s highest military leaders were doomed to the firing squad today for treasonable activity against the Red Army they headed. No appeal remained from the death sentences handed down long before dawn by the military tribunal of the Supreme Court which branded the army chiefs as traitors in the spy service of a foreign power. The nation’s highest tribunal announced the verdict at 2 a.m. condemning Marshal Michail N. Tukhachevsky and seven generals, including important figures in the military hierarchy, to death “immediately.” Soviet custom dictates that such sentences must be carried out within 24 hours. The swift-moving military trial was deemed by foreign observers as probably the most important of the Soviet Union’s treason trials, since it disclosed disaffection in the army’s topmost ranks. Previous trials, which sent a total of 29 men to firing squads

Hendaye, Franco-Spanish frontier, June 12. (2)—Bilbao waterfront houses were set aflame today by combined aerial and artillery bombardment as an Insurgent offensive was reported to have cracked the outer lines of the city’s last standing defenses. The aerial attack concentrated on three objectives—the waterfront, militiamen’s barracks and the water reservoirs. Reports said a large force of planes shuttled between their base and the city, making forays against neighboring communities and Basque defense lines also. Air observers reported Generalissimo Francisco Franco’s heavy guns and air raiders combined to smash Bilbao with bombs and shells. They said they could see flames rising from several houses near the waterfront along the Nervion river. A squadron of 39 Insurgent bombers droned over Amurrio, Galdacano, and three smaller communities near Bilbao for 12 hours, raining bombs on the to

| MOSCOW, June 12.—(U.P)--The crumpled, bullet-riddled bodies of eight high army officers were believed to be in a Moscow prison morgue today, awaiting dishonored burial, in evidence of the swift, merciless punishment that Russia metes to traitors, The eight men, a marshal and seven generals—the marshal, Mikhail Tukhachevsky, regarded as Russia’s most brilliant soldier — were convicted on their own confessions of espionage in behalf of a foreign country unfriendly to the Soviet Union, The military collegium of the supreme court ordered that they be stripped of all military titles and honors and then shot summarily. The trial was secret and the government silent. But Pravda, official newspaper organ of the Communist party, said in its editorial: “The artfulness of the agents of Fascist intelligence services in our country has not helped and will not help them. . . . We have disclosed plan

1937-12-13.text: (By The Associated Press.) SHANGHAI, Dec. 14.—(Tuesday)—(”)—-The British gunboat Bee reported early today she had rescued eight Americans, seven of them seamen from the United States gunboat Panay, sunk in the Yangtze river above Nanking by Japanese warplanes Sunday. These rescues brought to 61 the known survivors among 72 persons believed to have been on the Panay when she was bombed. The report from the Bee further said it was understood two more Americans—not included in the 61—were safe ashore. One seaman died of wounds. Fifty-four were known to be ashore at Hohsien, about 85 miles upriver from Nanking, 15 of them wounded, some gravely. The eighth American picked up by the Bee was J. W. Pickering, of the Standard Oil, who apparently had not been aboard the Panay. In Shanghai the Japanese navy accepted full blame for the terrific aerial bombardment along the Yangtze in which the Panay

LONDON, Dec. 13.—(4#)—Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden today told the House of Commons that Great Britain and the United States were “in consultation” regarding Japanese attacks on their Yangtze river gunboats. The Foreign Secretary, who previously had talked with the American charge d'affaires, Herschel V. Johnson, and Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain, asked the Commons to refrain from further questioning in view of “the grave issues involved.” “His Majesty’s ambassador in Tokyo has made the strongest protest to the (Japanese) minister of foreign affairs, who had promised to make fullest inquiry,” Eden said, referring to the shelling of the British gunboat Ladybird. “The seriousness of these incidents needs no emphasis.” A great cheer arose from the members when the Foreign Secretary said “His Majesty’s ships opened fire in return” after they had been bombed.

Shanghai, Dec. 13--One nine Americans of the crew and refugees aboard the United States gunboat Panay when it was sunk in the Yangtze River by Japanese air bombs have been accounted for tonight. Others of the estimated 65 to 70 men aboard the warship may have reached places of safety but the British gunboat Bee reported that it had picked up only seven survivors and said two others were ashore. Reports were received here that 54 survivors had reached Hohsien and were safe in a mission but that could not be confirmed.

SHANGHAI, Dec. 13. WP Survivors of the United States Gunboat Panay, sunk almost without a trace on the Yangtze River by Japanese air bombers near Nanking, huddled on the river banks tonight, awaiting rescue by the British Gunboat Bee. The Bee, racing to the rescue, found only a launch stuck in the mud to tell of the Panay’s fate. In addition to the Panay, three Standard Oil boats were sunk or wrecked, and four British gunboats and two tugs were attacked. A British seaman was killed on the Gunboat Ladybird. How many were killed or wounded on the Panay and the Standard Oil boats could not be determined. It was officially announced that one seaman was killed on the Panay. Lt. Commander J. J. Hughes, the master, received a broken leg. Lieut. A. F. Anders, executive officer, was wounded, as was F. E. P. Gassie, clerk in the United States embassy at Nanking. SHANGHAI — A British gunboat, steaming at forced draught through shell fire along the Yangtze river, today reached the "hotspot" where Japanese airplanes in four separate attacks sank or wrecked the United States gunboat Panay and three American merchant ships. Its own decks pitted with the bullets and shell fragments of a Japanese army attack yesterday, the British gunboat, the Bee, found only a launch, stuck in the mud, to tell the fate of the Panay. Of the three merchantmen attacked, all Standard Oil vessels, there was no trace of the Meiping. The Meihsia was burning fiercely at a wharf on the south bank. The Meian was beached and deserted. At first there was no sign of any survivors. It had been reported that most of the survivors were landed at Hohsien, on the north bank of the river. Then the Bee sighted four men plodding down the south bank. They

London, Dec. 13.—Great Britain has protested strongly to Japan against yesterday's attacks on British warships and tugs in the Yangtze, Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden informed a questioner today in the House of Commons. (United Press), “The seriousness of these incidents needs no emphasis,” Eden declared. “In addition, a United States gunboat has been attacked with loss of life,” Eden continued. “The two governments are in consultation.” Eden at first was reluctant to answer questions and said he had nothing to add to previous statements, but the questioners were insistent. Asked whether he would bear in mind the desirability of asking for compensation from Japan, the foreign secretary replied: “Too, sir.” Eden's statement bore out earlier reports that Britain and the United States plan to proceed along the same lines, but individually and not in concert.

SHANGHAI, Dec. 13.—(Monday)—Japan's mighty war machine, striking furiously at stoutly-resisting Nanking and other Yangtze river ports, today was involved in a new Anglo-Japanese crisis. A British seaman was killed and a British naval officer and another seaman wounded at Wuhu, 4 miles upriver from Nanking, in one of several incidents arising from heavy Japanese aerial and artillery bombardments along 100 miles of the broad Yangtze waterway. The battle for Nanking, the capital from which the Chinese government fled three weeks ago, went into its fourth day with both sides reporting “satisfactory progress” in bloody fighting that claimed thousands of casualties. The Japanese, having thrust a foot inside the city, apparently had made little headway since and that little at great costs, although all available striking power in guns, planes and tanks had been unleashed against the city. 1937-06-27.text: VALENCIA, Spain, June 26.—The Spanish merchant vessel Cabo Palos, laden with foodstuffs, was reported tonight to have been sunk by a submarine off Point Ifach with the loss of five members of the crew. Forty-four survivors, including a woman who was aboard as a nurse, were taken to Alicante by another ship after they drifted six hours in lifeboats. The steamer was sunk at dawn today. Point Ifach is approximately 60 miles south of Valencia. The government made no immediate announcement of evidence as to the nationality of the submarine but it has repeatedly asserted the Spanish insurgents have no undersea craft of their own. Survivors were ordered to Valencia to make full reports.

Chicago, June 26.—(P)—The Herald and Examiner in a copyright story said tonight Robert Irwin, sculptor hunted throughout the country for New York's triple Easter Sunday slayings, had surrendered in the Herald and Examiner office. Detective headquarters and the Central police station reported they had received no word of the man’s capture. Two detectives of the New York homicide squad, Walter Laurie and John Spillane, who said they had been here three days trailing Irwin, joined Chicago police in a hunt for the youth. Not Official Authorities said they had no official report of Irwin’s seizure and had been unsuccessful in locating him. The paper said Irwin confessed the slaying of Veronica Gedeon, artist’s model, her mother, and (Continued on Page 17 )

(By The Associated Press) A new drive to capture Madrid and end the Spanish war appeared imminent last night (Saturday) as insurgents launched heavy attacks against the capital’s defenders. The offensive, preceded by shelling, came almost simultaneously with a prediction by Premier Benito Mussolini's newspaper, the Popolo d'Italia of Milan, that insurgents shortly would break Madrid’s ‘iron ring’ defense and win the war. It asserted a clean-up of the Basque territory was all that remained before Generalissimo Francisco Franco could throw the whole weight of his forces against Madrid. "The strong band around Madrid, like that around Bilbao which seemed impenetrable, will be broken," it said. Government commanders said insurgent attacks on Madrid, apparently in an effort to cut the highway to Valencia, temporary capital on the Mediterranean, were repulsed with heavy insurgent losses. Detroit, June 26.—(/)—The National Labor Relations Board, charging the Ford Motor Company with responsibility for "malicious and brutal assaults" on United Automobile Workers organizers, issued a complaint against the company today and set July 6 for a hearing. The complaint contended that the Ford Company is "interfering with, restraining and coercing" its employees for the purpose of discouraging membership in labor organization. Organizers Beaten Referring to the beating of union organizers attempting to distribute union literature outside gates of the huge Ford Rouge plant in suburban Dearborn May 26, the N.L.R.B. listed 14 persons, including three women, as having been "maliciously assaulted, attacked and beaten." It charged that the Ford Company "by its officers, agents, employees and representatives, instigated, encouraged, committed and acquiesced" in the assaults. Other charges

ANNAPOLIS, Md., June 26.—(*)—Democratic senators and congressmen brought back tonight from their picnic with President Roosevelt a more detailed description of a softball game than of legislative prospects. Like the contingent which preceded them to Jefferson Island yesterday, they reported virtually no serious discussion of national or congressional affairs. One house member said every time somebody edged up to the president for what might be pointed discussion, Speaker Bankhead or Rep. Rayburn, house majority leader, elbowed in or somebody started a song. Returning from the island, Bankhead remarked: “There really was no inside stuff at all.” He said there was no talk of adjournment and that “no one knows when we can adjourn.” “We had a softball game,” he added, “and tried to get young. Hollywood, Calif., June 26.—Now it’s Mrs. Buddy Rogers, Mary Pickford changed her name for the fourth time today when she became the wife of Actor-Orchestra Leader Charles (Buddy) Rogers. A double ring ceremony, performed by a minister of the Congregational church, whose ritual does not include the word “obey,” united the couple in the presence of 17 relatives and friends in the garden of the home of the Louis D. Lightons, in the nearby suburb of Bel Air. Rev. James Hamilton Lash was the parson. When Rogers placed Miss Pickford’s ring on her finger, she gripped her hand and squeezed the ring tightly. Under Tree They knelt on a white satin pillow for the ceremony out under a huge sycamore tree. Calla lilies decorated the tree. Red and white was the general scheme of decoration. Newspapermen were not admitted to the grounds until after the ceremony. When they came in, they found the newlyw

ANNAPOLIS, Md., June 26—President Roosevelt and a swany of democrats found today that, however wide and deep might be their differences on serious subjects, they could agree upon the merits of food and swimming, fishing and shooting. Even one progressive was lured into the procession of mercy makers that traveled to sun-splashed Jefferson Island, a dot in Chesapeake Bay, fifteen miles from Maryland's capital, for a second day of fun and frolic with the President. Representative Hinvenner of California, a progressive elected with democratic backing, was one of those who piled into four submarine chasers with twenty-odd eaters and more than 30 representatives for the trip to the island. Those who checked the guest list said he had an invitation. Thus far, however, the two days of frolicking on the island have produced little indication of any serious discussion of party policy.

HOLLYWOOD, Calif., June 26. — Mary Pickford and Charles “Buddy” Rogers were quietly married this afternoon on a hill overlooking the town that made them famous. It was a ceremony with a setting of complete intimacy. Never, in all the history of Hollywood, has an event been guarded with such rigid attention to detail. The estate where it took place is tucked away in the foothills on a lonely, one-way road. The garden where they stood is ringed with high fences and a barrier of trees. Police were outside and inside. Only 14 persons, the two families and a few friends, were in attendance. Mary and “Buddy” knelt on a pillow covered with white satin, beneath a spreading sycamore tree. Far beneath them, they could see the streets of Hollywood, and even the bustling movie studios where they worked and met, two years ago. Directly behind them were the groom's parents, Judge and Mrs. B. H. Rogers

1937-05-31.text: LONDON, Sept. 1—An unidentified submarine attacked the British destroyer Havock off Cape Antonio, on the east coast of Spain, during the night, the admiralty announced today. The submarine fired a torpedo at the Havock but did not hit it, the admiralty said. The attack occurred about 64 miles south of Valencia, in an area where mystery submarines—the Spanish Nationalist Navy is credited with having only one—have been attacking Loyalist and foreign merchantmen. Immediately on learning that a German fleet had opened fire on the Spanish Government-held port on the Mediterranean, Premier Blum called representatives of the British and Soviet governments to his office for a hurried conference.
