LONDON, May 31.—(UP)—Germany and Italy withdrew today from the Spanish non-intervention committee and the international control scheme, threatening a grave European crisis. Germany withdrew after her ships had bombarded the Spanish port of Almeria, causing many casualties, in retaliation for the bombing of the German pocket battleship Deutschland by Loyalist planes. Italy, co-operating with Germany, withdrew until she is given satisfaction for the Loyalist bombing of the Italian merchant steamer Barletta at Palma, Mallesca, on May 24.

Geneva, May 29. (UP)—The League of Nations council compromised in the face of a behind-the-scenes dispute over foreign intervention in Spain today and adopted a resolution calling upon every League member to respect the territorial integrity and political independence of every other nation. It did not, however, give formal recognition to the Spanish government's contention that territorial aggression had occurred in Spain. The Spanish government has accused Italy of such aggression and, in lesser measure, has assailed Germany for permitting its nationals to fight on the side of the insurgents.

Berlin, May 31 (Monday) (4)—All shore leaves in the German navy were cancelled, it was learned early today, following a cabinet decision “to take measures” because of the bombing of the pocket battleship Deutschland by Spanish airplanes. Every warship flying the swastika flag was waiting with steam up for further instructions, Orders cancelling all leaves were issued after the news of the Deutschland bombing off the Balearic Island of Ibiza had been relayed from ship to ship around the world. An official announcement early today placed casualties aboard the warship which docked at Gibraltar at 23 dead, 19 seriously wounded and 64 slightly wounded. The cabinet met in a hastily called session in the chancellery yesterday, Reichsführer Hitler and a number of others flying to Berlin for the meeting. The government, an official communique announced, decided that “this new criminal onslaught o

1937-07-24.text: Wimbledon, England, July 26 - After surviving a marathon 28-game first set, America’s top tennis ace, Don Budge, defeated Charles Edgar Hare, 15-13, 6-2 and gave the United States a crucial break with Great Britain in the opening singles matches of the Davis Cup challenge round today. Budge's triumph came after Bunny Austin, British stylist, had trounced Frankie Parker of Miltown, 6-8, 6-2, 7-8.

(By The Associated Press) LONDON, July 23 - The fight of a humorist turned crusader against the “holy deadlock” of England’s rigid divorce laws was victorious today. Parliament completed enactment of far-reaching changes in the conditions for terminating marriage. Adultery is now the only grounds for divorce in England. When the new law becomes effective Jan. 1 these will be added: Desertion without cause for at least three years; cruelty; incurable insanity for five years. The new law will apply only to England and Wales, not to Scotland or Northern Ireland. Scotland already recognizes desertion as grounds for divorce. Attempts to have incurable drunkenness, life imprisonment, and sexual abnormalities added to the list of divorce grounds were defeated during the act's course through parliament. The Church of England refused to fight the bill. The Archbishop of Canterbury, its Primate, d

London, July 24 (‘UP)—The British freighter St. Quentin has been damaged by an aerial bombardment and has three feet of water in one hold, the captain wired to the owners today from Valencia. Tugs with pumps were helping to keep the ship afloat.

Hongkong. (2) Two pirates were killed and four captured today when their band attempted to commandeer the British coastal steamer Tinsang which runs between Canton and Foochow. The boat's guard fought off the pirates and a British gunboat accompanied the Tinsang on its journey.

Madrid, July 23 (7)—Newly shattered buildings and blood-splashed pavements today reminded Madrid that it is still besieged and within range of enemy cannon despite recent successful thrusts of its defenders. After two weeks free from bombardment, while the government offensive bit into insurgent lines west of Madrid, the capital was heavily shelled twice in 24 hours. The city counted 15 killed and 20 injured, many in the squares and main avenues of the city. Workmen scrubbed at red stains on the pavement and cleared away the rubble. Including casualties in other bombardments 15 miles from Madrid and in Toledo province, a total of about 70 dead and 150 wounded was added to the war's toll. Armed forces struggled on two fronts, one 15 miles west of Madrid where the government entered the third week of its drive, the other 100 miles east of the capital where the insurgents aim at Valencia. G

MALERID, July 24.—(UP)—Nationalists, in one of the most terrible airplane bombardments of the civil war, set fire to the villages of Brunete, Villanueva del Pardillo and Villanueva de la Canada on the west Madrid front today. The villages are key points in the battle that is expected to decide the fate of the Nationalist siege of Madrid. For days Loyalists and Nationalists have attacked and counter-attacked throughout the area. For six hours today a Nationalist fleet bombed the area with incendiary bombs while Nationalist artillery put the Brunete-Villanueva de la Canada road under heavy fire. The Nationalist attack came after Loyalists had taken the initiative on the front northwest of Madrid and just east of the bombed area. Loyalist shock troops went out at dawn today, it was understood, on an attack in the important La Rozas-Majadahonda area northwest of the city. Infantry charged th

HENDAYE, Franco-Spanish Frontier, July 24 (4)—Generalissimo Francisco Franco today claimed a “brilliant victory” on Madrid's western front. A communique from his general headquarters, while acknowledging a lack of information as to details, asserted the insurgents were victorious in a counter-drive against government troops in the Brunete sector, 15 miles west of Madrid, near the Guadarrama river. It was known, however, the communique said, that Franco's men had captured a large amount of war materials. Government troops still held Brunete, tip of the 100 square-mile slice cut from insurgent rearguard positions, the communique disclosed. It added, however, that fall of the strategic point was “imminent.” Brisk engagements continued today in the Brunete and other sectors, it was stated, with insurgents pressing on to encircle Brunete. (Dispatches from Madrid did not confirm the insurgent

BRUSSELS, Belgium, July 24. — Establishment of an international organization to attempt solving the problems "which menacingly confront humanity" was urged today by King Leopold. A letter to Premier Paul Van Zeeland, who returned from economic conferences with President Roosevelt in Washington, set forth the monarch’s recommendation for a world economic institute relying on the cooperation of experts in industry, trade, agriculture, finance and labor from all nations. "If we wish to avert a war and bring the nations back to a more peaceful frame of mind, we must have the courage to tackle the economic question in its entirety; distribution of raw materials—the distribution of means of exchange—industrial distribution of labor—equilibrium between the agricultural and industrial nations," the king wrote. "I am convinced that the moment is favorable and we can hope to find not merely the su

1937-11-30.text: LONDON, Nov 30 ()—Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain and French Foreign Minister Yvon Delbos issued declarations today indicating they planned broad consultations with other powers looking toward a general settlement of world unrest. Chamberlain’s statement said Germany's colonial demands could not be considered “in isolation.” It declared France and Britain were ready to cooperate with other powers in protecting both their rights and treaty obligations in the Far East. The statement, outlining the French and British position, was made to the House of Commons after the heads of both governments had completed a two-day review of their problems and destinies in world danger spots. The prime minister told Commons: “The ultimate object we have in view is a general settlement. “It is obvious that a general settlement cannot be arrived at merely by conversations between two, or even among thre

7 Pt, | HONGKONG, Nov. 30 (2) —4- British naval communique said 2 British planes were fired on by an unidentified vessel today while engaged in maneuvers near Hongkong. The planes were not hit. Naval authorities immediately began an investigation.

LONDON, Nov. 29.—(/)—The premiers and foreign ministers of Britain and France today decided in a “successful” eight-hour discussion of major world problems were not yet ready to grant any German political or territorial demands. French Premier Camille Chautemps said the British and French ministers were in “full solidarity” in their search for peace. “We made a tour of the world,” he said as he left Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain’s official residence. The diplomats appeared pleased with their first day's work and authorized this official five-point account of the conference: 1. France fully understood the limited scope of Lord Halifax’ exploratory talk with Reichsfuehrer Adolf Hitler and agreed with Britain it fulfilled its purpose; 2. The ministers discussed the Colonial question in all its aspects and agreed it required further examination; 3. Both governments expressed themselves

LONDON, Nov. 30. (UP) — Ger- many’s colonial demands must be considered in consultation with other countries and not by Britain and France alone, Premier Camille Chautemps of France said today in a communique at the end of two days of talks between French and British statesmen. Chautemps said the colonial problem was not an isolated one, but a matter of general concern. The communique pointed out that during their stay in London, Chautemps and Foreign Minister Yon Delbos had several conversations with Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain, Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden, and Viscount Halifax, who gave an outline of his visit to Germany. The communique said that Chautemps and Delbos were happy to state that the discussions had given new proof of the community of attitude between the two governments.

LONDON. (7). Humorist A. P. Herbert plunged the House of Commons into gales of laughter in an attack on the government’s “Nosey Parker” bill, designed to find out why Britain is not producing more babies. Herbert recommended “holidays with pay by the sea” as a remedy. Other members joined the humorist in ridiculing Sir Kingsley Wood's population statistics bill, which the opposition labeled “an insult to the nation’s women.” The measure reportedly would give the government broad liberties in prying into family confidences. ‘I am a grandfather,” Herbert declared. “I think I have ceased to breed, but no one is going to ask me about that until I die.” Herbert also recited one of his own compositions, two lines of which were: The babies studied musketry while mother filled a shell And everybody wondered why the population fell. Wood argued that the present population decline, if continued, w

(United Press Staff Correspondent) London, Nov. 30 — (UP) — Great Britain and France were understood today to be prepared to recognize in principle Adolf Hitler's rights to colonies in exchange for a German guaranty to subscribe to European security. At the termination of Anglo-French discussions, an authoritative source reported that statesmen of both nations favor solution of the colony question by the creation of an international territorial pool. Powers holding League of Nations mandates would contribute to the pool which would be offered to Hitler for exploitation. However, 'there must be still considerable study' of the proposal, the informant said. The entire question was said to be linked with general European security and progress depends entirely on what guarantees Germany offers. Apparently Germany's return to a 'piece in the African sum' now depends largely upon what concrete
Hong Kong. Nov. 30 (UP)—An unidentified surface vessel fired on a navy plane from the British aircraft carrier Eagle today.

SHANGHAI, Nov. 30—Japanese naval forces today seized the American-owned steam tug Feiting, hauled down its American flag and threw it into the Whangpoo River. They also seized two Italian flags. It was the first time the Japanese had touched an American flag, although they had bombed points flying that flag. The American vessel was seized at the Kinleeyuan wharf in the French concession. The Japanese removed from the bridgehouse a sign indicating its American ownership, struck members of the Chinese crew with the sign, and steamed downstream. It was understood that United States Consul General C. E. Gauss registered a strong protest with Japanese authorities after which he made a formal report to the State Department in Washington. It was understood that the Italian Embassy also protested to the Japanese authorities who promised an investigation. The Japanese towed the Italian and Americ

1937-11-10.text: By United Press LONDON, Nov. 10.—Leaders of all political parties, friends and enemies, paid tribute today to James Ramsey MacDonald, Britain’s first labor prime minister, while the liner Reina del Pacifico aboard which he died last night, made its way to Bermuda. Men who had denounced him as a pacifist and as a traitor to the Labor Party, joined in praising MacDonald as a man who had fought hard for 50 years for the things he thought were right. Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain, Conservative; Sir Archibald Sinclair, Liberal, and Maj. Clement Attlee, Labor, leaders of the three great parties, were expected to speak in the House of Commons in praise of him. It was expected that MacDonald’s body, after its arrival at Bermuda Monday, would be returned to Britain for burial at Lossiemouth, Scotland, his birthplace. There, in the little fishing village overlooking Moray Firth which he loved

LONDON, (AP).— The British government today was seeking its closest cooperation with the United States since the World War, advocating a “hand-in-hand” policy in the Far East and elsewhere on the troubled world diplomatic front. The strong movement apparently was the outgrowth of President Roosevelt’s Oct. 5 Chicago address which encouraged Britain, after close scrutiny, to believe the Washington government might relax somewhat its traditional policy of isolation. Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain, who in a speech at Birmingham Oct. 8, had welcomed the Roosevelt plea for concerted action for peace, went a step further last night in a speech at Guildhall, calling for fuller British-American collaboration. The Prime Minister hailed the United States participation in the current Far Eastern peace conference.

LONDON, Nov. 9 (®)—The abrupt departure of Max. im Litvinoff from the Brussels conference was seen tonight as meaning either or both of these things: 1. A protest against what Russia considered a Brussels maneuver to leave her out of any Chinese-Japanese mediation conferences while leaving Italy in, 2. A preliminary to a Soviet defense council on how to meet Italy’s adherence to the German-Japanese anti-comintern pact, Litvinoff left Vladimir Potemkin, Russian ambassador to France, in charge of the Soviet delegation, but the fact Russia still was represented did not lessen the belief his sudden departure was significant.
WASHINGTON, Nov. 10.—(N- The treasury announced today: $4,000,000 worth of gold would be shipped to England tomorrow. It will be the second gold export from the United States this week.

London, Nov. 10 (4)-The News Review, a weekly news magazine, today published what it said was a telephone conversation between the Duke of Windsor and King George and said the Duke postponed his American trip on the advice of the king. Before the postponement was announced, the magazine said, the Duke called his brother from Paris and complained: “They know I am not a Fascist. I have been misled by friends and misunderstood by the public.” The king was said to have replied that he was sorry about the affair and that if he could do anything he would be only too glad. “Whatever your advice may be I will follow it,” the Duke was quoted as saying. The King thought for a moment, the magazine said, then expressed the view that because of what had happened he considered it wise to cancel the trip or postpone it indefinitely.

MOSCOW, Nov. 10 (AP) — The Communist party organ, Pravda, declared today that the real purpose of the Italian-German-Japanese anti-Communism agreement was to grab territory in a new world war. The newspaper urged collective action by the United States, Britain and France against the three powers. "The interests of peace call for opposition to block the Fascist war incendiaries by a united front of countries interested in strengthening collective security on a basis of the individuality of peace," Pravda said. "An end must be put once and for all to the policy of protecting the aggressors. Italian and German fascists and Japanese militarists must be made to understand that attempts to provoke a new world war for territorial plundering will bring collective resistance from all peaceful countries. "The sooner the necessity of the policy of collective defense of peace is realized by all gove

WASHINGTON, Nov. 10 UP~ President Roosevelt issued the following statement today on the death of J. Ramsay MacDonald, former prime minister of Great Britain, "Because Ramsay MacDonald labored long and successfully for the good of his fellow men, he will be mourned by those throughout the world who call themselves liberals. I am glad to have known him as a friend and I deeply regret his death."

London, Nov. 10, ()—David Kirkwood, Laborite, was suspended today from the House of Commons, by vote of 178 to 104, after a stormy scene in which he shouted from the floor “I don't give a d-—— for the lot of you.”

1937-05-08.text: NEW YORK, May 8, p—The final quota of coronation visitors from America, Capt. Dick Merrill and Jack Lambie, hoped to start today from Floyd Bennett field on a non-stop flight to London. In case of unfavorable weather, the start may be delayed until tomorrow. Merrill, with a record of two Atlantic crossings behind him, said: “It's a tough flight and I know it, but life is like that—and you can’t see a coronation every day. And with Jack Lambie sitting next to me, up forward there, we're going through like a knife through cheese.” The only thing new in the flight, as far as Merrill is concerned, he said, is that he’s flying a Lockheed Electra instead of the big Douglas which he handles on his regular passenger run between New York and Miami. Lambie is his regular co-pilot. The silvery monoplane has been equipped with 13 gasoline tanks capable of giving the ship a range of 4300 miles. The g

London — Italy's action in banning all but three English newspapers and recalling Italian correspondents now in London was officially ignored here today. One person in authority said: “Really now, the British empire will be able to withstand the horrible impact.” Some sources said they felt the Rome announcement was timed to coincide with the usual long weekend of British officialdom during which no official consideration could be given to the ban and no retaliation might be exerted.

London, May 8. (AP)—The Yankee in King Arthur’s court may have felt stranger, but he would have to come back to prove his point to the wide-eyed legion of Americans discovering London amid its coronation trappings today. Most of them are first-time visitors. They crowd the ancient Cheshire Cheese Tavern, in Fleet Street, where pompous old Dr. Johnson used to sit with his Boswell, and Ye Olde Cock Inn where Charles Dickens held forth to literary lights of the day. They guzzle tea and marvel at Englishmen wearing raincoats and carrying umbrellas in the bright sun that for seven days, now, has been something of a marvel to Englishmen themselves. They wander through Piccadilly and the Strand, through Haymarket and Trafalgar Square and along the Thames Embankment. They peer up at Parliament and Big Ben, the tallest thing in a city given strictly to four-story buildings. They try to find Westm

BY RALPH HEINZEN (United Press Staff Correspondent). PARIS — Great Britain and France reconsidered today the offer of Gen. Francisco Franco, Spanish insurgent leader, to grant safe conduct of women and children war refugees through his troops encircling Bilbao. Although it appeared likely that further evacuations of the refugees from the Basque capital might be delayed while Franco's proposals were being studied, reports from Saint Jean De Luz said the French steamship Caramare left for Bilbao today, convoyed by three French warships. It was to embark 1,090 refugees. Under Franco's plan it would be unnecessary to continue the difficult and costly task of evacuating the non-combatants by sea which would become increasingly dangerous if Gen. Emilio Mola's army should capture the Heights of Sollube and bring the mouth of the Nervion river, leading to Bilbao, under artillery fire. Franco sug

- London, May 8—London dressmakers were driven to the verge of a nervous breakdown today by a welter of last-minute coronation orders which swamped their workshops. Some peeresses delayed ordering their robes until almost the “zero hour,” while others, exercising woman's age-old prerogative, changed their minds three or four times concerning details—piling up extra labor on workrooms already jammed. Lights burn in the sewing and embroidery rooms until after 10 o'clock nightly. The crush is so great that one firm is working its 300 girls in two 10-hour shifts. Peeresses are getting serious on the coronation problem. They bring jewels to last-minute fittings in order to try them with their robes. They visit coiffeurs, carrying their coronets as casually as a basket of peaches for coronation coiffure dress rehearsals. Some have decided to avoid the early-morning hair-dressing problem by wea

- LONDON, May 8 (AP)—London’s millions, cast in the role of unwilling pedestrians, trudged to work with their soles thinner but their tempers still good today as the bus strike entered its second week. There were no signs of settlement, but some newspapers predicted the 5000 buses would be back on their routes by nightfall or by Monday at the latest.

LONDON, May 7.—(7)—Barnum said: “Greatest show on earth”—and the eyes of American visitors to the coronation already are popping at the gaudy calliope chorus of the empire's multi-million-dollar coronation spectacle. Great Britain is staging an immense show, and the millions of her people watching the pageantry are hoping business of one kind or another will draw the English equivalent of a half billion dollars into the box office. Americans though are pouring in on the boat trains from Southampton, Liverpool and Plymouth. There's a honeymoon couple from Ardmore, Okla., and there's dignified Gen. John J. Pershing. There's an old man from New Jersey and there's Rudy Vallee. There are Americans from the East, the West and the South and there's former Ambassador James W. Gerard looking for a knee-breeches tailor. Today the man from Oklahoma told what one Mayfair landlady with rooms overlook

ROME, (UP). It was officially announced that the government has ordered the recall of all Italian correspondents in London because of the alleged antifascist campaign of British newspapers. The government also banned the sale and distribution of all British newspapers in Italy, except the London Daily Mail, the Evening News and the Sunday Observer.

1937-02-03.text: London (JP) — Three Spanish government airplanes dropped three small bombs near the British battleship, Royal Oak, off Europa Point, Gibraltar, official sources reported today. The ship was not damaged. Official sources said they “assumed” the planes mistook the battleship for a Spanish insurgent ship, but George Ogilvie-Forbes, British Charge d’Affaires in Spain, was instructed to “bring the matter to the attention of the Valencia socialists administration.”

Forbes, British embassy: datelines in Spain, has protested to the loyalist government against the dropping of bombs yesterday near the Battleship Royal Oak by what were believed to be loyalist airplanes. Guilvie-Forbes demanded that the government take measures to prevent a recurrence. According to reports here, three monoplanes flew over the Royal Oak near Gibraltar at 11:30 a.m. yesterday, dropped three bombs in the vicinity, and vanished. It was said that the planes mistook the Royal Oak for the nationalist cruiser Canarias.

LONDON, Feb. 3 .pr-The foreign office has received what it regards as confirmation that a fresh contingent of Italian “volunteers” for the Spanish nationalist army landed at Cadiz last Friday night, it was understood today. The number of men was not specified. Italy and other powers have agreed to cease dispatch of men to Spain if all nations can agree to do so at once.

UM ARE PUL MAE Aah ee Shanghai, Feb. 3—Fifty passengers and crew were reported drowned when the launch Yungslun ran on the rocks near Ping Wang, south of here while crossing Hangchow Bay from Huchow bound from Shanghai.

PARIS, Feb. 2 (®)—A vast program to strengthen France’s armed forces over a four-year period at a cost of 19,000,000,000 francs (about 874 million dollars) was disclosed to the Chamber of Deputies today by Defense Minister Edouard Daladier. His speech outlining the plan was cheered wildly and at its conclusion the government was accorded a vote of confidence, 405 to 186, endorsing the national defense policy. Designed to match German military preparations, the plan includes: Extension of the concrete and steel “Maginot Line” along the Belgian and Swiss frontiers to stand as a barrier to invasion between Dunkirk on the English Channel and the Jura Mountains. Construction of roads paralleling frontiers to facilitate swift movement of men and materials. Increases in the size of mechanized army divisions, creating a corps of 15,000 specialists to strengthen professional shock troops, and mor

Madrid, Feb. 2.—(#)—Fighting was renewed on all Madrid fronts today, with both socialist government and fascist insurgent troops attempting to press an offensive. On none of the fronts was there an important change in positions. Madrid's food-control committee announced that, beginning Friday, milk will be sold only by medical prescriptions, which will be given for none but babies, persons ill, those wounded in the war and those who donate blood for transfusion and operations.

Madrid, Feb. 3 (UP)—Rebel artillery at the Getafe airport opened a vigorous bombardment of Vallecas today, presumably, loyalist officers said, in preparation for a drive on Madrid by way of the Valencia highway. Loyalist artillery returned shell for shell against the insurgent battery. From the University city area, on the west, came a relief rifle and machine gun attack as activity was resumed all along the line. Rebel movements were observed in the Casa De Campo sector. Loyalists tightened their net of street around an estimated 1,000 rebel troops besieged in the hospital Clinico.

TOKYO, Feb. 3—(AP)—The new cabinet of Premier Senjuro Hayashi, after canvassing the knotty problems inherited from the Hirota government, decided today to ask voluntary suspension of the diet for a week while they draw up a general platform of policies. Re-examination of the gigantic budget of the previous government, dissolution of the diet and re-drafting of bills that brought an open break between political leaders and the army were paramount problems. The premier will visit the grand shrine of the sun goddess at Ise Saturday to inform her he has assumed leadership of the government.

1937-04-01.text: WASHINGTON, April 1—()— Secretary Hull said today that the United States is not planning an international disarmament conference, and is not making any proposals to European nations through Norman H. Davis, now in London, for such a meeting.

HOLLYWOOD, April 1 (Bj John Barrymore’s milk bill is $34.25 —and overdue, He listed that item today as one of $70 owed to Los Angeles, New York and London creditors in filing a schedule of $261,597 assets and $161,503 liabilities in a debtor's petition in bankruptcy.

LONDON, March 31.—As Norman H. Davis, American ambassador at large, reached London today, there were authoritative indications President Roosevelt may employ him to feel out the possibility of a new move toward disarmament. Although Davis’ immediate mission is to head the United States delegation at the international sugar conference, the British press emphasized the significance of his arrival in connection with larger questions of world peace and economic co-operation. “Not Far Fetched.” A member of Davis’ suite said some of the newspapers’ conjectures were “not far fetched.” An authoritative source said that although the ambassador ostensibly is here only to talk sugar with experts of other nations next week he may also, in talks with more highly placed statesmen, find time to re-emphasize the three basic points of American foreign policy: Peace, disarmament and international economic

Copyright 1937 by United Press Paris, via London, April 1 (UP) —The European race for armaments is also a race in the output of human beings—potential cannon fodder in a future war. Behind the staggering expenditures and tremendous building programs of such nations as France, Italy and Germany, lies a determined effort to step up the birth rate. In the case of France, the declining birth rate causes acute preoccupation. The rate of 16 per 1000 compared to 19 per 1000 before the World War means, according to statisticians, that France’s population in 1940 will be 44,000,000 compared to Germany’s 80,000,000 if the present ratio continues. It is Germany that France chiefly fears. Subsidies Granted By propaganda and humorous methods of subsidization France is trying to increase births. Direct state subsidies range from 120 francs ($5.52) for the third child to 540 francs ($24.82) for the fif

LOS ANGELES, Calif., April 1. () — Japan’s urgent need for steel in her military and industrial expansion today found her buying construction machinery that was used in building the mammoth Boulder Dam. The Nailsea Court, chartered British tramp steamer, took 450 tons of the machinery from Los Angeles harbor today, bound for Yokohama. ———_—_—_—_—_~<>- PROTEST COAST DRILLING AUSTIN, April 1. (P) — A delega-

London, (#)—A British restaurant manager decided today Diane Raye's strip tease dance was art and gave the American girl a job. Starting April 5 Diane will perform the act, mostly undressing to music, which was banned by the producer who brought her from the United States to introduce the strip tease as Broadway knows it to London. He took one look, decided it was "too hot for England" and went into hiding while Miss Raye went looking for another job.

LONDON, March 31—President Roosevelt was reported Wednesday night to be organizing a world peace offensive in an effort to avert Europe’s headlong plunge into a general war arising from the Spanish holocaust. The president's recognition of Europe’s bitter plight—through his roving ambassador, Norman H. Davis—came at an hour when the Spanish revolution, and perhaps the jealousies and hatreds of heavily armed nations, appeared to be working up steam for a “blow-off.” General Francisco Franco's military rebellion seemed on the verge of a crack-up as internal revolt and a combined military and diplomatic offensive reaching out to three continents gave the odds of victory to his loyalist enemies. European statesmen foresaw brave possibilities from the crowded events of the day, which included: 1—Davis’ arrival in London to confer with British statesmen on what well-informed observers believed

LONDON, (AP).—Any feelers by President Roosevelt's ambassador-at-large toward disarmament in a hastily rearming Europe will get a chilly reception, it appeared today after disclosure that might be a mission of Norman H. Davis. A member of the ambassador's suite said British press conjecture placing such additional construction on Davis’ presence for the international sugar conference was “not far fetched.” This, however, was the lineup of major powers’ reaction of the prospect of such a move by the American envoy: Italy—opposed to disarmament. Germany—close-mouthed, “unless Davis makes an official statement.” France—favorable in principle but reserved concerning success of such a large scale attempt at this stage of the game. Britain—no comment but willing to listen.

1937-03-22.text: (By The Associated Press) New London, Tex., March 22 — Supt. W. C. Shaw, a frail man torn with grief since the London school blast killed 455 of his pupils and teachers, broke down today during the testimony before a military court of inquiry and was taken from the witness stand to an adjoining room.

London, March 22 (UP)—Lifeboats fought through blinding smoke today to rescue the crew of the British steamship Marie Moller, burning fiercely fore and aft off Holyhead on the Welsh coast. Holyhead lifeboats took off about 40 of the crew, mostly Chinese, and returned for the rest of 72 whom the ship carried. All were taken ashore safely. The condition of the ship was considered hopeless. The ship’s master wirelessed 2 fire boats from Liverpool after two explosions started a fire aboard. The flames burst high from the decks and the ship fought its way to within 2½ miles of Holyhead, where it anchored in the moderate sea.

(By The Associated Press) | New London, Tex., March 21.— Evidence that an unauthorized gas connection supplied fuel for the school blast that killed 455 children and teachers weighed down tonight on an already stricken community, occupied with a second day of continuous funerals. Testimony of D. L. Clark, Parade Gas Company foreman, before the military inquiry court, bore on the theory that accumulated gas, either in the walls or under the floor, burst the London consolidated school in the world’s greatest child disaster. Earlier, the court heard testimony that economy dictated a change of plans for the school's heating system, pointed to by experts as the source of gas for the rending blast. In the rambling band rehearsal hall, a stone's throw from the wreckage of Thursday's catastrophe, Clark told the court: “I know that no person had permission to connect the school line to the Parade

LONDON. (®). A spokesman for Scotland Yard asserted that the famous police headquarters knew ‘nothing about reports it was investigating a suspected plot against the life of King George VI. The newspaper Sunday Referee reported such an investigation in progress. It said detectives had raided the room of an unknown man and found a throwing knife wrapped up in a map of the route of the coronation procession.

New London, Texas. (INS)--Supt. W. C. Shaw of the New London consolidated schools today took the witness stand before the military court of inquiry investigating the nation’s worst school disaster here and told his story of the explosion that killed 455 children. The superintendent admitted he was one of the persons responsible for cutting a wet gas line of the Parade Oil Company for fuel for the school’s heating plant without permission of the pipeline company. He also had been warned against the change to wet gas from dry, last January. Shaw's Son Killed Shaw was in the building at the time of the blast. He escaped with minor injuries. He had a son killed in the tragedy, however. “I was partly responsible for the laying of the pipeline. No one made an agreement with the Parade people,” he said. “We had a discussion on the subject but they (Parade company officials) told me that if the

HOLLYWOOD, Cal., March 21. (P)—President Roosevelt heads the list of the 10 most handsome men in the world as selected by Movie Actress Madeline Carroll today. The blonde British actress has looked over the Hollywood crop of actors and hasn’t found any who threatens her estimation of good looks. Her No. 2 man is George Bernard Shaw and the others are Sir Anthony Eden, British statesman; Averill Harriman, railroad president; Raymond Guest, polo star; Baron Gottfried von Cram, German tennis player; Charles A. Lindbergh, Gene Tunney, Admiral Richard E. Byrd and Signor Toscanini, musical conductor. “Use of the word ‘handsome’ to describe mere good looks is all wrong,” Miss Carroll said. “Few young men are handsome, in my opinion, for a man becomes 80 only after he has attained his goal through effort that tries his courage and develops his intellect.”

| LONDON. (UP). Believing even its 7.5 billion dollar rearmament program may not protect civilians against bombing attacks in wartime, the British government intends to spend millions more in precautions against poison gas and incendiary bombs. The home office, which in less troubled times devotes its energies to such matters as preventing cruelty to animals and administering prisons, is now the scene of almost as much war preparation as the out and out military departments. Its special air raid precautions division has asked parliament for an appropriation of $23,087,500 for the next 12 months alone, more than three times as much as it is spending during the 12 months ending March 31. There was a time when Britons could face the possibility of war secure in the knowledge that, win or lose, the civilian population was safe behind Britain’s grey warships. Air raids during the World War we
NEW LONDON, Tex., March 2: The official Red Cross tabulation of the toll taken by the New London schoolhouse explosion follows Identified dead— 426. Seriously injured—49, Reported missing—15.

1937-10-13.text: BY LR Mmastesaleo Pies. Shanghai, Oct. 13 (Wednesday) — Anglo-Japanese tension hardly subsided since Japanese flyers machine-gunned the British ambassador to China, seemed destined today to be renewed, The issue was over the shooting, 14 miles south of Shanghai yesterday, in which it was disclosed that four Britons and one Russian were subjected to machine gun fire from warplanes identified as Japanese. No one was injured. The Japanese today took the stand that the incident was the fault of the British, who they charged, failed to inform Japanese authorities concerning the procession of two automobiles and a truck, traveling from Nanking to Shanghai. Japanese Explain. Japanese asserted that the Japanese navy was informed that a party of Britons was coming to Shanghai, but that the army was not advised and for that reason the flyers were uninformed, The British embassy maintained that the

BANGOR, Me., Oct. 12.—(AP)—The notorious Al Brady's boast he would “make John Dillinger look like a punk” was abruptly silenced by G-man bullets today. The 35-year-old Indiana bandit-robber-killer, one-time neighbor of the deadly fingered Dillinger, was cut down with one of his mobsters, Clarence Shaffer Jr. in an early morning ambush in a Bangor sporting goods store. A third Brady gangster, James Dalhover, surrendered after a police bullet had furrowed the bridge of his nose. Agent Wounded. The only casualty among the federal men was Walter Walsh, who was nailed in the shoulder by a gangster bullet. For nearly five minutes whistling lead shrilled through Bangor’s busiest street as the gangsters, each with a price of $500 on his head, returned the withering bar- (Continued on Page 9? fin) 91

BALTIMORE, Oct. 13 (4)—Maybe it works and maybe not, but Mrs. W. W. Matthews said most of the visitors to Wallis Warfield's former home sit in the bathtub for luck. Mrs. Matthews, “hostess” at the little house on Biddle Street, explained an English woman started the practice shortly after the house opened as a museum. “She said it was good luck to sit in the tubs of famous women,” Mrs. Matthews related. “She said she had sat in lots of famous tubs all over Europe—Cleopatra’s and Marie Antoinette’s. She was determined to get into the tub and she. The tub doesn’t look like a talisman—it's just an ordinary white bathtub on legs, the sort found in lots of old houses. It doesn’t match the flashing facsimiles of the five crowns Edward, King of England, gave up to marry Mrs. Wallis Warfield. Mrs. Matthews said she doesn’t know whether to believe all that about the tub, but her visitors do. “Nin

London, Oct. 12—British and French conferees moved tonight to give the international ‘hands-off Spain’ committee a brief last chance to try to get Italian troops out of Spain. At the same time, it was understood that Great Britain and France were agreed to treat alleged Italian activity in the Balearic Islands, off the Spanish east coast, as a separate problem. (French foreign office technicians were reported yesterday to have discussed the possibility of inviting Italy to join with Britain and France in occupying the islands to safeguard them for ultimate government of Spain, without referring to their conviction that Italian soldiers and sailors already are established firmly there.) The possibility arose that Great Britain and France might try to get all Mediterranean powers together on this supposed menace to the security of trade routes in the Mediterranean. Both problems were thras

LONDON, Oct. 13.—France and Great Britain, conceding to Premier Benito Mussolini another diplomatic triumph, intend to offer to submit the Spanish volunteer problem to the committee on non-intervention, it was understood today. Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden and Yvon Delbos, French foreign minister, agreed to this plan in negotiations conducted through the French embassy here and the British embassy at Paris. Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain approved the proposal and it remained only for the British and French cabinets to give their formal assent. The British cabinet met today and heard Eden's report on the situation and the French cabinet is to meet tomorrow. It was believed that immediately after the French cabinet meeting the British and French governments would begin to draft an offer to submit the problem of withdrawing foreign volunteers from the Spanish civil war to the non-inte

LONDON, Oct. 13—British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain today took the unusual step of calling Maj. Clement R. Attlee, leader of the labor opposition in parliament. The conference was such as rarely occurs when parliament is not in session—except when important government decisions are under consideration. The usual reason for such a move is to obtain opposition support for government policy in times of crisis. Follows Cabinet Meeting The move followed a cabinet meeting to consider the next move in the Spanish intervention impasse between Italy on one side and Britain and France on the other. The ministers met in an atmosphere of pessimism resulting from reports that Premier Mussolini had called up 50,000 blackshirt reserves. Rome, however, denied any of the troops were destined for the Spanish civil war in which the Italian premier is supporting the insurgents. It was possible, howev

LONDON—British brokers today accused Wall Street operators of causing an international break in security prices. They advanced manifold reasons why London was not guilty of starting the steep price slide, but financial men confessed they were unable to give a valid conclusive explanation why the slump started and why it continues. Brokers asserted nearly every recent break stemmed from Wall Street and the London security market was forced to follow. On several occasions, they added, the London market bid up prices before Wall Street opened and then got its fingers burned when Wall Street started business at lower levels.

DUBLIN (*) — Enigmatic President Eamon De Valera indicated today that he was grooming a “mystery man” to run the new State of Eir, which is to be set up under the constitution adopted by the Irish Free State last July. The New York born president, who disclaims any attempt to assume dictatorial powers through the constitution, apparently will not offer himself as a candidate for the presidency of the new state. This construction was placed on a speech he delivered at a Fianna Fail party conference last night.

1937-12-19.text: BALTIMORE, Dec. 18—(AP)—Robert Worth Bingham, United States ambassador to Great Britain, died tonight at the age of 66—victim of a rare and obscure disease diagnosed by an operation this week. The North Carolinian who became publisher of Louisville’s two newspapers—the Courier-Journal and the Louisville Times—and one of the first New Deal diplomatic appointees, died in Johns Hopkins Hospital of “abdominal Hodgkins.” Only after his death did doctors disclose the nature of the illness which defied diagnoses in European medical centers last summer. Physicians disclosed a hospital staff doctor went to England to bring the ambassador here. Unconscious Three Days Death came at 6:21 p.m., CST, after the diplomat had been unconscious for three days, following a diagnostic operation performed by Dr. William F. Rienhoff, Jr., Tuesday. “He was in bad shape when he came to the hospital,” said Dr. Hu

LONDON, Dec. 16.—(0)—The British admiralty tonight was reported secretly speeding preparations to send part of the Mediterranean fleet on a forced run to the Orient at a moment's notice. Although no formal decision has been made, one diplomatic source said the British foreign office believed strengthening the British Far Eastern fleet virtually was inevitable and the admiralty was waiting word from the cabinet to send reinforcements. Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden and Charles Corbin, French ambassador, were understood to have discussed the feasibility of taking some British dreadnaughts from the Franco-British naval patrol of the Mediterranean. The newspaper Evening Star said (Turn to Page 6 Part 2 Col. 2)

BALTIMORE, Md., Dec. 18 (INS) - Robert W. Bingham, 66, ambassador to Great Britain, died at 7:21 o'clock tonight at Johns Hopkins Hospital where he had been ill for several weeks. The ambassador, publisher of the Louisville Courier and Journal, succumbed to abdominal Hodgkin's disease. Kennedy Will Get Post The ambassador, who had been ill for several months, underwent an operation five days ago. He had improved somewhat after the operation, but suffered a relapse tonight, and death ensued quickly. The ambassador's poor health had caused him to seek relief from his official duties, and plans had been made to supplant him. Joseph P. Kennedy, head of the maritime commission, now vacationing in Florida, is to be the new ambassador, according to high officials. Career In Many Fields Bingham rose to the top of America’s foreign diplomatic corps after a long and successful career in the law, t

By The Associated Press SHANGHAI—(Sunday) — The cruiser Augusta, flagship of the United States Asiatic fleet, today cancelled her scheduled sailing for Manila shortly after another American died of wounds received in the Japanese attack on the gunboat Panay. Seaman Edgar William George Hulsebus, of Canton, Mo., died of wounds caused by bomb fragments just a few hours before surviving members of the Panay’s crew had expected to leave war-torn China on the Augusta. His death brought fatalities from last Sunday’s attack to four foreigners, three of them Americans. The Augusta, on which the Asiatic fleet’s board of inquiry is conducting its inquiry into the Panay incident, had expected to reach Manila by Tuesday. The board of inquiry shrouded in secrecy its swift investigation of the attack on the Panay. Its findings were expected soon to be in the hands of President Roosevelt and Secretary

TOKYO, Dec. 19 (Sunday) (AP)—The Japanese foreign office disclosed today that Japan would reply first to the second United States protest on the sinking of the American gunboat Panay. Partial Informed sources said the reply would be a complete denial that surface vessels attacked the gunboat after she was bombed by the Japanese war planes in the Yangtze river above Nanking last Sunday. Authoritative sources also indicated that Japan’s second answer, which would reply to the United States’ original representations, would include iron-bound guarantees from the Japanese navy against any recurrence of naval or air bombardments that might endanger foreign shipping. It was believed the reply regarding charges that Japanese surface craft machine-gunned the sinking Panay would be delivered Monday and that the second answer would be made later. United States Ambassador Joseph C. Grew would make n

Madrid, Dec. 19— (Sunday), (4)— A government communique said today that the last defenses of Teruel, strategic Insurgent city in eastern Spain, had fallen before the government’s surprise offensive. The army high command, the communique said, would make a final assault upon the city this morning after civilians had been given a chance to escape. The prisoners of war were sent into Teruel last night, carrying a government promise of safety for all civilians and Insurgent soldiers who would leave the city and enter government territory before 9 a.m. The first eye-witness accounts of battle for Teruel told of fierce fighting in a blizzard reaching a velocity of 50 miles an hour and in bitter cold. Snow was from six to 36 inches deep on the mountain battle ground. Just before the news of Teruel was received by jubilant government officials, it was announced that 16 persons were killed and 32

Paris, Dec. 18 (4?)-A link between a widespread French revolutionary plot and the Spanish insurgents was disclosed today by government investigators. Police found that quantities of uniforms, seized as part of the equipment cached by the secret revolutionary committee, had first been consigned by a Paris merchant to San Sebastian, ostensibly for use by the Spanish insurgent army. Quantities of cartridges found in at least one of the series of raids came from a Toledo, Spain, arms factory, police said.

HENDAYE, Franco-Spanish Frontier, Dec, 18 (UP)—Fall of the walled city of Teruel, important Nationalist base on the Aragon front, within a few hours was predicted tonight by jubilant Loyalist forces. The government said its forces had captured the last important defensive position and taken a mill northwest of Teruel, the key point of resistance to the city. Agence Espagne claimed it marked the collapse of Nationalist defenses in this sector. More than 100,000 troops were engaged in the battle, which is regarded as a possible turning point in the Spanish civil war.

1937-08-15.text: LONDON. (4)--The Panamanian motor tanker George W. McKnight was reported in messages received early Sunday by Lloyd's to be blazing off the Tunisian coast after she was shelled by an unidentified warship. The vessel was abandoned and one message said all hands were picked up by the steamer British Commodore. Advices to Lloyd’s from the British freighter Mostyn, which relayed a message from a Tunisian radio station, said the George W. McKnight sent out her first distress signal at 9:13 p.m. Saturday night. A later message said: "Now cleared. All hands picked up safe by British tank steamer British Commodore. Ship still burning; nothing can be done about it."

Moscow, Aug. 14.—)— Soviet Russia launched a widespread search tonight for Sigesmund Levaneffsky and his five companions who were believed forced down on an Arctic ice floe on a transpolar flight from Moscow to Alaska and the United States. Three crack Arctic fliers were believed en route already from Moscow to Rudolf Island, 560 miles from the pole, to comb the Arctic wastes for their countrymen while other fliers and two ice breakers were ordered to join the search. The Soviet party encamped on a floe drifting in the vicinity of the North Pole was advised to convert its station into an air base for the search planes. The flight committee here tonight announced it was believed the airmen had landed on an ice floe, The official announcement said faint radio signals had been heard which were thought to be from the plane, the faintness taken as indicating it was down on ice, Three fliers w

SHANGHAI, China, Sunday: (UP)—Chinese threatened today to renew aerial attacks on warships of the Japanese third battle fleet lying on the waterfront. The threat again threw the international settlement into confusion. Scores of fires raged throughout the city in the wake of the thunderous aerial bombardment yesterday, in which many foreigners, including three Americans, were killed. It appeared that huge Chinese armies south of the city were determined to destroy the foreign area, unless the United States, British, and other officials of the international settlement yield to China's demand that all Japanese armed forces and warships be withdrawn immediately from the foreign controlled areas and their vicinity. Ask Equal Rights The Chinese contend that if Japanese are permitted to use the international settlement as a basis for military operations, they must have and will exercise the sa
HANOVER, Germany, Aug. 13.—(®)—Eight mechanics and engineers were killed here today when a German three-engined plane crashed and burst into flames while on a test flight from the local airdrome.

BY MORRIS J. HARRIS SHANGHAI, Aug. 15.—(Sunday)—(P)—A Chinese typhoon today swallowed the war horrors of Shanghai where Chinese air bombs killed 836 civilians, including three Americans, and injured at least 1,140 in this teeming international city. Police of the international quarter said 40 foreigners were among the dead, but that a complete check had not been completed. Japanese naval guns thundered—spasmodically from ships anchored in the Whangpoo river and machine guns rattled an answer in isolated sections. Otherwise blood-soaked peace settled on the stricken city, heaped with the broken bodies of bombing victims and its hospitals crowded with suffering wounded. Tension in the international quarter, scene of the worst carnage in Saturday’s tragic aerial attack, seemed relieved as heavy wind and rain swept in from the sea. Extremely poor visibility seemed to allay fears of any immed

Tokyo, Aug. 15.—-(Sunday)——(/)—After a three-hour cabinet session the Japanese government early today asserted that latest developments in China, including those in the Shanghai area, made it necessary for Japanese authorities to resort to “firm, resolute measures.” These measures would be taken to make the Nanking government and the Kuomintang effectively reconsider past positions, the statement said. (The Kuomintang is the national people’s party of China.) Japanese authorities said they did not intend any harm to the Chinese masses in general and that their aim was still for cooperation between China, Manchoukuo and Japan, Kawai Grieves Tatsuo Kawai, a foreign office spokesman, expressed “horror and distress” over the Shanghai bombing, in which hundreds were killed. He said the foreign office had learned the Chinese government had warned all foreigners except Japanese to evacuate the

HENDAYE, Franco-Spanish Frontier, Sunday, Aug. 15. (U.P)—General Francisco Franco’s northern Insurgent armies opened a smashing offensive against Santander, last stronghold of the Basque republic, early today. Nationalist reports said the Insurgents column broke the government lines in two places, the Insurgents driving through north of Palencia and occupying the towns of Queto, Puentevaldeceboila and Sabedilla, and the northern part of Castilloval de Lamar. A radio communique from Salamanca said the Nationalist troops smashed through outer Basque entrenchments along the Santander front, capturing 500 prisoners, including officers, and seized much war material. Losses on the government side were tremendous, the report said. The attack was led by the famous “Black Flame” division, which struck from the Sancillo and Valdecebolla sectors, about 69 kilometers from Santander.

WASHINGTON, Aug. 14—(AP)—Senate judiciary committee members forecast today the committee would vote Monday to approve the nomination of Senator Black (D-Ala.) to the supreme court—although there were telegraphed protests and demand for delay. Senator Burke (D-Neb.) one of the few publicly committed opponents of confirmation, predicted the committee majority would override objections Monday and recommend that the senate approve President Roosevelt's nomination of the liberal Alabama Democratic senator. Opponents of the nomination could delay action on the senate floor as long as they wanted, but in view of the adjournment fever, many believed the confirmation would be voted after a brief flurry of debate. A check-up of the judiciary committee members disclosed a line-up of ten to three for the Alabaman, with four senators still publicly uncommitted. Members of the committee said the teleg

1937-04-14.text: (By Associated Press) Italian Fascists pointedly disparaging Great Britain's sea strength advised Spanish insurgent warships to sink “enemy” vessels indiscriminately. Coupled with growing insistence by British ship owners that their cargo vessels be protected within Spanish territorial waters, informed sources feared the Italian jibe might have considerable importance. A semi-official Italian Fascist paper taunted Britannia for being able no longer even to protect her own shipping. Charging Britain was “competing with France and Russia” in supplying the Spanish government forces, the paper urged insurgents “to have no nervousness in launching torpedoes and sinking enemy ships.” Conservative ship owners and labor leaders joined forces in London against Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin's cabinet which assured the British Union Jack protection up to but not beyond Spanish territorial waters.

London, April 14 (4P)—Conservative shipowners and labor party leaders massed their opposition against the Baldwin cabinet today in an effort to force the British government to guarantee protection to British merchantmen in Spanish waters. The move to bring out in the open the opposition to the government’s handling of the Spanish civil war came as Insurgent Generalissimo Francisco Franco disclosed further plans to menace shipping by mine laying along the coast. The formal motion of censure, offered by Opposition Leader Maj. Clement Attlee in a bitter denunciation of the government, was designed to open up for debate not only the stand Premier Stanley Baldwin's cabinet has taken on the Bilbao incident but the government's conduct of efforts to isolate the Spanish civil war. Baldwin, backed by Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden, decided to defend the government's policy from the attack in parl

London, April 14 (UP)—The opposition, seeking to force Premier Stanley Baldwin’s government to extend its protection of British shipping in Spanish waters, moved a vote of censure in the House of Commons today. The House was packed as Major Clement R. Attlee, labor leader, moved the vote. The diplomatic gallery was crowded, including the ambassadors of Argentina, Belgium, Poland, Russia, Spain and Czechoslovakia. It was a full debate, with the oratorical guns of the three big parties — conservatives, labor and liberal — taking part.

LONDON, April 14—(UP)—The government, defending itself against opposition attack, informed the House of Commons today that it had just warned Gen. Francisco Franco, Spanish rebel chief, that it would not tolerate interference with British shipping. Sir John Simon, Home Secretary, speaking for the government, disclosed that despite the government's decision to warn British ships not to jeopardize themselves by risking the mined approaches to Bilbao, Spain, "the government within the last few hours has communicated directly with France intimating that we refused to recognize the belligerent rights (of the rebels) or tolerate interference with British shipping."

Berbera, British Somaliland, April 14. ()—Stories of terrorism and hardship under Italian rule were told by more than a thousand refugees who fled across the border from Ethiopia. Spokesmen for the refugees said thousands of Ethiopians all over the conquered country died in Italian reprisals after natives wounded Viceroy Rodolfo Graziani last February in an attempt on his life. Among the fugitives were many women and children and some wounded men. Their leaders said Ethiopian natives were living in terror of the Italian colonial rule, in constant fear of frequent raids on farms and numerous executions.

London, April 14—Warships of five nations riding the choppy waters of the Bay of Biscay last night brought closer menace of an international incident which might explode international hatreds caused by the Spanish civil war. Mightiest of all was the British battle cruiser Hood, biggest in the world. It poked its 15-inch guns toward the loyalist seaport of Bilbao - where Gen. Francisco Franco's naval blockade threatens thousands of Basques with starvation. Germany sent two cruisers. Norway sent a mine-layer. France patrolled the three-mile limit with sleek destroyers and the Spanish rebels strung a barrier across Bilbao Harbor with a battleship, three cruisers and numerous armed trawlers. The Bilbao blockade—and Britain's decision to give it virtual recognition—engulfed British statesmen in a bitter political feud. Labor Party leaders, the official opposition in Parliament, decided to mov

Oshawa, Ont., April 14—(Canadian Press)—Mayor Alex Hall, acting on his own initiative, telegraphed an “ultimatum” today to United Automobile Workers union officials demanding United States workers of General Motors be called out on strike unless the Canadian motor strike is speedily settled. The dapper young mayor, a supporter of the walkout from the big General Motors plant here by the union affiliated with John L. Lewis’ Committee for Industrial Organization, said if his “ultimatum” is ignored he would advise Canadian workers to abandon unionism. His telegram—sent on the seventh day of the strike of 3,700 workers, in which negotiations are deadlocked—was addressed to Homer Martin, Detroit, president of the CIO union. “The Oshawa Strike,” Mayor Hall wired, “is going into its second week. Negotiations deadlocked on internal union issue. Oshawa workmen lost time during January in the Unit

TORONTO, Ont., (UP).—Premier Mitchell F. Hepburn has requested the resignations of David A. Croll, Ontario minister of labor, and Attorney General Arthur W. Roebuck, it was announced today. The request was an outgrowth of the premier’s demand that his cabinet “be solidly behind me” in his reaction to the General Motors of Canada strike at Oshawa. Croll and Roebuck opposed Hepburn's fight “against the forces of John L. Lewis, C. I. O. chairman, and Communism which are marching hand in hand.”

1937-03-11.text: | Staggering Blow To Madrid LONDON, March 9. ~ Spanish government officials anxiously sought today to learn the fate of the crew and passengers, reported to include two Americans, aboard the mystery freighter Mar Cantabrico when the crashing guns of an insurgent cruiser sent her to the bottom of the Bay of Biscay. 'It was believed all aboard the freighter which carried “huge quantities of war stores” for the Spanish government had been picked up by the cruiser Canarias after they leaped into a pounding sea, lighted by the blazing hulk last night. The British destroyer Echo reported to the admiralty here the Mar Cantabrico’s “crew are aboard the Canarias.” Cargo Worth $2,700,000 Although the message was taken to mean that some 40 men under Capt. Joe Santa Maria had been saved from a watery grave, their fate at the hands of their captors was unpredictable. Aboard the Spanish government fre

LONDON, March 11 — (P) — Sir Samuel Hoare, First Lord of the Admiralty, told the House of Commons today that Great Britain, by the end of the year, “will have under construction the remarkable number of 148 new warships.” Sir Samuel introduced the 1937 naval estimates. These call for 60 more new ships to cost $525,325,000. With the ships already started, these will bring the total to be under construction by the end of 1937 to 148, he said.

LONDON, March 11,—(UP)—Sir Samuel Hoare, first lord of the admiralty, in announcing the new naval estimates in the house of commons today, said the house is asked to vote more than 100,000,000 pounds ($500,000,000) and approve the construction of 80 new warships, bringing the total under construction by the end of the year to 148. “We are forced to telescope into two or three years what ought normally to be carried out in a decade,” Sir Samuel said.

LONDON, March 10.—(UP)—Britain is prepared to support a plan to guarantee Belgium's neutrality in event of a new European war, diplomats understood tonight. The scheme, which was discussed at today’s cabinet meeting, would provide that: 1. Belgian air fields would be available to the British air force in event of an emergency. 2. The British armed forces would have the right to supervise sound detectors strategically scattered along Belgian land frontiers to reveal the approach of hostile aircraft. 3. Certain arrangements would be made for disembarking British expeditionary forces at Belgian ports if desired. The scheme envisages transformation of the existing French-British-Belgian defensive military alliance into a guarantee of Belgium’s neutrality by Britain, France and Germany.

Washington, March 11. — The Committee for Industrial Organization will recommend to the forthcoming world textile conference an international agreement regulating working hours of employees in textile mills throughout the world, it was learned today. Great Britain, France, Belgium and Czechoslovakia already have indicated that they would be represented at the meetings scheduled to open here April 2. Officials said Germany was not expected to send a representative. The CIO, now working on preliminary plans for union organization campaigns in the cotton mills of the South and the rayon and woolen centers of the East and New England, was said to believe that it would be futile to recommend establishment of an international minimum wage because of the differences in money and labor costs throughout the world. But the labor organization was reported to feel that much could be accomplished if

(By The Associated Press) Irthlingborough, Eng., Mar. 11.—With the shouts of 300 girl laundry workers—‘We want Ernie’—ringing in their ears, union and company officials of a local laundry tried today to settle the absorbing question of where Ernie Greasley was going to go. His employers thought a promotion for Ernie as foreman of another plant would be nice. The girls, however, insisted they would strike unless Ernie, he is “Clark Gable” to them, was left at his present post. “Negotiations,” officials said, “are in a delicate state.” Adding to their delicacy was the incessant chant of the girls, whose admiration drove Ernie into hiding: “Do not give in, we know what we want. We want Ernie!”

SAN FRANCISCO, March 11.— Five ships were in distress today in Pacific waters. One vessel sank off the California coast after a collision with another ship; a Chinese steamer went aground at the southern end of Formosa; a British motorship was afire off Honolulu, and an oil tanker was aground at the entrance of San Francisco Bay after a collision with the Dollar liner President Coolidge. The trawler Normandie, from San Francisco, sank after a collision with the motor freighter Alamer when 11 miles off Humboldt Bar, off the Northern California coast. The Normandie’s crew of 10 was rescued by a fishing boat. The British motorship Silverlarch radioed the Coast Guard at Honolulu that a fire in its No. 3 hold was under control and that immediate assistance was not needed. The ship sailed March 4 from San Pedro, Calif., for Manila. Globe wireless reported the Chinese steamer Hopsang went agrou

MADRID, March 10 (4)—Veteran troops, hurled into the breach to smother an insurgent advance through Guadalajara province, stood their ground today, the government reported. After two days of admitted reverses, war office communiques declared the defense line now was holding and vulnerable gaps in it had been closed. Tanks, armored cars and a few artillery units, pushed to the newly developed battlefront northeast of Madrid last night by Gen. Jose Miaja, commander of all government troops in central Spain who spent the day touring the front lines, were said to have bolstered the resistance.

1937-10-02.text: LONDON (UP).—Soviet Russia demanded in a note to the Spanish non-intervention committee today that the Spanish Loyalists be accorded the right to buy arms openly abroad and to receive volunteers from abroad. France, in a note delivered at the same time, cited her views on the Spanish non-intervention situation and was believed to have intimated strongly that action is needed to end breaches of the neutrality agreement. It was assumed that both notes were timed to coincide with the expected delivery to Italy this weekend of a British-French invitation to discuss withdrawal of foreign volunteers from Spain—an invitation that is to be supplemented privately by a warning that if Italian troops remain in Spain, the French frontier will be opened for the flow of men and arms to the Loyalists.

By The Associated Press. Jerusalem, Oct. 1—British authorities swept down on Arab leaders in Palestine today in a coup designed to crush the Holy Land's long months of terrorism. Several high Arab leaders were arrested and held for deportation.

PARIS, Oct. 2.—A sharp break in the franc today brought a lengthy statement from the French cabinet that France's financial condition was sound and that any weakness in the currency was due to speculation induced by world unrest. In London, the Franc, barometer of France’s fortunes, dropped from 144.50 to 151.50 to the pound ($.0326) as the foreign onslaught on French currency continued. The statement of Premier Camille Chautemps’ cabinet followed an extended conference of the ministers with President Albert Lebrun at the presidential summer palace at Rambouillet. It did not indicate what specific measures the government would take to strengthen the franc other than that there would be no foreign exchange control.

SHANGHAI (UP). Chinese defenders of Shanghai sent back word from their pillbox trenches they were holding their own along the Shanghai front and counter-attacking Japanese in some sectors. They told of routing Japanese troops in the vicinity of Kiangwan, north of Shanghai. Japanese admitted the Kiangwan civic center buildings had been evacuated, but said their lines to the rear were unchanged. When skies cleared during the evening, Chinese planes roared over Shanghai in a reconnaissance flight. Japanese anti-aircraft guns blasted at the fliers apparently without effect. Shell fragments fell into the international settlement. Japanese bombardment of Hankow and the Hankow-Canton railway Sept. 25 drew sharp condemnation from Rear Admiral Harry Yarnell, commander of the U.S. Asiatic fleet. The admiral branded as erroneous a Japanese spokesman’s statement Ambassador Nelson T. Johnson had advi

Hendaye, Franco-Spanish Frontier —(®— The ancient village of Covadonga, sacred to patriotic Asturians as the burial place of their first king, was reported today to have capitulated to the thrust of a Twentieth century war machine. The village, 12 miles inland from the Bay of Biscay and some 30 air miles southeast of Gijon, was the extreme eastern end of the Asturian defense line against which a Spanish insurgent army has been hammering for weeks. The daily insurgent communique reported Navarrese troops swept across ridges and through villages of eastern Oviedo province yesterday, north of Covadonga, and then after heavy fighting took the town. The insurgent high command admitted the Asturians put up a fierce resistance but said they were overpowered by artillery and bombing planes. Within Covadonga the fighting was heaviest around the Sixteenth century abbey and church of La Virgen de l

Moscow, Oct. 2—()—Abdullah Rakhimaieff, premier of the Soviet Republic of Tadjikistan and chairman of the central executive committee of the U. S. S. R., was removed today as a “spy of a foreign Fascist country.” Treason charges were brought against Rakhimaieff, President Shirinsho Shotemor and three commissars of Tadjikistan in a drive on anti-Soviet separatist movements. Disclosure of the charges left no doubt that all five were under arrest. Removal of Rakhimaieff, who had a harem of three wives, was a foregone conclusion after Pravda, the Communist Party newspaper, denounced him recently as a Bourgeois Nationalist “who sold himself to the intelligence service of a neighboring foreign state.” Executions again were reported from several places in the provinces.
