, PARIS, Oct 2.—(U.P)—The cabinet, after a three-hour meeting on the financial situation today, issued a formal declaration asserting that the position was sound and that therefore there was no basis for heaviness of the franc exchange or for speculation of the franc. Coincidently the cabinet announced six resolutions providing measures to deal with the situation. The resolutions are: 1. To oppose firmly all foreign exchange control and to maintain the principles involved in the French-American-British (tripartite) monetary agreement. 2. To continue a policy of peace, trying with Great Britain to obtain effective non-intervention in Spain and at the same time defending the vital interests of France fully. 3. Authorizing Premier Camille Chautemps to issue decrees to increase production by taking measures to modify the 40-hour working week laws. 4. Appealing to workers and employers to ref

TOKYO, (4P)—Japanese secret service men and Tokyo criminologists began an investigation today of the theory that the mysterious creeping death plague in Fukuoka prefecture was the work of a human germ spreader. The plague, spreading rapidly, already has killed more than 800 persons since Monday and caused the serious illness of 6,789. A majority of the dead were children.

1937-10-23.text: LONDON (U.P.) — Hope for agreement on withdrawal of foreign volunteers from the Spanish civil war was all but abandoned Saturday. Well informed quarters predicted that either the powers must be content to let the Civil war drag on to exhaustion or definitive victory, or they must find a way to mediate between the rebels and loyalists. It was feared that at a meeting of the chairman’s sub-committee of the Spanish non-intervention committee Tuesday, delegates of the nine powers represented must agree to refer the entire volunteer problem back to the main committee with the confession that they were deadlocked. That would mean in effect the collapse of withdrawal efforts. Sub-committee negotiations reached an impasse Friday when Russia refused to agree to a “token” withdrawal of volunteers based on repatriating an equal number of men from each side, rebel and loyalist, and Italy refused to

LONDON, Oct. 20.—The Evening Standard’s diplomatic correspondent reported “authoritatively” from Rome today that Premier Benito Mussolini had agreed at the last moment to withdrawal of foreign volunteers from Spain, in order to break the deadlock in the non-intervention committee. LONDON, Oct. 20.—Italy is ready to accept creation of a Spanish mission to solve the volunteer questions, Dino Grandi, Italian ambassador, informed the sub-committee of the non-intervention powers today. At the afternoon meeting of the sub-committee, which opened in a pessimistic atmosphere, Grandi announced that Italy accepted without reservations British plans for a definition of belligerent rights. The alternative to some agreement this afternoon was expected to be an adjournment without date of re-meeting of the chairman's sub-committee. This is what happened last August 6 when a break was imminent. But thi

IGHAT, (AP)—A Chinese spokesman declared to Chinese troops, attacking in concert on many fronts, that the battle for the mastery of Shanghai had taken a turn from the Japanese and were threatening to cut their advancing forces. Determined to save Tazang and their supply lines to the northern border of the International Settlement, the forces of Chinese moved throughout last night to a sector 12 miles to the northwest, where the fiercest fighting was in progress. By five different routes the Chinese were converging on Japanese troop bases to the rear of Wentsaopang Creek, and claimed capture of five villages. Japanese claims of further progress toward Tazang were partly substantiated by American military observers who said they spotted machine gun and rifle fire from Chinese defenses on the outskirts of the town. They placed the main body of Japanese at more than a mile away. Both Chinese

By The Associated Press. Hendaye, France-Spain Frontier, Ort. 22.—Generalissimo Francisco Franco, armed with more complete power than ever before as dictator of Insurgent Spain, today turned his attention from the conquered Northwest to the vital Eastern fronts. While the two-thirds of Spain under his control celebrated the fall of Gijon and collapse of Government resistance in the Northwest, Franco tightened his hold on the reins. It was disclosed that the decree setting up the Fascist National Council gave Franco the right to secretly name his own successor as dictator of Spain. It provided that all executive power shall be exercised by Franco and his ministers, ten of whom he is expected to name shortly. Insurgent officers said the greater part of nearly 100,000 Insurgent troops who have been fighting in Asturias would be transferred soon to the Aragon and Madrid fronts. Only small fo

Moscow — (4) — Twelve more death sentences were reported today in the Soviet rural regions, Under the recent decree providing longer prison terms for so-called wreckers, courts have been imposing more prison sentences.

SHANGHAI Oct. 22—Chinese and neutral sources reported tonight that Japan is withdrawing troops in large numbers from Chinese fronts to meet a new threat of a dangerous uprising in Manchuria. Thirteen Japanese troop trains reportedly left Tientsin for Mukden and Kwantung. Army leaders are said to have informed the Japanese command in North China they could provide no further help for Japan's conquests below the Great Wall. Dispatches from Peking and Tientsin indicated Japanese troops are being pulled off North China fronts in large numbers, although no reason was assigned. In Nanking, both Chinese and foreign sources said the situation in Manchoukuo, brewing with threats of trouble for several weeks, is becoming critical. Any serious uprising in Manchoukuo would leave Japan's important northern Asiatic frontier vulnerable to a Soviet attack. None of the reports was confirmed by Japanese s

| PORT COQUITLAM, B. C., Oct. 23,—A brown and white springer spaniel was credited today with saving the lives of three persons in a boating accident which claimed four victims at Pitt Lake, 10 miles north of here. Three men and a four-year-old girl were drowned when Emil Anderson's 12-foot boat overturned with its eight occupants and sank. Yesterday, Anderson clutched the dog as he struck water and was towed ashore. Anderson seized five-year-old Jacqueline Hayes and pulled her to safety with him. “Bunnie,” the spaniel, swam back to where the others struggled in 10 feet of water. He was clutched by Mrs. Harold Raulty, whom he towed to shallow water and safety. In a launch, Cliff Thompson, a logger, rescued Mrs. Robert Hayes, mother of Jacqueline. None of the party could swim the 20 feet to shallow water.

BORDEAUX, France, Oct. 23. (U.P) — Nationalist airplanes bombed and sank the Spanish Loyalist destroyer Ciscar and about 40 smaller vessels were captured or sunk while attempting to flee from Gijon, it was charged today. Thirty-eight sailors from the Ciscar arrived aboard the Spanish steamer Pluto and described the Nationalist aerial attack on the vessel and a Loyalist submarine during the confusion of the mass exodus from northern Spain of more than 7,000 refugees. The sailors were believed to be the last to leave Gijon before the Nationalists entered the city and checked the wholesale evacuation.

1937-01-03.text: ROME, Jan. 2—(4)—Great Britain and Italy signed a pledge today to respect each other's rights in the Mediterranean — high road to Britain’s empire and key to naval defense of the Italian peninsula. A brief communique announced the agreement, centering on these objectives: (1)—Furtherance of good relations to peace between the two nations, (2)—Respect for rights of other nations in the Mediterranean. (3)—Continuance of existing British and Italian positions in the Mediterranean and liberty of navigation, Signed by Count Ciano The communique stated tersely that the document was signed in the Chigi palace by Count Galeazzo Ciano, Italian foreign minister and son-in-law of Premier Mussolini, and Sir Eric Drummond, British ambassador to Rome. Thus Italy, worried lest her power in the Mediterranean be challenged ever since Britain took the lead in invoking sanctions during the Ethiopian campai

London — (4) — London’s most famous burglar—the elusive “Flannel Foot”—had a new price on his capture Saturday and a new reason to chuckle at the law. To the policeman who can bring in Flannel Foot goes $50 and a two weeks’ holiday—the first time Scotland Yard has resorted to such a means to encourage its men in pursuit of a public enemy. It's a tribute to Flannel Foot’s ingenuity: to the desperation of one of the grimmest organizations in the world. For years now Flannel Foot has burgled his way in and out of London suburban homes. For years he has tormented the police. He telephones them when he takes a holiday. He telephones them when he returns—ready to work. There are hundreds of pages of memorandums about him in Scotland Yard. There is a large map covered with cotton strings to show his activities. No ordinary burglar—Flannel Foot uses strips of flannel around his shoes. He works e

PARIS, Jan. 2— (4) —German attack against a Spanish government freighter followed by the shelling of a French ship by Spanish fascists roused official quarters here tonight to grave concern lest the peace of Europe be disturbed. ) The Valencia socialist government declared it was prepared to “reply in fitting manner” to shelling of the freighter Soton by a Nazi warship and termed the attack an “act of war.” Basque authorities at Bilbao ordered warships to fire on German ships or ships of any other nation if the attacks were repeated. The French foreign office pressed diplomatic and consular representatives in Spain for full reports on shelling of the French vessel by three insurgent trawlers. (The German government followed its announcement the Soton had been shelled and the Spanish freighter Aragon captured with the declaration such measures would be continued.) The French merchant vess

BERLIN, Jan. 2.—The German government tonight followed up its announcement that German warships have taken drastic action against two Spanish vessels with a flat declaration that such measures would be continued although the Spanish Basque regime at Bilbao regards them as “acts of war.” The ministry of propaganda announced German warships already had “retaliated” against two Spanish steamers for the recent seizure of the German freighter Palos by the Bilbao regime. The pocket battleship Grafe Spee had seized the Spanish freighter Aragon and forced it into an undisclosed Spanish insurgent port, it was announced. The cruiser Koenigsberg with shell fire had driven the freighter Soton aground on the coast. Nazis further were irritated tonight by a Salamanca report of the shooting of a German, Lothar Guedde, who was sentenced to death by a Bilbao court Dec. 30, allegedly for Fascist activity.

ANDO, Vall. a. ade Basque government warned Germany Saturday night that shellfire will answer any new attempt to interfere with Spanish socialist merchant ships. Provoked by attack against the Spanish freighter Soton by the German warship Koenigsberg, the autonomous Spanish regime invoked the order "to uphold the dignity of the Basque republic." Patrol boats in the Bay of Biscay area were ordered to fire on any vessel of any nation attacking Spanish merchantmen. The Basques charged German warships were being harbored at Guetaria, a coastal city near Bilbao and San Sebastián. "The Basque government is not also opposed to permit any German interference violating international law and has given orders for the most extreme measures if necessary, fully realizing what may be the international repercussions of these measures," the official announcement said. Mellon, secretary of the Treasury in the Hoover administration, had offered his $19,000,000 art collection to the government and that President Roosevelt would recommend that Congress accept it. Correspondence between the President and the Pittsburgh multi-millionaire disclosed that Mellon also had offered to build at his own expense an $8,000,000 or $9,000,000 "National Gallery of Art" here to house his famous collection and other art treasures. Mellon and administration officials have been sharply at odds in the past over the proposed gift and other matters. In a suit which the United States Board of Tax Appeals now has under advisement, the government has sought to collect $3,075,102 from the former Treasury chief as back taxes and penalties. This exceeded the $750,000,000 Harry L. Hopkins, Works Progress administrator, is un- made known that he was looking into the idea of transferring funds from some other source to augment this $850,000,000, A bulky report was left at the White House by Paul Betors, secretary of the mayors’ conference, whose members had surveyed relief conditions in 100 major cities, Basing its estimate on an average pay of $63 a month, the report said $877,500,000

BOLLYWOOD, Cal., Jan. 2, (AP) — Ross Alexander, wisecracking young film actor, was found dead in the barn back of his home in Van Nuys tonight. His wife of six months, the former Anne Nagel, film actress, said she believed he committed suicide. She was too hysterical to talk coherently. But a maid said, “Between 7:30 and 8:30 tonight, Mr. Alexander took his pistol and went out to the barn. He said he was going to kill a duck. We heard a shot. And then he did not come back.” The pistol was found beside the actor’s body. Alexander's first wife, Aleta Fricle, a stage actress, committed suicide about a year ago. Six months later, he married Miss Nagel, a newcomer to the movies.

1937-07-19.text: | Wimbledon, England, July 19, (UP)—The United States ran up a 2-1 lead over Germany in the interzone final Davis Cup series today when Don Budge and Gene Mako defeated Baron Gottfried Von Cramm and Henner Henkel in the doubles match, 4-6, 7-5, 8-6, 6-4. The doubles victory put the United States within one point of gaining the right to challenge England for possession of the historic trophy which has been held on this side of the Atlantic for ten years. In the first of tomorrow’s two final singles matches, Byran (Bitsy) Grant will play Henkel and in the second one Budge will play Van Cramm. The match was one of the most thrilling in Davis Cup history and was marked by brilliant comebacks by the U. S. forces. Particularly was this true of the fourth and final set in which the Americans lost three consecutive games at love, including a service break against Mako, and trailed one game to fo

LONDON (#)—The admiralty announced Sunday that the British famous as a blockade runner under the name of Seven Seas Spray, had been “captured by an Insurgent warship inside Spanish territorial waters.” A few hours after the merchantman’s capture Saturday morning, the British battleship Royal Oak and the destroyer Basilisk sailed from St. Jean de Luz, France. The Basilisk had been under orders to leave Spanish waters Saturday night, but at 4:45 p. m. she received orders to sail immediately. At 5:45 the destroyer started off in the direction of the Spanish coast at full speed. The Royal Oak left just as suddenly at 8 p. m. Saturday, while five of her officers were ashore. This group took a speedboat and overtook the battleship. Officers at St. Jean de Luz expressed belief these movements were connected with the capture of the Candleston Castle, but in London an admiralty spokesman said, “w

London, July 19.—In stinging words that left no doubt of his meaning, British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden today told Premier Mussolini to keep his hands off British interests in the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. The strongest language that any British cabinet officer has used in the House of Commons for many years was employed by the youthful foreign secretary in stressing Britain’s determination to preserve her colonial sovereignty. He made it abundantly clear that the government is prepared to go the limit should her interests be endangered and repudiated the frequent Italian charges that Britain is seeking “revenge” for her humiliation by Mussolini in the conquest of Ethiopia.

LONDON, July 19. U.P)—British sources indicated today that no action would be taken by Britain over the seizure of the English steamer Candleston Castle in Spanish territorial waters. The Admiralty announced yesterday that several Insurgent warships captured the Candleston Castle and were understood to be taking it to the Insurgent port of El Ferrol. It was the second capture of a British ship by Insurgents within a week but no protest will be made, since British ships have been warned that they enter Spanish waters at their own risk.

TOKYO, (AP).—A Donei (Japanese) news agency dispatch from Tientsin tonight said the Japanese army commander had served a virtual ultimatum on the Chinese military declaring it would “take independent action” unless all Chinese firing against Japanese ceased immediately. This threat followed a renewal of fighting in the zone west of Peiping where Japanese and Chinese troops had been in intermittent conflict since July 7. Japanese military forces said Chinese soldiers making a concrete pillbox near Lukuochiao fired on a Japanese detachment, gravely wounding a Japanese captain. The attitude of the Japanese command was described in dispatches as the most determined it has yet assumed in the North China crisis. Its grim notice to the Chinese was said to declare that unless all Chinese firing ceased the Japanese would begin action Tuesday, presumably any time after midnight, (11 a.m. Monday E.

MADRID, July 19.—(WUP)—Na- tionalist and loyalist armies, the pick of men from many nations who are fighting in the Spanish civil war, fought today with every means of warfare from airplane to trench knives and fists the most savage battle, the biggest and probably the most important in a nightmare year of struggle. Sixteen miles west of the capital the nationalists, gambling all they had, were trying for the third day to take back the positions they had lost in a loyalist offensive. Attack in 3 Sectors. After a night in which the roar of gunfire and the flash from gun muzzles gave no chance for rest, they attacked furiously again to be in three sectors west of the capital, Brunete, Villanuevo Del Pardillo and Quijorna. The reply, while expressing willingness to retire central government troops from Hopei province, reiterated Nanking’s insistence on assuming authority over local northern affairs, destruction of which has been Japan's principal objective. MADRID, July 19.—Sixteen miles west of Madrid, the pick of the nationalist and loyalist armies fought out today with every arm of warfare from airplanes to trench knives and fists the most savage and probably the most important battle of the civil war. Sources close to the general staff estimated that between 5,000 and 7,000 men of both armies were wounded or killed yesterday. Red Cross ambulances fought for space on the road back to Madrid with men and truckloads of material on the way to the front. Hospitals here were filling fast. The operation was a desperate nationalist counter-attack intended to throw the loyalists out of the deep salient they cut southward into the insurgent lines in the Brunete area west of the capital. The loyalists were forewarned and were prepared. Loyalist leaders asserted their confidence that their lines would hold. If they break the attack, the siege of Ma

China's “open door” will be slammed shut against American, British and French commerce when this is accomplished, but the process will be gradual, and accompanied in constant Japanese protestations to the contrary. Japan's strategy, it was revealed by the unimpeachable authority, is to capture and occupy by military force all of China's coastline, from the extreme north down to Indo-China in the south, past Britain's stronghold at Hongkong. Thus, by controlling the lengthy coastal plain, Japan would cut off the Chinese government and military forces from all sources of supply. PEEBLES, Scotland, Dec. 18, P— Mrs. Helen Buchan, mother of Baron Tweedsmuir, Governor-General of Canada, died today. Before his elevation to the peerage, Lord Tweedsmuir was John Buchan, noted writer.

London, Dec. 18.—Alarmed at the Japanese advance toward South China in the vicinity of Britain’s crown colony and naval base at Hong Kong, the British government today moved rapidly to take drastic precautionary measures. International News Service learned that the government has launched preparations for dispatching a “substantial naval squadron” to Hong Kong. British authorities, it was revealed, have decided that Britain must act alone, irrespective of American cooperation, if there is any further serious threat against British interests in China, especially at Hong Kong, or any more attacks are registered against British warships.

London, Dec. 17.—(/P)—Great Britain looked to the defense of her Far Eastern possessions tonight as reports indicated Japan's undeclared war against China soon might be extended to the south. A high diplomatic source predicted an increase in British naval strength in Chinese waters "by early in January" with or without the United States taking parallel action.

BULLETIN, Tokio.--(P)-Emperor Hirohito tonight received a detailed report on the sinking of the United States gunboat Panay from Premier Prince Fumimaro Konoye. News of the premier’s action, in an unusual step in the Japanese system, lent weight to reports that some expression concerning the Panay affair might come from the emperor, Tokio.--(P) The Japanese foreign office disclosed today that United States Ambassador Joseph C. Grew had delivered a second American note in connection with the sinking of the gunboat Panay. The nature of the new representations was not made known, but they were reliably understood to concern reports that the Yangtze river patrol ship had been machine gunned by Japanese launches before it sank under the pounding of aerial bombs last Sunday. The naval court hoped to complete its investigation before the United States cruiser Augusta, flagship of Admiral Harry E. Yarnell, commander of the United States fleet in Chinese waters, sails for Manila tomorrow. Naval officials aboard the Augusta said they were informed a Japanese officer had boarded the Panay seeking information when the gunboat was 10 miles down the river from the scene of attack. They said, however, the officer’s call had no connection with the bombing. Armed Japanese troops boarded the Panay under protection of a field gun which was trained on her and questioned Lieut. Comdr. James J. Hughes, her commanding officer. It was announced today that the United States Cruiser Augusta, flagship of Admiral Harry E. Yarnell, American navy commander in chief in Chinese waters, would leave for Manila tomorrow on the first tide. Had it not been for the Panay attack, he would have gone Tuesday. ROME (P) -- Countess Edna Mussolini, daughter of the Italian Premier, today gave birth to her third son. He was named Marzio. The father, Foreign Minister Count Galeazzo Ciano, immediately informed Mussolini, who was overjoyed at the news. To the Italian masses the event meant that the Countess was showing herself a wife conforming to the big-family ideal of Fascism.

1937-12-05.text: The statement of policy undertaken as a result of the last two days’ developments in Shanghai including the “victory march” of Japanese forces through the International Settlement, was understood to have been called for after consultation with Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden. It was evident that government leaders regarded the Far Eastern developments as the most serious since the outbreak of the Chinese-Japanese war, despite the withdrawal of armed Japanese from the western defense zone in the International Settlement. Angry attacks upon the government’s handling of the situation are expected Tuesday when Eden faces questioners on the floors of the House of Commons. Laborites and liberals are expected to assail the government for continuing what they regard as “a policy of retreat since 1931” in dealing with foreign affairs. The attack on the government will be led by two powerful labori

LONDON, Dec. 4. (WP) — The Spanish Insurgent radio station at Salamanca warned neutral shipping tonight that the Insurgent navy would use “all means within its power” to prevent trading with Loyalist ports. Generalissimo Francisco Franco's navy had strung a blockade around Valencia, Barcelona and other Loyalist ports on the Spanish east coast. The warning, it was explained, was based on “the obvious reason of war” and also “the fact that those dealing with the red government make themselves accomplices to an iniquitous offense.”

WARSAW, Dec. 4.—(7)—A sudden snag in the Franco-Polish talks on a new collective security arrangement for Europe was reported authoritatively today to have "been hit even before the conversations began." While French Foreign Minister Yvon Delbos was entertained cordially by Polish statesmen, the French embassy staff worked behind the scenes with Polish officials to iron out the difference of opinion over the complex relations of Poland, Germany and Czechoslovakia. Delbos’ talk with Marshal Edward Rydz-Smigly, inspector of the Polish army, however, was considered a hopeful sign. The length of their conversation was taken to indicate the Franco-Polish military alliance had been strengthened. Authoritative reports from both French and Polish sources agreed France had insisted Poland's relations with Czechoslovakia be included in the discussion of ways toward general European peace. PARIS—Alexandre Barmine, former Russian charge d’affaires in Athens who fled to France and then resigned his post in defiance of orders to return to Moscow, asserted Saturday night that "paid killers" of the Soviet are following him around Paris. Barmine, a Russian diplomat since the days of the revolution, sent an imploring letter to the League for the Rights of Man, appealing for the protection of colleagues who, like himself, have disapproved of Dictator Joseph V. Stalin's purge. Friends of Barmine said that he was renouncing all diplomatic immunity to become a political refugee, and refused to reveal his hiding place. The League for the Rights of Man would not discuss his whereabouts or plans. Washington, Dec. 4,—(P)—The Senate wound up two weeks of wordy debate on the farm bill today by agreeing to limit future speechmaking on the measure. A substitute farm program proposed by Senator Lee (D. Okla.) was exempted from the delegate limitation agreement, after Lee had protested he had no opportunity for a full discussion of his measure. Lee’s bill differs from the pending agriculture committee measure in that it would be entirely voluntary. Democratic leaders expressed hope the committee bill would pass the Senate next week. May Go Back There was sentiment, however, for recommitting the bill to committee for further study. Some senators argued objections to the legislation raised by Secretary Wallace could be more expeditiously met by committee action. Middletown, Conn., Dec. 4.—(AP) Little Miss What’s-Her-Name was worth a fortune tonight, No one knew when it happened. No one knew why. But everyone knew she once was a penniless orphan, and was now, overnight, an heiress. Name Not Known Rockefeller millions lay in her lap, and the world didn’t know her name. She was the little blond girl at the Muriel McCormick Hubbard estate, a little blond girl too young to wonder why it should happen to her when there are thousands of orphans. She was the adopted great-granddaughter of the late John D. Rockefeller and a probable heiress to part of the McCormick reaper fortune as well. Everything will not turn to gold for the little blond girl, but most things will shine for her with a golden tint. Two things, oil and harvesters; two names, Rockefeller and McCormick, will see to that. (Continued on Page 7.)

MIAMI, Fla., Dec. 4.—(AP)— President Roosevelt started the first leg of a 1,450-mile trip back to Washington by sea and land today, interrupting a fishing cruise to return for dental treatment of a slow-healing gum. The vacationing chief executive deemed it advisable to cut three days from his southern journey in view of the delay in the closing of the wound where an infected ad was removed Nov. 18. Officials still insisted his general condition was good and that the early return was being made solely for the purpose of resuming treatments believed to have been sufficient when he left Washington on Nov. 27. A radio message from Secretary James Roosevelt said the yacht Potomac, with the president and his seven guests aboard, got under way for Miami at 1 p.m. today from the Dry Tortugas Islands, 300 miles southwest of here in the Gulf of Mexico. The white-moustached clerk, Francis Stephenson, at first presented his monarch’s preference for a woman over an empire, and determined to thwart him from carrying out his historic decision. He decided to stop the divorce which would make it possible, But today, touched by the plaintive note of former King Edward's farewell broadcast when he said, "I cannot continue to discharge my duties without the woman I love," the little, bespectacled clerk stepped aside from the affairs of state and cupid. He withdrew his objections and Sir Boyd Merriman, president of the British divorce court, formally dismissed the charge of “collusion,” a barr

NEW LONDON, Tex. Mar. 20 (UP) The latest tabulation of the New London explosion toll: Dead 425. Injured 125, of whom 48 remain in hospitals. Identified dead 415. Unidentified dead 3. Unidentifiable dead 7. In building at time of explosion approximately 900. Number who escaped unharmed 350.

(By the Associated Press) Injured—Estimated at 175. Cause—Still officially undetermined, but W. C. Shaw, superintendent, said it undoubtedly resulted from accumulated gas. Unusual Facts—The London Consolidated School was reputed to be the wealthiest rural school in the United States; located in the world’s greatest oil area; students attended from a 30-square-mile area; physicians said that nearly every victim died from a fractured skull; bodies were carried to towns within a 50-mile radius to be prepared for burial; martial law temporarily in force. Rescue Work—Workers, haggard by their grim toil, were hampered by a heavy rainstorm; Red Cross workers arrived, wet. Austin—Gov. James V. Allred sent expert investigators to the scene and ordered a military court of inquiry. The legislature adopted a resolution calling for a legislative investigation.

TYLER, Tex, (UP) — The Tyler Morning Telegraph said this morning that Capt. Zachriah Combs, judge advocate of the military court which will investigate the explosion at the New London school, had obtained evidence that the blast was caused by nitroglycerine. The military court began its hearing this morning. The newspaper said Capt. Combs’ information came from W. ob. Thompson and Jess Vaughn, oil field workers, who dug up two sections of sewer pipe from beneath the ruins of the schoolhouse. The pipes would indicate that the explosion occurred inside them, rather than above them, as they were forced outward and broken at the edges, the Morning Telegraph reported. Thompson and Vaughn were said to have advanced the theory that ten ounces of nitroglycerine flushed in the sewer would explode upon impact with the obstruction. Capt. Combs was reported to have told the men that their theory wou

NEW LONDON, March 19 (#)— Gas flares from the forest of oil derricks surrounding this city of sorrow cast into eerie relief tonight a scene of quiet strangely at contrast with the frenzied activity last night when a thousand men burrowed through wreckage seeking their dead, Exhaustion from a day and night of feverish labor kept some within their homes. Sorrow at home and sympathy for neighbors held many more. Scene Is Deserted. The shell of the New London Consolidated School building where 425 died yesterday in a disastrous explosion, lay silent, its steel and bricks and shards of tile scattered over a vast area as workers sought to rescue the living and found the dead, Occasional muffled sobs of anguished parents, most of them shut in their homes with their grief, broke the funeral quiet. Around the scene of the blast itself, where last night men groaned in anguish and tremendous labor,

NEW LONDON, Texas, March 20 —(UP)—Rosters of the dead will carry the names of two persons who were not even near the New London schoolhouse when it exploded. Mrs. Alma Stroud, 40, searched all night for her missing daughter, Helen, 16, who had been at the school. She found the child in a morgue at Overton and immediately fell dead of a heart attack. George L. Hardy, 63, was at Arp when he heard about the tragedy. He sped to New London, watched rescue workers bring bodies of children from the wreckage, and fell dead of shock.

1937-11-28.text: London, Nov. 27 (4)—Millions of Britons breathed moderately fresh air again tonight after three, choking days of a fog that was blamed for the loss of 12 lives. Before the fog—one of the heaviest in London's history lifted, the thick, soupy gloom had “blacked out” half of England, cutting visibility in many places to a scant two yards. There were scores of accidents as pedestrians made torches of newspapers to guide their way along the street. Oftentimes they formed chains as they grouped along the sidewalks. Buses ran behind schedule, or quit altogether. Trains generally were late. Automobiles were convoyed by flares. Three persons walked into water reservoirs and were drowned while several were saved from a similar fate. Several persons were injured at Nottingham station in falls from the platform because they were unable to see its edge. At sea, Trans-Atlantic liners wirelessed they w

mV The Associated Press LONDON—Great Britain today ordered her ambassador to Tokyo to inform Japan that Britain insisted on being consulted before any changes were made in the Chinese maritime customs. As British anxiety shifted from Europe to the Orient, some quarters suggested recent Japanese moves to take over the government of conquered Shanghai might lead Britain again to try to bring the United States into a joint British-French-American program.

PARIS, Nov. 27.—(U..)—The foreign office announced tonight, on the eve of Premier Camille Chautemps’ departure for London, that France refuses to sacrifice her military alliances in central Europe as the “price” of Germany’s collaboration toward a permanent peace. “France wishes to obtain relaxations in the international tension and to co-operate with all powers, but that does not mean she is ready to give up her ideals,” the foreign office spokesman said. “France does not regard it as timely to loosen her diplomatic ties, which threaten no one. Each people can have their own internal policy, but this does not prevent a joint foreign policy.” The announcement was a pointed warning to Fuehrer Adolf Hitler of Germany, and to the British statesmen who will confer with Premier Chautemps and Foreign Minister Yvon Delbos, that France will not give up her sources of military assistance for the

Hendaye, Franco-Spanish Frontier, Nov. 27 (4)—Spanish insurgent advices said tonight that Generalissimo Francisco Franco had sent the government an ultimatum demanding unconditional surrender before December 5. The advices said Franco threatened to launch a general drive, ready since November 10, if the government refused to accept his terms. Although the insurgent generalissimo declared yesterday that he would accept no armistice or compromise, authoritative sources said he had accorded a 25-day delay of his offensive in the hope that government capitulation might spare many lives. The nature of the government reply, if any, was not known, but the advices indicated there was little chance Franco's demands would be met. A general offensive was expected to begin next week on several fronts.

SHANGHAI, Nov. 27.—(U.P)—Japanese forces tonight slowly tightened a death grip on China’s main arteries, the great Yangtze and Whangpoo river valleys, through which flows the rich revenue-producing trade of the Orient. While Japanese authorities in Shanghai moved into possession of customs, telegraphs, telephone, and postal departments, the vanguard of the Japanese army was reported to have reached Wutsin and Thing, almost within artillery range of the capital at Nanking. A shortage of foreign food was reported in the capital. Take Over. Radio, a group of Japanese plainclothesmen and municipal police arrived at the Chinese government radio administration building to find the place deserted. Chinese personnel had removed all equipment. The Japanese embassy said that the work of taking over the customs and communications would be completed soon, adding, however, that it had been necessary

HENAYE, Franco-Spanish Frontier Nov 27 Q.A—The Spanish nationalist and loyalist regimes tonight rejected neutral efforts to bring about an armistice before Christmas and 500,000 troops moved up into advance positions along a 900-mile front. “WIN BY ARMS” Apparently in preparation for the nationalists’ long-heralded offensive that may be launched at any point along the curving front from Jaca to Almena, insurgent airplanes roared over enemy bases in Aragon on bombing and machine-gunning raids. Generalissimo Francisco Franco of the nationalists, in an announcement from his Burgos base in the north, said: “I will win this war by arms. There will be no mediation and no armistice. The enemy must surrender unconditionally.” “WE WILL FIGHT ON” Simultaneously Premier Juan Negrin of the loyalist government at Barcelona asserted: “We will fight on, firmly convinced that the final victory will be o

WASHINGTON, Nov. 27. (®)— President Roosevelt gave Congress a strong hint today that he wanted the cost of the new farm program held to half a billion dollars a year. In a letter to Senator Barkley, the Democratic leader, the president reinforced earlier budget-balancing statements with the emphatic assertion: "It is obvious that a constant increase of expenditures without an equally constant increase in revenue can only result in a continuation of deficits. Soundness Threatened "We can not hope to continue on a sound basis of financial management of government affairs unless the regular annual expenditures are brought within the revenues." Mr. Roosevelt said he felt "that every effort should be made" to keep spending under the new farm program within an already-voted $500,000,000 appropriation. But if this were impossible, he added, "I then urge that steps be taken to provide the necess

Washington, NOV. 2 (AP) — Secretary Hull, concerned for the future of China's commercial "open door," warned Japan today the United States could not look with equanimity on any attempt to tamper with the Chinese maritime customs system. Acting on his instructions, American Ambassador Joseph C. Grew formally notified the Tokyo foreign office the American government would be "very much concerned" if the Japanese conquerors of Shanghai and other parts of China disturbed the integrity of the Chinese customs service. The secretary of state announced also the State Department was maintaining close contact on the subject with other governments, some of whom, notably Great Britain, have lodged similar representations with the Japanese government. Fear Real Officials here did not attempt to disguise their growing anxiety over the possible consequences to American trade and financial investments i

1937-11-13.text: | BOULOGNE-SUR-MER, France— (P)—A runaway sausage balloon of the British Royal Air Force, trailing a cable across high tension wires, escaped pursuers today on its madcap course over northern France. The balloon, carrying thousands of dollars worth of meteorological instruments, cut high tension wires last night near Andruicq, causing a short circuit and setting the town's post office afire. The homes of an estimated 1,900,000 inhabitants of northern France were plunged into darkness. The balloon, which snapped its mooring at an airdrome near Ramsgate last night and crossed the English Channel, was reported drifting toward Belgium. Although its cable still dangled, its contact with electric wires had not damaged it. The balloon was described in London as one of a number stationed at Royal Air Force airdromes throughout England to register wind currents and temperatures at various heights

LONDON (2?) — British authorities today studied the possibility of adopting more rigid precautions to safeguard King George VI during his public appearances. It was pointed out that the Armistice Day incident at the Whitehall Cenotaph yesterday showed the ease with which an attacker might break through the guard lines and approach the King. It appeared certain that 43-year-old Stanley Storey, who shouted “all this is hypocrisy” yesterday during the two minutes of silence for the war dead, had not planned an attack on the King, but he had struggled through the guards almost to where the monarch stood.

London, Nov. 12 ()--A new attempt to settle Europe’s pressing problems by Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain’s favored method of informal discussion was developing today in diplomatic moves involving Britain, Germany and Italy. Reichsfuehrer Adolf Hitler's insistent colonial demands and Premier Benito Mussolini’s desire for recognition of Italy's Ethiopian conquests were believed to be subjects of the new negotiations. These followed Chamberlain’s speech Tuesday expressing a desire for better relations with Germany and Italy and the belief they could better be achieved by informal discussion than by “public declamation.” Conferences yesterday in Rome and London were seen by diplomats as a new approach to the Anglo-Italian understanding which is the cornerstone of Chamberlain’s peace policy. Lord Perth, the British Ambassador, met Count Galeazzo Ciano, Italian Foreign Minister, in Rome, w

WASHINGTON, Nov. 12—(I.P.—State Department officials reluctantly indicated tonight that they were considering the idea of following Great Britain’s lead in indirectly and unofficially recognizing the regime of Generalissimo Francisco Franco in Spain. They indicated this with the admission that Secretary of State Cordell Hull has decided to reopen the American consulate at Bilbao. Consul W. E. Chapman has been designated to reopen the consulate, officials admitted after first denying the report. They asserted that Chapman would have no diplomatic status in his position as consul, but this denial was questioned in some circles in view of the earlier denial of the same officials that the consulate was to be reopened. Hull, questioned at his press conference, evaded a direct answer. He said that Chapman had gone into Bilbao on several occasions. The consulate was closed because of the danger

LONDON, Nov. 13.—(Saturday)—(#)—A runaway Royal Air Force balloon, trailing more than two miles of mooring cable, was believed headed toward Belgium today. The balloon broke away from its mooring at an airdrome near Ramsgate last night and crossed the English channel. The dangling cable struck high tension wires in France and cut off electric current in the cities of Bethune, Boulogne and St. Quen. Royal Air Force planes were forced by darkness to turn back after chasing the balloon over the channel in an attempt to locate it and shoot it down.

Shanghai— (?) — A Japanese gunboat successfully crossed the partly broken boom obstructing the upper Whangpoo river today after armed Japanese naval launches had swept the stream of mines, exploding several harmlessly. The exploratory voyage up the Whangpoo and the trip of two other armed launches up the Soochow creek indicated Japanese preparations to use both streams to transport military supplies to its armies advancing westward toward Nanking. Japan has declared officially they intended using Soochow creek to transport supplies through the international settlement. Foreign defense officers avoided possible friction, recognizing the creek was an open waterway. (United States marines guard a section of the international settlement bordering the creek. Before the Chinese withdrawal from Shanghai, British officials prevented armed Japanese launches from proceeding up the creek.) TRAFFIC

(By the Associated Press) Shanghai, Nov. 13. (Saturday)—On new battlefields 20 and more miles west of Shanghai the Chinese-Japanese war raged on today with all signs pointing toward an early Japanese drive on Nanking, capital of the Chinese nation. It had become a rapidly shifting war of movement, covering hundreds of square miles. After three months of terrific pounding, Shanghai itself knew peace once more. With the Japanese in complete possession of this metropolitan area, silence reigned, although great fires still burned in Pootung and Nantao. Japanese Flag Run Up Japan's refusal to cooperate with the Brussels conference's search for peace was received by Chinese as notice the war would go on. In Nanking a government spokesman commented: “Japan's action is consistent with her policy of flaunting international agreements and her determination to continue aggression.” The final episod

Brussels, Nov. 13.—()—Norman H. Davis, chief of the United States delegation to the far eastern peace conference, today told the representatives of 18 other participating governments there were “compelling reasons” for Japan to cooperate with the conference. Davis expressed a hope Japan would “still see the way clear to doing so.” He reiterated, however, the conviction that respect for treaties and observance of the pledged word were the only possible basis “for an equitable, lasting solution of the Sino-Japanese conflict.” Japan, a signatory of the nine-power treaty to protect China, under which the Brussels conference was called, had refused two invitations to participate in the international efforts to find an avenue to peace in her war with China. Davis spoke with the heads of other delegations in consideration of the latest Japanese rebuff at the start of deliberations on a possible

1937-12-14.text: London, England, Dec. 14.—(>)— Japanese Ambassador Shigeru Yoshida today apologizes to Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden for Japanese attacks on two British gunboats in the Yangtze River Sunday. This was the second official apology in two days for the incident, a military attache having expressed regrets to the British War Office yesterday. The ambassador said his government was not yet in full possession of the facts, but was actively pressing inquiries. The gunboats, the Ladybird and the Bee, were not seriously damaged. Despite the apologies, Britain was understood to be preparing to dispatch a severe note to Tokio, and Eden indicated he would make a new statement to the House of Commons later in the day. There were growing indications that the British government would look to President Roosevelt for leadership in the next move if protests fail to gain full satisfaction for the attacks on

London, Dec, 14—Bitter winter weather disrupted communications and transportation in the British Isles today, and caused at least nine deaths. Huge snow drifts, some 12 feet deep, blanketed Scotland and northern England. Two persons died of exposure, two track workers were killed, four persons were killed in a Royal Air Force plane crash and a sailor was washed overboard in the Irish Sea.

JERUSALEM, Dec. 14.—(AP)—Shooting, looting and sabotage swept the Holy Land today. An armed band killed a Jewish constable in Tiberias and wounded a British policeman at Haifa as both police and British troops exchanged fire with marauders. Several homes in the Jenin district were raided by men who snatched money, jewels and furnishings at gunpoint. Communication lines were the objects of attack throughout Palestine.

LONDON. (®). Great Britain and the United States worked in close concert in the grave far eastern situation growing out of Japanese attacks on gunboats of both nations on the Yangtze river. Members of the House of Commons cheered Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden's statement that British ships had fired on Japanese planes after they had been bombed and shelled. Eden told Commons the British ambassador to Tokyo had “made the strongest protests” to Japan for the shelling of the British gunboat Ladybird at Wuhu, up the Yangtze from Nanking. Eden conferred with both Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain and Herschel V. Johnson, the U.S. charge d'affaires, before making his cautious statement to Commons that the two Anglo-Saxon powers were “in consultation” on the serious international developments in Japan's undeclared war with China. The British foreign office was understood to be watching Americ

BALTIMORE, Dec. 14 (P).—Robert W. Bingham, ambassador to England, was operated upon today at Johns Hopkins Hospital in an effort to determine the exact cause of his illness. Dr. William F. Rienhoff, Jr., the surgeon, said a definite diagnosis had not been made, and that the operation had been decided upon to aid the physicians.

Peiping, China. (4) Garland Leonard, Pentecostal missionary from Yale, Iowa, was shot and killed by Chinese soldiers at Yuanping, North Shansi province, on October 7, reports received here said today. A message from the British Baptist hospital at Taiyuanfu, through Domei (Japanese) news agency, said Mrs. Leonard was safe at Taiyuanfu. Yale is in Guthrie county, northeast of Guthrie Center.

LONDON—(UP)—British cabinet ministers met in emergency session today to consider action in protest against Japanese attacks on British men of war. The half dozen key men who attended the meeting delegated foreign secretary Anthony Eden to make a new statement of policy in the House of Commons this afternoon in an effort to appease angry public sentiment. Eden, after a morning of study of dispatches from the Far East, conferred separately with Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain. It was understood that a strong British note to Japan would be completed tonight and submitted to the entire cabinet at its regular meeting Wednesday. The government continued to maintain closest possible cooperation with the United States government in an effort to assure parallel action on Japanese attacks against American and British warships. There were frequent telephone calls between London and Washington. I

SHANGHAI—Japanese suggestion that U. S. and Britain move their ships if they want to be safe is rejected, and suggestion is rescinded. Admiral Harry E. Yarnell, commanding U. S. fleet in China, said any warning “would be ignored. TOKYO—Japan delivers four-point note to U. S., apologizing, promising indemnity, punishment of offenders and steps to prevent future incidents such as Panay bombing. PEIPING—Japanese proclaim new government in North China. WASHINGTON—President Roosevelt insists on direct apology from Japanese emperor, officials say. LONDON—Cabinet members in emergency meeting; Britain expected to draft strong protest note. BERLIN—Germany makes representations to Japan on bombing of ship housing provisional German embassy headquarters at Nanking. ROME—Italy awaits outcome of U. S. action before deciding whether to take steps about death of ace Italian war correspondent on Panay.

1937-08-28.text: London, Aug. 27. (4P)—Britain’s demands for ‘full satisfaction’ for the shooting of her ambassador to China by Japanese airmen were imparted officially to the Japanese government today. While Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden gave Japanese Ambassador Shigeru Yoshida a bad half hour at the foreign office here, it was authoritatively understood instructions had been sent to the British embassy in Tokyo to make a similar forceful presentation of the British stand. Yoshida had called at the foreign office to express formally Japan's ‘regrets’ over the shooting Thursday on the road between Nanking and Shanghai, in which Sir Hughe Montgomery Knatchbull-Hugessen was gravely wounded. Sir Hughe, his back broken by a Japanese machine gun bullet, lay in a Shanghai hospital, his life still in danger. The admission in quarters close to the government that the possibilities for full satisfaction were ‘ve

London, Aug. 28 (P) — Stanley Wooderson, English foot racing star, cracked the world record for the one mile run today by negotiating the distance in 4 minutes, 6.6 seconds in a specially arranged handicap race. This clipped two-tenths of a second off the listed record of 4:06.8 made by the American, Glenn Cunningham, at Princeton, N. J., in 1934.

SHANGHAI, Aug. 28. The British freighter Shenking was questioned as to identity by a Japanese warship off the mouth of the Whangpoo River today, but was in no way molested under the Japanese blockade of the Chinese coast against Chinese vessels. The warship signalled to the Shenking and asked its identity, permitting it to pass when the Shenking complied. The Shenking is under charter to British naval authorities to assist in evacuating refugees from Shanghai to Hong Kong and to bring British naval and army supplies to Shanghai on the return trip.

London, Aug. 28. — The Exchange Telegraph Shanghai correspondent reported today that the British steamship Shengking, a 3,000-ton freighter, was stopped off Woosung at the mouth of the Whangpoo today by Japanese warships. It was the first report of Japanese interference with foreign shipping under the new blockade of the China coast, and the victim was Great Britain—already angry over the wounding of its ambassador to China by a Japanese airplane machine gun. The Exchange Telegraph correspondent reported that the British commander in chief forwarded a protest at once to the Japanese authorities and asked an explanation. Under the blockade—at least as so far outlined—only Chinese ships were to be subject to the blockade. A Japanese navy spokesman at Shanghai said today that any Chinese ship which did not comply with orders to halt would be shelled.

(By The Associated Press) SHANGHAI—Japanese and Chinese armies locked in battle north of Shanghai; thousands killed or wounded; Japanese claim capture of Lotien, key town; Sir Hughe M. Knatchbull-Hugessen, British ambassador to China, shot Thursday by Japanese airmen, reported improving. LONDON--Britain demands from Japan “full satisfaction” for shooting of her ambassador to China; financial and other informed quarters speculate on chances of diplomatic break between Britain and Japan. WASHINGTON—Secretary Hull announces United States has served notice on Japan and China it would demand respect of all its rights and interests in the far east; officials study probable effects of Japan’s “peaceful blockade” of China coasts. NANKING—Nearly 150 Chinese civilians killed in devastation series of Japanese air raids; foreign ambassadors ask Japanese understanding not to bomb non-military parts o
